Active nests usually escape if spraying is used because it delays cutting for a week or so, but swathing can destroy many of the later broods (Burton et al. 1999). Reed, Sedge and Grasshopper Warblers also nest occasionally in rape fields but, like Reed Buntings, their breeding seasons are ended by the harvest.

FIG 61. A rape crop in seed (left), and pale unripe rape seeds (right) in the gullet of a Linnet Linaria cannabina, as shown in a live bird by blowing apart the neck feathers (Ian Newton). Rape seeds now form a major summer food of Linnets and other small seed-eaters.

In winter, well-developed rape plants provide an insulating layer over the soil, so thrushes and other ground-feeding birds can concentrate to feed there at times when the bare surfaces of other fields are frozen over. In addition, owing to winter flooding or grazing by pigeons and other animals, rape fields often have patches that are bare or sparser than the rest of the field. These patches are used for nesting and foraging by Skylarks and other birds which are absent from the rest of the well-grown crop.

FIG 62. The Reed Bunting Emberiza schoeniclus is commonly found nesting in rape fields (Richard Chandler).

All the brassicas grown on British farmland, including rape and forage kale, as well as vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts, were derived from a single wild plant, Brassica oleracea. When grown to feed livestock, they are usually sown in spring (May–June) and then strip-grazed through the winter, using a moveable electric fence. The leaves of all brassicas are eaten by a range of bird species, and those of kale, cabbages, sprouts and turnips can form major foods of Woodpigeons at times when smaller plants are buried under snow.

Forage kale crops are usually grown in small acreages, but are often of great value to wildlife, sometimes providing the only tall cover in an otherwise bleak winter landscape. Their leaves are eaten by pigeons and game birds, especially at times of snow, and their seeds (produced in the second year) are eaten by various finches (Table 4). On one Derbyshire farm, 5–6 ha of kale were grown every year (Wareing 1973). The crop was cut section by section with a forage harvester and fed fresh each day to cattle housed in yards. While it lasted, the crop provided a roosting and feeding area for hundreds of birds, sometimes as many as 3,000–4,000. It was used as a roost by Wren, Dunnock, Linnet, Greenfinch, Reed Bunting and Yellowhammer, and it served as a feeding area for these species plus Chaffinch, Brambling, Corn Bunting, Pied Wagtail, Song Thrush, Blackbird, Fieldfare, Lapwing, Golden Plover and Woodpigeon. It also provided cover for game birds and Snipe. Some species used only the bare areas post-harvest, while others fed unseen under the crop canopy. Predators such as Kestrel, Little Owl and Barn Owl took advantage of the abundant prey. These observations refer to a single kale patch, but the crop is widely known for the birds it supports.

FIG 63. Left, kale is grown mainly to feed cattle in winter (Richard & Barbara Mearns); below, kale crops are often rich in weeds which attract seed-eating birds such as these finches and Skylarks mainly after the kale has been eaten off (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Other minority crops

Some other crops were previously grown in Britain more widely than they are now, while others were introduced only in recent decades. Linseed (flax) was widely grown both for its stem fibres used in clothing (linen) and rope manufacture, and for the oil in its seeds. The growing crop is short and sparse, and can hold high densities of Skylarks, offering suitable nesting conditions throughout the breeding season. The seeds are readily eaten by Goldfinches, Linnets and Greenfinches, and occasionally by other finches, House Sparrows and Woodpigeons (Table 4). The biggest Goldfinch flock I have ever seen, totalling more than 1,500 individuals, fed in winter on an unharvested linseed field in northeast Scotland. Sunflower is a recent introduction, restricted to the south because of its need for warmth and sunshine: its seeds are taken by a range of larger seed-eaters, together with the Greenfinch among the smaller species. Goldfinches can eat sunflower if the seeds are small or soft enough for them to de-husk, and in some areas Bullfinches and Hawfinches take them from bird-feeders. On parts of the continent, buckwheat is widely grown for human consumption, and in Britain it is a frequent component of game-cover crops and wild-bird seed mixes; its seeds being eaten by some waterfowl, game birds, corvids and doves (Table 4). Borage is occasionally grown as a crop in Britain for its seed oil. Its flowers attract bees in abundance, while Greenfinches eat its seeds. Other minority field crops, grown specifically for game or other wild birds, are discussed in Chapter 20.

Horticultural crops

Fruit, green vegetables and flowers are grown in relatively small areas (total 174,000 ha), and some of them increasingly under polythene or glass. They are found across the country, with major concentrations in the southeast. Top-fruit crops, such as apples, pears, plums and cherries, provide different habitat from field crops, and attract many breeding birds that would otherwise nest in hedges and bushes. Birds also obtain food from various fruit crops. Bullfinches attack the blossom buds and sometimes the opened blossom of apples, pears, plums, cherries, currants and gooseberries, and the mature fruits of cultivated blackberries and raspberries; Blackbirds commonly eat cherries, raspberries and other soft fruit, while Starlings are especially fond of cherries. Various thrushes also feed heavily on apples and pears, but mainly in autumn after the unharvested fruit has fallen. Of these species, only Bullfinches (for eating buds) and Starlings (for eating cherries) have been considered as major pests of fruit growing in Britain, but both have declined greatly since the 1960s (Chapter 2). Blackbirds cause problems mainly in private gardens, where protection of fruit by netting is often feasible.

Energy crops

In recent years, some farmland has been used to grow biomass or biofuel crops. Most involve conventional crops such as beet or maize, which are harvested green, chopped and then fed into anaerobic digesters. As they rot, they produce methane (biogas) which is used for various purposes, including power generation. The residue is spread back on the land as compost. It is partly the increased number of digesters which has led to greater maize production, with its attendant problems for soil management (Chapter 5). Other energy or biomass crops are grown on a smaller scale, and include the introduced perennial grass Miscanthus and short-rotation coppiced willow or poplar. All these crops are water-demanding. Miscanthus is cut annually in spring, while coppice stays in the ground for many years, with the shoots harvested every 2–3 years to provide mulch, pulp-wood, chip-wood or fuel for heating and power generation. In 2012, these crops covered more than 10,000 ha in Britain (Defra 2012). Some have the potential to support a range of bird species, providing pesticide use is limited (Sage & Robertson 1996, Sage et al. 2010). As stubble in May, Miscanthus holds open-land species at similar densities to arable and grassland, but from July, when it has reached 2 m tall, it can hold more birds, mostly scrub-dwelling species. Short-rotation willow coppice usually contains more individuals of more species than Miscanthus, but bird densities in both crops are increased by patchiness and weediness. The growth of energy crops conflicts with food crops, as both require the same type of land.

Soil-improving crops

All crops leave a legacy in the soil, the structure changed by the rooting system, and the organic content by the residue of dead matter left behind. Some crops are grown primarily because of the effects they have on the soil. Nitrogen-fixing legumes raise fertility, while other so-called 'cover crops' benefit soil structure, reduce erosion, or hold nitrogen and other soluble nutrients over winter and stop them washing away. Fodder radish serves several of these functions. It is grown overwinter to improve soil structure by deep root penetration, and by covering the soil it reduces erosion. It is direct-drilled in late summer after the cereal harvest, grows up, and dies down in spring. During its growth, it absorbs nitrogen and other nutrients, and releases them as it rots in spring, ready to support the new crop, direct-drilled after an application of herbicide.

Importance of crops to birds

Owing to their ability to fly, birds need to minimise their body weights. For this reason plant-eating birds tend to have relatively simple digestive systems, compared to plant-eating mammals. They tend to select foods of high nutrient content and digestibility, a need which is reflected in the habitats, plant communities, plant species and plant parts that they exploit.

As food-crop plants became more productive, digestible and nutritious for humanity, they also improved as a source of food for birds and other wildlife. This holds for grains which are bigger and more nutrient-rich than wild types, grass and other leaves which are more nutritious and digestible and less toxic, and roots which are larger and more nutrient-packed than the underground storage organs of wild plants. In natural habitats, herbivorous birds are extremely selective in their feeding, normally feeding from only a small proportion of the plant species present. They can also preferentially feed on particular individual plants and parts of plants. When these eaten parts are analysed, they are often found to be more nutritious than the same parts from other plants which are not eaten. But when birds feed on crops, they have before them high-density monocultures of the same species, whose edible parts are uniformly nutritious and palatable. They do not need to pick and choose, so their rates of energy and protein intake are much greater than is possible in most natural habitats, as repeatedly shown by studies on geese and others (Fox et al. 2016). It is little wonder that many birds select crops in preference to wild foods, and that on this rich food supply some species have reached numbers that cause substantial economic damage.

Nowhere is this effect better illustrated than among wild geese, which during the 20th century took increasingly to feeding on farmland (Box 4). For example, Greenland White-fronted Geese traditionally overwintered by feeding on below-ground storage organs of bog plants, but increasingly shifted to adjacent low-intensity pasture and then to intensively managed grassland and cereals (Fox et al. 2005). Wintering Brent Geese formerly fed almost exclusively on intertidal eel-grass, but now feed on various agricultural crops, and in some places on golf courses and other amenity grassland (Rowell & Robinson 2004). Intensive agriculture has created a sequence of seasonally abundant foods which are highly attractive to geese, swans and other avian herbivores. Spilled grain on cereal stubbles is relished by all goose and swan species, as well as by some duck species. Waste from root crops, sequentially harvested through the autumn and early winter, provides sugar beet, turnips, carrots and potatoes, all eaten by various species of geese and swans. Modern grass varieties, young growing cereals and rape have been implicated in promoting recent population growth and distribution shifts in various waterfowl in Britain and elsewhere (Fox et al. 2005, 2016, Gauthier et al. 2005).

BOX 4. Farm crops and waterfowl populations

All six species of native wild geese in Britain were probably once restricted to inland or coastal marshes, but they now feed primarily or partly on farm crops. Some of them seem to have made this switch in relatively recent times, since the mid-20th century in the case of some populations of Barnacle and Brent Geese. This switch occurred at a time when their natural coastal marshes were shrinking, owing to reclamation projects, and while their numbers were increasing, mainly following from reductions in shooting pressure. But farmland now offers high-density, high-quality foods through the winter, providing much more nutritious feeding than is available on natural marshland. All goose species in Britain eat grass, young growing cereal and rape leaves, although in their mainly coastal habitats Brent and Barnacle Geese seldom gain access to cereals and rape. When given the choice, almost all these geese prefer the nutritious nitrogen-rich cultivated grasses of leys over the largely indigenous grasses on unfertilised older pastures. Most of the crop damage caused by waterfowl occurs in spring, when they remove the young growing leaves of forage grasses needed at this time for the 'early bite' for cattle and lambing ewes. In addition, during periods of wet spring weather, when feeding on young growing cereals, the geese puddle the soil, causing the green shoots to become coated with mud which then hardens, inhibiting further growth and creating bare patches in the fields. Geese can be present in spring in flocks of hundreds or thousands, and can soon devastate a field of young grass or cereals. This is a relatively local problem, however, involving only a tiny proportion of farmers in Britain, but on their farms the effects may be far from trivial. In some areas, under conservation funding, special fields are managed and sacrificed for geese. Coupled with regular scaring from other fields, this practice can do much to alleviate the conflict.

Swans, geese and various dabbling ducks eat cereal grains, picking them from stubble fields after harvest, or (less frequently) taking spilled grains at the time of sowing. Mallard seem to do this more than other ducks, but Gadwall, Pintail, Teal and Shoveler also forage on stubble fields. Grain-eating in this way does not normally constitute damage.

Species of grey geese also eat the harvest waste of root crops. By removing this material from harvested fields, geese cause no damage to the crop. Waste potatoes, sugar beet and carrots are eaten by both Greylag and Pink-footed Geese, and at least the first two by White-fronted Geese, but only the larger-billed Greylag seems to tackle the hard flesh of unharvested turnips. In the past, turnips were grown more widely than now to provide winter food for cattle and especially sheep, which were often folded on the unharvested crop. The geese fed in these same fields, mainly on roots that had already been nibbled by sheep, but because they took material that was otherwise still available to sheep, this activity was classed as damage. To my knowledge, the smaller-billed Barnacle and Brent Geese have not been recorded feeding on cultivated root crops to any extent (but see How et al. 2015). Introduced Canada Geese have now increased sufficiently to cause substantial local damage to farm crops, especially leys, young cereals and potatoes ready for harvest. Swans also take growing grass, cereals and rape, and in some areas wintering Whooper and Bewick's Swans take waste potatoes. As resident Mute Swans have increased over recent decades, they have also taken increasingly to feeding in midwinter on farm crops close to water, especially the leaves of oilseed rape (Spray et al. 2002). Some dabbling ducks, notably Mallard and Pintail, take waste potatoes from harvested fields in autumn, while Wigeon graze on young grass and cereal leaves. While geese and swans feed in fields mainly during the daytime, ducks seem to visit fields chiefly at night, which may mean that their dependence on agricultural crops has been underestimated.

Wintering geese are restricted to particular parts of the country, feeding within a few kilometres of their wetland roosts. While the increase in their numbers followed greater protection from shooting, it may also have been helped by the nitrogen-rich grass which became increasingly available on British farmland from the 1960s, allowing the geese to accumulate substantial body reserves in spring. In several species, the reproductive rate of individuals, and of populations in different years, has been found to correlate with the body condition of the adults in spring, before their return to northern breeding areas (Ebbinge & Spaans 1995, Newton 2013a). Good nutrition resulted in good body condition, which in turn resulted in good breeding. The Greenland White-front is the only wintering grey goose in Britain in which part of the population still feeds in winter primarily on natural habitat (peat mosses). In these birds, survival and reproductive rates are lower than in the larger part of the population which now feeds on rich agricultural land (Fox et al. 2005).

Most of the big waterfowl that feed largely or entirely on farmland in winter have increased in recent decades. During the period 1970–2000, the numbers of Bewick's Swans wintering in Britain increased by about 3-fold, Whooper Swans by about 3-fold, Pink-footed Geese by about 4-fold, Greylag by about 1.5-fold, Greenland White-fronts by about 4-fold, Svalbard Barnacle Geese by nearly 8-fold, Greenland Barnacle Geese by 2-fold, Dark-bellied Brent Geese by about 4-fold, and Eastern Light-bellied Brent by 3-fold (Owen et al. 1986, Cabot 2009). The European White-fronted Goose declined in Britain over this period, and Bewick's Swan more recently, apparently because of migratory short-stopping, with birds wintering closer to their breeding areas and not reaching Britain in such large numbers as previously, a change attributed to climate warming. The Greenland White-fronted Goose also declined recently, owing to deteriorating conditions on its breeding areas, probably resulting from competition for food with increasing numbers of dominant Canada Geese (Fox et al. 2005).

FIG 64. Barnacle Geese Branta leucopsis feeding on farmland on Islay (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

In northwestern Europe, it is frequently impossible now to recognise ancestral natural habitats of geese because the birds have become almost wholly dependent on farmland for survival between breeding seasons. Some of the original habitats may now have gone from most areas, but in any case the geese gain from shifting from remaining natural to agricultural habitats (Fox et al. 2005, 2016). Farmland offers food of much higher density and greatly improved nutritional value compared to adjacent 'natural' habitats. Experiments showed that herbivorous waterfowl rapidly switch from unfertilised to fertilised swards, benefiting from the nitrogen applied (Fox et al. 2016). Changes in agriculture since the 1950s have almost certainly made a major contribution to the rapid growth of northern hemisphere goose populations. The same presumably happened at various times in the past among other crop-feeding birds, such as pigeons, finches, sparrows, buntings and larks.

LIVESTOCK

The major livestock species in Britain, from Neolithic times on, have included cattle, sheep, pigs, horses and poultry. Within historical times, goats seem to have been of minor importance, and horses are now kept mainly for recreation. Nowadays, more than 80% of agricultural land in Britain is used to support livestock, and there is also a large import of foodstuffs. This situation arises partly because the climate and relief over much of Britain favour a pastoral economy, and partly because of our liking for a protein-rich diet. Big changes occurred in livestock numbers in Britain during the 20th century, with cattle, sheep and pigs increasing, and draught horses almost disappearing. Chickens and turkeys increased enormously, while ducks and geese declined. On a global scale, cattle and other livestock in their present numbers have highly adverse impacts on the environment. They are the main cause of deforestation to create more pasture, they have massive food and water needs, and produce abundant greenhouse gases, such as methane and nitrous oxide which derive from ruminant digestive processes and manure.

Cattle

The original wild Aurochs probably lived mainly in open woodland, with scattered trees and grassy meadows and wetlands. Over much of their European and central Asian range, they occurred alongside Bison. Both species are ruminants, with complex digestive systems suited to a high cellulose diet, especially grasses. Among domestic animals, cattle are best equipped to deal with such a diet, followed by sheep and then by goats which, like deer, can more readily digest soft woody tissue.

Domestication of wild Aurochs produced smaller more docile animals. This size difference was apparent even in Neolithic times, when domestic cattle and wild Aurochs coexisted in Britain for a time. The threat of hybridisation may have provided additional incentive for people to get rid of wild Aurochs, because interbreeding would have rapidly undone the beneficial effects of domestication. For most of their time in Britain, domesticated cattle were used primarily as draught animals, their meat and milk being minor products. In the 14th century, cattle were much smaller than modern beasts, and their milk yields are thought to have averaged 500–600 litres per cow per year, less than one-twelfth of that of a modern dairy cow (see here). It was in the latter part of the 18th century, with the growing demand for meat and milk from new industrial towns, that attention was devoted to breeding faster-growing, earlier-maturing cattle specifically for meat, and later still for quantity of milk. This selection has continued, and during recent decades a handful of high-performing breeds have come to dominate all others.

In the years around 2015, the cattle population of Britain was calculated at nearly 10 million animals, about one to every seven people (Defra 2016). More than half these cattle were used for milk and other dairy products, and the others (mainly of different breeds) for meat, with some 2.2 million animals slaughtered per year. In financial terms, milk has long been the single most important agricultural product in Britain, contributing one-sixth of total agricultural output in 2015 (Defra 2016). If they are to produce milk at maximum rate, dairy cattle need care and attention. Although most are kept in productive grass fields in summer, and brought in twice each day for milking, dairy cattle are generally housed inside over winter, and fed on stored foods, in the past mainly hay and fodder roots and in recent decades mainly silage. In the first half of the 20th century, the main milk breeds were the native Ayrshire and Shorthorn, the Channel Islands' Guernsey and Jersey, and the British (formerly Dutch) Friesian. But in recent decades all these breeds have been largely replaced by the more productive Holstein from North America (originally bred from Friesians), which now accounts for about 95% of all dairy cattle in Britain. To support an average annual yield of around 7,600 litres of milk (Fig. 65), each cow needs the equivalent of about 100 kg of productive rye grass per day, and unlimited access to water. Increase in milk yield was brought about not only by selective breeding and change to a more productive breed, but also by better disease control, increased use of artificial foodstuffs and increased intensity of grassland management (Chapter 12).

FIG 65. The Holstein, the commonest milk-producing cow in the world. Through selective breeding and good nutrition, the milk yields of Holsteins have tripled since the mid-20th century, now averaging around 7,600 litres per cow per year, with some exceptional individuals producing up to 12,000 litres (more than 32 litres per day). The animals need a nutrient-rich and easily digestible diet to produce at this level (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Native beef breeds are in general less demanding than dairy breeds, and can be grazed on poorer pastures. The main native beef breeds are the Hereford and Aberdeen Angus, both of which under appropriate management produce high-quality well-flavoured beef, with a marbling of fat through the muscle. Important regional beef breeds include the Galloway and Highland, the latter often also kept as a decorative park animal. As the health dangers of saturated fats became known from the 1950s, native breeds were largely replaced by less fatty continental breeds, such as Charolais, Simental and Limousin, the latter now being the most popular beef breed in Britain. Beef breeds can be kept outside year-round, although upland animals are mostly brought to lower ground for the winter. In summer, most cattle are fattened on grass, but in winter most are now held in enclosed yards, formerly fed on roots, kale and straw, or in more recent times more on barley-based feeds or silage.

As may be seen from their bony appearance, most milk breeds are not built for meat, and for obvious reasons calves have always been surplus to needs. Most of the calves from dairy cows are now fathered using semen from a beef-breed bull, giving them greater potential for meat production. Most of these hybrid calves are sold on to farmers who specialise in rearing them for slaughter, taking advantage of seasonal grazing wherever they can get it. In northern Britain, crossing different beef breeds is also common practice, because hybrids between some breeds grow faster than either parent on the same diet. This is true, for example, for Hereford × Aberdeen Angus hybrids. Otherwise, the old breeds are kept today mainly because of their ability to survive on poor forage, their lower growth rates producing more flavoursome beef for a niche market.

The main impact that cattle have on birds is through their effects on habitat, as huge areas of grassland and arable crops are devoted to producing their food. In the past, fields of root crops grown as winter fodder supported an abundance of weeds, which in turn fed many finches and other seed-eaters. Such crops have now been largely replaced by silage, which, under intensive management, is perhaps the least bird-friendly crop grown in Britain at the present time. Intensive silage grass is cut too frequently to allow ground-nesting birds to breed successfully, and on intensive pastures cattle are grazed at such high densities that nests of ground-nesting birds are trampled before they can produce young (Chapter 12). Such fields contain few plants other than modern grass strains. However, the old-style byres used to house cattle still provide nest sites for Swallows, and the aerial insects that cattle promote provide an important food source. Starlings, Yellow Wagtails and other birds feed around grazing cattle, exploiting the insects disturbed, but Skylarks tend to avoid them.

FIG 66. Highland cattle, a traditional slow-growing beef breed of the Scottish Highlands, which can survive year-round on poor vegetation on the open hills (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Cattle benefit Starlings in a different way. In Denmark, the breeding densities of Starlings in different localities in the mid-1990s were correlated with the abundance of dairy cattle which in the warmer months were turned out daily to graze the grass (Heldbjerg et al. 2016). Regional declines in Starling numbers between 2001 and 2014 coincided with the loss of intense grazing pressure, as cattle were increasingly kept indoors. At the national level, the long-term decline in Starlings paralleled a long-term decline in the numbers of dairy cattle grazing outdoors. The short grass of grazed pastures enabled Starlings to forage efficiently on soil-dwelling prey throughout the breeding season. So it was not only the extent of grassland that affected Starling densities, but also the continued grazing needed to keep it short. The same presumably applies in Britain, where far fewer farms now support cattle than a few decades ago, and many of those that do keep cattle house them inside year-round (Chapter 4).

Sheep

Domestic sheep were derived from the Asiatic Mouflon of southwest Asia. For most of their history since Neolithic times, sheep were kept in Britain primarily for their wool, and only to a small extent for milk and meat. Wool production was probably the first organised large-scale industry to develop in Britain. By the 16th century, exported wool is said to have accounted for around one-half of the nation's wealth, bringing great prosperity to regions such as East Anglia, the southern downs, the Cotswolds and the uplands of northern England and southern Scotland. But with the development of man-made fabrics from the 1950s, the market for wool has slumped, and the main emphasis is now on meat. This change reduced the value of sheep, for instead of producing two useful products, most now produce only one. There are still more than 50 different breeds of sheep in Britain, regional types which fall into three main groups: the small hill sheep suited to mountain pastures, the somewhat larger short-wool sheep of the downs, and the even larger long-wool sheep of the lowlands. Sheep require little in the way of housing or fixed equipment, and are generally wintered outside.

Small hardy breeds have persisted in the uplands, becoming by far the main agricultural product of these areas. On some hill farms, sheep are the only livestock kept. Despite the severe winters, heavy rainfall and damp windy weather, some breeds of sheep can still give birth and rear lambs on the hills. Some of the toughest breeds include the Herdwick in the Lake District and the Blackface in the Scottish mountains. These sheep can utilise the poor rough grazings year-round, but pregnant ewes need hay or other supplementary food in winter. The use of the uplands to provide breeding stock and lambs for subsequent fattening in the lowlands has proved to be an efficient way of producing meat.

In the uplands sheep increased greatly in numbers and densities into the 1990s, with substantial impact on upland vegetation and its associated birdlife (Chapter 19). Since then, under a changed subsidy system, their numbers have been reduced to more sustainable levels. In contrast, sheep numbers in the lowlands declined during the 20th century, and smaller breeds came to prevail. This change can be attributed to the high labour costs of managing folded sheep on arable land, a consumer preference for smaller joints which favours the smaller hill breeds over lowland ones, and competition from imported lamb. Remaining sheep in the lowlands are found mainly on grassland, and to a smaller extent on arable farms, where they still perform a useful role in scavenging crop residues. Overall, the total number of sheep and lambs of Britain in 2015 stood at more than 33.3 million, about one per two people (Defra 2016)

Most lowland sheep are now brought under cover for lambing, and most upland sheep to lower enclosed ground nearer the farmhouse. And while most domestic animals are born throughout the year, sheep are mated so that lambs are born in late winter or spring in time to take advantage of the 'early bite' of young grass. The peak lambing month varies from January to May, depending on region and elevation. Unlike cattle and pigs, therefore, sheep have retained a distinct birthing season, like their wild ancestors. Most of the lambs are slaughtered over a long period from summer through to the following summer, depending on their growth and market demand. The percentage of twins is greater in the lowlands than in the uplands, and mortality rates are lower. In good lowland areas, there may be 1.6 lambs per ewe in summer, while in many upland areas the ratio is nearer 0.6 lambs per ewe.

Sheep are important to birds for two main reasons, first through their widespread impact on vegetation, which affects the structure and composition of grazing land. In this way they affect all other plant and animal life on which birds might depend. Overall, sheep have probably had more impact on the vegetation of Britain than any other animal, most obviously in the uplands. Secondly, they are important because they are kept mainly out-of-doors, and through their mortality in the hills they provide a source of carrion for many scavenging birds, and in spring also a source of placentas and stillborn lambs (Chapter 19). These items come in late winter and early spring, at times when other foods eaten by scavenging birds reach their lowest levels of the year. Various raptors, corvids and gulls are the main beneficiaries.

FIG 67. Feral goat photographed in the Galloway hills, southwest Scotland (Keith Kirk).

Goats

Domestic goats were derived from the Bezoar of southwest Asia, and were brought to Britain in Neolithic times to yield wool, skin (leather), meat and milk products. However, at least in historical times, they seem never to have played a major role in the economy of the British countryside, with only a small specialist market for their milk and cheese (and more recently meat). In 2012, they numbered around 73,000 in Britain, compared with 1.84 million dairy cows (Defra 2012). In feeding habits, goats are more versatile (and hence more destructive) than sheep, as they are browsers as well as grazers. Like cattle, they have been selected for high milk production, and in modern breeds individuals can produce around 3.5 litres per day. In addition, various feral herds live wild in upland Britain, some supposedly derived from Neolithic animals, and occurring, for example, in the Galloway, Langholm, Moffat and Kielder hills, as well as in parts of the Scottish Highlands, Snowdonia, and southwest England. Their impact on birds is similar to that of sheep, mainly through their effects on vegetation and (in feral herds) as a source of winter–spring carrion.

Pigs

The pigs brought in by Neolithic farmers were already quite different from their wild ancestor, the Wild Boar of the forests and marshes. From the start they were kept primarily for their meat. Their ready domesticity, fecundity, richness in fat, and ease of meat storage by salting and smoking all favoured their use as a source of human food. Moreover, they eat almost anything organic, so could be kept by the poorest of people.

During the latter half of the 20th century, the rearing and fattening of pigs for pork and bacon became concentrated, as an intensive form of production little related to the nature of the land. Domestic pigs are the most sensitive of all farm animals to cold and damp, and consequently they are largely excluded from the uplands. In lowland areas, they are either kept indoors or in sheltered fields in which they are given small huts in which to sleep. Unlike other livestock, they cannot be reared on grass, but depend on more concentrated foods such as waste potatoes and other roots. Nowadays, they are mostly fed on manufactured concentrates made primarily from grain. They are often kept at high densities in special buildings on relatively small holdings, with all the food bought in. Pigs are prolific, with two large fast-growing litters per year, and the young ready for slaughter in five months. Pigs can therefore fluctuate greatly in numbers during the course of a year. On the basis of the June censuses, there were more than 7 million pigs in Britain in the late 20th century, but owing to competition from imported pork their numbers then dropped to 4.7 million in 2015. Pig units are widely distributed through the lowlands, but tend to be concentrated in areas of intensive vegetable or root production, as in parts of East Anglia. This pattern has persisted, even though the pigs are now fed largely on bagged concentrates rather than on crop residues.

In former times, when pigs were allowed into forests to feed on autumn mast crops, they no doubt influenced the forest ground flora, exposing soil-dwelling invertebrates by rooting, while removing large seeds otherwise available to pigeons, corvids and squirrels. But this method of husbandry had almost stopped by the late 19th century. Subsequently, apart from their influence on the crops that are grown, pigs probably had little impact on bird populations until the introduction, mainly from the 1950s, of processed concentrated food. This material, fed as a powder or mash, proved attractive to some birds, notably House Sparrows, Starlings, Rooks, Crows, Jackdaws, and various gulls. Because pigs were increasingly kept inside bird-proofed buildings, this source of food was progressively shut off from birds. However, those pregnant and farrowing sows that are kept in outdoor units, with individual shelters spaced around muddy fields, are still fed in outdoor troughs. In these situations, it is practically impossible to exclude birds, and pig fields attract large numbers of corvids and gulls, which get part of their food from the pig troughs and part from the soil, continually churned over by the pigs themselves. Their rooting behaviour makes soil-dwelling invertebrates more accessible for birds, and the small numbers of Stone-curlews which now overwinter in East Anglia can often be seen in pig fields. The dry soil makes the area ideal for outdoor pig keeping, and once the pigs are removed from a field, it quickly grows up with Fat-hen and other weeds, whose seeds attract Stock Doves and other seed-eaters. In 2015, outdoor pigs in the UK occupied about 9,000 ha of land nationwide (Defra 2016).

FIG 68. Outdoor pigs in Norfolk, along with some of the birds that benefit from the food provided and from invertebrates in the well-manured soil (Chris Knights).

Horses

The domestication of the Wild Horse brought under human control an animal that revolutionised transport, trade and warfare, and eventually also agriculture. But strangely, at least in historical times, it seems that horses were never milked or eaten in Britain, as they are in other parts of the world, and in contrast to other draught animals, such as cattle, water buffaloes or camels. The Wild Horse (Tarpan) seems to have been eliminated from Britain up to 2,000 years before domesticated horses were imported in Neolithic times. To judge from archaeological records, domesticated horses began to appear across Europe from about 6,000 years ago (Clutton-Brock 1992), and in Britain they increased in frequency through the Bronze Age. The earliest evidence that horses were used for work in Britain dates from the Late Bronze Age, in the form of harness artefacts. At that time, horses could have been widely used for load-pulling, pack-carrying and riding, enabling people to travel further and faster than before. By the end of the Iron Age, according to accounts by Julius Caesar, horses were used in warfare in Britain, valued for their speed in long-distance raiding and rapid escape. The earliest evidence for wheeled vehicles dates from the Iron Age, around 2,500 years ago (Bendrey 2010). The two-wheeled chariots used by Queen Boudica (Boadicea) in her battles with the Romans figure prominently in childhood history books.

Although long used in agriculture, it was not until the 18th and 19th centuries, with the development of bigger and stronger animals, that horses widely replaced the ox teams of earlier centuries. For around 200 years, until the mid-20th century, they were the major source of power on British farms. At their peak in 1910, working horses numbered 1,137,000 individuals. Their subsequent decline, associated with the introduction of tractors, brought a major change to the countryside, through a decline in the amount of pasture, hay and oat crops needed to feed them. Oats and their associated weeds provided a major winter food supply for seed-eating birds, especially in hill country where few other arable crops were grown. The small stubble fields helped to sustain upland populations of Linnets, Twites and other seed-eating birds, which have since declined there. Smaller horses (ponies) were used in hill districts, with different breeds in different regions, but again their use greatly declined during the 20th century, especially with the introduction of motorised quad-bikes. In contrast, horses for riding became more numerous in Britain from the 1950s on, with an estimated 500,000 now kept for recreational purposes. As horses cannot be fed on silage, they provide an incentive for continued hay production, and the small short-grass fields in which they graze are used by foraging birds chiefly in winter.

Unlike the Wild Horse, the Wild Ass never occurred naturally in Britain. It was domesticated probably in North Africa, and introduced to Britain in the Late Iron Age. Whereas horses are specialist grazers which can thrive in our climate, donkeys are adapted to warm dry stony areas with scrub on which they can browse. They need sheltered housing through British winters. Unlike in much of southern Europe, therefore, the donkey and its infertile hybrid, the mule, have played a trivial role in British agriculture, except perhaps in Roman times. Their bones are poorly represented in the archaeological record, compared to those of horses (Johnstone 2010). Their impacts on birds and their habitats can be considered as little different from those of horses, relating to the grass and other crops needed to feed them.

Poultry

Modern chickens all derive from the wild Red Junglefowl of India. More than 100 different breeds are now known in Britain, mostly kept as ornamentals, but different commercial types are kept for either egg or meat production, different breeds for different purposes. Until the mid-20th century, chickens were kept on every farm and in many back yards, but since then, like pig keeping, poultry keeping for eggs and meat has become an intensive industry in which the nature of the land plays little part. Into the 1950s, most chickens were kept on grass outside, provided with sheds in which they could roost and lay, and fed largely on grain, some of which was inevitably taken by wild birds, especially House Sparrows. But chickens are now kept in intensive indoor units closed to wild birds, and fed on pelleted food, made mainly from grain with additional protein. Poultry units are widely distributed, but largely for historical reasons they tend to be concentrated in the same districts as pigs.

The numbers of fowls in Britain were estimated in 2015 at more than 156 million, and the numbers of turkeys, ducks and geese at more than 11 million (Defra 2016). These numbers reflect those alive in June, at the time of the census, but in such prolific, fast-maturing birds, the total production during each year must have greatly exceeded these figures. Modern laying chicken breeds start to produce eggs at 20 weeks old, lay at maximum rate for about 18 months, and can produce more than 300 eggs per year, while modern meat breeds can be ready for the table in less than six weeks. The major changes in the industry have been the increase in production of broilers, the output of which increased 15-fold since the 1950s, and the increase in turkeys at the expense of ducks and geese. In the 1950s, broiler chickens took 100 days to grow, but now, under selective breeding, only 36 days. Within two decades, chicken meat moved from a rare luxury in Britain to become the cheapest and most frequently eaten form of animal protein, now providing about 40% of all meat consumed.

The switch to indoor poultry rearing probably had another indirect impact on wild birds because of the effect it had on human attitudes to Foxes. In the past, when many people kept outside chickens, everyone was against Foxes, and much time and effort was devoted to killing them. The incentive for such relentless control largely disappeared as poultry were progressively brought indoors, and reduced persecution may have been one of the factors permitting the growth in Fox numbers over recent decades. Nowadays, only game-rearing estates are serious about killing Foxes, although in some upland sheep-rearing areas, there is still frequent control using dogs or poison (both practices illegal).

Domestic geese were derived from the wild Greylag, and in earlier centuries played a much bigger role in the agricultural economy of Britain than they do now. They were often kept on village greens (the so-called 'green geese' of old cookery books). Around the Fens, flocks of hundreds were tended by a gooseherd (or gozzard), just as sheep were tended by a shepherd, and were taken regularly to pasture and to water. They were bred partly for their meat, but were also plucked for their down and feathers four or five times per year (for use in human bedding and quill pens). In autumn they were driven to town markets, walking around 15 km a day. Selected birds were kept and fattened for Christmas, and part of their decline can be attributed to their replacement by the turkey, introduced from North America in the 16th century. Most domestic ducks are derived from the wild Mallard, and are still kept commercially mainly for their meat, but only on a small scale. Most of the duck carcasses sold in Britain are now imported.

FIG 69. Wild Greylag Anser anser, the ancestor of most breeds of domestic geese, which were once kept in much greater numbers than now on British farms (Ian Newton).

The impact of poultry on wild birds in Britain was probably large in the past, owing to the food being provided in accessible situations, but it is now small, apart from the crops that are grown to feed them. However, poultry share various diseases with wild birds, which gives potential for cross-infections (Chapter 7). Fewer are kept by householders than in the past, but garden poultry are usually fed in open sheds or pens, which still provide grain for House Sparrows and Collared Doves.

Importance of livestock to birds

Livestock largely determine the vegetation over most of Britain. Almost all the grassland and about half the arable land is currently devoted to feeding livestock. But the presence of cattle and sheep on farms is generally beneficial to birds. Without these animals, there would be much less need for grassland, which provides habitat and feeding opportunities for many bird species, especially those, such as corvids, thrushes, Lapwing and Starling, that eat soil-dwelling invertebrates. For these species, grazed grass provides a valuable foraging habitat in summer when other crops are too high for them, and even more so in winter, except when the ground is frozen or snow-covered. Grassland also provides grazing areas for wild geese and swans, and for grazing mammals such as deer, rabbits and hares. In addition, the outdoor sites where livestock are fed in winter provide feeding opportunities for many bird species. Grain-based cattle feeds attract corvids, Yellowhammers and other seed-eaters, but silage attracts few if any birds (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986).

Livestock may alter the vegetation they graze to create more or less suitable conditions for particular bird species, or make prey more or less available to them. Grazed wet grassland provides nesting habitat for Yellow Wagtails and various waders, while heavily grazed dry grassland provides nesting habitat for Wheatears, Lapwings and Stone-curlews. In the longer term, livestock grazing can keep habitats open by preventing tree growth, but too much grazing in upland areas can destroy heather and other dwarf shrubs, and lead to their replacement by grass, with adverse impacts on some bird species (Chapter 19). Traditional methods of grazing, using cattle, sheep or ponies, are increasingly used on nature reserves to keep the vegetation in suitable condition for particular wild animal and plant species. This would not be profitable for a farmer making a living, but it is a cheap and efficient method of grass management that can be seasonally controlled, perhaps removing the animals while ground-nesting birds are breeding.

Livestock also have more direct effects on birds. Starlings are frequently seen on the backs of sheep, probing into the wool, and are assumed to eat any parasites living there. Wagtails and Starlings take insects disturbed from around the feet and noses of grazing cattle and, during periods of severe weather, livestock often break through snow in the course of their feeding, giving birds access to food otherwise unavailable. Across Britain, summering Swallows are often associated with cattle, nesting within the byres and feeding on the flies that cattle and their dung promote (Henderson et al. 2007a). Cattle-grazed pastures are favoured foraging areas for Swallows. Adverse impacts of livestock on birds result from their stepping on the nests of ground-nesting species, a hazard which increases with the densities of the animals concerned (Chapter 12).

FIG 70. Associations between livestock and birds: upper left, Starlings Sturnus vulgaris feeding on insects disturbed by grazing sheep (Richard & Barbara Mearns); lower left, Jackdaw Corvus monedula collecting nest material from a cow (Richard & Barbara Mearns); right, Yellow Wagtail Motacilla flava feeding on insects disturbed by a grazing cow (Richard Chandler).

Cattle dung pats can hold dozens of invertebrate species, including dung beetles in the genus Aphodius. These animals play an essential role in the breakdown of organic matter, and recycling the nutrients that it contains. Without such recycling, pastures would soon become covered with rank patches of grass of low digestibility and nutrient value, eventually becoming unsuitable for grazing (Gittings et al. 1994). Several bird species exploit the insects associated with animal dung, wagtails picking off the surface insects, and corvids, Starlings, Lapwings, Black-headed Gulls and others breaking open dung pats and turning over the pieces to expose the insect larvae and beetles within. Choughs, in particular, exploit the invertebrates associated with dung year-round. Oystercatchers nesting on inland pastures first pick the flies and beetles off the surface of fresh cow pats, and 10–15 days later they start to probe into the pats for beetle larvae, and after two months when the pat has mostly rotted, they probe in the soil beneath for earthworms (Briggs 1984). However, animal dung is now a much less productive source of bird food than it once was, because the anthelmintic drugs used to treat livestock kill many of the insects that could otherwise live in the dung, as well as others that occur in the soil below (Chapter 8).

FIG 71. Manure offers a source of invertebrate food items for Rooks Corvus frugilegus and other birds that can move it around (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

FIG 72. Other corvids that probe among livestock dung for food items include: left, Jackdaw Corvus monedula; right, Hooded Crow Corvus corone, as indicated by the manure on its beak (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

In addition to fresh dung deposited by grazing livestock, manure heaps attract many birds, with wagtails and corvids seeking mainly invertebrates, and House Sparrows, Yellowhammers and others picking out undigested cereal and grass seeds. The warmth of the manure makes muck heaps attractive feeding sites when other ground is frozen. Rotted farmyard manure spread over the fields increases the densities of soil-dwelling invertebrates, including earthworms, and brings them closer to the surface within reach of soil-probing birds (Scullion & Ramshaw 1987, Tucker 1992). In specific studies, large numbers of earthworms, bibionid flies and leatherjackets were found in areas where dung or slurry had been applied in the previous season (D'Arcy-Burt & Blackshaw 1991, McCracken et al. 1995, Edwards & Bohlen 1996). These are all important prey items for birds, and are usually less abundant under inorganic fertilisers.

LOW-INTENSITY FARMING

While most of this book is concerned with high-intensity modern farming, we should also take a brief look at some remaining areas of low-intensity farming. Over millennia, people around the world have shaped landscapes through farming, and their local traditions and cultures have in turn been influenced by their food-production systems. Many wild plant and animal species have become adjusted to, or even dependent on, such traditional agricultural systems. Some European birds, for example, are now largely or entirely dependent on traditional production landscapes found in particular regions: for example the wooded pastures of southern Portugal (montados) and southern Spain (dehesas) or the Crau steppe of southeast France. All these landscapes are man-made but exceptionally rich in wildlife, holding many species which are rare elsewhere. Terms such as traditional, marginal, extensive, and low-intensity are often applied to such farming systems. They all involve low inputs of energy and chemicals, but often require large inputs of human labour. All such areas in Europe now face threats arising from depopulation, poverty and loss of indigenous knowledge, cultural values and management systems. They do not match up in terms of 'efficiency' as usually applied to agriculture, because they exploit the sustainable natural potential of the land, rather than attempt to modify this potential by expensive (usually subsidised) inputs of energy and chemicals from elsewhere (Table 5). The nearest we have in Britain to low-intensity farmed areas, managed in largely traditional ways, are some lowland nature reserves, such as heaths or wet grasslands, which are managed specifically to maintain their wildlife populations. Parts of the uplands of Britain are also farmed in more traditional ways, although they suffered in the late 20th century from greatly increased (and unsustainable) grazing pressures (Chapter 19).

TABLE 5. Characteristics of low-intensity livestock and crop-based farming systems. Adapted from Beaufoy et al. (1994).

CONCLUDING REMARKS

This review indicates how much modern crop plants and livestock have changed from their ancestral forms, as a result of continuing selection. These changes speeded up greatly with the increasing application of science in the last century or so. Few if any of these man-made plants and animals could survive in the natural world of competitors and predators but, nurtured and protected on modern farms, they can produce food for people in quantities unimaginable from their wild ancestors, or even from the crop plants and livestock in vogue a century ago.

But as crop plants became more productive, digestible and nutritious for humanity, they also improved as a source of food for wildlife. Throughout their history, crop plants have been eaten by wild animals, including birds, and almost certainly the population sizes of many farmland species were influenced by the amount of crop food available. When production was lower, waste greater and birds more numerous, substantial parts of some crop types could be taken by one species or another. This was an inevitable consequence of arable agriculture. Bird damage to farm crops is now much less serious than it once was, and no birds can be said now to reduce food production in Britain on a scale that matters nationally. This is partly due to declines in some former 'pest' species and partly to more efficient crop sowing, protection and harvesting and to more secure storage and animal housing. In consequence, arable crops now provide much less food for birds and other animals than in the past, and this has been a major factor in reducing bird numbers over recent decades (Chapter 10). Nevertheless, some grazing birds can now feed extensively on the nutrient-rich leaves of oilseed rape and autumn-sown cereals, both of which provide an important winter food source, rape mainly for pigeons and cereals for geese and swans. The increased acreage of oilseed rape has almost certainly promoted the recent increase in Woodpigeon and Stock Dove numbers in Britain, and the same may have been true of winter cereals and waterfowl. Herbivorous waterfowl in Britain seem nowhere near the limit of their potential food supplies on agricultural land, although they may be in some localities, causing serious losses to individual farmers. Together with captive raised pheasants and partridges, these various species can, in some circumstances, reduce the yield of growing crops on which they feed, or lead to uneven growth and ripening across a field, but again such local effects are trivial in the national scheme of things. The effects of farm crops, livestock, and their production methods on bird populations are discussed in more detail in later chapters. But it is first worth discussing the other plant and animal life which is important to birds on farmland, which takes us on to the next chapter.

## CHAPTER 7

## Weeds, Pests, Diseases and Birds

THIS CHAPTER EXPLORES SOME aspects of farmland ecology that centre around plant or animal pests, or around livestock diseases that involve birds. Farms exist primarily to produce food for people. So any organisms that seriously reduce food production are considered pests, and farmers strive to get rid of them. Control of weeds and animal pests has therefore long been integral to farming. Like their wild ancestors, crops and livestock suffer from diseases, some of which have little obvious effect, while others can reduce the growth, breeding or survival of infected individuals. Farmland also hosts beneficial insects, such as pollinators and predators of pests, birds and mammals which eat pests, and subterranean organisms that enhance soil fertility.

The earliest statutes relating to the killing of birds to protect farm crops date from the 15th century in Scotland, and the 16th century in England and Wales. Bounties were paid for the destruction of all species regarded as serious crop pests, including Rooks and other corvids, pigeons and sparrows which ate grain, and Bullfinches which ate fruit buds. For centuries, bird scaring has been a regular and necessary activity in croplands. Many old paintings or tapestries depict crows and other species feeding on precious cereal crops, or people scaring them away. Some species considered as pests, such as Woodpigeons and Rabbits, have reached their present numbers largely because of the widespread abundance of food provided by crops, and these species in turn influence other farmland wildlife.

PLANT PESTS

Perhaps the greatest challenge to farmers through the ages, however, has been the eternal war on 'weeds'. These are often defined as plants out of place, unwanted within the crops. Like the crop plants themselves, arable weeds thrive on regular disturbance and short growing periods. They can compete with the crop for water, nutrients and light, restricting its growth and reducing its yield. Some weed species can still cause heavy crop losses but, with improved methods of control, many weeds are now so uncommon that their conservation is becoming more important than their control, at least for naturalists. Owing to the use of herbicides, cereal fields are now often described as virtual deserts for wild broad-leaved plants and their associated insects. Where native broad-leaved weeds survive, they are largely confined to the field edges, where herbicide application is less efficient and soil is more compacted than further out. Moreover, the removal of half the hedgerows and other field boundaries in Britain since 1945 has further reduced the amount of margin habitat in which wild species might otherwise survive.

Arable weeds are important to birds for two main reasons. First, their seeds form major dietary components of various species, which pick them directly from the plants or from the ground below; and secondly they support a big variety of insects which in larval or adult form feed on the leaves, flowers or seed-heads, and comprise another important food source for birds. Particular weed species often support specific kinds of insects which cannot persist without their own food plants. And it is not just strict 'insectivorous birds' which suffer from a shortage of insects, but some seed-eaters too which require insects to feed their young, such as the Grey Partridge, various buntings and sparrows.

Most farmland weeds are native to Britain, and their remains date back to Palaeolithic or Mesolithic times, but they were presumably much rarer and more localised before the advent of agriculture. Others could have been introduced along with crop-seeds from areas outside Britain, probable examples being wild oats, while some indigenous weeds may have been reinforced from imported crop-seed in the same way. Some common broad-leaved weeds, such as Persicaria, Fat-hen and Knotgrass, are favoured by seed-eating birds, and were once also eaten by people. The greatest variety of arable weeds was found mainly on the light sandy and chalky soils of the southeast. The most important plant families whose leaves or seeds are consumed by herbivorous birds on farmland include the Poaceae, Polygonaceae, Caryophyllaceae, Brassicaceae, Asteraceae, Chenopodiaceae and Lamiaceae (Wilson et al. 1999, Holland et al. 2006).

FIG 73. Persicaria (or Redshank) Persicaria maculosa was formerly a common weed of arable land whose seeds are relished by seed-eating birds, picked from the plant or the ground below (Ian Newton).

Most weeds of arable land are annuals which can complete their short life cycles from germination to seeding within the growth period of the crop. Species with the shortest life spans can fit in several generations per year: Shepherd's-purse and Groundsel can produce seeds in as little as six weeks after germination, and these seeds can grow at almost any time of year given enough warmth and moisture. Most arable weeds also produce prodigious quantities of seeds (Box 5), some of which can lie dormant in the soil for years until conditions again become suitable for their growth. These natural attributes of arable weeds may have been accentuated under centuries of cropping, as they became progressively more adapted to crop rotations and other farming practices. For centuries, weeds of cultivation were spread widely with seed-corn as it was broadcast, and most were not eliminated in a fallow year. It is now hard to say what the original habitats of many familiar weeds might have been, but it was probably areas of unstable soil, such as land-slips and scree slopes, places where wild pigs had rooted up the soil, or any other areas where perennial vegetation could not establish. But since the advent of farming, for hundreds and possibly thousands of years, such weeds could have spread and provided a widespread food source for several finches and other seed-eaters, including the Linnet and Twite, Chaffinch and Brambling, Greenfinch and Goldfinch, as well as various sparrows, buntings, larks and others, which became some of the commonest farmland birds (Newton 1972).

BOX 5. Average seed production by individual plants of some common farmland weed species favoured by seed-eating birds

Among the once-common weeds of farmland, some of the species important to birds produce seeds in prodigious quantities. For example, in round figures Charlock Sinapis arvensis produces 1,000–4,000 seeds per plant, Fumitory Fumaria officinalis 1,600, Corn Spurry Spergula arvensis 1,000–10,000, Chickweed Stellaria media 2,500, Sticky Mouse-ear Cerastium glomeratum 6,500, Shepherd's-purse Capsella bursa-pastoris 3,500–4,000, Greater Plantain Plantago major 13,000–15,000, Fat-hen Chenopodium album 3,000, Orache Atriplex patula up to 6,000, Knotgrass Polygonum aviculare up to 1,000, Persicaria Persicaria maculosa 200–1,200, Broad-leaved Dock Rumex obtusifolius 5,000–7,000, Curled Dock Rumex crispus 30,000, Groundsel Senecio vulgaris 1,000–3,000, Ragwort Senecio jacobaea 55,000, Dandelion Taraxacum sp. 2,000–5,000, Cat's-ear Hypochaeris radicata 1,000, Sow-thistle Sonchus oleraceus 40,000, Smooth Sow-thistle Sonchus arvensis 13,000, Creeping Thistle Cirsium arvense 4,000–5,000, and Spear Thistle Cirsium vulgare 4,000–8,000.

(Mainly from Salisbury 1961)

Another important feature of most arable weeds is that their seeds can survive for long periods in the soil. Typically, most seeds produced by a plant are likely to germinate or die within the first year, while progressively decreasing proportions survive through successive years. Seed longevity gives an obvious advantage to plants living in a habitat which may be unsuitable for them for long periods. When the soil surface is sufficiently damp and warm, germination is stimulated by exposure to light. In fields that are regularly cultivated, fresh batches of seeds may be exhumed and germinate every year. The periods that seeds can remain viable in the soil vary between plant species, but some of the commonest arable weeds have shown seed dormancy periods of up to several decades. For example, some seeds of Common Orache, Broad-leaved Plantain and Persicaria germinated after more than 30 years in the soil, Shepherd's-purse and Fat-hen after 35 years, and Curled Dock and Knotgrass after 60 years (Salisbury 1961). These periods may not represent the maximum possible longevities for the seeds of any of these species, but they demonstrate an important attribute of common arable weeds that enables them to persist until they again find themselves near the soil surface in conditions suitable for germination. During the First World War of 1914–18, the association of Poppies with the disturbed soil of the trenches and shell-holes of Flanders arose from the long-term dormancy of the seeds, able to survive for decades under grass yet spring into life when conditions became suitable. The old adage 'one year's seeding means seven years' weeding' is clearly a big understatement for many of the common weeds favoured by seed-eating birds. At the other extreme, Corncockle seeds can survive for just a few months, which explains the current extreme rarity of this plant; in the past, before mechanised seed-cleaning, it was re-sown with every grain crop.

FIG 74. Growth of poppies in a rape field, Lincolnshire (Ian Newton).

The importance of the buried seed-bank to birds is not only that it enables their major food plants to persist through periods of adversity, but that some seeds are turned to the surface with each ploughing, becoming suddenly available again. In the past, when weeds were more abundant than they are now, it was common to see flocks of finches, sparrows, buntings and larks, sometimes thousands strong, feeding on newly turned soil. This freshly exposed food source was important because it became available mainly in late winter or spring, when fields were ploughed for planting, a time when most other accessible seeds had been eaten. In recent decades, with the decline in broad-leaved weeds, such flocks have been seen much less often, but can still occur when land that has been under grass for 50 or more years is ploughed, revealing once again its buried treasure.

In contrast to arable weeds, most broad-leaved weeds (or 'wild flowers') of grassland are biennials, seeding in the second year (such as Spear Thistle and Teasel) or perennials, growing and seeding from the same root stock year after year (such as Knapweed, Meadowsweet and Dock). Such plants are able to withstand grazing, but can be eliminated by regular ploughing. Most produce seeds in large quantities, but these seeds are normally available to birds only from the plant. Once they are shed, they fall into the herbage below and become inaccessible. With some exceptions, such as Dock, most are likely to have seeds with short dormancy periods. For when long-term grassland is ploughed, it is usually the typical arable weeds that grow, rather than grassland species. This was evident when some long-term grasslands were ploughed in the early years of the Second World War (1940–41). We can see the same phenomenon today when, after a period of drought, an old pond or reservoir dries up and the exposed mud becomes carpeted with the seedlings of arable weeds.

FIG 75. Left, Linnet Linaria cannabina taking the seeds of Dandelion Taraxacum sp.; right, Goldfinch Carduelis carduelis taking the seeds of Creeping Thistle Cirsium arvense (Richard Chandler).

Weed control

The first major step in weed control came in the early 18th century with the development of the seed-drill which buried crop-seed in rows. This made it easier subsequently to hoe out the weeds between the rows of growing plants. Before this, when crop-seed was scattered by hand, much of it was taken by birds before it could germinate, and as the crop grew, hand-hoeing was practically impossible. The second development came with improved methods of screening harvested grain to remove weed seeds, preventing them from being re-sown with the next crop. The traditional flail and winnowing methods were replaced in the late 19th century by threshing machines and from the mid-20th century by combine harvesters. Both machines were fitted with screens and sieves designed to remove all small weed seeds and other impurities, which could then be destroyed (Salisbury 1961).

A third main development in weed control came from the 1940s with selective herbicides, which could be sprayed on a cereal or other crop to kill only the broad-leaved weeds, leaving the crop unharmed (Chapter 8). Crop spraying was at first small-scale, but became widespread from the 1970s. Repeated annually, it led to gradual decline of many weed species, and to progressive depletion of the seed-bank in the soil, as growing plants were killed before they could seed. Some species with short-lived seed, such as Cornflower and Corn Buttercup, declined rapidly in the 1950s–60s, but others with longer dormancy periods persist to this day, depending on the seed-bank and an occasional chance seeding. On many farms, 60 years of herbicide use has failed to eliminate totally some once-common species of arable weeds, and given an opportunity, they could quickly return.

Early selective herbicides could not kill narrow-leaved plants, however, so their use enabled 'grass-weeds' to proliferate, with Black-grass and Barren Brome now being major problem plants on arable land. To these, we can add Cleavers, whose surface hairs prevent herbicides from properly wetting the leaves. Specific grass-killing herbicides were developed in later years, but Black-grass became resistant to most of them. It is now one of the most rapidly increasing plant species in Britain, the bane of many cereal growers (Carey et al. 2008). It can out-compete wheat, reducing the grain yield, as it more readily extracts nutrients from the soil. It sheds its seeds in summer before the crop is harvested. The seeds germinate mainly in autumn, when the young plants can be killed by a general herbicide (glyphosate) if the soil is dry enough to allow tractor access.

The seeds of wild grasses are much less important to seed-eating birds than are those of broad-leaved weeds, although buntings eat some of them. These weeds all thrive under contemporary cereal farming; although they have little seed dormancy, they are highly responsive to nitrogen and resistant to many herbicides. So although many common weeds of farm crops date back to Neolithic times, different species have predominated at different times, under changing circumstances. Nevertheless, since the advent of selective herbicides, mainly from the 1940s, almost all broad-leaved weed species have declined greatly, thus removing a major food source of seed-eating birds.

In grassland, as opposed to arable land, many weeds (= wild flowers) were eliminated simply through the use of inorganic nitrogen fertilisers. These compounds can be taken up particularly well by modern grass varieties which then grow so vigorously that they out-compete most broad-leaved weeds, while the remaining resistant ones such as thistles can be eliminated by spot treatment with herbicides. Fertilisers were thus a major cause of the loss of the much-loved 'wild flower meadows' of Britain. Even the wild grasses of lowland pastures have greatly declined since the 1960s, as most areas were 'improved' by ploughing and reseeding with modern strains of mostly non-native grass species (Chapter 12). Wild indigenous grass species – though few in number – now predominate chiefly in the open uplands, which cannot easily be 'improved' in this way. Despite these changes, the seeds of broad-leaved grassland plants are still important to seed-eating birds, first in the fields as they are produced, and secondly in any resulting hay that may be fed to out-wintered livestock. Sparrows and buntings, in particular, search hay for the grass and weed seeds it contains. However, intensive silage production now allows few plants of any kind to seed, so that these seed sources have also greatly declined in recent decades (Chapter 12).

ANIMAL PESTS

Some native animals that could have created major problems in crop and livestock production disappeared from Britain at the end of the last Ice Age or in the Mesolithic Period, long before agriculture developed. Others disappeared later, at various dates between the Neolithic and recent centuries, and for at least some of these species, such as Brown Bear and Wolf, human killing was almost certainly the primary cause. Most significant current mammalian pests of agriculture and food storage were introduced to Britain from other parts of the world. Some have become key species in farmland ecology, and important prey for various predatory birds.

Deer

Of the four native deer species of Britain, the Reindeer died out soon after the last glaciation and the Moose in the Bronze Age, while the Red Deer and Roe Deer remained widespread but uncommon into the Middle Ages, but gradually lost ground in later centuries. Killing by meat-hungry country folk could have caused their demise. By the 19th century, the native Red and Roe Deer had become largely confined to the Scottish Highlands and a few other areas, while the Fallow Deer (introduced in Norman times) still occurred mainly around their original release sites in lowland parks and private estates.

During the 20th century, however, deer populations in Britain increased massively, not only the native Red and Roe Deer, but several alien species that had escaped from parks and other collections. Besides the long-established Fallow Deer from southern Europe, they include the Sika, Reeves' Muntjac and Chinese Water Deer, all brought from eastern Asia in the 19th century. So from being only locally distributed in the 1950s, deer of one or more species are now found over most of the country. Since the 1970s, the geographical ranges of Red and Roe Deer in Britain have more than doubled, while the ranges of three of the introduced species have increased more than tenfold, but the Chinese Water Deer much less. Deer are probably now more numerous and widespread in Britain than at any time in the past 1,000 years. In some areas, their densities exceed 40 individuals per km2, with up to four different species in the same area. In lowland they are centred on woodland (Chapter 17), but they emerge mainly at night to feed on farm crops, especially grass and cereals, eating both the growing plants and the ripening seed-heads. Complaints of their damage are increasing.

FIG 76. The two extant native deer of Britain: left, Red Deer Cervus elaphus (Chris Knights); above, Roe Deer Capreolus capreolus (Chris Knights).

Several factors have contributed to their recent increase, including reduced human hunting, the lack in modern Britain of large predators capable of controlling their numbers, greater areas of woodland to provide cover, reduction of competing livestock in woodland (with loss of wooded pasture), and the extensive planting of autumn-sown crops, which in the lowlands have provided a rich winter food supply. Milder winters may also have fostered good overwinter survival. In these favourable conditions, hunting at current levels has done no more than slow the rate of increase, until their numbers reach the point at which large-scale starvation prevails.

At their current high densities, deer have therefore become ecologically important in much of modern Britain, mainly through their effects on vegetation. They are important to birds for three main reasons. First, through their browsing, they have a huge impact on woodland structure, gradually removing most of the vegetation below the 'browse line'. They thereby reduce the habitat and food supplies of shrub-nesting birds, such as Bullfinch, Dunnock, thrushes and warblers, most of which have declined in Britain in recent decades (Chapters 2, ). Secondly, they consume the fresh young shoots of trees, shrubs and herbaceous plants, which would otherwise support many of the insects and insect larvae eaten by birds. In the uplands, some of the plants that are heavily browsed by deer, such as heather and bilberry, are themselves important food plants of various grouse species. Thirdly, they have a positive impact, in that their mortality in the open uplands provides a supply of carrion for scavenging birds, such as eagles and corvids (Chapter 19). To this carrion can be added the gut-piles ('grallochs') of deer that are shot and gutted in the hills.

Rabbits

The Rabbit was once restricted to the western Mediterranean basin, and is thought to have been introduced to Britain by the Normans in the 11th or 12th centuries, possibly after earlier failed attempts by the Romans (Fig. 77). For several further centuries, it was kept in semi-captivity, and managed in artificial warrens for its meat and fur (Sheail 1971). By the 13th century, commercial warrens were widely established, especially around monasteries, and Rabbit meat and fur came to provide a major source of protein and clothing for rural people. The species gradually became established in the countryside around the warrens, but it was not until the 18th and 19th centuries that its numbers mushroomed. Its rise coincided with two major changes in the countryside: first, the establishment of winter fodder crops (such as turnips) for livestock which also provided winter food for Rabbits, and secondly the control of its predators by gamekeepers, along with generally milder winters. So from the 18th century the Rabbit was increasingly regarded in the lowlands as an agricultural pest, and strenuous efforts were made to reduce its numbers, although with little lasting effect. In terms of crop damage, Rabbits are probably the most important agricultural pest in Britain today, causing losses estimated at more than £183 million per year (Williams et al. 2010). Without Foxes and other predators to kill them, their damage could be very much greater.

FIG 77. Rabbit Oryctolagus cuniculus, one of the major pests of farmland, with most damage caused by the grazing of grass and growing cereals (Keith Kirk).

In the early 1950s, Rabbit numbers in Britain were estimated at 60–100 million, and the damage they did to growing crops was greater than today. The species is noted for its high reproductive rate, and it is the continual production of naive young, rather than the numbers present at any one time, which supports the several predator species that depend largely on Rabbits (Buzzard and other raptors among birds, Foxes, Polecats and Stoats among mammals). From 1954, the introduced viral disease myxomatosis wiped them out in many places, causing an estimated 99% decline in their overall numbers nationwide, and put an end to the remaining commercial warrens, as at Lakenheath in Suffolk (Sheail 1971). The decline in Rabbits was accompanied by obvious declines in their predators, including Buzzards, Foxes and Stoats.
