Over time, however, as Rabbits became more resistant to the virus or the virus became less virulent, their numbers began to recover, reaching an estimated 37.5 million in the early 1990s. The species is now numerous and widespread, but fluctuates greatly, the disease usually striking again whenever numbers rise substantially. The recent spread over much of Britain of another pathogen – Rabbit haemorrhagic disease – has also reduced their numbers in some areas, but immunity seems soon to develop (Macdonald & Tattersall 2001).

The crash in Rabbit numbers in the 1950s had some striking effects on vegetation and other wildlife, besides predators (Flowerdew et al. 1992, Lees & Bell 2008). Overgrazed woodlands started to regenerate, herbs that had not flowered for years burst into bloom, while grass and cereal production rose. Through their relentless grazing, Rabbits had prevented vegetation succession and suppressed competition among plant species, with the result that, when Rabbits declined, some plants became commoner and others rarer. The low vegetation – such as that on closely grazed calcareous downland – tended to become rank, species-poor and invaded by scrub. Taller, denser grassy vegetation suited Field Voles, which increased along with their Weasel predators in some areas, as Rabbits declined (Flowerdew et al. 1992). These changes demonstrated how ecologically significant in lowland areas Rabbits and their grazing had become.

Apart from deer, Rabbits now constitute the largest biomass of any wild terrestrial mammal in Britain. They are important to birds for two main reasons. First, they graze down the grass on some heathlands and downlands almost to ground level, creating ideal nesting habitat for birds such as the Stone-curlew and Wheatear (which also nests in Rabbit burrows). They also prevent scrub and tree establishment in these habitats. Secondly, Rabbits provide an important food source for some predatory birds, especially the Buzzard and Great Black-backed Gull, and are also eaten as carrion by other species, such as the Red Kite, Raven, Carrion and Hooded Crows, and other large gulls. Rabbits are now so important to Buzzards that in many areas Buzzard breeding densities and success are closely correlated with local Rabbit numbers (Dare 1961, Newton 1979, 2013a, Graham et al.1995). As an introduced alien in contemporary Britain, the Rabbit is therefore another keystone species, with major effects on the farmland ecosystem. Nevertheless, according to BTO surveys, its numbers in Britain have halved in the 20 years since 1995 (BTO website).

Rats and mice

Two species of rats became established in Britain accidentally, the Black Rat supposedly in Roman times, supporting the flea that later transmitted the Black Death, and the Brown Rat much later, in the 18th century. The Black Rat is found naturally in southern and southeastern Asia and the Brown Rat further north in eastern Asia. Both species arrived as stowaways on ships, and thrived in the towns and countryside of Britain, especially around farms and game-rearing sites. When they come together, the bigger Brown Rat (at around 500 g) usually eliminates the smaller Black Rat (340 g), which is now restricted in Britain to a few port towns and some offshore islands (such as the Shiants) which have not yet been colonised by its larger and hardier relative. In the past, they were both major pests of stored grain, causing enormous post-harvest losses, and damage to containers.

FIG 78. Prey and predator: left, Brown Rat Rattus norvegicus, a major pest of stored grain and other foods, formerly found in large numbers in cereal ricks (Keith Kirk); above, Barn Owl Tyto alba brood with rat (Andrew Everitt).

Where rats have access to a regular food source on farms – whether grain or processed animal feed – their numbers can build up rapidly, and their presence becomes obvious. Before the advent of combine harvesters, rats lived in cereal ricks, being displaced at threshing time as the ricks were dismantled. In a study in Oxfordshire in 1939–41, the numbers of Brown Rats built up steadily from an average of 18 animals per rick in September to an average of 79 in April, after which many dispersed into the countryside (Venables & Leslie 1942). When based in the ricks, they had to leave frequently for water and thus became repeatedly available to Barn Owls and other predators hunting around the farm (Box 6).

In addition to the damage they cause, rats spread disease to people and farm stock, not only the infamous bubonic plague which killed so many people in earlier times, but others such as leptospirosis (or Weil's disease) to which the rats themselves are fairly resistant, but farm animals and people are susceptible. They can also contaminate human and livestock foods with bacteria such as Salmonella.

Rats are important to birds in two main ways: first as a food source, as they are eaten by a range of predators, particularly Barn Owls nesting in farm buildings; and secondly as predators of other birds, mainly of eggs and chicks but sometimes also of adults. They can climb well, so can reach the nests of shrub-nesting species, and also readily explore holes and crevices for the nests of cavity-nesting or burrow-nesting birds. On offshore islands, they have caused the declines and often local extinctions of several seabird species, notably burrow-nesting Puffins and petrels (Newton 2013a).

Introduced House Mice have lived in Britain as human commensals at least since the Iron Age. In the past, they also colonised cereal ricks from late summer, and fed on the grains until the ricks were dismantled months later (Southern & Laurie 1946). As for rats, ricks provided an ideal environment for House Mice in terms of shelter, warmth, and protection from predators, so that numbers could increase rapidly, feeding on the grain. On average, numbers doubled every two months, so hundreds could be exposed at threshing time, representing between 1 and 14 mice per cubic metre of rick. Like rats, they acted as important prey for Barn Owls and other predators.

After threshing, the grain was stored indoors, usually in stone buildings more difficult for rodents to penetrate, and often in an upper storey, but still the entry of a single pregnant female could soon populate a store. Clearly, rats and mice were a major cause of grain loss during storage at least into the 1960s, a loss which has now been almost totally eliminated, following the introduction of the combine harvester and rodent-proof bins and silos. There can be few, if any, farms on which rats and mice occur in similar numbers nowadays as in the past; food is less available for them and chemical rodenticides are in constant use.

BOX 6. Rodents, ricks and Barn Owls

Into the 1960s, stack-yards typically contained 2–6 cereal ricks, constructed of bound sheaves with seeds still attached. They were built at harvest time in August–September, and dismantled for threshing at any time up to the next July. While they lasted, ricks provided warm and food-rich housing for rats and mice, which bred continuously to reach peak numbers in spring.

In a stack-yard of six ricks, rats and mice in April might together number about 1,200 individuals, confined within a small area and venturing outside mainly for water (Venables & Leslie 1942). They provided a constant source of food for Barn Owls, especially important at times when field rodents were scarce or hidden under snow. Not surprisingly, Brown Rats and House Mice were more important in the diet of Barn Owls in the early 20th century than they are now. One study revealed that the two species formed about 58% of the Barn Owl diet by weight (Collinge 1924–27), and in another study these rodents formed 43% of the bird's diet by weight (Ticehurst 1935). More recent studies, conducted mainly after the demise of cereal ricks, revealed much lower proportions. In an analysis of 48,000 prey items from Barn Owl pellets collected in many parts of Britain during 1960–71, the percentage of Rats averaged 2% numerically but 11% by weight (1 to 28% by weight in different regions), while the percentage of House Mice was 1% by number and weight, varying up to 3% in different regions (Glue 1974). In all regions in these later studies, the single most important prey item was the Field Vole, which inhabits rough grassland and formed 40–60% of the diet by weight in different regions.

Other indications of high rat densities in the days of cereal ricks stem from the numbers of rats killed by gamekeepers (Twigg 1975). For example, in 1903 a single gamekeeper on an estate in East Anglia killed 14,662 rats. In 1926, over 10,000 were killed, but by 1942 following the introduction on this estate of the combine harvester and the disappearance of the cereal rick, the number of rats killed decreased to 1,500 per year, even though the gamekeeper pressure remained the same. The last total in 1966 was 466 rats, about 3% of the number killed in 1903. Current populations of rodents around farm steadings can rarely equal those provided by the old rick-yards.

The change almost certainly affected Barn Owl numbers. In 1932, in a national survey of Barn Owls, cereal regions of central and eastern England were shown to hold the highest densities of 10–20 pairs per 100 km2. Following major changes in the threshing and storage of cereals, these regions experienced the biggest subsequent decline in Barn Owl numbers, falling in the 1980s to an average of only 0–5 pairs per 100 km2 (Shawyer 1987). In these same regions, organochlorine pesticides caused many Barn Owl deaths, and may have contributed to their decline (Newton et al. 1991). However, Barn Owls could have recovered in subsequent years, as organochlorines were phased out, but another change then became important, namely a reduction in the area of old grassland, with its abundant Field Voles. In recent decades, this change probably had the most important negative impact on Barn Owl numbers.

Other rodents

Out in the fields, in the early growing season, the mainly nocturnal Wood Mice make use of both cropland and hedgerows, as well as other semi-natural habitats, whereas the mainly diurnal Field Voles are found in long-term grassland, living within the matted growth of uncut areas, as in neglected fields, field boundaries, ditch sides and newly planted woods (Chapter 19). A blanket of snow affords Field Voles added overhead cover from most predators, and an insulating layer that creates a warm microclimate throughout their network of grass tunnels. These conditions enable voles to breed through the winter, increasing to high levels in spring, and promoting good breeding success among their predators. However, by protecting voles from predation, prolonged periods of snow result in big losses among Barn Owls and Kestrels, which often show conspicuous population crashes during occasional hard winters.

Various voles and other small rodents of farms and farmland form the prey base, not only of predatory birds, but also of predatory mammals, such as the Fox, Badger, Polecat, Pine Marten, Stoat and Weasel. Some of these predators also take birds and their eggs, the Fox having the biggest impact overall. The Fox has long been known as a predator of poultry and recently born lambs. This latter predation is now a problem mainly in upland areas where sheep lamb outside. Where sheep are brought inside for lambing, the problem has been largely eliminated, and similarly Fox predation on poultry has been much reduced now that most commercial poultry are kept enclosed. Nevertheless, Fox numbers have grown substantially in recent decades, especially in towns but also in the countryside, so we can expect their impact on wild bird populations to have increased greatly in this time (Chapter 2, Box 1). On estates with gamekeepers, the numbers of Foxes killed per year more than doubled between the 1950s and 1990s, reflecting greater numbers in the wider countryside (Tapper 1999). However, since 1995, their numbers counted on BBS plots have declined by about 40% (BTO website).

FIG 79. The Kestrel Falco tinnunculus preys largely upon Field Voles Microtus agrestis, found in rough grassland (Frank Snykers).

Over the centuries, rodents around farm buildings were controlled by use of traps, domestic cats and terriers, as well as by wild Barn Owls which were encouraged to nest in farm buildings. In the southern two-thirds of Britain, many farms held at least one pair, although their numbers fluctuated greatly from year to year depending on rodent numbers. In years of high rodent densities, two or more pairs could nest close together on the same farm, and sometimes in the same building or straw stack (Shawyer 1987). Nowadays in lowland Britain where farmsteads hold fewer rodents, and rough grassland suitable for Field Voles occurs mainly in strips along wood edges, field edges and ditches, it has been calculated that each Barn Owl pair requires some 15–25 km of edge habitat, assuming a mean strip width of 5 m (Shawyer 1987). In a study in southern Scotland, radio-tagged Barn Owls hunted up to 1 km from their nest sites, giving roughly circular home ranges of around 3 km2 (Taylor 2002).

In continental Europe, another species, the Common Vole, also occurs in grassland, and is regarded as a serious pest, because numbers sometimes increase so much that valued grass fields are eaten bare, and then the animals start to dig out the roots, with damage spreading outwards from field to field across a landscape. Aware of this potential problem, Dutch farmers mostly plough and reseed their grasslands every second year to kill any voles present and prevent them from reaching plague proportions. These voles can be twice the weight of Field Voles, and are favoured food items for many birds of prey. While absent from most of Britain, they occur on five of the Orkney Islands, to which they are assumed to have been introduced in Neolithic times, the oldest known radiocarbon-dated fossil being 4,600 years old. These voles are hunted on Orkney by Hen Harriers, Kestrels and Short-eared Owls.

Other pests

The damage caused by some bird and mammal species to crops or livestock is often highly visible. Most of these 'pest' species can be legally killed, but in the presence of such readily available food, killing must be maintained year after year if their numbers are to be kept to levels acceptable to the farmer. Often 'scaring' rather than killing is used to protect crops against bird damage, because it can be applied by individual farmers to particular vulnerable fields at appropriate times. With modern crop-guns or other banging devices, scaring is less costly and time-consuming than attempting to kill large numbers of the pest species involved. The inefficiency of controlling Woodpigeons and Rooks by contemporary shooting practices was demonstrated by detailed studies (Box 7), and it is no longer encouraged by subsidies on cartridges as it was in the past. Crop damage caused by the millions of Pheasants and Red-legged Partridges, artificially reared each year for shooting, is generally tolerated.

The smaller organisms which damage crops, such as insects and various disease-causing pathogens, were in the past much more difficult to control, or even to identify. In earlier centuries, farmers relied on natural predators and used indirect methods, such as crop rotation, to keep their numbers in check, but from the mid-20th century suitable methods of chemical control were developed. These various pesticides have had a major impact on farmland and its wildlife in recent decades, as discussed in Chapter 8.

DISEASES OF LIVESTOCK

Some diseases have had major impacts on livestock farming in Britain over recent decades, and have sometimes involved wild bird populations. In the past, before veterinary drugs became available, all farm animals were more or less permanently infected with a range of parasites, some of which had little impact, while others reduced growth and reproductive rates and were occasionally fatal. Some parasites and pathogens were specific to particular kinds of livestock, while others were shared between species, including people. Cattle and pigs were intermediate hosts for tapeworms which completed their life cycles in people, but these parasites are now effectively extinct in Britain. Nowadays, while some diseases of livestock are simply tolerated as before, others are reduced through husbandry practices, or through the use of vaccines, antibiotics and other drugs.

Because farm animals are now kept in larger numbers, at much greater densities than in the past, they could have become increasingly vulnerable to infectious diseases. Some such pathogens can also be passed to people, with recent examples including avian influenza, TB (tuberculosis), SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome) and BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy). Moreover, as sheep and cattle are continually moved around, sometimes over long distances, the potential for the spread of diseases is correspondingly greater than in the past.

BOX 7. Pest control: Woodpigeon and Rook

Many bird species considered as agricultural pests in Britain can be killed openly at any time of year to lessen their numbers or scare them from crops. A general finding in agricultural pest control worldwide is that pest-birds can often be killed in large numbers year after year without causing any long-term population decline, and often without achieving much reduction in damage (Newton 1998). Before embarking on a control programme aimed at population reduction, it is first helpful to study the natural factors affecting the reproductive and mortality rates of the species concerned. The additional level of kill that must be achieved to cause population decline can then be assessed, as can the time of year when this could most readily be accomplished. Often this critical level of control may not be feasible or economically worthwhile (that is, control would cost more than the damage the pest would inflict if left alone). These issues can be illustrated by two species long regarded as agricultural pests in Britain.

WOODPIGEON

For many years, the killing of Woodpigeons was encouraged by the payment of a subsidy on cartridges (Murton et al. 1974). The pigeons were killed like game birds, using double-barrelled shot guns, usually by small numbers of people shooting at birds as they entered woodland roosts in the evening. One feature of this control method was that, regardless of flock sizes, it limited the numbers of birds that could be killed from each flock, because after two shots the gun had to be reloaded, by which time the flock had passed. So as populations rose and flocks became larger, a steadily increasing number, but decreasing proportion, of birds was killed. On this method of control, shooting became 'inversely density-dependent', and above a certain population level it could not control numbers.

Another problem with traditional pigeon control was that, although permitted year-round, most shooting occurred in autumn and early winter, when numbers were at their annual peak. But this was only a few weeks before these numbers were reduced naturally by large-scale starvation. Such shooting merely removed part of a number that was doomed to die from food shortage in the ensuing weeks (Murton et al. 1974). This type of control was clearly ineffective in reducing the nation's Woodpigeon population, and also in reducing crop damage, which did not occur at this time of year. So in 1965 the subsidy on cartridges was withdrawn. In subsequent years, no increase occurred in Woodpigeon numbers, which instead declined in response to agricultural changes that reduced the winter food supply (Inglis et al.1990, 1997). Only when rape was introduced as a widespread crop from the 1970s did pigeon numbers rise again, a trend continuing until around 2010 (Fig. 16). Woodpigeons are still shot as they enter winter roosts, or over decoys in fields where they are feeding, but more for recreation than for control. More Woodpigeons are shot each year than any other wild bird.

ROOK

In Britain, Rooks have long been 'controlled' by shooting young birds as they leave their nests in April, although without the backing of a government subsidy. At this time, the young birds are sitting targets. Again, however, numbers are reduced only temporarily because a month later shooting is compensated by lower natural losses when numbers are reduced by the seasonal shortage of earthworms and other soil-dwelling invertebrates which form the main summer food before grain becomes available (Dunnet & Patterson 1968, Murton 1971). This natural population reduction occurs a few weeks before the survivors begin to cause potential damage by feeding on ripening cereal grains. To reduce numbers further, it would be better to insert control measures between the periods of natural mortality and subsequent crop damage, but this would involve much more effort than shooting fledglings, and would probably not be economically worthwhile. As in the Woodpigeon, it appears more sensible to concentrate remedial action at the places of crop damage, rather than attempting widespread population control.

In general, the success of any control operation in reducing the population levels of birds depends not merely on the proportion of birds killed at one time, but on whether the deaths from control operations increase the overall annual mortality of the species or simply replace deaths from natural causes, so that the overall mortality remains much the same. To reduce numbers effectively, control operations should follow the main period of natural loss, and not precede it. Most of the birds that are considered pests of farm crops in Britain move around from farm to farm, so that scaring (by banging devices, visual devices, or direct shooting) is a fairly effective way to protect vulnerable crops for short periods. The birds move from field to field, distributing their feeding widely around the neighbourhood, rather than concentrating on the same field or the same farm. For species of conservation concern, such as some types of wild geese, scaring is the main method used to reduce crop damage, but fields of sacrificial crops may be grown especially for the birds, these being the only fields from which they are not driven away. In places where sacrificial crops are grown, farmers are paid from government subsidies or conservation funds.

Involvement of livestock in wildlife diseases

Sometimes, domestic livestock act as reservoirs of infection for wild birds. The transmission of the disease louping ill from sheep to Red Grouse is an example. This disease is caused by a flavivirus which affects the central nervous system. Infected sheep often develop a characteristic louping gait, in which the front legs move forward together, followed by the back legs. Typically, about one-tenth of infected sheep die. The louping ill virus was probably brought to the British uplands in sheep where it is now patchily distributed and transmitted between hosts by the Sheep Tick. The mortality that occurs in Red Grouse in areas where louping ill is established is often sufficient to reduce grouse to low densities, but continuing infection depends on the presence of sheep or other alternative hosts, and also on ticks as vectors (Duncan et al. 1979). In some areas, alternative hosts include Red Deer and Mountain Hares.

FIG 80. Two game birds that can be affected by parasitic diseases originally derived from domestic livestock: above, the Pheasant Phasianus colchicus is sometimes afflicted by gapeworm Syngamus trachea from domestic poultry (Stan Wilson); right, the Red Grouse Lagopus l. scoticus is prone to infection by louping ill virus from sheep (Stan Wilson).

Following infection, adult grouse are much less likely to die than chicks. Studies in northern England revealed that, in areas with ticks and louping ill, grouse chick survival was about half the level found in areas with ticks and no louping ill, or in areas with neither ticks nor louping ill (Hudson & Dobson 1991). The removal or routine vaccination of sheep can eliminate louping ill from grouse stocks, providing other potential hosts, such as hares and deer, are scarce. Adult grouse sometimes contain antibodies to the virus, suggesting that they have developed some immunity. With continued exposure, Red Grouse could in time become more resistant to louping ill.

Since the 1990s, louping ill seems to have affected Red Grouse in areas where it was not previously recognised. This could be due to mild winters allowing better survival of ticks, or to increased numbers of alternative hosts such as Red Deer. But it could also be due to the transport of sheep between different parts of the country, thereby introducing the disease to areas previously free of it. Fencing is now sometimes used to exclude deer or sheep from valued grouse moors, and the killing of Mountain Hares as alternative hosts is becoming widespread, despite continuing opposition.

Another example of disease passing from domestic to wild species involves the nematode worm Heterakis gallinarum. This parasite is a carrier of the protozoan Histomonas, which causes the disease blackhead (histomonosis) in gallinaceous birds, including domestic turkeys. Until the 1960s, when large numbers of domestic fowls were kept free-ranging on farmland, this parasite was frequently passed to Grey Partridges, causing substantial mortality. But now that most poultry are kept indoors, and can be treated with appropriate drugs, this transfer no longer occurs on any scale, removing this source of mortality from Partridges and other wild game birds (Potts 2012).

Another nematode parasite which can pass between domestic poultry and wild game birds is the gapeworm Syngamus trachea, which infests the trachea, causing frequent gaping, and occasionally killing the host. Eggs laid in the trachea are coughed up, swallowed and passed out in faeces. They then get into an intermediate host, such an earthworm or snail, from which they pass back into another bird. The first recorded instances in Britain occurred in domestic poultry, but now the parasite is more often found in Pheasants, especially where they are reared in the same pens year after year. Like domestic poultry, Pheasants can be treated with an anthelmintic drug, such as ivermectin.

Among contagious viral diseases, Newcastle disease can affect many domestic and wild bird species. First recorded in 1927, it can sometimes cause severe epidemics in poultry. It is also transmissible to humans, in which it causes temporary flu-like symptoms. Other game bird diseases, such as coccidiosis and strongylosis, may also have originated in domestic poultry, but this is not known for certain.

In other cases, agriculturalists often view wildlife as a source of infection for livestock, and when a virulent disease outbreak occurs among farm animals, its arrival and spread are often blamed on wild birds. Eventually the facts emerge, and often the disease can be attributed instead to movement of domestic stock or animal products. This was the case in the spread of the H5N1 strain of avian influenza among poultry, and in various foot-and-mouth disease outbreaks among cattle and sheep. Bird flu usually takes the form of an inconspicuous viral infection that is maintained in bird populations by oral or faecal routes of transmission. The viruses involved have been found in at least 105 wild bird species, but most often in waterfowl, terns and waders (Olsen et al. 2006). These viruses change rapidly in nature because their genetic components continually mix in bird bodies to form slightly different subtypes. The previously unrecorded subtype (H5N1) emerged among poultry in China in 1996. It soon spread over most of Asia, and also reached Europe and Africa, mainly through the transport of poultry and poultry products (Gauthier-Clerc et al. 2007). The disease also passed from domestic ducks to migratory waterfowl, which suffered massive mortalities, and may have played a minor role in its spread. The virus caused widespread public concern because it infected some people, most of whom died. However, following the rigid control and burning of infected poultry imposed by the agricultural authorities, the virus soon disappeared.

Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is another highly infectious viral disease which affects cloven-hooved animals, including cattle, sheep, pigs and deer. The virus causes a high fever for 2–3 days, followed by blisters inside the mouth and on the feet where they may rupture and cause lameness. Adult animals rarely die, but become debilitated, with effects on body condition and milk yields; young animals more often die. FMD can rapidly spread by animal-to-animal contact, or from contaminated equipment and vehicles, clothing or fodder, and by scavengers that feed on infected carcasses. Standing water, and uncooked food scraps and feed supplements containing infected animal products, can also harbour the virus and give additional routes of infection. The containment of FMD demands constant monitoring, restrictions on movement of livestock, quarantines, and the elimination of infected herds.

It has often been claimed that migratory birds, especially Starlings, periodically bring FMD from the continent to Britain. The virus does not become established in bird tissues, but captive Starlings that were fed on virus-contaminated food then excreted it for 10–26 hours, while it persisted for up to 91 hours on their plumage (Eccles 1939). It is therefore conceivable that birds could carry the virus from farm to farm. However, no convincing evidence for this possibility has yet emerged to set against the overwhelming alternative view that people, livestock and vehicles move the virus around. In 1951, when an epidemic occurred in England, outbreaks in autumn were clustered around seaports, which was hardly consistent with the broad-front migration of birds into Britain. Moreover, FMD did not reach Britain during the war years 1939–44 in spite of widespread outbreaks on the continent. Birds still migrated, but shipping and passenger traffic were much reduced (Murton 1964). In a major outbreak in 2001, the role of livestock and vehicle movements in the spread of the disease were well documented from the pattern and sequence of outbreaks, and wild birds were deemed irrelevant. Another disease involving domestic and wild animals is bovine TB, which has become a major challenge for cattle farming in Britain, especially in southwest England. Birds are not susceptible to TB, and have not been implicated in its spread, but it illustrates a disease where the culling of a wild species (the Badger) may be needed to protect livestock.

CONCLUDING REMARKS

In Neolithic times, when farming was introduced to Britain, all species of livestock would have been in competition with their wild relatives for forage, susceptible to some of their diseases, and at the same time vulnerable to wild predators of one type or another. As the more important of these competitors and predators were eliminated from Britain, and in more recent times smaller livestock (such as poultry) were increasingly moved indoors, competition and predation have ceased to be significant factors in nationwide livestock production. Remaining predation mostly concerns sheep, whose lambs are vulnerable for a short time to predators such as Foxes, Crows, Ravens and large gulls, and in hill country also to Golden and White-tailed Eagles. People who keep poultry as a hobby may lose some individuals to Foxes and perhaps other predators, but this is no longer a serious economic problem nationally. However, disease transfer between wild and domestic animals is a continuing but sporadic threat. Although some diseases may have originally spread from domestic to wild animals, the latter may now have become the main source of re-infection of domestic stock. The controversial role of Badgers in transmitting TB to cattle (and vice versa) is the only current economically important example.

Into the 1970s, competition from weeds clearly limited the productivity of plant crops, and much manpower was expended in reducing their impact. Nowadays, this control is accomplished much more quickly and effectively with chemical herbicides, but weed control has huge adverse consequences for birds and other wildlife. The broad-leaved weeds involved provided much food for seed-eating birds, and also supported many insects and other invertebrates which themselves acted as additional food for birds. The reductions in these sources of bird food have almost certainly contributed to declines in the bird species that depended on them (Chapter 10).

Most of the wild birds that in the past were considered serious pests of farm crops are now much less of a problem, mainly because of quicker and more efficient sowing and harvesting methods which have reduced the period over which grain crops are vulnerable. Rodent-proof storage containers have also helped to reduce the once-huge losses of stored grain to insignificant levels. Most remaining crop damage attributable to birds involves species that eat the green leaves of farm crops, such as Woodpigeons, game birds and some large waterfowl. Rabbits and deer are also clearly important in the modern farmed environment, not only competing for food with grazing livestock but having major impacts on vegetation and the wild animals dependent on it. They also act as significant food sources for predatory and scavenging birds.

While veterinary medicine has greatly reduced the day-to-day impacts of livestock diseases in Britain, compared with former times, four aspects of modern agriculture promote the spread of diseases, namely: (1) the high densities at which some farm animals are kept (as for example in modern poultry, pig and dairy cattle units); (2) the frequency of long-distance dispersal of farm animals, as they are moved around the country from farm to farm (as is usual in sheep and cattle husbandry); (3) the importation of live animals, meat and meat products from abroad which can act as a source of new disease outbreaks; and (4) the feeding of animal-based products back to live animals, especially herbivores (as in BSE, Chapter 4). Livestock and wildlife (including some birds) share many important diseases, giving the potential for transmission from livestock to wildlife (as in Red Grouse and louping ill), or from wildlife to livestock (as in Badger and bovine TB).

In conclusion, a relatively small number of wild animal species in Britain play crucial roles in the ecology of farmland, and support many of the predators that live there. Some of these key species are indigenous to Britain, while others are introduced. Many of them feed on farm crops or stored food of one sort or another. Some are important to birds because they influence habitats and food supplies, others because they figure prominently in the diets of birds, and yet others because they share diseases with domestic livestock. Many of these species have declined in recent years in association with changes in agricultural practices, while others (notably deer) have increased. This chapter, together with the previous two dealing with farmland ecology, sets the scene for the rest of the book, in which the effects of recent agricultural practices on bird populations are examined in more detail.

## CHAPTER 8

## Pesticides and Birds

THE CONTROL OF WEEDS and pests has long been a major concern of farmers, because of their potential effects on crop yields. The first attempts to use chemicals for weed and pest control were in the 19th century, but it was not until the 1950s that the practice became widespread and routine. The name 'pesticide' is now applied to any chemicals used to kill unwanted plants and animals, whether marketed as herbicides, insecticides, molluscicides, fungicides, or any other '–cides'. These chemicals are viewed as a boon to human food production and livestock health worldwide. But their use also has detrimental effects, notably a massive destruction of other plants and animals, including birds. Depending on the chemical and mode of application, birds may be poisoned directly, or they may ingest a sub-lethal dose which then affects their physiology or behaviour, predisposing them to other forms of death or affecting their reproduction. However, pesticides also affect birds indirectly by reducing their food supplies, including many of the 'weeds', insects and other small animals which these chemicals routinely destroy. All three types of effects can reduce bird numbers.

Pesticides are now applied every year to almost all the arable land in Britain and some of the lowland grassland. They are also used in forestry, horticulture, plant nurseries and amenity areas such as golf courses, and in veterinary products used against parasites. Since the 1950s, their overall use in Britain has risen more than tenfold, as measured by the weight of active ingredients applied. There have been increases in the proportions of farmland treated, the numbers of applications per year, and the variety of chemicals used. Over this period, the numbers of active chemical ingredients approved for use as pesticides increased from only a few dozen to several hundreds, formulated in thousands of registered products. Their annual usage in Britain is monitored by the Pesticide Usage Survey (PUS), which produces regular reports available online. Fungicides have become the commonest group of pesticides in use, accounting in 1996 for about 48% of all applications in terms of area covered, with herbicides accounting for an additional 33%, insecticides for 11%, growth regulators 7%, molluscicides 1%, and other compounds less than 1%.

Some early pesticides were highly toxic and were often applied haphazardly, with little regard to health and safety. Some farm workers died as a result of their exposure. As years passed, the dangers of some of these chemicals became increasingly apparent, and much more care was imposed on their development, manufacture and use. Changes to sprayers and their nozzles allowed pesticides to be used at lower concentrations and more precisely targeted than before. Since 2003, sprayers have been subject to annual checks under the National Sprayer Testing Scheme (NSTS).

Pesticides may be sprayed in liquid form on crops to kill foliage pests or on the ground to kill soil-dwelling pests, such as leatherjackets. Some may also be applied in powdered form to seeds intended for sowing, acting against soil-dwelling insects or fungi. Or they may be made into granules to control soil organisms, or mixed with baits to control slugs or larger animals, such as rats and mice.

FIG 81. The Grey Partridge Perdix perdix is one of the major casualties of herbicide use which kills the 'weeds' on which insects suitable for partridge chicks depend (Chris Knights).

In Britain, birds are not normally targeted directly by pesticides, but they are exposed incidentally, mainly through their food. Seed-eating birds often eat treated seeds that have been spilled on the soil surface or recently planted, and can thereby ingest a lethal dose of insecticide. Also, some birds swallow pesticide granules picked from the field surface, apparently mistaking them for food or grit (which they habitually take to help break up food in the gizzard), and these granules can also cause mortality (Best & Fischer 1992). Some pesticides persist in animal bodies, contaminating and sometimes killing their predators by 'secondary poisoning'. In addition to contaminating food items, crop spraying sometimes results in pesticide being applied directly to birds, perhaps being absorbed through the skin or preened off the feathers. Birds that sit tight on their ground nests may be sprayed as the boom passes over, or their eggs may be sprayed and the residue absorbed into the eggs or through the brood patch into the incubating adult. Nestling birds, lacking feathers, may be dowsed in chemicals. However, the aerial spraying of farm crops, which led to widespread spray drift, has been banned in Britain since the 1980s.

IMPORTANT FEATURES OF PESTICIDES

If pesticides destroyed only their target pests and then quickly broke down to harmless by-products, problems from their use would be minimal. But most pesticides are non-specific (or 'broad spectrum'), and kill a wide range of other organisms besides the target pests. Many of these non-target organisms might act as food for birds. In addition, while some pesticides break down rapidly, others last for weeks, months or even years in the environment, able to affect organisms long after they were applied. For the farmer, such chemical stability is usually beneficial, because it enables the pesticide to remain active over a longer period. But this same feature allows some chemicals to accumulate progressively in the bodies of non-target animals. Accumulation results when the rate of chemical intake exceeds the rate of elimination, so that the animal can repeatedly acquire small doses until the chemical in its body reaches a lethal level. The concentrations of some persistent chemicals can also increase at successive steps in a food chain, as one type of animal eats another, each time acquiring further pesticide; that animal in turn may be consumed by a third, and so on. Depending on their chemical properties, all pesticides vary in their toxicity and specificity, and in their persistence and cumulative propensity. Where a pesticide stands in these various respects affects its environmental impacts. Generally, chemicals marketed as insecticides and fungicides do not affect plants at the concentrations at which they are normally applied. Nor do herbicides generally have strong direct effects on insects or plant diseases, but some fungicides kill insects, pyrazophos being a noted example.

Pesticides drift on wind, or wash from land into rivers and lakes, sometimes reaching areas and organisms far removed from places of use. The potential impacts on non-target species are therefore not confined to farmland. The wide dispersal of some pesticides became shockingly apparent in the 1960s when residues of the insecticide DDT were detected in penguins and other Antarctic birds, thousands of kilometres from places where DDT was made or used (George & Frear 1966).

Other problems have resulted from pesticide manufacture which, through accidents and discharges, repeatedly pollutes rivers, lakes and coastal areas, causing loss of aquatic life. Added to these major spills are many local accidents and abuses, excessive application and careless disposal. Some of these same points apply to some other chemical pollutants, but because pesticides are specifically designed to kill plants or animals, are used routinely in Britain by more than 200,000 farmers and farm workers, and are applied each year to large land areas, the problems they cause are widespread and ever-present.

Lack of specificity

Lack of specificity in pesticides can be illustrated by an experimental trial involving a commonly used carbamate insecticide, carbaryl, which was applied to one of two adjacent one-acre (0.4 ha) patches of millet (Barrett 1968). Applied in July, the carbaryl remained toxic for only a few days, but in this time the numbers and biomass of insects and other arthropods on the sprayed plot declined to almost nil. Populations took seven weeks to recover in biomass, and longer to recover in numbers and diversity. The chemical also affected other organisms not studied, including micro-arthropods, earthworms and other soil-dwellers, as evidenced by the greater build-up of leaf-litter. The unsprayed control plot maintained its fauna throughout. Several North American studies that examined the effects of aerial forest spraying with DDT recorded up to 90% declines in overall insect populations following single applications, and similar reductions of aquatic insects in forest streams (Adams et al. 1949, Hoffmann et al. 1949, Crouter & Vernon 1959). Among more recent pesticides, the organophosphate dimethoate applied to wheat caused 80–95% mortality of field-layer invertebrates (Vickerman & Sunderland 1977). These and other studies exemplify the effects of a single application of a broad-spectrum insecticide: in each case, a large range of insects and other organisms was killed, and not just the target pest. Almost all the organisms involved would have had no effect on the crop, and some may have been beneficial. For birds dependent on these organisms, the spraying would have brought a sudden sharp reduction in food.

In small field trials, invertebrate populations usually recovered within two months of spraying, but in such trials recovery probably depended largely on immigration from surrounding unsprayed areas. Immigration is much less likely nowadays in modern intensively farmed landscapes, where the treatment of almost every hectare leaves few refuges in which vulnerable insect species can survive in sufficient numbers to re-colonise sprayed areas quickly. Recovery is likely to depend mainly on reproduction by the few individuals that survive, taking much longer than recovery by large-scale immigration. In cereal fields in Sussex, many arthropods took more than a year to recover from spraying with a broad-spectrum insecticide, while sawflies took up to seven years (Potts 2012).

Long recovery periods may be good for the farmer, but not for the birds and other animals that depend on those insects. Imagine the impact on a community of insectivorous birds in the breeding season if 90% of the insect biomass in their habitat were removed with a single spraying. This is exactly what happened in those experimental trials. Now imagine the same process conducted at different dates through the growing season, applied over the 4.6 million hectares of arable and horticultural land in Britain every year. It is no wonder that insects are strikingly scarcer now than in the recent past.

On recovery from a single spraying, some pest species can become more abundant than before because their predators (being scarcer, with longer life cycles) take longer to recover than they do. This usually leads to further pesticide applications – the so-called 'pesticide treadmill' – so that many invertebrate species become depressed over even longer periods. Species differ greatly in their susceptibility to any particular pesticide, but in general the higher the concentration applied, the greater the range of organisms killed. Application of broad-spectrum insecticides can cause treated fields to become almost devoid of insect life, and, if the products are persistent, the fields may remain depleted for weeks. Birds usually attempt to compensate for loss of food locally by foraging elsewhere, but there are limits on how far they can fly and return regularly to a nest with food for nestlings.

On cereal farms in Sussex, attempts were made to link declines in invertebrates with particular chemicals (Ewald & Aebischer 1999). Five invertebrate groups studied showed declines with the use of insecticides, and four of them also with the use of fungicides. All five groups responded strongly to pyrethroid and organophosphate insecticides, but none of them showed noticeable decline under pirimicarb, a more selective insecticide used primarily against aphids (but sparing their main predators, ladybirds). In other words, broad-spectrum insecticides such as dimethoate were most damaging to the insect fauna as a whole. Similarly, the molluscicide methiocarb was found to be toxic to a wide range of other animals, including carabid beetles (Purvis & Bannon 1992).

Broad-spectrum insecticides can kill bees and other pollinating insects. This can lead to poor pollination of food crops, reducing the quantity and quality of produce. In many orchard areas, natural pollinators have been reduced so markedly that hives must be brought in for some weeks each spring to ensure adequate pollination. This is common practice now in most fruit-growing areas of Britain, and has become a substantial industry in the major fruit-producing regions of California and elsewhere. The need arises partly from insecticides killing wild bees and other pollinators, and partly from herbicides killing the flowering plants which would support pollinators for the rest of the growing season. In parts of the Far East, owing to heavy pesticide use, some fruit crops now achieve an adequate yield only if they are pollinated by hand, demanding huge inputs of human labour.

Over the years, pesticide development and manufacture have been increasingly in the hands of multinational companies who, given the costs involved, are interested mainly in broad-spectrum pesticides that kill a wide range of organisms, making them suitable for use on a variety of pests on different crops across the world. For more specific pesticides, the sales are usually considered too small to be worth the costs involved in development and manufacture.

Resistance

One of the anticipated results of long-term pesticide use is the development of resistance in some of the target species. More than a dozen insect pests in Britain have become resistant to one or more insecticides, while rats and mice are now resistant to the rodenticide warfarin and some similar chemicals. Among plants, an early example was provided by Groundsel, which became resistant to the pre-emergence herbicide simazine. Herbicide-resistant Black-grass has become a major problem for cereal growers, because it can now tolerate all seven groups of selective herbicides which can be used on cereal fields. This grass can currently be controlled chemically only by using glyphosate, a broad-spectrum plant-killer that can be used in the intervals between crops that it would otherwise kill. The use of pesticides has therefore led to a costly arms race between pests and chemical companies, the one developing resistance and the other ever more effective products. Non-target organisms are caught in the crossfire.

THE MAIN TYPES OF PESTICIDES

In the late 19th century, the earliest chemicals used as pesticides were inorganic compounds based on sulphur or metals, such as arsenic, mercury, copper and tin. They all carried serious risks for the operators, and were used chiefly on high-value crops such as fruit and hops. Then from the 1940s, more serious attempts were made to find chemicals that were effective as pesticides but less harmful to people. Hundreds of organic chemicals were synthesised and tested against various plants and insects, selecting the most toxic ones. It was largely a hit and miss business, but the first 'hormonal herbicides' (MCPA and 2,4-D) were introduced in the 1940s, as were the first modern insecticides (DDT and BHC). Their discovery opened a new era. They were the forerunners of agrochemical manufacture as a huge multinational industry often linked with the pharmaceutical industry. Typically, each active ingredient has several trade names, often marketed by different companies, with different formulations. Some (systemic chemicals) can be absorbed from the soil or through plant leaves and incorporated into plant tissues, where they protect against fungi or insects. Two or more pesticides are sometimes applied together as approved tank mixes of compatible chemicals, while others may be applied at different times to the same crop. Their effects may be additive or synergistic, one accentuating the effects of another. Quantities of active ingredients of only 1–2 kg per sprayed hectare may seem small to have such great biological effects, but they are usually far in excess of the levels needed to kill the target organisms, and many others besides.

By 1955, some 37 different compounds had been approved for agricultural use in Britain, rising to 136 by 1970, and to 344 by 1997, progressively widening the range of plant and animal species that could be controlled (Ewald & Aebischer 1999). The overall area of land treated each year by different types of pesticides increased by several-fold during the last 30 years of the 20th century (Fig. 33). Most arable fields came to receive multiple applications per growing season, depending on the crop. Autumn-sown cereals, which are in the ground for longer than spring-sown cereals, are sprayed more often, potentially with up to a dozen different chemicals (Thomas et al. 1996). Winter wheat can receive an average of ten different treatments during its life, winter barley around eight, and spring barley less than five. Autumn-sown rape can receive up to 20. However, pesticide use also fluctuates from year to year according to weather and prevailing threats, as do the types of chemicals used. In general, though, we can surmise that the indirect effects of pesticides on bird populations, via depression of their food supplies, are likely to have increased substantially since the 1940s. The 1970s saw a big increase in herbicide use, and the 1980s in insecticide and fungicide use. Interestingly, these were the years of most severe decline in different bird populations (Chapter 2).

Herbicides

Non-selective methods of weed control such as the flame gun, or drastic herbicides such as sodium chlorate, arsenical weed-killers, petroleum oils and coal-tar acids proved useful on railway tracks and other situations requiring long-term soil sterilisation. But for use in fields, the need was for selective herbicides which would kill some plants but not others – weeds but not crops. Monocotyledonous plants, such as grasses and cereals, have somewhat different physiology and leaf structure from dicotyledons, such as broad-leaved weeds, providing a basis for selectively controlling one group without the other. In the 19th and early 20th centuries various chemicals were trialled for their selectivity, and some came into limited use: for example, dilute sulphuric acid or copper sulphate to control broad-leaved weeds in cereals.

Physical features of the plant can affect the uptake of herbicides. In general, the broader a leaf, the more easily is herbicide absorbed. Features such as hairy leaves and the presence of a waxy cuticle can hinder take-up and cause water-based compounds to run off without being absorbed. This latter problem was overcome in the 1970s by the addition of wetting agents to the spray. The annual weeds of arable land proved easiest to control. The destruction of perennials (mainly found in grassland) required translocation of the toxin through the plant into the roots and other underground parts. These are often controlled by 'spot treatment' of individual plants.

Most early herbicides had chemical names too cumbersome for everyday use, and they were commonly designated by abbreviations, such as DNBP (used for weed control in leguminous crops), MCPA and MCPB (both used against broad-leaved weeds in cereal crops), DNOC (useful for weeds resistant to other hormone weedkillers), TCA (used against grass weeds, such as Couch and Wild Oats), 2,4-5-T (used against woody perennials), and IPC (used against grasses). These chemicals gave some idea of the degree of selectivity possible in plant-killing operations. Most were also much safer to use than some earlier compounds, and had the additional advantage that they broke down quickly in the soil, without having big effects on soil microorganisms. An exception was DNOC, which proved highly toxic to people and animals, and so was discontinued when safer compounds became available.

Even within the same group of plants, different species vary in their susceptibility to particular herbicides. Many of these early herbicides did not give complete control of their target species. They were poor at controlling Polygonum species which were important food plants for seed-eating birds and for some insects eaten by birds. Herbicides for controlling these plants became available from 1962, and were particularly significant because they removed Knotgrass and other food plants of the insects that provided the main foods of Grey Partridge chicks (Potts 1970). Root crops were also susceptible to many herbicides used against broad-leaved weeds, and for years they could not be sprayed. They therefore remained important sources of weed seeds for seed-eating birds. But all this changed when pre-planting and pre-emergent weed control came into use from the mid-1960s, using soil-acting herbicides. Weed seedlings could then be destroyed before the crop plants – whether cereal or root crops – grew above the ground, allowing the later emerging crop plants to grow for a time free of competition.

The number of herbicidal compounds approved for use on cereals and root crops in Britain increased from one in 1960 to nearly 40 in the late 1980s and beyond. There was a massive increase in the use of herbicides from the 1970s on, and arable weeds and their dependent insects rapidly declined over this period (Wilson et al. 1999, Firbank & Smart 2002). It was a period when Linnets and other seed-eating birds began to decline. In one long-term study in Sussex, the numbers of weed species per square metre on cereal fields more than halved between the 1930s and 1970, with similar declines elsewhere in Britain and Europe over the same period (Potts 1986). Declines have continued to the present day, and most cereal fields are now almost clear of broad-leaved weeds and their associated insects.

Herbicides also had a fundamental impact on farming practices, facilitating reductions in crop rotation and changing the main season of cultivation from spring to autumn. These changes were also inimical to wildlife (Chapter 10).

Herbicides and genetically modified crops

The herbicide glyphosate (Roundup) is used to achieve a total kill of all herbaceous plants. In the United States, it is used mainly in association with genetically engineered glyphosate-resistant crops, making it possible to destroy all the plants in a field except for the resistant crop. Both the glyphosate and the resistant crops are marketed by the same company, Monsanto. If crops genetically modified for glyphosate resistance became widely adopted here, almost the entire food-base of many insects and birds on arable land could then be removed, probably bringing further decline in their populations. In due course, strains of some problem weed species might evolve resistance to glyphosate, as has happened in North America, but no doubt they could be controlled by other chemicals. Glyphosate has been described in the industry as a 'virtually ideal' herbicide for farmers, owing to its broad spectrum and low toxicity to animal life. However, in 2015, the World Health Organization cast a shadow over the halo, classifying glyphosate as 'probably carcinogenic in humans'.

Fungicides

Like other pesticides, the early fungicides were based on sulphur or toxic metals such as copper and mercury, but from the 1960s other organic chemicals were developed for controlling plant fungal diseases. The early ones controlled mainly mildew, but from the 1980s the triazoles made it possible to control a wider range of fungi, including rusts on cereals. Nowadays, fungicides are used both as seed-dressings to control seed- and soil-borne diseases and as foliar sprays to control other diseases (such as mildews and rusts) on growing crops. The use of foliar fungicides increased greatly in the 1980s, particularly on cereals, but large amounts are also used on fruit and vegetables. Repeated applications are needed through the growing season to keep fresh leaves free from fungal infections. In cereals, up to four sprays are applied per growing period, and in apples an even greater number to keep the fruit free of blemishes such as those caused by 'apple scab'. Some fungicides also control insects, either through direct poisoning or through reducing their fungal food supplies. At the same time, they allow other insects to increase through depressing the fungal pathogens that would normally control them. The commonly used fungicide benomyl has this effect. In addition, the use of fungicides has supported the switch to winter cereals, especially to winter wheat, which is more susceptible than barley to disease problems. However, most fungicides are still preventative rather than curative, because it is hard to eradicate fungal infections once they have become established through a crop.

Insecticides

Insecticides that came into use during the late 19th century were based either on inorganic substances such as copper and mercury, or complex compounds, such as derris, pyrethrum and nicotine, derived from plants. More modern insecticides are all synthesised, some to mimic naturally occurring pyrethrum and nicotine. They are used as seed-dressings against soil-dwelling pests or as foliar sprays on standing crops. Some are also used as fumigants in glass houses, and as veterinary medicines, as in the dips to control sheep scab (caused by mites) or fly blow (maggot infestations). Since the 1960s, almost the entire area of cereals, roots and vegetables grown in Britain has been sprayed annually with insecticide, sometimes with several applications per year, and until 1992 the process of sheep dipping was mandatory.

Insects form more than 80% of all known animal species, so it is not surprising that they form the majority of crop pests. But they are also eaten by almost all farmland birds, and are essential in the chick food of many more, so any substantial reduction in their numbers can be expected to affect birds adversely. The main types of insecticides are as follows:

• Organochlorines, such as DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) and lindane (gamma-hexachlorocyclohexane), came into wide use in the late 1940s, mainly as crop sprays, killing a wide range of insects and other organisms. About 20 years after its introduction, DDT was found to cause serious eggshell thinning in certain raptors and other birds, leading to reduced reproduction (Figs 82 & 83). More toxic compounds, such as aldrin, dieldrin and heptachlor, were introduced from 1956 and were used mainly as seed-dressings. They proved to be highly toxic to birds and mammals, and were responsible for very large kills of seed-eating birds and their predators during 1956–62 (see below). In addition, DDT, lindane and then dieldrin were used in sheep-dips.

In terms of their direct effects on birds, the organochlorines proved more serious than other types of pesticides, causing worldwide declines in several bird species, often in areas far removed from farmland. Studies of their modes of action revealed some important principles. Besides being toxic, organochlorines were chemically extremely stable, persisting in the environment for years. They were soluble in fat, so at sub-lethal levels they were able to accumulate in animal bodies, passing from prey to predator, affecting species further up the food chain. They were also dispersed widely away from farmland in air and water currents, and in the bodies of migrating birds, reaching regions far removed from where they were made and used. Their residues were found in the bodies of birds all over the world, from the High Arctic to the Antarctic. Moreover, different kinds of organochlorines had different modes of action, both lethal and sub-lethal, which acting individually or together caused serious declines in some bird populations. Widespread declines in birds of prey were caused by the combined effects of reduced reproduction (resulting from eggshell thinning caused by DDT and its metabolites) and increased mortality (caused by the much more toxic aldrin, dieldrin and heptachlor).

FIG 82. Modes of action of DDE (from the insecticide DDT) and HEOD (from aldrin and dieldrin) on raptor populations. From Newton (1986).

For a time, organochlorines were widely used throughout the developed world, but during the 1970s and 1980s they were banned progressively in one country after another, as their environmental impacts and potential risks to human health became increasingly apparent. They continue to be used without regulatory constraint in some tropical and subtropical countries. In Britain their use was reduced progressively from the 1960s, until they were banned almost totally by EU legislation in 1986.

FIG 83. Eggshell thickness index of Sparrowhawks Accipiter nisus in Britain, 1870–1997. Shell thinning became quickly apparent from 1947, following the widespread introduction of DDT in agriculture. Shell thickness improved from the 1970s, following progressive restrictions in the use of the chemical, which was banned altogether from 1986. Each dot represents the mean shell index of a clutch (or part-clutch), and more than 2,000 clutches are represented from all regions of Britain. Shell index was measured as shell weight (mg)/shell length × breadth (mm). Extended from Newton (1986).

• Organophosphates were derived from the nerve-gases used in human warfare. Most are highly toxic, but after application they are short-lived, and do not readily accumulate in animal bodies. However, some types, such as chlorfenvinphos, can persist in the soil for several weeks, especially when used in seed treatments. Organophosphates also replaced organochlorines in sheep-dips and were used in veterinary medicine to control parasites such as warble fly. For birds and mammals, some of the most toxic organophosphates used in agriculture were diazinon and chlorpyrifos, both of which have killed thousands of birds worldwide and created chronic health problems for some of their human users (Pretty 1998).

• Carbamates are used to kill plants or animals. Most are highly toxic to a wide range of invertebrates, and are especially effective in soil against nematodes and slugs. Aldicarb is used as a nematocide, methiocarb and metaldehyde as molluscides, pirimidon as an aphicide, and carbofuran as a general soil insecticide. To birds and mammals, some of the most toxic carbamates include carbofuran and methomyl. These chemicals have killed millions of birds worldwide, and have also impaired the health of many people (Mineau 2005, US EPA 1989).

• Pyrethroids came into wide use from the 1990s. One of the most commonly used is cypermethrin, which is toxic to a wide range of insects. Pyrethroids are moderately persistent, and are also especially toxic to aquatic organisms. At extremely low concentrations of two parts per trillion of water, they proved lethal to mayflies, gadflies and other small creatures that form the base of many aquatic food chains, some involving birds. When cypermethrin was first used as a sheep-dip (replacing organophosphates), it contaminated many upland streams, killing aquatic invertebrates, with knock-on effects on fish and birds extending for tens of kilometres downstream. In Britain, it was withdrawn as a sheep-dip from 2010.

• Neonicotinoids are the latest major group of insecticides to be developed, coming into wide use from 1994. They are chemically similar to nicotine, a natural insecticide found in tobacco leaves, and are currently used mainly as seed-dressings. Like most other insecticides, neonicotinoids act on the nervous system. They are of relatively low toxicity to mammals, so are safer than some earlier pesticides for farmers to use, and as they are relatively new, few pests have yet become resistant to them. They are moderately persistent in soil, lasting in measurable amounts up to several years, and accumulating year on year as more is applied (Goulson 2013). However, neonicotinoids differ from most other insecticides in two important respects. First, they are highly soluble in water, so they easily leach into wetlands where they can have devastating effects on some aquatic invertebrates (Mineau & Palmer 2013, van Lexmond 2015). Secondly, they are systemic, being readily absorbed by plant roots or leaves to be retained in the tissues. Used as seed-dressings, they can be taken up into the growing plant, and can then pass to any insects which eat the leaves or pollen, suck the sap or drink the nectar. In Britain, they have been applied as seed-dressings to several crops, and especially to rape to protect the growing plants from the flea beetle Psylliodes chrysocephala, against which they are said to confer protection for about 10 weeks post-planting. However, there is particular concern over their effects on bees. Although the concentrations in nectar or pollen are very low, bees can gradually accumulate higher concentrations in their bodies; if the bees are not killed outright, they suffer a variety of behavioural and physiological effects (Pisa et al. 2015). Other studies have revealed that contaminated dust arising from seed-drills at the time of sowing neonicotinoid-coated seeds can have serious effects on bees, and firm evidence has now emerged for colony declines in both bumblebees and Honey Bees resulting from field exposure to neonicotinoids (Whitehorn et al. 2012, Budge et al. 2015, Godfray et al. 2015). In the case of Honey Bees, most of the evidence refers to imidacloprid, the most toxic neonicotinoid yet released.

Because of concern over bees as food-crop pollinators, the EU placed a two-year moratorium on neonicotinoid use from December 2013, giving time for more information on their environmental impacts to become available. This recent research produced stronger evidence for colony failures in Honey Bees linked to imidacloprid use on rape seeds (Budge et al. 2015) and also suggested that neonicotinoids could have serious effects on a wide range of other animals, including birds (Box 8). Butterfly populations in Britain declined markedly during the period 2000–2009, but in 15 out of 17 species, declines were strongest in localities with greatest neonicotinoid use (Gilburn et al. 2015). Further work is needed to test for a causal relationship in butterflies, because their annual numbers are also related to summer weather and to numbers in the previous year. It further emerged that, owing to their persistence in soils, neonicotinoids could be taken up by any plants, not just the crop. One study found that most of the neonicotinoids present in pollen taken to Honey Bee hives in arable landscapes came from wild flowers. The concentration of neonicotinoid in wild plants growing along hedgerows was up to eight times the highest level found in the adjacent crop (Botias et al. 2015). With different plant species flowering at different times, contaminated pollen and nectar were available to bees over a much longer period than from any one crop.

BOX 8. Effects of neonicotinoids on birds

Introduced in 1994, neonicotinoids are the latest group of pesticides to be used on a wide scale. They are popular with farmers, but evidence of their wider environmental impacts is emerging year by year. One major concern is that they will reduce insect pollinators enough to reduce crop yields, as well as affecting many wild plants. A review of 150 studies of the direct (toxic) and indirect (food-chain) effects of neonicotinoids on vertebrate wildlife focused on two neonicotinoids, imidacloprid and clothianidin (Gibbons et al. 2015). Studies confirmed that imidacloprid at field levels was toxic to many birds, exerting both lethal and sub-lethal effects. Sub-lethal effects, as studied mainly in captive birds, included lethargy, impaired immunity, reduced growth and reproduction.

The registration of pesticides for widespread use requires their prior testing in laboratory conditions on standard species, often Mallard and Quail among birds. But subsequent field studies revealed that some songbirds are more sensitive to neonicotinoids than are these standard test species. A recent review of mainly North American studies concluded that 'a single corn kernel coated with a neonicotinoid can kill a songbird. Even a tiny grain of wheat or canola [rape] treated with the oldest neonicotinoid, imidacloprid, can poison a bird' (Mineau & Palmer 2013). Even with the less toxic clothianidin or thiamethoxam, a few seeds would suffice. Laboratory evidence suggests that neonicotinoid insecticides can debilitate birds at a much lower fraction of a lethal dose than other pesticides, and that the debilitation can last for much longer.

So far, however, most of the field evidence for the effects of neonicotinoids on birds is circumstantial, as it results from correlations between neonicotoid use and declines in bird populations, usually through effects on their insect prey. Population trends in insectivorous birds over the years 2003–09 at different sites in the Netherlands were negatively correlated with the concentrations of imidacloprid found in local waters (Hallmann et al. 2014). This relationship was apparent in 14 out of 15 bird species considered, and was statistically significant in nine species, as well as in the overall bird community, all species combined. In areas with imidacloprid concentrations in water greater than 19.4 ng per litre, bird populations had declined, on average, by 3.5% per year. The spatial pattern of bird declines became apparent only during the period of imidacloprid use from the mid-1990s. It was not apparent in earlier years when other pesticides were used instead. The authors suggested that birds had been affected indirectly by declines in their insect prey caused by imidacloprid, which had been used mainly as a seed treatment. There had been no other major land-use or management changes over this period.

A similar correlative study in North America also examined bird trends in relation to neonicotinoid use in 30 different areas of the Canadian prairies. The neonicotinoids were spread mainly in granular form as seed-treatments. Allowing for variations in other land-use practices, bird declines were strongest in areas of heaviest neonicotinoid use, including such widespread species as Magpie, American Robin, Horned Lark, Meadowlark, European Starling and House Sparrow (Mineau et al. 2005). Other birds, such as Tree Swallows that nest near prairie wetlands, showed obvious symptoms of food shortage in areas of heaviest neonicotinoid use, with lower adult body weights and lower feeding and growth rates of chicks (Morrissey et al. 2013). As in other areas, wetlands with the highest neonicotinoid concentrations held the lowest numbers and diversity of insects (Morrissey et al. 2013, van Lexmond et al. 2015).

Insects have been declining progressively in Britain and other parts of western Europe since the 1950s, in parallel with the progressive intensification of agriculture, but regular monitoring suggests that the rate of decline has steepened from the 1990s, coinciding with the period when neonicotinoids were in wide use (van Lexmond et al. 2015). There is no proof that neonicotinoids were largely to blame, but they were considered the most likely among a number of possible causes discussed at a meeting convened to discuss the problem in 2009 (van Lexmond et al. 2015). When used as seed-dressings, only 2–20% is absorbed by the crop, the rest degrading, washing out of the soil into waterways, or being absorbed by subsequent generations of plants, including 'weeds' (Goulson 2013). So banning neonicotinoid use on flowering crops does not prevent their use on cereals, and then getting into the next crop of rape or other plants on the same ground. In addition, dust created at sowing could introduce these chemicals into other non-cropped habitats around the farm. Clearly, future decisions on whether to approve, restrict or ban these powerful insecticides could have profound environmental consequences throughout the developed world.

• Fipronil is another broad-spectrum insecticide (a phenylpyrazole) which became available at the same time as the neonicotinoids. It has some similar properties, and is now widely used around the world, but only in small amounts in Britain. In addition to its effects on insects, studies in North America have found that concentrations of fipronil in some wetlands were high enough to also kill fish and some birds (Gibbins et al. 2015). In toxicity trials, game birds were killed at lower doses than waterfowl and songbirds. Owing mainly to its supposed effects on bees, a moratorium was placed on some of its uses in the EU, along with the neonicotinoids. There are concerns over its environmental and human health effects.

Pesticide mixtures

Most of the research on pesticides has been concerned with individual or closely similar chemicals. But in the wild, plants and animals are often exposed to mixtures of different chemicals, present on vegetation or in soil or water. These mixtures could have greater effects on some organisms than the individual chemicals, especially when one enhances the effects of another (synergism). Recent research has suggested that the cocktails of pesticides and other man-made chemicals now found, mostly at low levels, in many wetlands may be a factor in the declines of amphibian populations.

DIRECT EFFECTS OF PESTICIDES ON BIRDS

Public awareness of the side effects of pesticide use in Britain was first aroused in the late 1950s, when thousands of birds were found dead and dying in recently sown cereal fields (Cramp 1962). The grains had been dressed with the newly released organochlorines, namely aldrin, dieldrin and heptachlor, in order to protect them against insect attack in the soil. But these pesticides proved also to be highly toxic to birds and mammals, killing many individuals that fed on treated grains spilled on the soil surface. The birds usually died in convulsions, but were otherwise in good condition; chemical analyses revealed organochlorines in their body tissues. Affected species included not only seed-eaters such as finches, buntings, pigeons and game birds, but also raptors, such as Sparrowhawks, which fed on the dying birds. The many thousands of carcasses found around arable land were assumed to form a tiny proportion of the total birds killed. The situation was exemplified in a letter from a Norfolk landowner: 'The place is like a battlefield. My keeper has found innumerable corpses, including masses of small birds... this slaughter... is going on all around here and quite apart from the game, the destruction of wildlife is quite pitiful.' The slaughter continued every spring for several years, and some raptors disappeared from much of their range in this time, especially the bird-eating Sparrowhawk, Peregrine and Merlin.

Mammal predators were also killed: in the East Midlands alone during the winter of 1959–60, at least 1,300 Foxes were found dead after eating Woodpigeon carcasses contaminated with organochlorine seed-dressings (Blackmore 1963). Over the same period, large numbers of Badgers perished, causing a national decline in their numbers (Jefferies 1969), and Otters disappeared from most of the country, accumulating their organochlorine residues mainly from fish, following the contamination of lakes and rivers (Chanin & Jefferies 1978, Mason & Macdonald 1993). Over the same period, alkyl-mercurial compounds were also used as seed-dressings, and had similar properties and similar effects on birds and mammals, but they were used much less in Britain than in Sweden and other parts of Europe (Borg et al. 1969).

FIG 84. Three major victims of organochlorine pesticide use in Britain: above left, Peregrine Falco peregrinus (Edmund Fellowes); above right, Merlin F. columbarius (Edmund Fellowes); left, Sparrowhawk Accipiter nisus (Keith Kirk).
