Field evidence for lethal effects of pesticides on birds has come mainly from carcasses found around farmland, as in the above examples, with the cause of death confirmed by chemical analysis. Some studies also included counts of live birds before and after an application of pesticide, comparing them with counts in nearby untreated areas. Such studies mostly involved chemicals that are very toxic to birds, and often revealed local population reductions exceeding 70%, with total elimination of some species from sprayed areas (Newton 1998). Providing the spraying was not repeated, songbird numbers usually recovered in about 1–3 years, or longer in the case of slower-breeding species (Brown 1978). Experimental studies of this type were done mainly in the 1950s and 1960s, since when most of the toxic chemicals concerned have been replaced by others which have less direct impacts on bird populations.

FIG 85. Pink-footed Geese Anser brachyrhynchus, frequent victims of carbophenothion use in the 1980s (Chris Knights).

Although many modern pesticides kill birds, sometimes in large numbers, they break down more quickly than organochlorines, so do not have such lasting or far-reaching effects. Nevertheless, poisoning of wild geese by organophosphate seed-dressings occurred in Britain during the 1970s–90s. Most such incidents involved less than a hundred birds at a time, but collectively several thousands of birds may have died over this period, mainly Pink-footed and Greylag Geese and in some areas also Brent and Canada Geese, Bewick's and Whooper Swans (Stanley & Bunyan 1979, Fletcher 1994). Fifty or more geese and swans lying dead in a field at the same time is a memorable sight. The main chemical involved was carbophenothion. This compound was later replaced by chlorfenvinphos, which posed a lower risk to geese, but killed large numbers of Woodpigeons, with recorded incidents occurring throughout the 1980s. This chemical was in turn partly replaced by fonofos, which carries a lower risk to pigeons, but still killed some (Burn 2000).

All these incidents involved seed-dressings. But in the 1980s, many other wildfowl were poisoned by grazing on winter wheat treated in February–March with the insecticide triazophos. Three incidents involved around 50, 60 and 80 Brent Geese, and others involved 30 Greylag and seven Bewick's Swans (Fletcher 1994). As a result of these incidents, this material was banned from use after the end of December each year.

FIG 86. Red-legged Partridge Alectoris rufa, frequent victim in Spain of neonicotinoids used as seed-dressings (Richard Chandler).

In a recent study of Red-legged Partridges in Spain, the density of treated seeds on the soil surface after sowing was 11.3 ± 1.2 seeds per square metre in the centre of fields and 43.4 ± 5.5 seeds/m2 on the headlands (Lopez-Antia et al. 2016). This was enough to provide, in an area between 6 and 50 m2, doses of six active ingredients above the median lethal level (LD50). Cereal seeds represented more than half the total mass of food consumed by partridges from October to February, and pesticide residues were found in a third of the crops and gizzards examined. Dressed seeds clearly represented a serious threat to partridges and other birds in Spain, where up to 30 species were seen consuming treated cereal seeds in recently sown fields. Comparable studies in Britain are needed.

The number of birds that die each year in Britain from direct pesticide poisoning could be greatly underestimated, especially for small birds such as Corn Buntings. Only if sizeable birds die in large numbers at a time are incidents likely to be reported, but not if they die in ones and twos across the country, even though they could add up to a large number in total. This would appear little different from natural everyday mortality, which is seldom noticed or recorded, mainly because carcasses in small numbers are quickly removed by scavengers. Bear in mind, too, that animals killed by poison are usually in good condition, and that confirmation is not simple. Standard veterinary laboratories are seldom equipped for the job, and carcasses must be sent to specialised laboratories to confirm the pesticide. Nevertheless, since the organochlorine era, direct mortality of birds is unlikely to be as high per unit area in Britain as in North America, where more highly toxic pesticides have been used over longer periods (Mineau 2002, 2005).

Sub-lethal effects

At sub-lethal levels, some pesticides have debilitating effects on birds and mammals, through their temporary influence on physiology or behaviour. These responses can in turn reduce an individual's reproductive success, or increase its susceptibility to death from some other cause, such as predation.

Probably the best-documented example of a sub-lethal effect leading to population decline is DDT-induced eggshell thinning among some predatory birds (Fig. 83). Other sub-lethal effects documented in captive birds include disruption of the nervous system, alteration of hormone levels, and impairment of immune function. Chemicals found to affect the endocrine system, especially in young individuals, include synthetic pyrethroids, organochlorines (DDT, BHC, dicofol, endosulphan and toxaphene), and the herbicide atrazine. All but the pyrethroids have now been banned in Britain, and they are probably no longer killing birds, despite small quantities persisting in the environment.

Carbamates and organophosphates kill animals by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which is involved in the transmission of nerve impulses. Studies on birds have shown that when cholinesterase activity drops below 50% of normal, behavioural and physiological irregularities become apparent, and as activity drops further, death becomes increasingly likely (Hill & Fleming 1982, Shimshoni et al. 2012). At sub-lethal levels, experimentally affected birds may show impairment of memory and learning, inability to thermoregulate properly, change in resting posture, tendency to hide in cover, and reduction in feeding and flying behaviour. They may recover within a few hours, but in the meantime they are more at risk than usual from predators. Similar responses occur in mammals, fish, reptiles and amphibians.

INDIRECT EFFECTS OF PESTICIDES ON BIRDS

These are due mainly to reductions in crucial food supplies (Sotherton & Holland 2002; Boatman et al. 2004; Morris et al. 2005). As mentioned earlier, problems arise largely because most pesticides kill a much wider range of organisms than the pests themselves. Most insecticides kill many kinds of invertebrates; some fungicides kill some invertebrates and remove the fungal food supplies of others; and herbicides may remove the food plants of some insects as well as the seeds eaten by granivorous birds. For example, cereal fields can hold 700–800 different insect species, only 10% of which may damage the crop, yet almost all these insects are typically removed by insecticide applications (Buckwell & Armstrong-Brown 2004). The widespread use of pesticides over many years has been associated with a massive and general reduction in the weed flora and insect fauna of the British countryside, and hence in the foods of birds. The use of pesticides is now so ubiquitous – usually with multiple applications per growing season – that insect populations over huge areas must be held permanently at much reduced levels, not only in the crops themselves but also in adjoining habitats to which the chemicals are carried by wind. The question of reduction in bird food supplies through pesticide use is taken up in greater detail in Chapter 10. It is probably the biggest cause of the recent population declines in a substantial proportion of farmland birds.

REDUCING THE IMPACTS OF PESTICIDES ON BIRDS

Almost certainly, far more pesticide has been used on British farmland over the years than was necessary for crop protection, as the following words from a farmer imply:

There are cases where spraying has become a yearly ritual, established partly because it is easier to spray than to have to decide whether weeds and other pests constitute a threat, and partly because out-of-season discounts encourage farmers to buy in advance before they have any real idea what the real problem is going to be. The third and equally dangerous side to this problem is vested interest. The majority of technical advice on spraying comes from advisors employed by the chemical manufacturers. These firms have to sell to survive, and so do their staff. Their advice is unlikely to be free of bias. (Wareing 1973)

These words were written in the 1970s, but in some respects the situation remains little changed. Open any farming magazine and you will see pages devoted to advertising one or other products of the big chemical companies, often with dire warnings of what might happen if the crop is left unsprayed. Following the ending of free independent advice to farmers (with the privatisation of the advisory service ADAS in 1997), the chemical companies are now in an even stronger position to dispense 'advice'. What has changed for the good, however, is the efficiency of sprayers, which can now deliver smaller quantities of chemical more directly to the target plants with minimal drift. The advent of precision treatment also allows the amount of pesticide or fertiliser released to be varied across a field, according to need. Pesticides are also relatively more expensive than they were, which presumably makes farmers more careful about how much they use.

Impacts on the invertebrate foods of birds can also be reduced by careful selection of the chemical to be used, and by less frequent and more careful timing of spraying. One obvious strategy is to select pesticides that destroy the pest species but only a minimum range of other invertebrates at the same time. For example, if aphids need to be controlled, aphid-specific chemicals such as pirimicarb have less overall impact on other organisms than do broad-spectrum compounds such as dimethoate (Ewald & Aebischer 1999). Care in the selective use of pesticides also reduces the impact of the spraying on beneficial insects such as aphid predators or bees. Pyrethroids in general seem to affect fewer insect groups than organophosphates, such as dimethoate.

Another obvious strategy is to spray, not as a routine preventative measure, but only if pest numbers exceed a certain threshold. Farmers now have the means to monitor the numbers of some pests, so they can then judge whether spraying is financially worthwhile, and when best to do it. Probably a large proportion of farmers now operate on this basis. 'Threshold spraying' is more difficult with fungal diseases, however, because most fungicides are preventative rather than curative, so they must be applied before the disease gets hold. Nevertheless, both fungal and pest outbreaks can often be predicted from weather and other conditions, which can avoid some unnecessary applications. Insect development depends largely on temperature so, with the help of weather forecasts, spraying can be timed to give maximum kill of the pest, and thus reduce the need for future sprays. Seed treatments have now become routine, but are also largely prophylactic, as they tend to be applied annually, regardless of levels of risk. Farmers buy the seeds already dressed, which can only increase the use of the chemicals involved.

Some farmers now practise integrated pest management (IPM), which aims to reduce pesticide applications to a minimum and support natural predatory arthropods, such as earwigs, anthocorid bugs, ladybirds and spiders. In sufficient abundance, such predators can control pest numbers and prevent outbreaks. Supporting them entails ensuring that some of their habitat, such as hedgerows and other field boundaries, remains pesticide-free in order to provide refuges for them in the periods between successive crops. Current agri-environment subsidies support various means of reducing pesticide applications and setting aside parts of the farm which can remain free from their use (Chapter 20).

Insecticides sprayed in spring (March–June) have a more damaging effect on the insects available to birds in the breeding season than those applied at other times. The most important insect groups for birds are largely absent from arable fields in winter and do not become established there before spring, when they are removed by any insecticides applied. Similarly, herbicides sprayed on cereal fields early in the growth of a crop have less effect on weed growth in the subsequent stubble than do herbicides sprayed later in the growth of the crop or after harvest.

The overuse of pesticides cannot be blamed entirely on farmers and salesmen. Much of the spraying of fruit and vegetables is done because of customer demands for fruit and vegetables that are free from insects and from insect and fungal blemishes.

OTHER PROBLEMS

In addition to the general depression of bird food supplies on farmland, other chemically induced problems have developed in recent decades.

Deliberate poisoning of raptors

In parts of Britain, mainly on game-rearing estates, birds of prey are often killed illegally with poison baits. Typically, gamekeepers apply the poison to carcasses of Rabbits or other meat-baits which they then lay out for raptors and other scavengers to find and eat. Habitual carrion feeders, such as Golden Eagle, Buzzard and Red Kite, are especially vulnerable, but almost any raptor species can be killed in this way, as can corvids, gulls and other scavengers. Over the years, various poisons have been used for this purpose, including strychnine, the narcotic alpha-chlorolose, the organophosphate phosdrin (or mevinphos), and various other pesticides, the current favourite being the carbamate, carbofuran. Such illegal use of poisons is almost certainly a major factor restricting the numbers and distributions of Red Kites and Golden Eagles in Britain, but every year it also kills large numbers of Buzzards, Goshawks and others (Newton 2013a).

Incidental poisoning of owls and raptors by rodenticides

Rodents can cause serious damage to grain and stored food on farms, and traditionally they were controlled using traps, cats and terriers, with help from wild predators such as Barn Owls (Chapter 7). Strychnine was a frequently used poison, but from 1949 some anticoagulant rodenticides came into wide use, the most popular being warfarin. These chemicals disrupt the vitamin K cycle and thereby reduce the production of blood-clotting agents, ultimately causing death by internal bleeding. However, in little more than a decade of widespread use, rats and mice in several areas became resistant to warfarin and similar products, and this resistance gradually spread over most of the country. From the 1980s, these early rodenticides were therefore largely replaced by newer compounds, such as difenacoum, bromadiolone, brodifacoum and flocoumafen. These 'second-generation' or 'single-feed' rodenticides act in the same way as warfarin, but they are more toxic and more persistent, giving rise to secondary poisoning of rodent predators (Newton & Wyllie 2002). As with warfarin, it may take several days for a poisoned rodent to die, during which time it can be caught and eaten by a predator. If the rodent is resistant to the poison in question, it can remain as a mobile 'poisoned bait' for even longer.

FIG 87. The Barn Owl Tyto alba is afrequent victim of rodenticide use in Britain, through eating contaminated rats and mice (Andrew Everitt).

Barn Owls killed by second-generation rodenticides have frequently been found in Britain since the 1980s, many showing typical symptoms of haemorrhaging. In one study, Barn Owls found dead were requested for analysis, regardless of how they had died. Among 836 owl carcasses examined over the period 1983–98, rodenticide residues were found in 28% overall, but the proportion increased over the years from 5% in 1983–84 to 40% in 1997–98, as these compounds came into wider use. However, only 7% of the contaminated owls (or 2% of the overall sample) were judged on postmortem symptoms and residue levels to have died from rodenticide poisoning (Newton et al. 1999, Newton & Wyllie 2002). This mortality seemed insufficient to have caused widespread population declines of Barn Owls in Britain, in contrast to the situation in some other parts of the world (Duckett 1984). This situation may change, however, if rodenticide use increases further in Britain.

Residues of second-generation rodenticides have also been found in many other birds of prey, including Buzzard, Goshawk, Kestrel, Red Kite, Little Owl and Tawny Owl. All these birds feed at least partly by scavenging, and would take any dead rodents they find. Like Barn Owls, Red Kites feed around farm buildings, as well as in the open countryside, so are especially likely to come across poisoned rats and mice. Among numbers of Kestrels and Red Kites found dead in Britain and analysed using the latest sensitive equipment, more than 70% contained rodenticide residues (Shore et al. 2015).

FIG 88. Red Kite Milvus milvus, another frequent victim of rodenticide poisoning (Peter Beasley).

A survey in 1997 suggested that one or more rodenticides were used on around four-fifths of all farms in Britain. In some woodland areas rodenticides were used for control of Grey Squirrels, and on some game-rearing estates they were used around Pheasant pens in woodland (McDonald & Harris 2000). The increasing use of these chemicals could result in many other rodents being contaminated, threatening a wider range of predatory and scavenging birds. Mammalian predators have also become widely contaminated, including Hedgehogs, Stoats, Weasels, Polecats and Foxes (Shore et al. 2015). The more potent of these chemicals (brodifacoum and flocoumafen) are allowed for use only in buildings or sewers, but if they were approved also for outside use – for which there is continuing pressure – they could kill much greater numbers of Barn Owls, Kestrels, Red Kites and other species. There is already considerable misuse.

Other types of poisons are used legally in the countryside to control Moles and Rabbits, but for these animals the poison is placed in their underground burrows, and to my knowledge, no effects on birds have been reported.

In other parts of the world, such as the oil palm plantations of the Far East, and the farmlands and date palm plantations of Israel, rodenticides have been replaced by Barn Owls as agents of rat control (Duckett 1984, Meyrom et al. 2009). Rodenticides are expensive, they kill non-target animals including predators of rodents, and eventually rodents become resistant to them, causing even bigger problems. However, Barn Owls feed almost entirely on rodents, and remain as effective predators even at low rat densities. In most of the farmlands and plantations involved, natural nest sites are scarce or non-existent, but Barn Owls take readily to any nest-boxes provided. This has proved a much cheaper and sustainable solution to the problem of rodent control, and as nest-box schemes increased in Israel, sales of rodenticides fell, crop damage declined and profitability increased. So satisfactory was this solution to crop damage that in recent years sales of anticoagulant rodenticides were banned, thus eliminating the poisoning of other wildlife, including storks and raptors. This could be one of the most successful known attempts at biological pest control, because the predator is more effective than chemicals, and causes no significant damage to other wildlife.

Kestrels also feed on rodents and nest in boxes, but in Israel they proved less effective than Barn Owls at controlling rodents. This was because, at low rodent densities, Kestrels switched to other prey, such as insects or birds, whereas Barn Owls continued to concentrate on rodents, preventing their numbers from rising. If rodent numbers increased rapidly, Barn Owls could respond more effectively, raising up to two large broods of 8–10 young per year, whereas Kestrels could raise only a single brood of 4–6 chicks (Meyrom et al. 2009, Y. Leshem in litt.)

Veterinary products

Some veterinary products also cause problems for wildlife. The most serious in Britain are the anthelmintics which are fed to farm animals to destroy parasitic worms in the gut. Among these compounds, the most widely used are the avermectins, particularly ivermectin, introduced in 1981 (Wall & Strong 1987). After dosing, livestock can excrete these persistent chemicals over a period of four or more weeks in their faeces, thereby affecting most of the insects that would normally feed on the dung, together with other invertebrates in the soil below, including earthworms (McCracken 1988, Madsen et al. 1990, McCracken & Foster 1994, Edwards 2004). Dung flies and dung beetles are major casualties. These insects had previously provided a food source for birds, particularly wagtails and corvids, but this source is now much reduced on British farmland. One incidental consequence is that cowpats, which in the past disappeared within weeks, can now remain in the fields for months. Newer compounds used as replacements for avermectins have similar effects. In an experimental study, ivermectin administered in the form of a sustained-release bolus was found to kill dung beetle larvae for approximately 143 days after treatment (Errouissi et al. 2001). Even where cattle are housed year-round in sheds or yards, soil-dwelling invertebrates are not totally protected from anthelmintics, which, being present in slurry or manure, may be repeatedly spread on the fields.

FIG 89. The numbers of various dung-feeding insects have been much reduced by anthelmintic drenches used to control parasitic worms in the guts of cattle and sheep: left, dung flies attracted to fresh cowpat; right, Pied Wagtail Motacilla alba, which often catches and eats these flies (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

The impact of this loss of food on birds has been little studied. However, in one study on the Solway made before anthelmintic drugs came into use, insects associated with dung formed more than 80% of the diets of adult and young waders (Rankin 1979). The abundance of dung-related flies in different areas was correlated with the densities of cowpats (but so was the proportion of eggs and chicks that were trampled by cattle). In addition, in the Chough, for which invertebrates in cow dung are particularly important, breeding success and juvenile survival were reduced in areas where ivermectin was used (McCracken 1993, McCracken et al. 1995). For other birds, use of these chemicals adds to other reductions in food caused by pesticides. Organic farms had significantly greater dung-beetle biomass and species richness than conventional farms (Hutton & Giller 2003). In any case, with some effort, steps can be taken to reduce ivermectin use without ill effects. For one thing, most parasitic worms are host-specific, so their life cycles can be broken by alternating cattle and sheep in a field. In addition, the monitoring of parasite egg numbers in the faeces of livestock, the avoidance of overstocking, and the judicious use of clean grazing all help to avoid unnecessary treatments. Anthelmintics have also become a standard part of Red Grouse management, and are usually fed to the birds as 'medicated grit' to rid them of strongyle parasites, but no side effects on other species have yet been identified.

Elsewhere, other veterinary products have had more direct effects on birds. By far the most significant are the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which are frequently fed to sick cattle, especially in the Indian subcontinent. Being sacred animals to Hindus, cattle are usually left to die natural deaths, when they become available to vultures. These birds can thereby acquire the drug, and as a result usually die within days. The most common symptom seen in dead vultures is a deposit of white uric acid crystals among the viscera, a condition known as 'visceral gout'. The large Gyps vultures are especially susceptible, suffering huge and widespread mortality. In consequence, the vulture population of the subcontinent became reduced by more than 99% over a 15-year period. At least three species were affected, and are now at perilously low levels, namely the White-backed Vulture, Slender-billed Vulture and Long-billed Vulture (Oaks et al. 2004, Newton 2013b). The main drug responsible was diclofenac (sold for human use in Britain under the name Voltarol), but other similar drugs, such as ketoprofen, have also been implicated. Occasional individuals of other raptors have been found dead from the same cause. The birds seem much less susceptible to a similar drug called meloxicam, which it is hoped will gradually replace the lethal ones, allowing vultures to recover. There are several other less widely used chemicals in this group, however, and it remains to be discovered which are toxic to raptors and which are not.

In 2013, nine years after the toxicity of diclofenac to vultures was discovered, diclofenac was approved for veterinary use in Spain and Italy. These countries hold over 80% of the European breeding population of the Eurasian Griffon Vulture, one of the species in which the toxicity of diclofenac has been demonstrated experimentally. These examples involving veterinary drugs offer a stark warning of the need for careful evaluation of the likely impacts of pharmaceuticals in the wider environment before they are passed for general use.

Risks to people

In addition to their impacts on biodiversity, some pesticides in the process of normal use present risks to farm workers, and to the general public through spray drift and contamination of food. These problems have lessened over the years, partly because some of the more toxic chemicals have been withdrawn, but also because farm workers are better protected than in the past, cocooned within their tractor cabs. The biggest known problems in recent decades have been caused by organophosphate pesticides, especially when used in sheep-dips. Some sheep farmers may have died as a result of contact with these chemicals, and hundreds of others have suffered lasting neurological and other health problems. For years official bodies and industry denied the connection, but in 1993 MAFF finally accepted that at least 529 cases of long-term human illness were related to sheep-dips, and since then the numbers have grown. Other unofficial estimates put the number as high as 6,000. Largely as a result of this issue, the dipping of sheep ceased to be compulsory in Britain. Here the Health and Safety Executive is ultimately responsible for regulating pesticide use, for overseeing the introduction and use of particular compounds, and for making recommendations on the way they are used. The primary aim is to reduce the risks to human health, but resulting restrictions are likely also to benefit wildlife. Nevertheless, the subsequent use of pesticides still depends on the good sense, skills and decisions of individual farmers.

DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS

Pesticides were originally developed 'in good faith' to enhance crop production, and in ignorance of their environmental impacts. There is no doubt that they have increased crop yields, and it is an unanswered question whether the rapidly expanding human population could have been supported at its current level without them. Nevertheless, widespread monitoring of bird populations, followed by appropriate research and experiment, has played a crucial role in highlighting some of the long-term consequences of pesticide use and in confirming pesticides as a major factor in reducing not just pest numbers but the entire spectrum of wild plants and animals in farmed landscapes (and beyond, in the case of organochlorines). Moreover, pesticides have had a far greater impact than the direct and indirect effects on birds discussed above, for they are central to the kinds of farming now practised throughout the lowlands of Britain and beyond (Shrubb 2003). Without an ability to control competitive weeds, insect pests and disease, more traditional forms of mixed farming would have had to be retained, and with them much greater diversity in the plants and animals of farmland, of which bird populations are just a part. The current specialisation in farming is therefore to a large extent a direct development from agrochemical use, both pesticides and fertilisers.

Looking back, the organochlorine episode had a big impact on the perception of pesticides by the general public. It highlighted for the first time the potentially severe environmental consequences that could result from the widespread use of chemicals, hitherto regarded by most people as wholly beneficial. The effects of DDT were not apparent immediately, but only after several years, and could not have been predicted by the testing procedures in operation at the time. They provided an early example of a genuine and well-documented global pollution problem, on a scale that we now take for granted. They led to wide debate on the value of circumstantial (correlative) versus experimental evidence, for at first the case against the organochlorines rested entirely on correlations, a point exploited to the full by the agricultural and agrochemical lobbies. This in turn led to the suggestion that the precautionary principle should be applied to pesticides, and that no new pesticide should be widely used until its potential effects were understood. This appreciation led to an overhaul in the procedures required for testing pesticides before they were cleared for general use. The system still has problems, however, not least because decisions depend on the attitudes of the arbiters concerned, and the extent to which they yield to pressures from vested interests.

Following the organochlorines, each major new group of chemicals has had some substantial impact on the natural world, often unpredicted despite aspects such as toxicity and persistence being tested beforehand. It is clearly difficult to predict all the environmental impacts that different chemicals might have, and which wildlife species are likely to be most vulnerable. Who could have guessed, for example, that vultures could have been brought to the brink of extinction by one particular group of drugs, widely and safely used on domestic animals and people? However thoroughly pesticides or drugs are tested beforehand on a limited number of organisms, we cannot necessarily predict their effects on others unrelated to the test species. Nor can we be sure how much predicted collateral damage regulating authorities will let through at different times as 'acceptable risk'. Only careful monitoring and study of wild populations can reveal such effects, as is the case now with the neonicotinoids. Encouragingly, though, the events of recent decades have confirmed that, if remedial action is taken and the offending chemicals are withdrawn, any remnant populations can and do respond by recovery. In other words, reducing or otherwise controlling the use of the more hazardous chemicals can rapidly restore measurable conservation benefits. The illicit use of pesticides for the wrong purposes, as by game managers, is a different matter. Prohibition requires much stronger enforcement of existing legislation and much heavier penalties for the offending landowners, as well as their gamekeepers. But the poisoned baits have still to be found and reported, and prosecutions secured.

Problems with testing and regulatory procedures

Reading this account of their impacts, you may well wonder why some of the chemicals concerned were ever cleared for widespread use. In practice, testing procedures for pesticides, on which decisions on the use of new products are based, have their limitations. For one thing, they are concerned only with lethal effects, and ignore sub-lethal effects which could predispose animals to deaths from other causes. Secondly, each new chemical is necessarily tested on only a small range of animals, and this procedure cannot allow for any differences between species in sensitivity. Most of the direct effects on birds have emerged only after the chemicals concerned came into wide use, reaching a bigger range of species. Thirdly, because in laboratory conditions some pesticides, such as diazinon, appear distasteful, it has often been assumed that birds in the wild would avoid them. This is not always so, however, and thousands of geese and other species have grazed their way to an early death on turf treated with diazinon (Mineau & Palmer 2013). Moreover, all animals on farmland are simultaneously exposed to some dozens of different agrochemicals, some of which act synergistically, with one enhancing the toxicity of another. The impact of chronic exposure to these chemical cocktails is not addressed by regulatory authorities and is poorly understood.

Generally speaking, the removal of non-target insects from crop fields is seldom seen as a matter of serious concern by regulators, and is not considered in registration reviews – whether in the EU or elsewhere. Moreover, it is sometimes difficult to establish unequivocally the link between the pesticide-induced declines in insect populations and the declines in bird populations that feed on those insects (despite some confirmed cases). Nevertheless, dramatic losses of insects from the countryside cannot fail to have had wider consequences, as in the many bird species that depend to varying degrees on the spring–summer flush of insect food to raise their young, or in the many plants (including crops) that require insects for their pollination. Over the past half-century, it took an average of 8–10 years for regulatory authorities to ban a pesticide after harmful environmental effects were first documented (Potts 2012).

Although studies of bird populations have played a crucial role in highlighting some of the long-term consequences of pesticide use, the number of well-documented case studies of indirect effects is limited (Chapter 10). This is because declines in bird numbers have mostly been gradual, and in recent years have seldom involved conspicuous large-scale kills. In addition, the effects of pesticides have sometimes proved hard to disentangle retrospectively from those of other procedural changes. Nevertheless, it is noticeable how many farmland bird species began declining in the 1970s, a period of substantial increase in herbicide use, and other species in the 1980s, a period of substantial increase in insecticide and fungicide use.

## CHAPTER 9

## Arable Land: Management and Birds

ARABLE FARMING INVOLVES replacing more permanent vegetation with a short-lived crop. The land must be cleared and cultivated, and the crop must be sown, grown and eventually harvested. Between the harvest of one crop and the planting of the next, the ground can be bare for days, weeks or months each year. Most crops are sown as monocultures which can complete their life cycles from germination to harvest in a matter of months. During its growth, the crop is nourished by manure or fertilisers, and is protected against competition from weeds and against damage from pests and diseases – nowadays mainly by pesticides. The crop is then harvested for its seeds, leaves or roots, as the case may be, after which the land is prepared for the next crop, usually of a different species. The fields in which arable crops are grown are thus subject to continual change. The periodic bareness of the ground (Fig. 90), the short life of the plants, and the contrived monocultures are all features which differentiate arable land from most natural or semi-natural habitats.

FIG 90. Fertiliser spreading and preparing a tilth on good-quality arable land, which is usually devoid of vegetative cover for part of each year (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Arable land now covers around 4.6 million hectares in Britain, about one-fifth of the total land area (Box 2, Carey et al. 2008). It is the most intensively managed of all farmland, receiving the highest inputs of agrochemicals. Most arable land in Britain is on the eastern side, where soils are generally more productive than further west, and the weather is warmer and drier, allowing the ground to be ploughed more easily and grain crops to ripen more readily (Chapter 5). The current dominant crops are cereals, altogether covering more than 3.1 million hectares, with oilseed rape on 0.67 million hectares, and a variety of other crops on the remainder.

Because of their simplicity as same-age monocultures, farm crops are inherently able to support only a narrow range of animal species, but some of these can periodically increase to become serious pests or disease agents, reducing the yield. Such outbreaks of specific organisms occur much more often in arable crops than in more diverse natural plant communities where most organisms have a more limited food-base and their own predators and diseases readily on hand to control them. Grown over large areas, monoculture crops are thus liable to turn previously inconspicuous arthropod species into serious overabundant pests.

Superimposed on the natural seasonal rhythms of growth and dormancy is a regular routine of farm operations through the year. Broadly speaking, this begins with spring ploughing and sowing, followed after a break by the harvest of silage or hay, peas and beans, then rape and cereals, followed by the autumn clearing operations, ploughing and sowing for the following year, and the harvesting of potatoes and other root crops. The timing of these operations varies with region, soil and weather, as well as with crop type.

All these operations offer specific feeding opportunities for birds. In particular, soil tilling brings soil-dwelling invertebrates and buried seeds to the surface, while harvesting clears dense stands of herbage, and makes previously hidden seeds, invertebrates and small mammals available to birds. Mixed farms provide the best seasonal spread of feeding opportunities for birds through the year, because different foods become available at different times, and operations occur close enough together for the same birds to move easily from field to field as needed. In contrast, specialised cereal farms tend to provide little activity for much of the year between sowing and harvest, and no short-grass pasture as alternative feeding areas. Birds quickly learn to associate farm work with food, and some species, such as gulls, seem to investigate any machine operating in a field at whatever time of year.

The main foods available to birds on arable land derive from the crops and their associated weeds, and from the insects and other invertebrates obtained from the soil or gleaned from the vegetation (including crop pests). However, modern crop management using pesticides generally destroys a large proportion of the wild plants and invertebrates that would otherwise occur on arable land, thus reducing most of the foods eaten by the majority of farmland birds. In addition, the eggs and chicks of ground-nesting birds breeding within the crops are at continual risk of destruction from agricultural operations.

BIRDS OF ARABLE LAND

The birds that feed on arable land can be divided into two broad categories: those which both nest and feed on the ground among the crops, and those which nest elsewhere but obtain their food from among the crops. The first category involves only a small number of species, most of which are now localised in distribution, namely the Skylark, Yellow Wagtail, Corn Bunting, Lapwing, Ringed Plover, Oystercatcher, Stone-curlew, Grey and Red-legged Partridges, Quail, Marsh and Montagu's Harriers and the extremely localised Great Bustard (formerly widespread but now nesting only in small numbers resulting from a reintroduction programme). In parts of Europe, Hen Harriers also nest in cereal fields, and may have done so in Britain when they were much more widely distributed than today, although I know of no firm evidence. All these birds tend to be most at home in the open fields, and some avoid areas near to trees, hedgerows, buildings or overhead wires. Some of them, notably the Lapwing and Stone-curlew, prefer to nest on bare or sparsely vegetated ground which gives a good all-round view, while others usually hide their nests in vegetation. All these birds are vulnerable to agricultural operations, such as ploughing, rolling, harrowing or harvesting. Spraying is physically less damaging because the tractor wheels run over a relatively small part of the field, leaving nests elsewhere undamaged (but see Chapter 10).

The second category, consisting of birds which feed on arable land but nest in trees, bushes or buildings, or in association with water, contains many more species, which are much less vulnerable to physical operations. On a regular basis, this group includes at least four species of corvids, eight finches, two buntings, two sparrows, two wagtails, three thrushes, Starling, three owls, four pigeons and doves, five gulls, six raptors, three geese, one swan and three ducks, plus many other species occasionally. Added to the ground-nesting species above, this gives at least 60 species which regularly feed on arable land in the breeding season (Table 1). Some other species occur on farmland in Britain only or chiefly in winter, increasing the number of thrush species seen on arable land to five, geese to eight, and swans to three (Table 2). Because food supplies are often short-lived on arable land, but occur locally in large amounts, many bird species occur on farmland in sizeable flocks, which can change in location from day to day or week to week, depending on changes in feeding conditions. Nevertheless, some species, notably geese, gulls and waders, have favoured fields which they use year after year. These tend to be large fields offering good all-round visibility.

FIG 91. Four uncommon waders of arable land nest on areas of bare soil or short growing crops, and avoid areas of dense taller vegetation. Upper left, Oystercatcher Haematopus ostralegus (Chris Knights); upper right, Stone-curlew Burhinus oedicnemus (Chris Knights); lower left, Ringed Plover Charadrius hiaticula (Bobby Smith); lower right, Little Ringed Plover Charadrius dubius (Chris Knights). The last two species are the most localised on farmland.

FIG 92. The Quail Coturnix coturnix was once a common bird of hayfields, but now nests in much reduced numbers mainly in cereal fields, and in numbers that vary greatly from year to year (Lior Kislev).

FIG 93. Two species which obtain almost all their food from arable land, the Corn Bunting Emberiza calandra (left) and Turtle Dove Streptopelia turtur (above), have now disappeared from much of their former range in Britain (Chris Knights).

Only two species in Britain seem to obtain almost all their food from arable land, namely the Corn Bunting and Turtle Dove. All the other species mentioned above also feed frequently in other habitats, such as grassland or heathland. However, many others feed mainly on arable land for at least part of the year, and several are most numerous in those parts of Britain with the most arable land. This holds especially for seed-eaters, such as Yellowhammer, Linnet, Tree Sparrow and Skylark (Fuller et al. 1997, Kyrkos et al. 1998, Robinson et al. 2001).

Among the 60 regular arable land species listed above, at least 25 have declined substantially in recent decades. Since 1970, the Corn Bunting, Tree Sparrow, Turtle Dove and Grey Partridge have declined by more than 90%, the Starling by more than 80%, and the Lapwing, Little Owl, Skylark, Yellow Wagtail, House Sparrow and Linnet by more than 60% (Table 3). Other rarer species, notably Stone-curlew and Montagu's Harrier, have maintained or increased their numbers on farmland only because of interventions to save their eggs and young from agricultural operations, while Cirl Buntings have benefited from other conservation measures (Davies et al. 2011, Chapter 21). Some of the most notable increases of farmland birds in recent decades have involved geese and swans which feed on the nutritious leaves of cultivated grasses and cereals and on grains of cereals and remains of harvested root crops. Other increasing species include the Woodpigeon and Stock Dove, which have benefited from the increased acreage of oilseed rape. Carrion Crows, Jackdaws and Magpies have also benefited from generally increased food supplies and reduced human persecution (Chapter 2).

FIG 94. Two pigeons have increased greatly in Britain since the 1970s when new varieties of rape began to be planted on a large scale, providing nutritious winter food: left, Stock Dove Columba oenas (Keith Kirk); right, Woodpigeon C. palumbus (Edmund Fellowes).

The challenge of life on arable land

Organisms inhabiting arable farmland must be able to survive the regular disturbance caused by the seasonal cycle of cultivation and harvest. Many invertebrates are killed by these processes, so in order to persist as self-sustaining populations, such species must be able to reproduce, or complete their life cycles, between successive lethal operations, say between sowing and harvest. This is also true of ground-nesting bird species, which must be able to nest successfully during a particular growth stage of the crop (say, before it grows too tall), or between successive destructive operations, such as ploughing and planting. Rearing a brood within an appropriate but undisturbed growth period is a major constraint for most ground-nesting birds on modern arable land. This is especially so for species that rear their young in the nest (such as Skylark and Corn Bunting), because they are tied to specific locations for longish periods, about 6–7 weeks from nest-building to independence of young. Some birds with mobile young (such as Lapwing) can lead their young after hatch to a different habitat, and thereby avoid some damaging operations. The Grey Partridge has mobile young, but has such a large clutch (up to 20 eggs) that the time from laying the first egg to hatching is as long as the whole breeding cycle of smaller birds (although most Partridges nest in field boundaries rather than in the crop). Because of routine farming practices, nest failure rates therefore tend to be high among ground-nesting birds on arable land (for Lapwing see Shrubb 1990, for Skylark see Donald 2004), and in some species persistent poor breeding has been a major contributor to recent population declines (Chapter 2). A propensity to lay another clutch after failure of an earlier nest is a clear advantage, but does not always end in success. Lapwings have been known to produce up to five clutches in a season without hatching a single egg (Klomp 1951). Rearing chicks can also be hazardous, but once the young can fly, they can more readily escape from moving machinery. Single-brooded species, such as the Lapwing, normally lay a repeat clutch only if the previous nest failed at an early stage, and not if it survived until late in incubation. Naturally multi-brooded species, such as Skylark, can raise more than one brood in a season, but may still lose some attempts to farm operations, as well as to predation and other natural hazards. In other words, whatever the species, producing enough young to sustain population levels is a constant challenge for ground-nesting birds on arable land.

BOX 9. The Great Bustard Otis tarda: an early casualty of agricultural change in Britain

The Great Bustard may have been the first bird species to become extinct in Britain mainly through agricultural change. It nested from some southern counties in England northward at least into Yorkshire and possibly into Berwickshire, mainly on open downs, wolds and arable land. The last recorded nest was on Thetford Warren (Suffolk) in 1832, although birds were seen in various areas for another decade or more. Its demise has been attributed to a combination of changing agriculture and human predation (Waters & Waters 2005). The enclosures rendered some previously wide open habitat hedged and unsuitable, and the development and widespread adoption of the seed-drill made nests unsafe. When grain was broadcast by hand, it was impossible to weed, so crops were left undisturbed until harvest. They formed the favoured nesting habitat of bustards, which laid their 2–3 large eggs in a scrape in the ground, safe and hidden. But once the grain was sown in rows, hand-hoeing to remove weeds became routine. Previously safe clutches were destroyed accidentally or taken for human consumption. Over the same period, improvements in firearms increased the ease with which the adults could be killed for the table. These various developments spelt the end in Britain of the Great Bustard – our largest farmland bird. Time will tell whether the current reintroduction project on Salisbury Plain succeeds in re-establishing a self-sustaining population.

FIG 95. Great Bustards Otis tarda on farmland (Chris Knights).

CHANGES IN ARABLE FARMING

As a reminder from previous chapters, the main changes on arable land during the 20th century included: (1) an increase in the total area of arable land in Britain from around 2.8 million hectares in 1938 (just pre-war) to around 5 million hectares into the 1980s, followed by a decline to 4.6 million hectares in recent years, most of the net increase being achieved though conversion of grassland; (2) a decline in mixed farming, with an increasing specialisation on crop production without livestock; (3) changes in the proportions of different crops that were grown, including declines in oats and fodder roots and an increase in rape; (4) enlargement of fields through removal of hedges and other semi-natural areas; (5) increasing use of fertilisers and decreasing use of manure; (6) increasing use of pesticides, as discussed in the previous chapter; (7) the change from mainly spring-sown to mainly autumn-sown crops, to be discussed in the next chapter.

Decline of mixed farms

This has been one of the most significant agricultural changes since the mid-20th century, as more and more farmers came to specialise in either arable or livestock production (Chapter 4). Traditionally, almost all lowland farms in Britain produced both crops and livestock as an integrated whole. Animal manure was used for fertilising arable crops and horses were needed to pull machinery. In crop rotations, legumes were used to maintain soil fertility and under-sown leys were used to produce fresh grazing following crops, some of which (such as oats and fodder roots) were grown as animal feed.

Several developments underpinned the change from mixed to specialised farms (Chapter 4). The arrival of tractors and inorganic fertilisers meant that arable production could for the first time be freed from livestock and the particular crops needed to feed them. It then became more efficient to concentrate on either arable or livestock in a single enterprise. Over much of Britain, farming thereby became less diverse, not just at the level of the individual holding, but across the country, as arable farming came even more to dominate in the east and livestock grassland in the west and north, fitting the geographical patterns in soil type, topography and climate. Only in northern Scotland do mixed farms still prevail.

Changes in crop rotations

In the past, crop rotation was widely practised as a means of limiting the weeds and pests associated with particular crops and of maintaining soil fertility. But rotation became less necessary following the development of agrochemicals. Fertilisers replaced legume crops and manure in maintaining soil fertility, and pesticides controlled the various weeds, pests and fungal diseases which previously might have risen to devastating levels if the same crop had been grown without break on the same ground. In these ways, agrochemicals largely did away with the need for traditional crop rotation, as well as for integrated crop and livestock production. Greater mechanisation also reduced the need to spread seasonal workloads, another factor important in traditional mixed farming. Nevertheless, on most arable farms, some measure of crop rotation has continued, with year-on-year cereal cropping being broken every third year or so with a broad-leaved crop, such as rape, beans or potatoes.

Fallow land

In earlier centuries, as part of the rotation, about a fourth or a third of arable land was left fallow for a whole year after harvest, and was therefore sparsely vegetated in spring. In this state, it attracted breeding birds such as Lapwings and Skylarks, and in some areas also Stone-curlews. There was no rolling or harrowing to destroy nests, and plant growth was slow so the habitat remained in a suitable sparsely vegetated state for nesting birds for much longer than cropped land. A major reduction in the area of annual fallow land in Britain occurred during the 18th century, when fodder roots replaced fallow years in crop rotations (Chapter 3). But during the 20th century, the fallow acreage was further reduced. In 1938, agricultural statistics record 146,595 ha of bare fallow in Britain, forming 5.2% of the arable acreage, but in 1970 there were 96,796 ha of bare fallow, only 2.3% of the arable acreage, declining further in subsequent years. However, the fallow area increased temporarily in the years of compulsory set-aside (1992–2007), when some land on every farm was left unplanted as a means of reducing crop surpluses (see later). This again provided prime nesting habitat for some open-land birds, such as Lapwing and Skylark.

Cropped land that lies bare overwinter attracts the same species of nesting birds as year-round fallow, especially Skylarks and Lapwings. These birds can often start nesting before the time of sowing, and although their nests are subsequently destroyed, they generally have time in spring-sown crops to make another attempt before the crop grows too tall. Such winter fallow greatly declined with the advent of autumn sowing, but it fluctuates in area from year to year according to weather, because a wet autumn can prevent ploughing, especially on heavy land.

Ecological consequences

As opposed to specialised arable or livestock farming, mixed farming provides a better environment for birds because most species need a mixture of arable and grassland, or a mixture of different arable crops, to supply their needs at different times. Birds can nest in one crop and gather food in another, or move from one crop to another during the course of a year. Rooks and other corvids rely on cereal grains in late summer and autumn and on invertebrates from freshly ploughed land or short grassland during the rest of the year. Ground-nesting Skylarks and Yellow Wagtails may switch from one crop to another for both nesting and foraging, raising early broods in one crop and later broods in another (Wilson et al. 1997, Gilroy et al. 2011); hedge-nesting Yellowhammers, Linnets and similar species move around, concentrating temporarily wherever food is abundant at the time (Stoate et al. 1998). Species whose young leave the nest soon after hatch may nest in one habitat, and then take their young to feed in another. For example, Lapwings frequently nest on spring-sown cereals, but take their young to more food-rich short-grass pastures, if they are available nearby (Galbraith 1988, Tucker et al. 1994); Stone-curlews nesting in spring-sown crops fly to nearby grazed pastures to collect food for their young.

It is the mixture of structural and feeding conditions continuously available in the same limited area that is important, allowing different birds to exploit different resources at different times, and thereby survive year-round in a constantly changing landscape. In addition, when almost every farm kept livestock, their food was grown, stored or bought into almost every farm. Grain-based foodstuffs often spilled and provided food for birds such as House Sparrows and Starlings, whether around the farmsteads or at feeding sites in the fields. But these foods ceased to be available on farms which shed their livestock. The specialisation in farming over recent decades has thus resulted in some sources of food that were once widely available becoming much more restricted in distribution.

FIG 96. Rooks Corvus frugilegus attracted by spilled grain on stubble fields during winter snow (Chris Knights).

The decline in mixed farms in eastern Britain has reduced the number of locations which offer a favourable combination of arable crops and pasture, or of different arable crops. Where birds live mainly in crop monocultures, they generally breed less well or for shorter periods each year (Chapter 10). Reduced reproductive output may have contributed to the population declines of some of these species. Nevertheless, the mobility of birds equips them well for exploiting sporadic food sources, such as invertebrates turned up by the plough or grain spilled at harvest. All these food sources are available temporarily at different times in different places, but in some places they may be available for only a day or two in great abundance.

Wider impacts of specialisation in farming on bird populations

Some bird species cannot persist in abundance through the year in an area that is either wholly grassland or wholly arable. Some have clearly responded to changes in the ratio between the two. For example, in the 1970s the optimum habitat for Rooks was found to be a mixture of arable crops and grassland (excluding rough grazing) in an approximate ratio of 45:55 (Brenchley 1984). Rook densities were lower in counties where the ratio of these two crop types shifted in either direction away from this optimum. In addition, between the national rookery surveys of 1944–46 and 1978, Rook numbers declined most strongly in counties where the grass/arable ratio had deviated most markedly from the optimum, as arable production expanded in the southeast and grassland in the north and west. Similarly, the breeding success of Rooks was greatest in areas where mixed farming was most frequent (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986).

For birds in general, the advantage of mixed over specialised farming became widely evident at the landscape scale (Atkinson et al. 2002). Bird counts in various plots scattered across the country showed that, in the breeding season, species were approximately twice as numerous in arable or mixed landscapes as in grassland ones. In winter, numbers in mixed landscapes increased further, while those in grassland landscapes declined. The number of species found in arable landscapes remained relatively stable year-round. These patterns were probably related to feeding requirements, as seed-eating birds tended to be most numerous in arable districts, which were more seed-rich, and invertebrate-eating species tended to be more numerous in mixed or pastoral districts, which were generally more invertebrate-rich. These findings again emphasised the importance of mixed habitats for farmland birds, particularly in winter.

Other factors affecting habitat diversity

Other changes over the past 60 years have also affected the structure of farmland. The number of farm holdings in Britain has fallen by about two-thirds since the 1950s, as smaller farms have been amalgamated into larger ones. This process has brought bigger areas under the management of single farmers, often with single-purpose aims. To accommodate bigger machines, fields were enlarged by removing hedgerows and other boundaries. This process improved the efficiency of operations, reduced the need for hedgerow maintenance and provided more ground for cropping. It was popular with farmers who no longer kept livestock, or who no longer kept livestock in fields. Remaining hedges tended to be cut shorter, and no longer needed to be stock-proof. Removal of field-boundaries was much more marked in eastern arable regions than in the pastoral districts of the north and west. Overall, however, at least half of all hedges and boundary habitats present on farmland in the 1950s were subsequently removed, greatly reducing the bird populations dependent on them (Chapter 18). In contrast to hedgerow-nesting birds, those of open land might be expected to benefit from hedge removal, but in practice their numbers became limited by other changes.

Uniformity was expanded further by a trend to grow the same crop in several already-enlarged fields next to one another (Fig. 97). This further reduced the time and manpower needed in management, but it increased the likelihood of pest outbreaks, so required good control (= pesticide use). It also vastly increased the monocultural nature of landscapes. For a time, whole farms in southeast England sometimes grew only a single crop, such as wheat or oilseed rape. This almost certainly led to more pest outbreaks developing, and to general declines in the diversity of insects found locally. For birds, too, large areas devoted to one crop would have limited foraging opportunities, especially in the nesting season, when adults need to feed close to their nests.

FIG 97. Block-cropping of oilseed rape. Sometimes farmers grow the same crop in adjacent fields, or even over the whole farm. This process increases the likelihood of pest outbreaks, so demands more pesticide use, and also reduces the diversity of foods available to birds (Ian Newton).

The importance of habitat diversity became evident in a number of studies which demonstrated higher breeding bird densities where the diversity of crop types was greater (Chamberlain et al. 1999a, 2000a). Even open-land species such as Skylarks nested at greatest density in places where 2–3 different crop types adjoined, a situation which allowed them to breed throughout the season, as crop structures changed (Schläpfer 1988, Jenny 1990). Under recent agricultural policy, farmland thus became less diverse at three main levels: the individual field, the individual farm and the landscape (Benton et al. 2003). This loss of heterogeneity was probably a major contributor to the declines of farmland birds and other wildlife, as well as to greater development of crop pests (Rusch et al. 2016).

Changes in crops

While areas of sugar beet, potatoes and legumes remained fairly stable over the years; the area under oats declined from around 36% in the 1930s to around 2% by the 1980s and beyond, mainly in association with the decline in horses. Fodder root crops, such as turnips, swedes and mangolds, fell from 9% in the 1930s to less than 2% in the 1960s, to around 1% in the 1980s, and even less subsequently. In 2010, less than 5,000 ha of turnips were grown nationwide. These root crops had been replaced as animal feed by silage, made mainly from grass but also from cereals. For a time (mid-1960s to late 1980s), barley became the commonest cereal in Britain, forming a basis for cattle feeds, but subsequently wheat took over as the most abundant cereal crop.

Since the 1980s, three arable crops – wheat, barley and oilseed rape – came to occupy more than three-quarters of all tilled land in Britain. The remaining crops of sugar beet, peas and beans, field vegetables and potatoes became largely concentrated in four counties in eastern England (Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk, Suffolk), with other major potato growing areas in eastern Scotland (Angus, Fife and East Lothian). However, following the development of new crop varieties and more effective husbandry, the yield per hectare of most arable crops increased greatly over the period concerned (Chapter 6).

Some of these changes in crop types were especially important for birds. For much of the 20th century, fodder roots were often full of weeds, which supported flocks of seed-eating finches well into winter, including Chaffinch and Brambling, Greenfinch, Linnet, Twite and Redpoll, as well as Tree Sparrow, Reed Bunting and Skylark. Root crops also provided food for leaf-eaters such as pigeons, and for species which feed on invertebrates such as plovers and thrushes. Other species, especially game birds, used root crops as a source of both food and cover, and in winter some invertebrate-feeders found food under the leaves of the crop, which gave some protection from frost. The leaves of tall brassicas, including kale and turnips, became a main winter food of Woodpigeons in snowy periods when lower plants were covered. Fodder root crops thus added several important food sources for a range of bird species. This is still the case in parts of northern Britain where turnips and swedes continue to be grown, although in progressively shrinking amounts. The decline in fodder root crops can only have brought a massive reduction of winter food supplies for birds, especially for seed-eaters.

In contrast, the area of oilseed rape increased from less than 1% of the arable acreage in 1970 to more than 18% in 2010. This is another useful plant for birds, because its leaves are eaten in winter by pigeons and other herbivorous species, and its seeds in summer by finches and other seed-eaters (Chapter 6). However, rape fields are usually ploughed soon after harvest, burying any seeds that remain on the surface. Only in northern Scotland are many rape fields left unploughed over winter, attracting flocks of small seed-eaters.

Reduction in the use of manure

Since the 1930s, inorganic fertilisers were increasingly used to promote crop growth, and by the 1980s, after a 20-fold increase, the average annual nitrogen input to arable land in Britain stood at 160 kg/ha per year, while much smaller amounts of phosphorus and potassium were also added. The loss of livestock from many arable regions meant that much less manure was used, greatly reducing the organic input to soil. This change is in turn likely to have greatly reduced the densities of soil-dwelling organisms dependent on humus, including the earthworms and other small creatures eaten by birds (Satchell 1955, Edwards & Bohlen 1996, Chapter 5). Organic input was not completely stopped, however, for cereals leave considerable residues to plough in, providing food for earthworms, while legumes decompose rapidly and leave little residue (Edwards & Bohlen 1996). Root crops, in which most of the crop is removed, tend also to support few earthworms, as do periods of fallow, which provide little humus.

Another activity which affected invertebrate numbers in arable soil was straw burning. As many farms in eastern Britain became wholly arable, they no longer needed straw for livestock bedding, and the easiest way to get rid of it was by burning in the field. For a period during the 1970s–90s, most wheat straw – more than 3 million tonnes per year – was burnt where it lay, and the atmosphere in arable districts was smoke-filled over several weeks each year. The flames destroyed a substantial proportion of seeds and invertebrates lying on the soil surface. Animals living beneath the surface were protected, but in the longer term they were presumably affected by the further reduction of organic input.

Straw burning was thus another factor which acted to reduce bird food supplies, but it also led to many accidental hedgerow fires. The drifting smoke led to road traffic accidents and to soot deposition on fruit and vegetable crops, freshly painted surfaces and clean clothes on washing lines. It did nothing for the popularity of farmers and, owing to public pressure, the practice was eventually banned. The straw was instead chopped and ploughed under, once again returning organic matter to the soil.

OTHER FARMING SYSTEMS

Organic Farming

So far, we have focused on conventional farming, as practised over most of Britain. But scattered among the majority of farms are some organic ones working to different principles. They aim to avoid the use of synthetic fertilisers or pesticides, to produce food of 'higher quality' free of pesticide residues, to manage the soil so as to maintain its organic content and minimise erosion, to avoid polluting the environment, and to manage semi-natural habitats sympathetically, working with wildlife rather than to its detriment. More attention also tends to be paid to animal welfare issues, particularly crowding, with antibiotics and other drugs used only when necessary, rather than as routine. Organic farming therefore relies largely on local resources and traditional methods, using crop rotations, manure and compost, and largely natural means of pest and disease control. In these respects, it resembles old-style traditional farming, having been defined as 'a production system that sustains the health of soils, ecosystems and people'. Organic farming is regulated in Britain by the Soil Association, which specifies those practices, methods of pest control, soil management and so on that are permissible if products are to achieve organic certification.

A series of studies over recent decades revealed that organic farms differed from conventional ones in many ways and not just agrochemical use. They were generally located in more diverse landscapes, and were often mixed rather than specialised, giving a level of structural and crop diversity which is now rare on conventional farms. They also tended to have more and bigger hedges and other uncropped areas (Norton et al. 2008, Feber et al. 2015). They put greater emphasis on spring-sown cereals, and often included grass–clover leys or other legume crops as part of a rotation. Not surprisingly, then, both native plants and animals were usually more plentiful on organic than on conventional farms. This was the case in both cropped and uncropped parts of the farm, albeit with big variation between farms. In one large survey, organic farms held an average of 30% more plant and animal species than conventional ones, many of them at much higher densities (Tuck et al. 2014). This difference has been maintained over at least 30 years, showing no sign of diminishing. Organic farms had greater effect on biodiversity as the proportion of arable in the surrounding landscape increased; in other words, their effect was greatest in the most intensively farmed regions.

Some groups of plants and animals responded more than others to organic farming. One of the main differences identified was in the weeds which are normally removed from conventional farms by herbicide use (Feber et al. 2015). The larger hedges and other uncropped areas on organic farms also supported greater numbers of wild plants, invertebrates and birds, both summer and winter (Piha et al. 2007, Kragten & de Snoo 2008, Chamberlain et al. 2009b).

Among open-land birds, Skylark nesting densities could be more than twice as high in organic cereal crops as in pesticide-treated crops, and in organic grassland up to five times as high as in intensive grassland (Wilson et al. 1997, Chamberlain et al. 1999b, Donald 2004). These differences were probably due to the greater densities of invertebrate food items found on organic farmland, along with the patchier less dense sward structure, which could provide nest sites throughout the breeding season. There were also longer intervals between cuts of organic grass silage, giving more opportunity than in conventional crops for nests to produce young.

Not every organic farm examined showed higher densities of all plant and animal groups, because other factors (such as location, isolation, soil type, field size and management) also played a role. For example, Skylark densities could be much lower on organic farms where the fields were small and enclosed by tall hedges, which Skylarks generally avoid, and their nest success could be lower in arable fields where weeds were controlled mechanically. Nevertheless, if organic farming became more widespread, it could help to restore some of the lost biodiversity across lowland Britain. In 2015, organic farms in Britain were estimated to cover around 521,000 ha, about 3% of the total farmed area (Defra 2016). The main limitation on their spread is their lower productivity: crop yields on organic farms can be around 20–25% lower than on conventional farms, and sometimes lower still (de Ponti et al. 2012, Seufert et al. 2012). To make a living, organic farmers rely on savings on agrochemicals and on higher returns from their crops, sold to people seeking pesticide-free produce but less concerned with blemishes. For feeding a population, however, organic production requires a correspondingly larger land area than conventional production to give the same amount of crop (or greater imports to make up the loss). It has received much less research than conventional farming (very little funded by government), so there may be more potential to raise its performance, particularly through better pest and disease control. From 1995, farmers could receive financial help to undergo the 2–5 year conversion process from conventional to organic, and receive additional annual payments for the environmental benefits (reduced pollution and enhanced biodiversity) that their methods deliver.

Integrated farm management

This is a name given to mixed livestock/arable farms which use a combination of old and new methods, and thus lie somewhere between traditional and modern farming. They aim to combine the best of the old with some of the new while maintaining or enhancing environmental benefits (Leake 2000). Crop rotations are designed to optimise weed, pest and disease control; biological and mechanical control methods are preferred over chemical ones, with pesticides used only as a last resort to avoid crop failures. Fertiliser inputs are based on crop requirements and soil analyses, and minimum tillage methods are used wherever suitable. As expected, bird populations do much better under this regime than under conventional management (see Chapter 21 for Titley Court Farm). An organisation called Linking Environment and Farming (LEAF) certifies integrated farming systems in the UK, and had 1,884 members in 2012.

Set-aside

By the 1980s, under the CAP, much more food was being produced than was needed, and the surplus could only be sold at a loss (Chapter 4). In order to limit crop production and reduce the storage costs and environmental damage, grant-aided set-aside was introduced in Britain from 1988, and became mandatory from 1992 to 2007. On this scheme, farmers were paid to leave a proportion of their land uncropped, either for one year (rotational set-aside) or for longer periods up to five years. Rotational set-aside had to be maintained unploughed between harvest and at least 15 July in the next year, although in the early years it was often treated with herbicide to prevent 'weeds' from seeding. Non-rotational set-aside was left untouched, and soon developed into rough grassland. While it lasted, the scheme provided stubble fields containing food for seed-eating birds over the first winter, and undisturbed nesting habitat for ground-nesting birds in spring (Thomas et al. 1996). All main groups of birds made use of it, and many occurred at higher density in set-aside than in winter cereals (Henderson et al. 2000, Firbank et al. 2003). Over the country as a whole, compulsory set-aside covered about 600,000 ha of arable land, forming about 10% of the whole arable area and second in area only to cereals.

Many studies assessed the value of set-aside to wildlife and how it could best be managed, as a result of which the rules on its management were changed from time to time. However, general features were that it should have some green cover (either regenerated naturally or sown), that it should receive no more than limited pesticide use, and that no crop should be taken (Donald 2004). An early regulation that the vegetation should be mowed in midsummer limited its usefulness for birds, and destroyed many nests. Easing of this regulation improved the situation for ground-nesting birds.

Many studies, summer and winter, revealed that most farmland birds occurred at higher densities on set-aside land than in cereals or rape. Set-aside emerged as an important nesting habitat for Skylarks, holding high densities through the breeding season, with no agricultural activities to destroy their nests. Nesting densities in eight different studies averaged 46 pairs per km2 (range 15–110 pairs per km2), compared with average densities on pastoral land of 18 pairs per km2, on arable land of 28 pairs per km2, and on mixed farmland of 22 pairs per km2 (Donald 2004). However, the way that set-aside was established and managed was crucial. The best type for Skylarks occurred when cereal stubbles were left unploughed and weeds were allowed to regenerate naturally. Skylarks benefited more from rotational set-aside, affecting different fields each year, than from non-rotational set-aside which was left in place for several years, allowing the vegetation to grow tall and rank. Skylarks nested most commonly in vegetation around 20 cm tall, with patches of bare ground to allow foraging (Henderson et al. 2001). Insects suitable as prey were more plentiful in set-aside fields than in cropped fields treated with pesticides. Skylarks also produced relatively large clutches in set-aside, and their breeding season was longer than in cereal crops, but their nest predation rates were still high (only one in five nests produced young). Nevertheless, a study in France estimated that, for Skylarks, set-aside was the most productive farmland habitat in terms of chicks produced per pair per year (Eraud & Boutin 2002). The total area of suitable set-aside in Britain was still too small to turn around the declining Skylark population nationally, but for a time it may have slowed the rate of decline. Other species found to nest at higher densities in first-year set-aside fields than in cropped fields include Grey Partridge and various waders (Watson & Rae 1997).

FIG 98. The Skylark Alauda arvensis was one of the main beneficiaries of first-year set-aside land, on which it nested at higher densities and with greater success than on most cropland. This juvenile was resting on nearby coastal gravel (Richard Chandler).

Set-aside land composed of cereal stubble with naturally regenerated green cover was used in winter by seed-eating birds (Buckingham et al. 1999). Five out of six declining species were found in significantly greater numbers on such set-aside areas than in farmland at large. This held over a wide geographical area, reinforcing other findings on the importance of stubble fields to seed-eating species (Chapter 10). The abolition of compulsory set-aside in 2007 caused a rapid loss of winter stubbles and other fallow land, suddenly reducing further the food of small seed-eating birds (Gillings et al. 2010).

By the time set-aside came in, harvesting procedures had become more efficient than formerly, and weeds were effectively controlled by herbicides. Far fewer seeds were therefore available on stubbles than in earlier times. Also, most of the cereal grain remaining on field surfaces was of autumn-germinating varieties, and these began to grow soon after harvest, reducing even further the value of set-aside for winter food. Nevertheless, some weeds developed in suitable autumn weather, depending largely on the level of weed control in the preceding crop. However, in the early years many farmers sprayed off any weeds growing on rotational set-aside after 15 April. This soon removed any associated seeds and insects, at a time when many birds were nesting.
