However, many other feeding opportunities had increased for Rooks over that period, including refuse dumps, outdoor piggeries, game-bird feed sites, roadside carrion and garden bird-feeders. Similar widespread increases in Carrion Crows and Jackdaws are implied by BTO monitoring schemes, and these species exploit many of the same food sources. However, more recent BBS data suggest that Rooks have declined considerably since the end of the 20th century.

FIG 133. Slurry spreading on a cattle farm, south Scotland (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

FIG 134. Corvids on grassland: left, Rook Corvus frugilegus (Richard Chandler); right, Jackdaws Corvis monedula (Richard Chandler).

LIVESTOCK AND NEST TRAMPLING

More intensive grassland management allowed more livestock to be fed on a decreasing area. This had a further crucial impact on ground-nesting birds in pasture by increasing the proportion of nests or chicks lost to trampling, as found mainly in studies of waders (Green 1986b, 1988a, Beintema et al.1985, Beintema & Müskens 1987, Shrubb 1990). In general, cattle proved more destructive than sheep, and among cattle, slow-moving milking or suckler cows trod on fewer nests than younger cattle which run around more. Losses of nests to trampling were therefore related to the type of stock – cattle or sheep – their ages, densities and lengths of time they spent in particular fields during the bird breeding season. While some larger birds, such as Oystercatcher and Curlew, can sometimes deflect sheep and cattle from their nests, smaller birds, such as Skylark and Yellow Wagtail, usually cannot (although they may occasionally attempt to do so; Wareing 1973).

Over many years, the nest success of Lapwings in Britain was significantly lower on grassland than in other habitats, such as spring-sown cereals, with figures of 58% and 70% calculated for the years 1962–85 from BTO nest-record cards (Shrubb 1990). Over this 24-year period, losses from the trampling of nests on grassland increased significantly in line with the increase in stocking densities. The same was true for clutch desertions, many of which could have been livestock-related. The problem of nest trampling by livestock is discussed in more detail in Chapter 13.

Given appropriate conditions, Skylarks often nest at the base of thistles or in the tall grass that grows up around dung pats. Because such sites are avoided by grazing animals, the birds gain some protection. However, trampling is not the only cause of breeding failure in grazed pastures. Many birds lose their eggs or chicks to predators, and livestock may accentuate these losses by putting birds off their nests, exposing the eggs to opportunist crows or gulls (Jönsson 1991, Hart et al. 2002). In addition, operations such as spring rolling, harrowing and slurry spreading also destroy nests, as mentioned above. Over the years, then, pastures have become increasingly dangerous places for ground-nesting birds. Nevertheless, many established pastures still support high densities of earthworms and other soil-living invertebrates, and can provide good feeding for birds, including for species that nest elsewhere, such as Starling, Golden Plover and the various corvids mentioned above.

The densities at which livestock are grazed in a field can markedly affect sward structure and bird content. In a series of experiments, Skylark nesting densities were six times higher on lightly grazed longish (15–25 cm) grass than on shorter (< 10 cm) heavily grazed grass (Wakeham-Dawson et al. 1998). The longer grass offered better nesting sites, and more food in the form of seeds and invertebrates. Similarly, on the Dee Estuary in northwest England, Skylarks reached the exceptionally high density of 120 pairs per km2 on ungrazed and moderately grazed coastal marshes, but fell to 50 pairs per km2 on heavily grazed marshes (C. E. Wells, in Donald 2004). Lightly grazed grassland also supplied better food supplies for wintering Skylarks, especially where grass species that bear seed through the winter were allowed to proliferate (Perkins et al. 2000).

REDUCTION OF FOOD SUPPLIES

Intensively managed grass fields are not only more dangerous places than their predecessors for birds to nest. They also offer less food. This is another result of some of the cultural practices described above, which act in different ways to reduce the abundance, diversity and accessibility of bird food items.

Declines in invertebrates

It can take up to four years for earthworms to recover their numbers after ploughing (Edwards et al. 1995). Grass fields are now ploughed and reseeded more frequently than in the past, so worm densities can be expected to be generally lower in intensive grassland than in traditional long-term grassland. Moreover, in the dry conditions of late summer, earthworms retreat to deeper soil, beyond the reach of probing birds. And following drainage, earthworms tend to move downwards earlier in the summer than before, and remain inaccessible for a longer period. In addition, grass leys are sometimes sprayed with an insecticide to kill leatherjackets in the soil, and prevent them from damaging the grass. This process can be expected to reduce other soil-dwelling invertebrates eaten by birds, as can soil compaction by livestock or machinery (Curry 1994, Vickery et al. 2001).

Above-ground invertebrates are also scarcer or less accessible in intensive grassland, owing mainly to its limited plant diversity, and more frequent cutting or grazing. Tall grass has a diverse structure which provides more niches for insects and others, but this structure cannot develop under constant grazing and is destroyed by frequent mowing. As the grass grows, arthropod numbers rise, but when the grass is cut and removed, their numbers crash (Curry & Tuohy 1978, Morris 2000, Kirby 1992, Macdonald et al. 2000). Timing of mowing affects the situation, as cutting in May is followed by more rapid recovery of arthropod numbers than cutting in July (Duffey et al. 1974). Through livestock grazing, most of the fresh growth on grass and other plants is removed as it appears, which greatly reduces the food supply for larval insects and others that depend on the same food source (Chapter 19). Moreover, whatever creatures they eat, most birds cannot feed easily within tall dense vegetation, but are normally restricted to areas of bare ground or short grass. The lack of tussocks and dead grass at the base of intensively managed swards reduces the opportunities for some invertebrates to complete their life cycles.

Short intervals between successive defoliations, as caused either by grazing or mowing, favour only short-lived, fast-breeding phytophagous insects which can fit in several generations per summer. But these species tend to be small-bodied insects, such as aphids, which are not much eaten by birds. Larger insects such as grasshoppers and lepidopteran larvae, which are favoured by birds, are also longer-lived, with only one generation per year. They do not have time to develop within the short period between successive grass cuts. Any larvae present are destroyed by cutter blades, incorporated into silage, or knocked to the ground where they are quickly consumed by the flocking birds which gather on freshly mown fields.

Not surprisingly it is the larger invertebrates, with their longer life cycles, that have most declined on modern farmland, with grasshoppers and butterflies being some of the most obvious casualties. Some underground beetle larvae take up to several years to develop into adults, making them especially vulnerable to periodic ploughing and cultivation procedures, as a field is reseeded. In addition, loss of botanical diversity has further reduced the range of insect food plants in the sward. Many insects require particular plant species for their development. While some butterflies feed from a variety of nectar plants, their caterpillars eat the leaves of only one or two particular species. Loss of these specific food plants results in the loss of the insects that depend on them. Other insect food sources, such as nectar, pollen and seed-heads, are also reduced in modern swards, whether through fertiliser use, mowing or grazing, as described above.

Long-term nitrogen application to grasslands reduces plant species richness but increases overall plant biomass. Parallel changes seem to occur in insect populations. Some 54 grassland plots that had been maintained at various rates of nitrogen input for 14 years were examined for insects (Haddad et al. 2000). Total species numbers declined in relation to the rate of nitrogen addition: more nitrogen meant fewer insect species. However, the overall abundance levels of the remaining species increased with the rate of nitrogen addition, with 13 of the most abundant insect herbivores increasing in line with their host-plant biomass. Insect communities seemed to change in the same way as plant communities: from variety to monotony but from lower to higher overall biomass. Long-term nitrogen loading thus seemed to have influenced the entire food chain, simplifying both plant and insect communities, although the changes were less marked in insects than in plants.

So under repeated nitrogen use, the arthropod community shifts increasingly to smaller species. Average body mass of arthropods in grassland has been found to fall steeply once the annual nitrogen input rises above 50 kg/ha (Siepel 1990, Beintema et al. 1991, Winspear & Davies 2005). This is well short of the levels usually applied to British farmland. The reduced plant diversity, denser growth, more frequent mowing and heavier grazing that result from nitrogen use are thus probably the main drivers of change in insect communities. In moths and butterflies, for example, decline may result both from the loss of food plants from the sward, and from the repeated grazing and cutting of those food plants that remain, preventing any caterpillars present from completing their development. In grasshoppers, population decline may result from vegetation so dense that the animals cannot warm up and function, as they do in more open sunny swards, and also from the destruction of nymphs during successive grass cuts. Other above-ground arthropods that tend to decline under fertiliser applications include bumblebees, crickets, beetles, flies, plant bugs, springtails and centipedes, most of which are eaten by birds.

By implication, a return to 'old-style' grassland management, with less nitrogen and no more than a single cut in late summer, could give greater opportunity for sward-dwelling grasshoppers, butterfly and moth larvae to complete their development and enable their populations to recover. For some other large invertebrate species, cutting intervals greater than one year, and rest periods spanning the whole winter, may be necessary to permit their recovery (Fry & Lonsdale 1991, Kruens & Tscharntke 2002).

Evidence confirms that shortage of large insects limits the breeding success of many grassland birds. The reproductive output of Cirl Buntings was constrained by the availability of grasshoppers (Evans et al. 1997), while the body condition of Corn Bunting and Skylark chicks was influenced by the availability of soft-bodied butterfly and moth larvae (Brickle et al. 2000, Donald 2004). In addition, Lapwing and other wader chicks in the early stages of their growth feed heavily on large surface-dwelling invertebrates (Beintema et al. 1991). In the Netherlands, these prey items were more numerous in wet-meadow nature reserves than in intensively managed grassland nearby, especially after the latter had been mowed in the first half of May (Schekkerman & Beintema 2007). In an experiment, captive-raised Black-tailed Godwit chicks were found to ingest 31% fewer prey items per unit time when foraging in cut agricultural grasslands than in uncut swards in nature reserves, a difference large enough to reduce chick growth and survival.

Declines in seeds

Traditional pastures usually contained some broad-leaved plants, such as thistles, Ragwort and docks, which were avoided by livestock, and were therefore able to produce seeds that were eaten from the plant by various finches. Traditional hay meadows contained a large variety of broad-leaved plants which seeded at different times through the spring and summer, producing a succession of seed crops suitable for finches and other seed-eaters. Dandelions seeded mainly in April and May, Sorrel and Cat's-ear in June, and knapweeds, thistles and others in July. Some of the grass itself produced seeds before it was cut, and some of these seeds were spilled during mowing. Nevertheless, the resulting hay retained enough seeds to provide food in winter, as they were shed wherever hay was provided for farm stock, attracting sparrows, buntings and partridges. Moreover, livestock which are fed on hay excrete the seeds in their dung, yielding another food source now largely lost to birds. Before the advent of motor traffic, horses in London were said to provide enough seeds from their nosebags and droppings to support the millions of House Sparrows that at that time lived within the city (Summers-Smith 2003).

Because modern monocultural silage fields are cut before seed is set, they can provide virtually no seeds, either during the growing season or through the winter when the resulting silage is fed to livestock. Modern hay fields are cut at a later stage of growth, but the range of seeds available is still smaller than in the past because of the narrower range of plant species that such fields now contain. Heavy grazing also reduces seed production within the sward, and hence the feeding opportunities for seed-eating finches and buntings.

Wider problems for seed-eaters

In the past, some seed-eating birds, such as Grey Partridge, Skylark, Yellowhammer and Reed Bunting, could survive year-round in grassland alone, without access to arable land. All these species eat some insects in summer, but feed on a wide range of grass and other seeds in winter. So their current absence from intensively managed grassland that is harvested before seeding may be largely due to shortage of seeds. Experiments revealed that, if rye-grass in modern grasslands was allowed to set seed, then seed-eaters moved in to take advantage of it (Buckingham & Peach 2006). In one experiment, four patches of final-cut rye-grass silage were allowed to regrow and set seed and were then left in situ overwinter. They attracted large numbers of Yellowhammers and Reed Buntings which fed on these seeded plots throughout the winter, confirming the importance of winter seed supplies. Quantity was important, and comparing different rye-grass plots, the usage by buntings was correlated with the densities of seed-heads, peaking at October densities of 400 seed-heads per square metre. More food meant more birds.

As the production of grass silage expanded over the years, cereal and other crops largely disappeared from some parts of the north and west, further limiting the feeding opportunities for seed-eaters. By the end of the 20th century, arable crops formed no more than 4–6% of farmland in some pastoral districts, and most of these crops were grown as silage, harvested before they could seed. The virtual disappearance of seed-eating birds, such as Grey Partridge, Yellowhammer, Corn Bunting, Reed Bunting and Tree Sparrow, from some western pastoral districts was attributed largely to shrinkage in the arable area (Robinson et al. 2001). This became especially obvious on hill farms, where the loss of turnip fields from some areas removed the main weeds important to farmland seed-eaters.

In conclusion, with the emphasis on silage production, seed-eating birds in pastoral areas have lost both summer and winter food sources. This shortage has been accentuated by the decline of arable seed crops (as opposed to silage crops) in pastoral farmland, although ways of mitigating these shortages have been trialled successfully (Mortimer et al. 2007, Buckingham et al. 2011). These changes have been more pronounced in pastoral areas in the southern part of Britain than further north, and not surprisingly some grassland birds have declined less in the north, although downward trends are continuing.

GRASSLAND AS A WINTER FORAGING HABITAT

Most of the problems discussed above result from conditions in the breeding season. But lowland grassland remains an important feeding area for birds in winter, and because most of it is short then, a greater area can be exploited than in summer. Species that feed mainly or entirely on soil-dwelling invertebrates from lowland grass fields in winter include Lapwing and Golden Plover, Black-headed and Common Gulls, Carrion Crow, Rook, Jackdaw and Magpie, Starling, Fieldfare, Redwing, Mistle Thrush, Song Thrush and Blackbird. Meadow Pipits and Pied Wagtails pick arthropods off the soil surface or low vegetation, while Snipe and other waders may occasionally be seen in ditches and other wet patches. Woodcock in winter often feed in fields at night, seeking mainly earthworms in damp ground or on the surface. Seed-eaters that feed on grassland in winter include various waterfowl, Pheasant, Grey and Red-legged Partridges, Woodpigeon and Stock Dove, and Skylark, Goldfinch, Greenfinch, Linnet, Chaffinch, Yellowhammer and Reed Bunting. The division between seed-eaters and invertebrate-eaters is not clear-cut, because many seed-eaters also take some green plant material and invertebrates, while some invertebrate-eaters also take fruit or seed.

FIG 135. Thrushes on grassland: left, Song Thrush Turdus philomelos (Richard Chandler); right, Mistle Thrush Turdus viscivorus (Ian Newton).

As in the breeding season, species in winter have strong preferences for different sward types, depending largely on their feeding and anti-predator behaviour. Wintering thrushes prefer to feed near trees and hedgerows to which they can retreat when disturbed, while plovers and geese prefer wide open areas away from trees, allowing them to spot any approaching predators from greater distance. Neighbouring habitats also influence the use of particular fields. For example, Jackdaws and Yellowhammers often feed on grassland next to cattle yards in which they also feed. Some species, such as Lapwing and Golden Plover, may rest in one type of field by day and feed in another type at night, providing it is light enough for them to see (Gillings et al. 2005b). By feeding at night, these two species may obtain earthworms more easily, and also avoid food-robbing by gulls (Barnard & Thompson 1985). In addition, the usual foraging behaviour of all species can be modified by weather, especially frost and snow or flooding.

Several winter surveys in different parts of Britain have examined the distributions of birds in relation to the field types present. At least three studies were concerned with birds in both grassland and arable (Tucker 1992, Wilson et al. 1996, Atkinson et al. 2002), and at least three others with birds in different types of grassland (Perkins et al. 2000, Barnett et al. 2004, Buckingham et al. 2006). The findings were broadly consistent between studies (Box 11), and all species concentrated in fields most likely to contain their particular foods in accessible form. Species that eat soil-dwelling or dung-dwelling invertebrates tended to select short swards, while species which eat sward-dwelling invertebrates or seeds tended to prefer taller swards with greater structural variability (Buckingham et al. 2006). Those birds that feed on soil-dwelling invertebrates (particularly earthworms) were also more numerous on permanent (unimproved) grassland, while generalists, such as corvids, were more numerous on improved grassland (Barnett et al. 2004). In addition, mixed farming landscapes which combined stock grazing with arable and overwinter stubbles supported greater numbers and diversity of field-feeding birds than landscapes covered entirely by autumn-sown crops or entirely by grass (Wilson et al. 1996). Considering grassland alone, mosaics of fields, some managed as short-term leys and others as permanent pastures with low-density cattle grazing over autumn and winter, provided the combination of heterogeneous sward structure, bare earth and some seeding plants that promoted a high overall use by wintering birds (Perkins et al. 2000). None of the areas studied held flocks of wintering geese; if they had, fields of young cereals (which other birds avoided) would probably have been more used.

BOX 11. Findings from studies on the use of different field types by birds in winter

• Of all field types, old ('permanent') pastures generally supported the highest densities of birds in winter. Where measured, they also supported the highest densities of earthworms and other soil-dwelling invertebrates on which many species fed. Ley grass and cereal stubbles supported moderate densities of a few bird species, while fields under bare till or growing cereals were generally avoided. Where leys (improved grassland) supported many birds, these were of a limited number of species, mainly corvids, Starlings or Black-headed Gulls. Carrion Crows often fed in longer grass than Rooks and Jackdaws.

• The use of grassland by several species, including Lapwing, Starling, Fieldfare and Redwing, increased following manure applications, which increased the densities of earthworms and other soil-dwelling invertebrates.

• Grazed grassland was generally preferred by species which fed on invertebrates (Buckingham et al. 2006). Grazing created variation in surface vegetation and some bare patches, providing more niches for invertebrates, and easier access for birds. The virtual absence of seed-eaters from grazed grass could be attributed to the scarcity of seeding plants. In addition, Lapwing, Golden Plover and (in coastal areas) Curlew all preferred pasture with short swards, but Snipe needed some cover. These species also appeared to prefer cattle-grazed over sheep-grazed pastures.

• Invertebrate-eaters used ungrazed grass fields less than grazed fields. In the studies involved, ungrazed fields were often short-term leys, used mainly for silage, and holding fewer soil invertebrates. However, ungrazed fields attracted more seed-eating birds, such as Skylarks and buntings, because some of the grasses and other plants had produced seeds after the last cut.

• Seed-eaters strongly preferred cereal and oilseed stubbles, in some cases to the virtual exclusion of other field types. These preferences were attributable to the crop and weed seeds that stubbles provided. Any kind of weed control reduced the usage of fields by seed-eating birds.

• Autumn-sown cereals were almost universally avoided during their growth, although organic cereal fields were used more by birds than those under conventional management.

• Summer grazing increased field usage in both summer and winter. Mown fields were also used in summer, and silage fields were strongly selected in winter if they were subjected to aftermath grazing by cattle. For these reasons, a wider range of fields became available to birds in winter than in summer. Cattle grazing and dunging promote invertebrates, the dung supporting fly and beetle larvae.

Details mainly from Townsend 1981, Barnard & Thompson 1985, Tucker 1992, Wilson et al. 1996, Milsom et al. 1998, Atkinson et al. 2002, Perkins et al. 2000, Barnett et al. 2004 and Buckingham et al. 2006.

In general, the structure and height of the sward had more influence on bird usage than its botanical composition, and for some species seemed just as important in winter as in the breeding season. The combination of short and long grass intermixed in the same field (created by appropriate grazing) provided the cover that many species seek, along with easy access to food in the short-grass areas. Some wader species were more sensitive to sward height than others (Milsom et al. 1998). For example, Lapwings and Golden Plovers, which have short legs and hunt by eye, preferred swards less than 6 cm tall, and avoided those more than twice this height. In contrast, Curlews, which are longer-legged and feed by both touch and sight, foraged in grass of all heights, but seemed to have difficulty in the tallest and thickest swards (Milsom et al. 1998). In the management of coastal grassland, a single cut in mid-October when growth stops proved sufficient to produce a sward suitable for winter use by all these waders, as well as by Brent Geese.

At more inland sites, Lapwings and Golden Plovers favoured old grassland or freshly ploughed fields, which offered more earthworms than other areas (Barnard & Thompson 1985, Village & Westwood 1994). Golden Plovers returned to the same old worm-rich fields year after year, on average preferring drier fields than Lapwings (Fuller & Youngman 1979). Black-headed Gulls often occurred in the same fields, obtaining much of their food by robbing the plovers of worms they had caught; Barnard & Thompson 1985). Winter Skylark densities were higher on swards around 10 cm high than on shorter swards, and decreased with sward density (Wakeham-Dawson & Aebischer 1998). Hence, for all these grassland species, sward structure and height emerged as a major factor in their choice of winter feeding area. This finding allows the management of grassland nature reserves to be targeted towards particular species.

FIG 136. Black-headed Gulls Chroicocephalus ridibundus chasing a Lapwing Vanellus vanellus for the earthworm it has caught (Chris Knights).

In one of the studies mentioned above, more than twice as many individual birds, consisting mainly of corvids, Starlings and Black-headed Gulls, were seen on improved fields, but were largely absent from unimproved fields, while Lapwings, Curlews, Snipes and thrushes were more abundant on unimproved fields (Barnett et al. 2004). This is somewhat different from the situation in summer, when the vegetation in many improved fields is too high for most birds.

Wintering waterfowl

The birds which most obviously benefit from modern grassland management are the wintering geese and swans that feed on intensively managed grass and cereal crops in winter and early spring before they return to their northern breeding areas. The young plants start to grow in spring earlier than in the past, and are rich in protein, enabling the birds to accumulate substantial body reserves in preparation for migration and breeding (Chapter 6). Intensively managed grassland can support remarkable numbers of wild geese in winter (Vickery & Gill 1999). For example, for Greenland White-fronted Geese, permanent pasture on Islay could support 100 goose-days per hectare, whereas newly reseeded pasture nearby supported 400–500 goose-days per hectare. For Greylag and Pink-footed Geese in eastern Scotland, modern grassland supported 1,300 goose-days per hectare, while for Brent Geese in southeast England newly established grassland supported 2,200–2,600 and a maximum of 4,500–5,000 goose-days per hectare. Some of these carrying capacities had been almost doubled by use of fertiliser. These data were useful in guiding the management of nature reserves established for wild geese.

FIG 137. White-fronted Geese Anser albifrons feeding on improved grassland in winter, benefiting from modern farming methods (Chris Knights).

CONCLUDING REMARKS

The first recorded declines in grassland birds, affecting mainly the Corncrake, began in the late 19th century, with the switch from scythes to mechanical grass cutters, which destroyed the eggs or young. Other changes during the latter half of the 20th century brought about further declines in a wider range of grassland birds. These developments included large-scale drainage and reseeding, a several-fold rise in the use of inorganic fertilisers, a switch from hay (with one cut per year) to silage (with multiple cuts per year), and increased stocking densities. As a result, the structurally diverse and species-rich swards of the past were largely replaced by dense, fast-growing, structurally uniform grass swards, sometimes consisting of a single grass cultivar. These changes brought about an enormous increase in grassland productivity, but at the expense of various environmental problems, including the loss of grassland birds.

On modern pastures, birds often have their eggs or chicks trampled by livestock, with losses depending on the types and densities of animals involved. Birds that nest in silage fields usually suffer such high rates of nest destruction or chick mortality when the grass is cut that their numbers cannot be sustained. The frequent cutting through the season, at 5–7-week intervals, more or less prevents birds of any species from nesting there successfully. It also largely eliminates flowering and seed-set, and thus reduces the food supplies for seed-eating birds. In the past, some nests were destroyed in these same ways, but livestock densities were generally much lower then, and grass cutting was a slower operation undertaken later in the season, after most birds had raised their young.

In addition, the food supplies for birds on grassland – whether invertebrates in the soil, arthropods in the grass sward or seeds from grasses and flowering plants – have all greatly declined in recent decades, perhaps having further effects on birds that traditionally bred or fed within the fields. Declines have been especially marked in larger species with longer development periods, such as grasshoppers and butterflies, which together with the loss of ants, spiders and tipulid larvae effectively removes most potential chick food for many bird species. Intense grazing or frequent mowing also prevent the build-up of grass litter at the base of the sward, reducing the habitat for small mammals, such as Field Voles, with repercussions on their predators, such as Kestrels and Barn Owls.

In winter when the grass is no longer growing, short-grass swards are the main field type available over much of Britain. Many birds then feed in these fields, including winter visitors from abroad. Most such species depend on soil-dwelling invertebrates, and include Starlings, various corvids and thrushes, Lapwings, Golden Plovers and various gulls. Several species of wintering geese also graze in grass fields, preferring nutrient-rich ley grass over most of our indigenous grasses.

Lowland grassland in summer provides perhaps the best example in British farmland of a so-called 'ecological trap'. In spring the habitat is attractive to birds, which settle there to breed, but once they have begun to nest, the grass grows and is either grazed or mowed, making it practically impossible for them to raise young. Such poor reproduction leads inevitably to population declines. Some of the most dramatic declines observed in recent decades concern the waders of wet grassland, discussed in the next chapter.

## CHAPTER 13

## Wet Grassland, Waders and Waterfowl

WET GRASSLANDS WERE ORIGINALLY created from natural marshland or riverine forest. Situated mainly in lowland river valleys or near sea coasts, they were subjected to periodic flooding and waterlogging, and were used primarily for summer grazing or hay production. Those that remain can support large numbers of waterfowl during winter floods, and in spring are home to breeding waders – mainly Lapwing, Redshank, Snipe, and in some areas also Black-tailed Godwit, Curlew, Oystercatcher, Dunlin and Ruff, the latter now very rare in Britain. These species derive from a range of different natural habitats, and only on wet grassland are they found nesting side by side, though each with specific requirements for feeding and nesting.

Other ground-nesting birds of wet grassland include the Skylark, Meadow Pipit, Yellow Wagtail, Whinchat, Cuckoo, and now very locally in Britain, the Corncrake and Spotted Crake. Along water-filled ditches, other species nest, notably the Mallard, Shoveler, Gadwall, Garganey (locally), Tufted Duck, Greylag, Mute Swan, Moorhen and Coot, all of which require open water, while the Water Rail, Reed Bunting, Reed Warbler and Sedge Warbler occur in the taller vegetation fringing the ditches and in the wetter parts of fields. In all these species, apart from the songbirds, the chicks leave the nest soon after hatch, and accompany their parents to suitable feeding areas. In total, over 40 bird species occur in wet grasslands in Britain, summer or winter, while around 500 plant species have been recorded in the meadows and associated ditch habitats. For at least four of the bird species (Dunlin, Black-tailed Godwit, Ruff, Corncrake), wet meadows provide their only remaining breeding sites in lowland agricultural land.

FIG 138. The four most widespread waders on wet grassland in Britain: upper left, Lapwing Vanellus vanellus (Bobby Smith); upper right, Redshank Tringa totanus (Ian Newton); lower left, Curlew Numenius arquata (Richard Chandler); lower right, Snipe Gallinago gallinago (Alan Martin).

Over the centuries, lowland wet grasslands in Britain have been progressively drained, with a major period of loss in the 1960s–80s. Nowadays, the main remaining areas include the Ouse and Nene Washes in Cambridgeshire (which are effectively banked-in river floodplains), the grazing marshes of the Norfolk Broads, the Somerset Levels, the Thames marshes, the Lower Derwent valley in Yorkshire, the Arun valley in Sussex and Otmoor in Oxfordshire, the latter re-created by blocking drains. Most of these areas are now nature reserves, managed as habitat mainly for waders and waterfowl. However, some also perform an important role in protecting neighbouring areas from flood and, in some cases, this prevents them from being managed to best effect for birds.

Most remaining areas of wet grassland are still flooded for part of each winter, and in most years the soil remains soaked and soft through the spring, giving ideal conditions for nesting waders. In the best areas, waterlogging also helps to delay grass growth and keep cattle and machinery off until late May or June, by which time most waders have produced their young. Around some of these wet grassland areas, arable land can provide harvest waste from cereals or root crops able to feed wintering waterfowl. Without flooded fields nearby on which waterfowl can roost securely, this abundant food source would go largely unused by these birds.

FIG 139. More localised waders of grassland: upper left, Dunlin Calidris alpina (Chris Knights); upper right, Black-tailed Godwit Limosa limosa (Richard Chandler); lower left, Ruff Calidris pugnax (Richard Chandler); lower right, Oystercatcher Haematopus ostralegus (Ian Newton).

STATUS AND HABITAT

The birds that breed on wet grassland have changed markedly in status over the last 2–3 centuries, and most have declined greatly in recent decades, associated with drainage. Declining species include not only the Corncrake, Quail and Whinchat, discussed in Chapter 12, but also waders. The Dunlin has now virtually disappeared from lowland wet grassland in Britain, apart from the machair land in the Hebrides and other parts of northwest Scotland, but it still occurs widely in damp parts of the uplands. For more than 150 years the Ruff has been scarce as a breeder in Britain, with few breeding records between the mid-19th and mid-20th centuries. Since that time, the Ruff and Black-tailed Godwit have been largely confined to the Nene and Ouse Washes, with only occasional breeding elsewhere, and the Snipe is probably now more numerous on these washes than anywhere else in lowland Britain (but is again more widely distributed in the uplands). The Oystercatcher is the only grassland wader which greatly expanded in numbers and breeding range during the latter half of the 20th century, accepting drier sites than most other waders. In the Netherlands, it occurs widely on inland wet grassland, but in Britain only rarely, choosing to nest on bare areas compacted by cattle or on spoil from ditch clearing; otherwise, it is found chiefly in coastal areas or near upland shingle-bedded rivers. The Curlew breeds occasionally in wet grassland, but mainly in rougher tussocky fields in the lowlands or much more commonly in lower parts of the hills. It seems less dependent on wet conditions for breeding than the Redshank and Snipe.

Most wader species leave their wet grassland nesting areas for the winter, some moving to the coast, and others to wintering areas further south. Although almost all such species have declined in recent decades, in association with the loss or degradation of their nesting habitat, none now seems to occur in all suitable areas, many of which remain vacant or at least not fully occupied. Breeding success is often poor, mainly due to predation or agricultural activities, and at times in the past some species may have been limited in their wintering areas, for example by shooting pressure. Into the mid-20th century, all grassland waders were extensively trapped or shot, for food or recreational hunting, and in many areas their eggs were harvested commercially for human consumption (Shrubb 2003, 2013). All these factors could have influenced the long-term trends in their numbers, and at times reduced them well below the level that the available nesting habitat could have supported. In the Europe of old, wet grassland was generally occupied by more species than now, with the Dunlin, Ruff and Aquatic Warbler being more widespread in lowland sites, and the Great Snipe breeding in meadows at least as far west as Schleswig-Holstein until about 1930 (Witt 1991).

In 20th-century Britain, it was from the late 1960s that substantial and widespread declines in the waders of wet grassland became evident. Over the years 1987–2013, numbers of breeding Lapwing, Curlew, Redshank and Snipe in England declined by an estimated 65%, 63%, 45% and 92% respectively (Fig. 16). Over the longer period 1968–2011, their distributions had declined in Britain as a whole by around 55%, 35%, 44% and 33% respectively (Balmer et al. 2013). Only the Oystercatcher had declined in numbers (–22%) but expanded in range (+28%). In other surveys on 851 lowland wet grassland sites in England and Wales, made in 1982 and repeated in 2002, Lapwing, Curlew, Redshank and Snipe had declined by 37%, 39%, 29%, and 62% respectively, while the Oystercatcher had increased by 51% (Wilson et al. 2005c). In the 2002 survey, birds were found only on a small number of sites, mostly nature reserves or other protected places. Two other species have been mainly confined to nature reserves at least since the 1960s, the Ruff showing little change in numbers or distribution, and the Black-tailed Godwit shrinking in distribution by about 40% (Balmer et al. 2013). In 2013, Ruffs in Britain were estimated at eight breeding females, and Black-tailed Godwits at 59 pairs (Hayhow et al. 2015a). In addition, the Woodcock, which often feeds in wet grass fields at night, declined nationally by nearly 30% between 2003 and 2013 (Hayhow et al. 2015a).

Many other studies recorded declines in grassland wader populations in particular localities and time periods, while hardly any recorded increases (Allison et al. 1974, O'Brien & Self 1994, Wilson et al. 2001, Henderson et al. 2002, O'Brien et al. 2002). Several compared wader and other bird populations before and after the drainage of particular areas, or between drained and neighbouring undrained land in the same year (Allison et al. 1974, Round 1978, Williams et al. 1983, Green & Robins 1993). In every case, drainage was associated with dramatic population declines, either abruptly from one year to the next or more slowly over several years. Clearly, all the commoner wader species of lowland wet grassland have declined greatly in the last 50 years or so. Conversely, the re-flooding of small areas for conservation reasons has usually led to increases (Phillips & Callaway 2002, Sills 2007).

Other species showed similar trends. Wet grassland was the main habitat of Yellow Wagtails in Britain, but numbers there fell by 65% in 20 years, 1982–2002 (Wilson & Vickery 2005). This left an increasing proportion of remaining Yellow Wagtails nesting mainly in spring-sown crops on arable land, which is probably now the main nesting habitat in Britain (Chapter 10). On wet grassland, the species prefers winter-flooded areas, with some bare ground and shallow-edged pools or ditches for foraging, and clumps of taller grass for nesting (Bradbury & Bradter 2004).

FIG 140. The Yellow Wagtail Motacilla flava was once found in damp grassland across southern Britain, but along with its habitat, has now much declined (Richard Chandler).

DRAINAGE, SOIL MOISTURE AND WADERS

Most of the big wet grasslands of Britain were drained in several stages over two or more centuries (Chapter 15). From year-round flood-land which was largely useless for agricultural purposes, early farmers gained whenever land that was under water in winter dried out sufficiently in summer to give access to cattle in May or June or to be cut for hay in July or August. After further drainage, it often became possible to reduce the duration and extent of winter flooding, and to lengthen the summer grazing season. The next step was to drain the land so thoroughly that it seldom or never flooded, and allowed the growth of more productive grasses or arable crops, including autumn-sown cereal varieties. This last step often involved pump drainage, and once the water levels in ditches could be reduced, fields could then be under-drained and water tables reduced by a metre or more. These three stages were still apparent in different parts of some low-lying areas of Britain well into the 19th century, including the East Anglian Fens and the Somerset Levels. However, in the 20th century, and especially in the 1970s–90s with the encouragement of grant aid, lowland wet grassland in Britain was even more effectively drained. When fields were pipe-drained during this period, many of the old water-filled ditches were filled in, reducing the brood-rearing habitat for ducks, Coots and Moorhens, and destroying the tall ditch-fringing vegetation that held Water Rails, Sedge Warblers and Reed Buntings. Along any remaining ditches, pollarded willows and bushes were usually removed to allow easier ditch clearing by machinery. Old willows had provided sites for hole-nesting birds, such as Stock Doves and Little Owls, and in some areas also for Mallards and other ducks. At the same time, the land surface was levelled, removing the minor undulations that were so important to breeding waders (see here). Less than one-tenth of the lowland wet grassland present in Britain during the 1950s survived through to the end of the century, largely confined to poorly drained pockets of land along river valleys, and totalling less than 260,000 ha (Shrubb 2003).

FIG 141. The Water Rail Rallus aquaticus is found in reed-beds and in well-vegetated ditch-sides in wet grasslands (Frank Snykers).

FIG 142. Drainage ditches through the Nene Washes nature reserve, habitat of Mute Swan Cygnus olor and various ducks and rails (Ian Newton).

Through drainage, ploughing, levelling and reseeding, the former semi-natural sward of varied wild grasses, sedges and rushes could thus be replaced by a uniform sward of productive grass cultivars capable of giving more hay or silage per cut, and more than one cut per year in some places. Alternatively, it could support greater livestock densities. With a lower water table, plant roots were no longer restricted by waterlogging and the drier soil warmed earlier in spring, so that grass growth began earlier than in the past, and could be boosted by the use of fertiliser. The timing of grass growth in spring has been further advanced by global warming. These changes allow grass cutting and livestock grazing to occur earlier in the spring than hitherto, increasing their overlap with the wader nesting season. Spring operations such as rolling, harrowing and muck-spreading also destroy the early nests of waders. The net result since the 1960s has been a massive reduction of both the breeding and wintering birds of wet grassland.

Importance of soil moisture

On remaining wet grasslands, winter flooding remains important, and not just for wintering waterfowl. By leaving shallow pools in its aftermath, flooding creates suitable feeding habitat for breeding waterfowl (Thomas 1980) and waders (Green 1986b, Ausden 1996, Sanders 2000). As the weather warms, botanically diverse wet grassland becomes rich in insects and their larvae, providing food for wader chicks. Ground water levels tend to remain high in spring and early summer, as waders and other birds begin to nest. A high water table increases the availability of soil organisms for feeding Snipe and other waders, by softening the soil for probing (Green 1986b, 1988a, Green et al. 1990). It also helps to keep the soil wet over a longer period, extending the potential breeding season, and thereby raising the seasonal productivity especially of Snipe (Green 1988a, Green et al. 1990). On the other hand, if widespread flooding persists into the breeding season, egg-laying can be delayed, by up to 70 days in the case of Snipe (Green 1988a).

Over the years, improved drainage has greatly reduced the period over which Snipe can breed each year, not just in Britain but also in the Netherlands where grassland has been similarly drained. In that country, recorded ringing dates of Snipe chicks over the period 1940s–80s showed that the start of the period in which ringers found Snipe chicks changed little over the years, but the end of the chick period became nearly two months earlier in the later years (from mid-August to mid-June), indicating a much shortened breeding season (Beintema et al. 1985). The resulting reduction in breeding output may have tipped Snipe populations into decline. Shortening of the season did not occur in the other four species (Lapwing, Redshank, Black-tailed Godwit and Ruff), which habitually bred over a shorter period than Snipe and were less dependent on soft soil and more dependent on pools. In these species, both the start and the end of breeding were advanced by about the same amount.

On peaty fen soils, as found in the Cambridgeshire Washes and Somerset Levels, the ideal water table for waders lies at around 20 cm below the surface (de Jong 1977, Round 1978). In such soils, capillary action is sufficient to carry water to the surface, thereby keeping the whole soil profile damp and soft enough for waders to feed by probing. If the water is much above this level, many earthworms can survive in the cold weather of winter, but in the warm weather of spring many die, so the total biomass of potential food items is then reduced. Although earthworm numbers eventually recover through the hatching of their cocoons, this takes time and numbers remain low if spring or summer flooding occurs frequently. On non-peaty mineral soils, an uneven surface can help to provide damp feeding areas through the breeding season, because drying occurs from higher to lower areas as the water table drops. This helps to provide a continuum of exposed soft-mud feeding areas for waders. To manage their land for wintering Snipe, farmers in Louisiana used to create a ridge and furrow system in their grass fields to produce the same effect (Tuck 1972), and a similar system has been adopted on Elmley Marshes in North Kent by Merricks (2010) and at West Sedgemoor in Somerset by the RSPB.

Spring–summer flooding

Despite the importance of damp soil, extensive flooding of wet grasslands in spring and summer can delay or completely prevent nesting in some seasons. At the Ouse Washes in 1983, spring floods persisted until the end of June, preventing the nesting of all but a handful of Lapwings, Redshanks and Black-tailed Godwits (Green 1986b). Some pairs nested in arable fields adjacent to the Washes but with low success. Snipe could breed later than the other species, and bred abundantly when the floods receded. Over a nine-year period, Snipe began to produce eggs at any time between mid-April and early July, but in each year soon after floods receded. Disruption of breeding by spring flooding therefore had less serious consequences for Snipe than for other species, with their shorter and less flexible nesting seasons (Green 1988a). Over the years, spring flooding has had a significant effect on the numbers of Black-tailed Godwits breeding on the Ouse and Nene Washes in England (Box 12).

Foraging behaviour of waders

During the breeding season, waders feed on a wide range of soil-dwelling, above-ground and aquatic invertebrates whose abundance is strongly influenced by the moisture content of the soil and the presence of shallow surface water. Pools and ditches differ in importance between species. On the Ouse Washes, Redshank nesting densities declined rapidly with increasing distance from a pool, Black-tailed Godwit densities declined less rapidly, and Lapwing least rapidly, reflecting the declining importance of aquatic feeding to these three species. Snipe occurred only at low densities, but they showed no obvious association with pools, except in very dry periods (Green 1986b). Curlews were absent from the Ouse Washes, but in other areas, despite their long beaks, they seem not to feed by deep probing in their breeding areas; nor do they show any particular association with pools and ditches, both chicks and adults picking most of their food items from the ground or vegetation. More recent studies in other areas have confirmed the importance of ditches and pools to Redshank and their lesser importance to Lapwing in terms of nesting location and success (Smart et al. 2006, Eglington et al. 2008, 2010).

After hatch, adult waders often lead their chicks from the nest area to a better feeding area until they fledge, especially if the vegetation in the nest area has grown too long and dense. On the Ouse Washes, Redshank, Lapwing, and to a lesser extent godwit broods concentrated around pools at this time, sometimes moving long distances from the nest to reach them. Snipe broods were often reared in fields without surface water and only moved to ditch edges and pools if earthworm abundance had been reduced by summer flooding or if the surface soil had dried out, preventing probing.

BOX 12. Spring flooding and Black-tailed Godwits in Britain

Black-tailed Godwits had nested on the Ouse Washes since 1952. After a period of increase through the 1950s and 1960s, the population stabilised for some years at around 50 pairs, but then declined (Green 1986b). The frequency of summer flooding increased from the early 1970s because of increased drainage of agricultural and urban areas and other changes in the management of runoff water. Godwits have a relatively short nesting season, with most clutches started in April and very few after 20 May, even replacements. Consequently, the opportunities for godwits to nest after late floods, or to lay replacement clutches after a summer flood, are limited. In the 30 years 1975–2004, godwit breeding on the Ouse Washes was significantly disrupted by spring floods in 16 years (53%) (Ratcliffe et al. 2005). Before 1975, spring flooding was less frequent, and godwit breeding was disrupted in only three (13%) of the 23 years 1952–74. In contrast to the decline from around 50 to around 3 pairs on the Ouse Washes, the Black-tailed Godwit population at the Nene Washes, only 30 km away, increased from 3 to 40 pairs between 1984 and 2004. A large area of the Nene Washes became a nature reserve in 1983 and large-scale re-establishment of wet grassland on former arable land and changes to grazing and mowing undoubtedly contributed to this increase. Moreover, the frequency of spring and summer flooding on the Nene Washes has been much lower than on the Ouse Washes. In only two of 21 years (10%) in the period 1984–2004 was godwit breeding on the Nene washes disrupted by flooding. Hence, there appears to be a link between the frequency of spring flooding (and resulting poor breeding) and the trends in Black-tailed Godwits breeding numbers in Britain.

GRAZING AND MOWING

Assuming that spring water levels are adequate but not at flood level, the numbers and kinds of birds that attempt to nest on wet grassland vary not only with the density of remaining pools (amount of remaining surface water), but also with the structure of the vegetation (height, heterogeneity and density). This structure in turn depends largely on whether the sward in the previous year was mown or grazed, and on the intensity of the grazing pressure. Research on the Ouse Washes in the 1970s showed that lightly grazed areas tended to be covered with Reed Canary-grass and Pond-sedge, with Reed Sweet-grass in the damper depressions. Moderate grazing gave a more tussocky sward with clumps of rushes or Wavy Hair-grass among the shorter grazed grass areas; while more intensive grazing or mowing produced a short even sward (Thomas 1980). While tussocks provided nest sites for ducks and most wader species, too many tussocks reduced the open short-grass areas which Lapwings used for nesting and all waders used for feeding. Young wader chicks also moved more easily on short grass than among longer vegetation (Chapter 12). Tussocks among short vegetation were also important in winter, for during floods the emergent stems trapped floating seeds and invertebrates, creating focal feeding sites for ducks (Thomas 1976). The grazed sward between the tussocks provided another food source for the ducks in the form of palatable grasses. The dung from cattle enhanced invertebrate populations, yielding more food for both ducks and waders. But to be suitable for a range of bird species, a good heterogeneous sward was required, created by careful control of cattle grazing to give a combination of tussocks and short-grass areas.

For wet grassland to remain suitable for waterfowl or waders in the longer term, grazing or mowing is essential. Without one or other, reeds and then shrubs take hold and spread, eventually leading to the loss of all ducks and waders, and their replacement mainly by reed-nesting and scrub-nesting passerines (Soikkeli & Salo 1979). Too much grazing gives entirely low vegetation and leads to the disappearance of all nesting waders except for Lapwings and Oystercatchers. The main challenge on nature reserves is to keep the short areas short for long enough each spring to enable waders to produce their young. A high water table helps to achieve this, because spring grass growth is then delayed, and in the absence of fertiliser, its growth is slow. Grazing when birds are on eggs would also keep the grass short, but at the risk of nest trampling, while mowing when the birds have either eggs or chicks destroys both (de Jong 1977, Chapter 12). The best nest success is achieved where access to cattle and mowing machines can be delayed until as late in the spring and summer as possible, say late May or June in southern England. Even then, late nests of Snipe, which have longer breeding seasons than other waders, are likely to be destroyed.

There is thus a dilemma in the management of wet grassland for waders, namely that grazing or mowing are needed to create and maintain a sward of appropriate structure, but both processes – if inappropriately timed – can lead to nest destruction and population decline. The problems for ground-nesting birds caused by mowing and grazing were described in Chapter 12, but are discussed further below, particularly in relation to waders on wet grassland, as studied by Round (1978), Beintema et al. (1985), Green (1986a, 1986b, 1988a), Beintema & Müskens (1987) and others.

FACTORS AFFECTING NEST SUCCESS OF WADERS

Most birds of wet meadows settle on their nesting territories in March, in preparation for egg-laying in April or May, before grazing has begun and when the grass is still short. The height and structure of the vegetation at this time is largely determined by grazing or mowing in the previous summer, but winter grazing by livestock or waterfowl can further reduce the height of the sward. On the Ouse Washes, the highest densities of nesting Lapwings and Black-tailed Godwits were in areas where vegetation was 10–15 cm high in mid-May, about two months after they had occupied these areas (Green 1986b), and elsewhere they abandoned sites when the grass grew taller (Lister 1964). Other species, such as Snipe and Redshank, usually nested within tussocks in taller swards of 15–20 cm (Mason & Macdonald 1976, Green 1986b). The degree of preference for short vegetation by these different species is also what might be expected from their nest defence behaviour. The nests of large waders which attempt to drive away intruders (such as Curlew, Oystercatcher, Black-tailed Godwit, Lapwing) tend to be on bare ground or in short vegetation, which provides good visibility. Other species (Ruff, Redshank, Snipe, Dunlin) nest in deeper cover and rely more on concealment. All these species tended to shun the tall, dense, uniform swards of heavily fertilised grassland. Chicks have difficulty in walking through such dense swards, and any prey items are less abundant or accessible (Chapter 12).

FIG 143. Two wader nests, showing contrasting degrees of nest concealment: left, Redshank Tringa totanus (Richard & Barbara Mearns); right, Lapwing Vanellus vanellus (Ian Newton).

Most wader species normally raise no more than one brood per year, but after early nest failures they can usually lay one or more repeat clutches, providing that the habitat and food supply remain adequate. In areas where the water table remains high into summer, the period over which individuals can breed is lengthened, giving more opportunities to compensate for earlier failures. But the degree of repeat laying varies not only with the state of the habitat and the length of the breeding season, but also with the body condition of the females, which in turn depends on food supplies, and whether they re-lay after losing chicks or only after losing eggs. Snipe have such a long potential breeding season that individual females would have time to produce two successful broods. None of the tagged females studied by Green (1988a) reared two broods, but all of the early breeding attempts he studied failed and were replaced.

Grazing, trampling and mowing

On wet grassland that is grazed, livestock can trample, defecate or lie on nests and may also push out or eat the eggs. Egg-eating by sheep or cattle has been seen mainly on acidic soils with nutrient deficiencies, but may be more widespread than is currently realised. On the basis of information collected on wet grassland, the chance that a nest will survive when exposed to a certain density of grazing livestock can now be predicted from knowledge of the area of the field, the number of stock present, the number of days for which the nest is exposed to risk, and a constant which is characteristic of the species of wader and type of livestock concerned. Such 'trampling constants' were estimated for various wader–livestock combinations in the Netherlands (Beintema et al. 1982, Beintema & Müskens 1987). These same constants also predicted accurately the nest destruction rates in England, where further data were added for Snipe (Green 1988a). The risks of individual wader nests in wet grassland being trampled, both per day of existence and over the laying–incubation period as a whole, are given for different species in Table 6. At a set density of cattle, Snipe and Redshank suffered the highest risk per day of nest trampling, followed in order by Black-tailed Godwit, Oystercatcher and Lapwing. However, because the laying–incubation periods varied between species, the Redshank emerged as the most vulnerable over the nest period as a whole, followed by Snipe and the others in the same order. The waders which mobbed intruders and drove them from the nest (Curlew, Oystercatcher, Black-tailed Godwit, Lapwing) suffered lower trampling rates than those which sat tight and then flew away from the nest when disturbed (Redshank, Ruff, Snipe).

TABLE 6. Nest survival probabilities for five species of waders in England and the Netherlands. The figures (called trampling constants) represent survival probabilities for a nest exposed to the risk of trampling by one cow in an enclosure of 1 ha. Figures in brackets show sample sizes. Mainly from Beintema et al. (1982) and Green (1986b).

The first two columns show the daily survival rates of the nests of different species, and the third and fourth columns the survival rates from laying to hatching. So throughout the nesting period a Dutch Oystercatcher nest has a 0.987 probability of surviving from one day to the next, and a 0.693 probability of surviving until the eggs hatch. The periods between laying of the first egg and hatching were calculated as 3 + 25 = 28 days for Oystercatcher, 4 + 28 = 32 days for Lapwing, 4 + 23 = 27 days for Black-tailed Godwit, 4 + 24 = 28 days for Redshank, and 4 +19 = 23 days for Snipe.

Differences between young and old cattle found in the Netherlands were not found in England. Beintema et al. (1982) also give trampling constants for sheep. According to their data, one cow is equivalent in terms of nest trampling to 2.52 sheep for Lapwing nests, 2.44 for Black-tailed Godwit nests, and 4.13 for Redshank nests. These numbers are not significantly different from one another, and the weighted mean of them all is 2.80 (that is, nearly three sheep per cow).

At a cattle density of only one animal per hectare, the proportions of nests likely to be trampled at some stage between the laying of the first egg and hatching of the last chick were calculated at 31% for Oystercatcher (Netherlands), 25% and 12% for Lapwing (England and Netherlands), 35% for Black-tailed Godwit (Netherlands), 41% and 54% for Redshank (England and Netherlands) and 39% for Snipe (England). With two cattle per hectare, loss rates would be twice as high. In reality, densities of cattle would often be higher than one per hectare, and nests would fail not only from trampling but also from predation and other causes. While in theory one day's grazing by 20 animals gives the same losses as 20 days of grazing by one animal, the consequences differ because the timing of losses affects the chance of re-laying. The earlier in the nesting cycle a clutch is destroyed, the more likely is the bird to lay again. All the figures above refer to inland wet grassland, but on grazed saltmarshes the effect of trampling by cattle on Redshank nest success emerged as more severe. On the Ribble Estuary in northwest England, nearly all (98%) Redshank nests were estimated to fail from trampling at a density of only 0.82 cattle per hectare (Sharps et al. 2015). So even light grazing can reduce Redshank nest survival to near zero.

In view of these findings, the later that cattle are allowed onto wader breeding areas, the greater the chance of waders nesting successfully. On nature reserves, postponing access until the end of May or early June greatly enhances the productivity of some species. The benefit is greater for Snipe and Redshank, which start breeding later than Lapwing and Black-tailed Godwit and have higher daily trampling risks, and, in the case of Snipe, a longer breeding season (Green 1988a). So any delay in the onset of grazing would be expected to give substantial benefit to Redshank and Snipe, and even further delay would particularly benefit Snipe, which can lay as late as July and have young into August. However, delaying the start of grazing might be detrimental for Lapwings, because tall vegetation in late May would reduce the amount of suitable foraging habitat and make the area less attractive for re-nesting.

The crucial finding from these and other studies was that a density of two or more cattle per hectare was too high to sustain a wader population, because cattle at this density destroyed so many clutches that insufficient young were produced to maintain breeding numbers. One cow per hectare was acceptable in some situations, but none at all was better, at least until June when most clutches had hatched (Witt 1991). Re-nesting occurred if eggs were destroyed early in the season, but in the drier conditions post-drainage, the potential laying season ended earlier than in the past, possibly because the adults were then unable to get enough food to produce further clutches (see here).

During the first few days after their release, young cattle and horses sometimes behave nervously, running back and forth over the fields. This behaviour disturbs incubating birds and chases them off their nests. Some of the clutches are crushed by the animals, while others are taken by opportunist crows and other predators (Jönsson 1991). Even at densities too low to cause much nest trampling, cattle and sheep sometimes keep birds from their nests, disrupting incubation and increasing the risk of egg predation. In coastal grazing marshes, Lapwing breeding densities in two out of three years were lowest on areas with most livestock, which Lapwings tended to avoid (Hart et al. 2002).

Once the chicks have hatched and can move around, they are largely but not totally immune to squashing by livestock, but such deaths have not been measured separately from other chick losses. In any case, survival of young waders to fledging is difficult to measure reliably, because the young are often hidden by vegetation, and over periods of days they can move long distances from the nest, making them difficult to follow. Nevertheless, some measures of chick loss have been made for Lapwing and other waders by intensive observation or by use of radio-tags to repeatedly locate the same broods (see later).

Mowing can be more destructive than low-density grazing, because it can destroy every nest or chick in its path, and also kill occasional incubating adults. So, as with grazing, delay of mowing date is beneficial, giving more time for nests to hatch and for chicks to move away. Delay is especially advantageous for Snipe, Redshank, Black-tailed Godwit and Ruff, the species most likely to keep their chicks in grass tall enough for mowing (Green 1986b, Kleijn et al. 2010). In contrast, Lapwings are likely to lead their chicks out of tall-grass fields onto shorter, grazed grass, providing it is available locally.

Management to enhance the nest success of waders may be acceptable on nature reserves, but many farmers who raise beef cattle keep their animals in units of one bull per 30 cows plus calves. The field sizes available in most wet grassland areas make it difficult to reach cattle densities low enough to avoid excessive nest trampling unless the animals are kept off the best wader areas altogether until the end of May or later, which is not always a practical option for farmers. In any case, by that time on many southern areas, the grass would be too high for Lapwings, especially if it had been fertilised.

Predation on waders on wet grassland

In addition to losses from trampling and mowing, waders and other ground-nesting birds often suffer high rates of nest predation. Many predators eat the eggs, chicks or adults of waders, including Foxes, Badgers, Minks, Stoats, Weasels, Otters, Hedgehogs, Dogs, Cats and Brown Rats among mammals, and Kestrels, Red Kites, Buzzards, Goshawks, Sparrowhawks, Marsh Harriers, Grey Herons, gulls and corvids among birds. Some of these predators take only the eggs, others only chicks or adults, while yet others take all three. Some take the adults of small species such as Snipe, but not of larger ones such as Curlew. The most significant predator species vary between areas, as do the overall rates of predation, depending partly on the state of the habitat and the food and concealment it offers, and partly on the abundance of the predators and the alternative foods available to them.

Many ground-nesting birds that breed in grassland have shown reductions in breeding output in recent decades (Sharpe et al. 2008, Kleijn et al. 2010, Roodbergen et al. 2012). In some studies, these reductions were due more to predation than to other factors, raising the questions: (1) to what extent could increasing nest predation have contributed to the declines in grassland waders, and (2) were higher predation rates due to increases in predator populations, or to changes in grassland management which made wader nests more vulnerable? In Britain, many potential egg and chick predators of waders have increased greatly since the 1950s, notably Carrion Crows, Magpies, Buzzards, Marsh Harriers, Foxes and Badgers (Chapter 2, Tapper 1999).

FIG 144. Some birds of prey that hunt wader chicks: above, Red Kite Milvus milvus (Alan Martin); right, Kestrel Falco tinnunculus (Richard Chandler).

FIG 145. Grey Heron Ardea cinerea, another significant predator of wader chicks on wet grassland (Frank Snykers).

FIG 146. Fox Vulpes vulpes shot while carrying away three Oystercatcher Haematopus ostralegus chicks (Chris Knights).

Across 15 areas in the Netherlands, the actual predators on wader eggs and chicks were identified by using temperature-loggers and continuous video-recording of 792 clutches of Black-tailed Godwits and Lapwings, and by radio-tagging and tracking 662 chicks (Teunissen et al. 2008). Overall levels of predation differed greatly between areas and years, as did the species of egg predators involved, but there was less variation in chick predators. In the 15 areas, 0–24% of chicks survived to fledging, depending on area. Most losses of chicks were traced to predation (70–85% in different areas) or to grass-cutting operations (10–15%), and the remaining 10–20% to various other causes such as starvation and drowning in ditches (Schekkerman et al. 2009). Godwits suffered less predation in long grass than in recently cut or grazed areas, while Lapwings suffered less predation in grazed than mowed fields. At least in godwit chicks, predation was predisposed by poor body condition (and food shortage), but whether the radio-tags themselves influenced predation rates remained an open question. Eggs were taken chiefly by mammals operating at night and chicks mostly by birds operating by day. In total, 22 species were identified as predators, of which the Fox and Stoat were the main consumers of eggs, and the Common Buzzard and Grey Heron the main consumers of chicks. This study thus confirmed that a wide range of birds and mammals eat the eggs and chicks of waders, and that predation rates could be high, depending on the habitat and predator species present. Agricultural practices predisposed some of this predation, but other agricultural losses were limited, because volunteers found and marked the nests, most of which could then be avoided by farmers at grass cutting. In the absence of this activity, agricultural losses would have been much greater, and predation less.

FIG 147. Two significant mammalian predators of wader eggs: left, Badger Meles meles (Chris Knights); right, Hedgehog Erinaceus europaeus (Ian Newton).

Other studies of predation concern Hedgehogs on the Outer Hebrides. These animals occur through much of mainland Britain, but were introduced in unauthorised manner to South Uist in 1974. Since that time, they have spread to two other islands linked by causeways, and wader numbers have declined markedly, including Dunlin, Ringed Plover, Lapwing, Redshank, Snipe and Oystercatcher. Predation on eggs became sufficiently high to account for these declines (Jackson & Green 2000, Jackson et al. 2004). Introduced Mink are also present on these islands, but their numbers have been controlled and they seem not to have had serious effects on waders.

Experiments at two sites in 1998 measured the effect of removing Hedgehogs from two fenced plots (Jackson 2001). Avian predators could not be excluded, but the subsequent hatching success of waders (Dunlins and Lapwings) inside the plots was roughly 2.4 times higher than in adjacent areas where Hedgehog densities remained high. These findings led to a programme aimed at removing Hedgehogs totally from these islands. Only time will tell whether the programme will succeed, and allow a recovery in wader numbers. Hedgehogs have created similar problems on islands off Germany and in New Zealand where they have also been introduced.

Further evidence that predators can have a big influence on the nesting success and subsequent breeding numbers of waders and other birds has come from other predator removal experiments. Once predators have been removed from an area, nest success typically shows a substantial increase, and in subsequent years breeding densities rise (Tapper et al. 1996, Newton 1998, Bolton et al. 2007, Fletcher et al. 2010, Merricks 2010). Most of these experiments were on nature reserves or other areas where livestock and mowing were not major causes of nest failures. Moreover, in the uplands, waders usually show greater nest success and nesting densities in areas where predators are controlled by gamekeepers than in other similar habitat elsewhere (Tharme et al. 2001, Douglas et al. 2014). More recently, fencing has been used to keep out mammalian predators from areas with high densities of nesting waders, and big improvements in productivity have been detected, compared with unfenced areas. In this way, Lapwing productivity rose from 0.23 fledged young per pair without a fence to 0.79 young per pair within an electric fence (Malpas et al. 2013a). The higher productivity was sufficient to allow a Lapwing population to increase (the replacement level being 0.6–0.7 young per pair). In another study, greater productivity in fenced areas was mainly due to improved overnight survival of chicks, suggesting that Foxes were largely responsible for their deaths (Rickenbach et al. 2011).

Modern grassland management could increase predation in at least three ways. First, the uniform sward structure, by reducing cover or camouflage, may increase the likelihood of a predator detecting nests, chicks or adults. In upland pastures of northern England, most losses of Lapwing clutches resulted from predation by corvids and gulls, but these losses were increased by pasture management that reduced the cryptic appearance of the clutch (Baines 1990). Over three years, 76% of clutches were taken by predators on improved pasture fields, compared with 47% on traditional pasture fields in the same area, a highly significant difference. Against the uniform green background of improved fields the eggs were more visible than against the broken green/yellow/brown background of unimproved traditional fields. Chicks up to 10 days old also had significantly lower survival on improved fields, yet food supplies seemed similar in both, so less effective camouflage may again have caused the difference.

The notion of reduced camouflage on the uniform green of improved fields was tested with dummy nests, using similar-looking Black-headed Gull eggs to simulate Lapwing clutches. After seven days, more than twice as many of the eggs had been taken from improved fields as from unimproved ones. This finding lent further support to the idea of reduced camouflage in improved pastures. Productivity on improved pastures was insufficient to maintain numbers, but for a time immigration from traditional fields helped to prevent decline there. Maintenance of numbers thus depended on the ratio of unimproved to improved fields, and as more fields were converted over time, overall Lapwing numbers were expected to decline (Baines 1994).

A second way in which predation may have risen over recent decades is through increased livestock densities. As well as treading on eggs and chicks, farm animals often flush birds from their nests, perhaps drawing the attention of predators or making the eggs more visible or accessible (Hart et al. 2002). The reduction in vegetation height caused by grazing might also make nests easier for predators to see, at least for those wader species such as Redshank that conceal their nests in tall vegetation. Over the years, both the exposure of nests caused by grazing and the 'flushing' caused by livestock would have been expected to increase in line with livestock densities. Moreover, improved pastures seem to attract larger numbers of Rooks and Jackdaws than unimproved ones, giving plenty of predators on hand to take advantage of opportunities that arise. Overall, then, recent management of pastures has probably increased the vulnerability of eggs and chicks to predation quite apart from any increase in the predators themselves.

Thirdly, modern grassland often contains fewer suitable insects and other invertebrates than traditional wet grassland, so offers less food for adult waders and their chicks (Chapter 12). Availability of food to wader parents may influence the robustness of their defence behaviour. When female Lapwings were weighed on the nest early in incubation using an automatic balance, it was found that lighter females were more likely to suffer egg predation than heavier females, and were also less likely to lay a replacement clutch after failure (Hegyi & Sasvari 1998). Females whose nests failed for reasons other than predation showed no such weight difference. So if females in better body condition were more able to deter predators from taking their eggs, we would expect birds nesting on improved pastures to be more prone to predation than those nesting on more food-rich unimproved pastures.

In addition to effects on adults, poor food supply in modern pastures almost certainly leads some chicks to starve (Round 1978, Beintema & Visser 1994, Kentie et al. 2013). Moreover, hungry chicks that are active and continually calling and searching for food are more obvious to predators than are well-fed chicks which spend much of their time resting motionless (Baines 1990). So food shortage for chicks could also predispose predation, and cause a further reduction in overall productivity (for Black-tailed Godwits see Box 13). It is usually hard to separate the influence of all these various factors.

BOX 13. Studies of Black-tailed Godwits in the Netherlands

Although some waders attempt to nest in modern grass monocultures, their success there is poor. Most of the losses are due to trampling or mowing, but any chicks that hatch in such fields do not grow or survive well, partly through shortage of food (Kentie et al. 2013). Among Black-tailed Godwits in the Netherlands, body mass at hatching did not differ between chicks from herb-rich meadows (nature reserves) and grassland monocultures, but at fledging those raised in monocultures were on average 14–16% lighter, and had bills 4% shorter. Moreover, the growth rates of chicks hatched on herb-rich meadows were similar to those in the meadows of earlier times, during 1976–85. In addition, apparent survival during the first year of life was 2.5 times higher among chicks hatched on herb-rich meadows than among chicks hatched on grass monocultures. Only in the meadows was chick survival good enough to maintain a stable population.

If this were not enough, the grazing and mowing dates on grassland are now earlier than in the past not only because of drainage and fertiliser use, but also because of climate change, which has brought warmer winters and springs (Kleijn et al. 2010). Ringing data indicate that, between 1945 and 1975, godwit hatching dates in the Netherlands advanced by about two weeks, as did median mowing dates.
