This facility is much reduced in arable land, because organic matter is continually turned to the surface where carbon can be oxidised to carbon dioxide, contributing to climate warming. Science has made us aware of environmental problems associated with the drainage of marshland that previous generations were oblivious to.

Impacts of marsh drainage on wetland birds

Our knowledge of marshland birds in prehistoric times is based chiefly on bone remains from archaeological sites, and in recent centuries also on written records, paintings and other evidence. The bones found by digging in lowland peat suggest an interesting past bird fauna, including the Dalmatian Pelican, whose bones have been found in the East Anglian fens, the Somerset Levels and elsewhere (Yalden & Albarella 2009). They also include the bones of White-tailed Eagle, White Stork, Crane, Bittern, Greylag, as well as many other waterfowl still found in those areas today. The range of species found in the ancient fenlands, with the predominance of Mute Swan, Bittern, Crane and Mallard, suggests a landscape with much open water, extensive shallows with reeds and grasses, and trees on higher islands. The historical record suggests that Little Egrets and Night-herons were also once abundant in fenlands (Bourne 2003), but they are strangely unrecorded from among archaeological material (although bones of Egrets can be easily confused with those of Bitterns; Yalden & Albarella 2009). Purple Herons, Spoonbills and possibly Great White Egrets and Little Bitterns were also present (Bourne 1999, 2003). The occurrence of the Crane in fenland is unsurprising, but the species was also widely distributed across most of lowland Britain and Ireland, as indicated by archaeological records and place names (Boisseau & Yalden [1999] list 225 place names). Most of these species later ceased (or almost ceased) to breed in Britain, but many of them figure prominently on late medieval menus. There is little doubt that many large wetland species bred here abundantly in earlier times (Bourne 1999, 2003, Stewart 2004, Yalden & Albarella 2009).

During the last four centuries, some specific losses were documented from the last recorded breeding dates, including the Crane (1620, re-colonised from 1980s), Spoonbill (1668, re-colonised from 1990s), Black Tern (1860–85, sporadic breeding subsequently), Bittern (1886, re-colonised from 1911), Marsh Harrier (1898, re-colonised from 1911), Avocet (1842 or later, re-colonised from 1941), Black-tailed Godwit (1850s, re-colonised from 1952), Ruff (1898, sporadic breeding up to 1922, then regular from 1963), and Savi's Warbler (1856 or 1885, re-colonised from 1950s, with very few pairs in recent years). In the early 19th century, Bearded Tits were reported as breeding in at least 10 counties in southeast England, Savi's Warblers bred in the Fens in Norfolk and Cambridgeshire and possibly in the Thames marshes in Essex, while Black Terns were widespread in at least seven southeastern counties from Lincolnshire to Sussex. At this time, the Spotted Crake also bred in many counties, but more commonly in the south than in the north (Holloway 1996). All these marshland species almost certainly occurred more widely than surviving records suggest, because suitable habitat occurred in many other places lacking written records.

FIG 169. Dalmatian Pelicans Pelecanus crispus, whose bone remains have been found in ancient drained marshland in Somerset and elsewhere in Britain (Frank Snykers). The species has since been eliminated from most of Europe, and now survives only in a few localities in southeastern Europe.

FIG 170. Historical evidence suggests that the above four species bred widely in southern Britain in medieval times. They then disappeared but have bred again in Britain in recent years. Upper left, Night-heron Nycticorax nycticorax (Frank Snykers); upper right, Purple Heron Ardea purpurea (Frank Snykers); lower left Spoonbill Platalea leucorodia (Frank Snykers); lower right, Little Egret Egretta garzetta (Allan Hale). The Little Egret has now spread widely as a breeder over much of Britain.

FIG 171. Black Terns Chlidonias niger bred at various sites in eastern England into the 19th century, and then ceased to breed, although they have appeared in numbers in most recent springs (Frank Snykers).

Following much habitat destruction by drainage, the final demise of some of these species has been attributed to overhunting (following the development of breech-loading guns) or egg-collecting. For some species, we cannot be certain that breeding by occasional pairs did not occur continuously or sporadically through their supposed period of absence, but remained undetected or unreported. Other species would almost certainly have disappeared during the 20th century were it not for special conservation measures, including habitat creation (see here).

Farming on drained marshland

In the 18th and 19th centuries, much drained fenland was used for pasture. Although often under water for much of the winter, in summer it dried sufficiently for cattle to feed on the natural vegetation. The ditches usually held water year-round, and were not managed rigorously, so water-lilies and other aquatic plants were common. Dragonflies and other insects were numerous. The human population was too low to pollute the water seriously, and little manure was used, so the water did not become too eutrophic. Although the main fenland areas had lost much of their native vegetation and most of the animals dependent on it, the rich flora and fauna of the dykes meant that the ecological interest of drained fenland was by no means negligible (Ennion 1942). This situation held until the general intensification of farming in the latter half of the 20th century.

Until this time, pastoral farming remained part of fenland agriculture, and graziers sought to maintain a high water table to promote grass growth through the summer; full dykes also provided water for livestock and effective field boundaries to constrain their movements. Subsequently, arable farmers aimed to lower water tables by up to a metre. This action influenced water levels over wider areas than those drained, and may have particularly affected species of wet grasslands such as Snipe and Black-tailed Godwit. Once more widely distributed, both species survive today in the lowlands mainly in two low-lying peaty areas, namely the Ouse and the Nene Washes, parts of which are managed as nature reserves. The Ouse Washes are now the largest area of neutral grassland in the East Anglian fens, about 31 km long and 1 km across; they consist of wet fields separated from each other by 140 km of functional ditches. In summer, the washes dry out sufficiently to allow grazing. More than half the area is under conservation management, and some of the bird studies there are summarised in Chapter 13.

Today, apart from nature reserves, almost all the original fenland in East Anglia is under arable cropping. Although the peat has disappeared from much of it, the land is still some of the most productive in Britain. Besides wheat and barley, the main crops include sugar beet and vegetables such as potatoes, brassicas, onions and carrots. In association with arable cropping, the ditches are kept 'well managed', cleaned out frequently and, with high use of fertilisers and pesticides in adjacent fields, they are now highly eutrophic and support little of the wildlife they held into the 1950s.

Opposition to land drainage

Through recent centuries, local people were generally opposed to big drainage schemes, because they saw their livelihoods threatened. Their way of life, with its common rights, was destroyed; wetlands provided abundant fish and waterfowl year-round, and hay in summer and thatch in winter. Drainage schemes were usually imposed on them from outside for 'the good of the nation', and often by wealthy businessmen who saw land drainage as a profitable investment. Major conflict marked the draining of the East Anglian Fens from the 1630s, when locals known as the 'Fen Tigers' tried repeatedly to sabotage the process. Similarly on the Somerset Levels, as late as 1769 goose owners stoned the local drainage agent and burnt his effigy before digging an open grave for a surveyor and offering a hogshead of cider to anyone who could catch him (Purseglove 2015).

The Land Drainage Act of 1861 set up a system of Drainage Districts and Commissioners of Sewers, each responsible for about 40,000 ha, with powers to improve and repair existing watercourses and outfalls. The work was financed by imposing a drainage charge on the land so 'improved'. In the continuing battle between graziers and arable farmers, the result was invariably in favour of arable.

During the main period of agricultural intensification in the 1960s–90s, lowland rivers and streams came to be increasingly regarded as sources of water for crop irrigation, and as drains to carry surplus water and pollutants as quickly as possible from land to sea. Much was done to speed the flow of water by dredging, straightening and 'canalising' existing river channels. These processes inevitably led to a general drying of the countryside. Gone were the meandering rivers, the oxbow lakes, the extensive floodplains and braided river channels of the past, all of which added greatly to the beauty of the countryside and the diversity of wetland habitats. Land drainage and river canalisation increased the risk of downstream flooding, and reduced the water flow in summer. Some of the drier parts of the southeast are now so well drained that irrigation is needed to maintain cropping, which can in turn result in reduced water levels in nearby lakes and rivers, and in extreme cases can cause smaller rivers to dry up totally in summer. Only at times of maximum flow in winter, when agrochemicals reach sufficiently low concentrations, can water be abstracted from some rivers for human consumption.

Throughout the 1960s–80s, the regulatory environment was heavily stacked in favour of drainage, as encouraged by government. The regional Water Authorities were strongly influenced by the network of Internal Drainage Boards, which regulated the process at a local level. They operated under a constitution free of public scrutiny, and were responsible for the destruction of thousands of hectares of wet grassland. Nature conservation interests suffered from the mechanism for approval of arterial drainage works. The drainage authorities had permissive power to undertake works deemed desirable by a majority of agricultural landowners to lower water levels, but all owners had to agree before works could be undertaken to raise water levels. During the 1970s, many case-by-case battles were fought between drainage bodies and agriculturalists who wanted to drain and plough the remaining marshlands of Britain, and conservationists who wanted to protect them. Almost always, the drainers won, and many important wildlife areas were lost, although a few – such as the Ribble Estuary in Lancashire – were saved at great expense.

FIELD DRAINAGE

For centuries, farmers in Britain depended on the ridge-and-furrow system for the drainage of individual fields. Crops were planted on the drier ridges and water flowed along the furrows into ditches. In the 19th century, however, various forms of underground tunnel were constructed on farmland in order to carry water to ditches. Early versions were used mainly to drain low-lying wet patches; trenches were dug and partly filled with stones or brushy material, and then covered with soil. Then, from the mid-19th century, clay pipe drains (called tile drains) were progressively developed. The most effective and durable were constructed of earthenware pipes, some of which survive to this day. They were typically laid just below plough depth in parallel lines 5–6 m apart, all opening into a ditch at the side of the field. Water entered through gaps between the short sections of pipe placed end to end. They improved surface run-off and caused the water table to drop. By the late 19th century, three-quarters of the farmed land in Britain had tile draining, and most of the remaining areas were on chalk or sand, which were naturally well drained. This development in under-draining transformed the lowland landscape, bringing declines in the species of wet grassland, such as Snipe and Redshank, as documented in ornithological texts of the time (Shrubb 2003).

From the 1880s, agriculture fell into a recession lasting more than 50 years (Chapter 3). During this period, tile drains slowly disintegrated and became less effective. Repair work and ditch cleaning was often neglected, grassland expanded and many fields became wet again. This led to an increase of Snipe and Redshank, especially in the south and east, as again documented in county bird books of the period (Parslow 1973, Shrubb 2003). How far the breeding populations of other birds of wet grassland were affected is unclear, but species such as Reed Warbler and Yellow Wagtail remained widespread.

The onset of the Second World War triggered a campaign to repair broken drainage systems and to return grassland to arable. Emphasis was on cleaning out ditches, enabling the old tile drains to work more effectively. At the same time, the deepening, canalisation and embanking of rivers and other watercourses ensured that the water was rapidly carried away. On really wet land, drainage sometimes required the construction of new watercourses and the installation of pumps where gravity flow was insufficient. Land drainage continued to be grant-aided at 50% or more of the cost until 1980, thereafter reducing to nil by 1988; but in some circumstances grant aid from the EU at 15% remained available. Between 1940 and 1980, some 1.91 million hectares – nearly 9% of Britain's total land area – were re-drained. This period of renewed land drainage saw the development of flexible plastic drainage pipes, laid by machines that dug the ditch, laid the pipe and covered it in one operation. Water enters via perforations in the pipe and, as with tile drains, the pipes open into ditches at the field edges.

During the 1970s–90s, damp grasslands everywhere were ruthlessly drained, and impacts on breeding waders were immediate and widely reported (e.g. Allison et al. 1974, Baines 1988, Fuller 1994, Chapter 13). In an attempt to stem the losses, nature reserves were established by the RSPB and other conservation bodies. Some remaining areas were thereby preserved, and others were re-created by raising water levels and re-wetting the land. Such sites were necessarily restricted to areas where water levels could be raised without affecting nearby land. Examples include Ham Wall in Somerset, Otmoor in Oxfordshire and Lakenheath in Suffolk, all managed by the RSPB. Such reserves soon came to support a wide range of birdlife, compared to the fields they replaced, and facilitated the recent breeding in Britain of bird species formerly lost (Box 14). However, as with many other semi-natural habitats in Britain, most remaining areas of marshland are too small and uniform to support all potential species.

BOX 14. The recent restoration of marshland birds in Britain

In the 20th century – as conservation gained momentum – several marshland species were able to breed again in Britain, mainly in newly created habitat, and some have since re-established sizeable nesting populations. By 2015, Bitterns had reached more than 150 booming males, Marsh Harriers more than 350 pairs, and Avocets more than 1,700 pairs (and more than 7,000 wintering birds). The Little Egret provides the most striking example of likely re-colonisation. After centuries of absence, this species began summering here in numbers from the 1990s; it was first recorded breeding on Brownsea Island, Dorset, in 1996, and near Cork in Ireland in 1997. By 2015, more than 800 nesting pairs were known, spread over much of southern Britain and southern Ireland, gradually advancing northwards. Cranes began to re-establish themselves in East Anglia in the late 20th century (first recorded breeding in 1981 in Norfolk), and in recent years have numbered around 20 nesting pairs in several widely scattered sites, including two in Scotland. They have also been reintroduced to southwest England, with 93 captive-raised birds released during 2010–15. In 2013, two unsuccessful nesting attempts were recorded, and by 2015, 16 pairs held territory, and three raised young to fledging (Great Crane Project website). Various other marshland species, formerly eliminated from Britain, have bred in small numbers in recent years, including Spoonbills, Great White Egrets, Purple Herons and Little Bitterns (Holling et al. 2016). Clearly, habitat restoration and other conservation efforts are paying off.

FIG 172. Cranes Grus grus on wet grassland. These birds were once widespread in Britain, but ceased breeding in the 17th century. The birds have since re-established a small breeding population in southeast England and have been reintroduced into southwest England (Chris Knights).

THE DOWNSIDE OF LAND DRAINAGE

Rainwater drains from land to sea, as it always did. But what has changed over the centuries, thanks to human action, is the speed with which this process happens. In the past, a rainstorm could have taken weeks or months to travel from hilltop through lowland to estuary. But the same journey can now be accomplished in a matter of hours, as one short-lived torrent. Because of drainage, the land can no longer absorb the water as it once did, and over most of the lowlands, winding rivers, marshes and natural floodplains no longer exist to hold and slow the water on its seaward journey.

Land drainage has also produced a much sharper distinction between land and water than existed naturally. There is now little of the intermediate marshy land so widespread in the past, so important to many wild plants and animals, and crucial to wise flood management. Whenever there are floods in the lower parts of rivers, whether affecting built-up or farmed land, the cry is always for more rapid drainage, river dredging and flood barriers. The latter are clearly necessary now to protect some low-lying towns, with buildings on former floodplains. However, a cheaper, more effective and lasting solution on many rivers would be to retain more of the water in the upper reaches of catchments from which it is naturally released more slowly into rivers. For in general, the faster the water is shunted downstream, the greater the risk of flooding in the lower parts.

One of the most ill-conceived activities of 20th-century agriculture was the drainage of upland peat bogs, in the interests of sheep and grouse. Peat covers large areas of rain-soaked hill country with an absorbent layer up to several metres thick. In its natural state, this peat acted as a huge absorbent sponge over many upland areas, soaking up rain as it fell and releasing it slowly over the ensuing weeks. The digging of drainage ditches through the peat not only reduced its ability to absorb rainfall, so that outflow became more rapid, but, as on the fens, it increased the drying, erosion and oxidation of the peat, adding further carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. The devastating floods of Lynmouth in August 1952, which destroyed much of the town and killed many people, were attributed partly to drainage of the upstream bogs on Exmoor so that they were no longer able to absorb torrential rainfall. Sixty years after the event, with the threat of more disasters, a programme was started to block and fill in the drains on Exmoor and Dartmoor, and restore the bogs to a more natural state. Intact peat bogs offer other benefits: they are rich in insects in summer, providing a crucial food source for many upland birds, including the recently hatched chicks of waders and grouse.

The fact that water drains away more rapidly than in the past is generally considered by farmers to be a good thing, but such rapid drainage has costs which are borne by society at large. After a period of drought, when ground is hard and compacted, water is carried away before it can fully replenish the soil or underground aquifers. It rushes towards the sea, causing rapid rises in river levels, sometimes flooding low-lying towns and villages, damaging bridges and flooding homes and properties, as has happened repeatedly in recent years. One hard-learnt lesson is that benefits accrue from slowing water down, with meanders and reed-beds, and allowing it to overspill river banks onto former flood meadows, instead of forcing it rapidly downstream. Some recent restoration projects have been aimed to 'de-canalise' rivers, to reinstate their original meandering courses, to stop unnecessary river dredging and to restore some former floodplains and other wetlands. In this way, natural processes can be used to prevent flooding of homes and properties, rather than resorting to costly engineering solutions with high maintenance needs. Wildlife requiring water and wet ground, including many bird species, would benefit from the additional habitats. In addition, if water travels slowly, it can deposit most of its silt en route, fertilising floodplains, instead of swishing it down to the sea to create more mudflat. Clearly, in these times of climate change and increased flood risk, land and water management need to change in Britain, giving less priority to intensive agriculture, and more to the absorption of rainfall by land in order to slow its seaward journey, a change that could bring greater net benefits to both people and wildlife.

All the time, the climate of Britain is getting warmer and wetter. The year 2000 was the wettest on record, followed by 2012, while January 2014 was the wettest month in almost 250 years. On 5 December 2015, the most rain ever recorded anywhere in Britain in a 24-hour period (341 mm) fell at Honiston Pass in Cumbria, with the previous record in 2009 also in Cumbria. At a national scale, the winter floods of 2015–16 were the most extreme on record, causing structural damage topping £5 billion, much more than the annual agricultural subsidy. So far this century, most of the major rivers in Britain have over-spilled their banks on one or more occasions, many flooding towns and villages. Such events have occurred in most of the counties in Britain, summer or winter. In each major event, hundreds of homes and other properties were flooded, and stone bridges that had stood for centuries were washed away. In the winter of 2013–14 the Thames Valley was inundated, the Somerset Levels lay under water for weeks on end, and part of the main railway line to the southwest was destroyed. Each event brought clamour for more expensive engineering solutions and more river dredging. Perversely, the deeper channels created by dredging allow high tides to move further upstream, forcing rivers to flood neighbouring land. The floods of recent years result from a combination of climate change and recent agricultural and land drainage policy. Natural flood prevention entails undoing some of the damage caused by this policy, to create more space for temporary water before it reaches the towns.

FIG 173. Flooding of the River Nith near Dumfries in winter 2012 (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

CONCLUDING REMARKS

The creation of large arterial drainage channels in Britain extends back at least to Roman times, but the process became widespread during the 17th and 18th centuries. The resulting drainage of major areas of marshland led to the loss from Britain of huge areas of natural habitat, together with the many marshland bird species that this habitat supported, including Cranes, various herons, egrets and others. In addition, under-drainage of existing farmland (field drainage) became widespread from the 19th century. Up to two-thirds of all lowland farmland in Britain now depends on artificial drainage. In the past, wet grassland habitats such as grazing marsh, floodplain grassland, wash-lands and water meadows were valued agriculturally for their spring growth, resistance to drought and annual influx of water and fertile sediments. However, in the latter half of the 20th century, agricultural 'improvement' of these areas through better land drainage, more intensive grassland management and conversion to arable resulted in the loss of most wet grassland, and the birds and other wildlife it supported.

Through land drainage, Britain is a much drier place than in the past, and marshland and wet grassland are more localised, but damaging floods and water shortages have become more frequent. The widespread damaging floods of recent years can be attributed to a combination of climate change bringing more extreme rainfall events than in the past, coupled with recent land drainage policy. In particular, the drainage of upland peatland, the straightening, dredging and canalisation of rivers, and general field drainage speeds the flow of water from land to sea, and causes flooding of low-lying towns. In the past, much of the water that fell on the land was held there, being released more slowly over a longer period; floods were less extreme, and affected mainly natural floodplains.

Given the current human population and its distribution in Britain, it is naive to think that any more than a small part of the original wetland could be restored, but the creation in appropriate places of more marshland and wet grassland than is currently present could bring major benefits to flood control, recreation and wildlife populations.

## CHAPTER 16

## Open Waters

WETLANDS ADD BEAUTY AND diversity to any landscape, but on low ground in Britain they do not exist in isolation from intensive agriculture. They are important not only for the aquatic species they support, but also in providing a base for others that can feed on the surrounding farmland, and a food supply for visiting terrestrial species (Chapter 1). With so few insects in modern farmland, wetlands have become increasingly important foraging areas for hirundines and other insect-eating species. Some wetlands, including farm ponds and flood meadows, form integral parts of farmland, whereas lakes, reservoirs and rivers might be considered more independent. However, all these waters act as centres for birds that feed on farmland, and all are polluted by agrochemicals. They are therefore relevant in the context of this book.

Freshwaters can conveniently be divided into still waters, such as lakes and ponds, and moving waters, such as rivers and streams. Together with various forms of marshland, these wetlands now occupy only 3.3% of the total surface area of Britain, but are estimated to hold around 10% of all plant and animal species. They provide water for domestic, agricultural and industrial use, and have great recreational, cultural and scenic value. However, owing mainly to pollution and uncaring treatment, many freshwaters in Britain now support only a fraction of the plant and animal life they once held. Threats vary from pollution, recreation activities and water abstraction to invasive non-native plant and animal species. Whereas in the 19th and early 20th centuries, most pollutants in freshwaters in Britain came from industry, since the mid-20th century they have come increasingly from agriculture, chiefly in the form of fertilisers and pesticides. According to the 2013 State of Nature report, some 57% of freshwater-related animals and plants (out of 1008 species assessed) have declined within the last 60 years, about half of them strongly so (Burns et al. 2013).

FIG 174. Two contrasting lakes: top, the oligotrophic Loch Druidibeg on South Uist, Outer Hebrides. Shrubs and small trees have survived only on the loch islands that cannot be reached by sheep (Ian Newton); above, Castle Loch, Lochmaben, Dumfriesshire, a natural lake which formerly held a rare fish species, the Vendace Coregonus vandesius, which disappeared in the 1990s probably partly through eutrophication (Ian Newton).

Aquatic plants range from floating species (such as duckweeds) and submerged species rooted in the bottom with leaves underwater or on the surface, to emergent plants which protrude above the surface. Some animal species, such as aquatic worms and fish, spend their entire lives in water; while others, such as mayflies and dragonflies, have life cycles that are completed partly out of water. Birds use freshwater habitats for foraging, nesting and roosting; they particularly exploit the concentrated food supplies created by large numbers of midges and other insects emerging simultaneously from the water, while waders and others find food in soft damp mud around the water's edge.

LAKES, PONDS AND CANALS

Unlike upland lakes, most of which survive in a fairly natural state, most lowland lakes in Britain are man-made and relatively recent. Many result from sand and gravel extraction, mining subsidence, landscaping operations or water storage schemes. Other small water bodies have developed in old quarries, clay pits, brick pits and the like. Fishponds date back to remote antiquity and were prevalent in the 12th–16th centuries, owned by the nobility and church, but subsequently declined. Streams were dammed to provide ponds to drive mills, or to create the shapely sheets of water in landscaped parks. Even the natural-looking Norfolk Broads developed from the large holes left by peat digging, mainly in the 11th–13th centuries. Canals were constructed mainly in the 18th–19th centuries, chiefly to facilitate the transport of heavy materials over long distances, and thereby helping industrial development. They were soon replaced by the railways and, as their original purpose declined, many became overgrown, providing better and less disturbed habitat for birds. They also brought stretches of open water to areas that formerly lacked them. Paradoxically, during a period of relentless land drainage during the 20th century, the numbers of open waters in Britain increased greatly, mainly through the creation of gravel pits and reservoirs. The Countryside Survey 2007 (CS2007) estimated the total area of standing water, canals and ditches in Britain at about 284,000 ha, forming 1.3% of the total surface area of Britain (Carey et al. 2008).

FIG 175. The Chesterfield canal, cleaned out in recent years, now supports a wealth of fish and birdlife (Ian Newton).

Open waters vary in several significant respects, including the nutrient content of the water, the depth and surface area, the structure and length of shoreline, and the nature of the edge vegetation. All these features influence their bird populations. Many upland lakes are large and windswept, of low nutrient status (oligotrophic), with deep water and bare stony shorelines. In contrast, the more productive (eutrophic) lowland lakes tend to be shallower with muddy shores, often supporting lush reed-beds and other waterside vegetation. Not surprisingly, eutrophic lakes support more birds of more species than similar-sized oligotrophic lakes. Many species – including Great-crested, Little and Black-necked Grebes, Little Egret, Cormorant, Mute Swan, Gadwall, Garganey, Shoveler, Tufted Duck, Pochard and Coot – normally occur on eutrophic waters, while a smaller number of species – including Red-throated and Black-throated Divers, Common Scoter, Goldeneye, Red-breasted Merganser and Goosander – are found primarily on oligotrophic waters, although some also gain food from the sea in the breeding season as well as in winter. Other aquatic birds, such as Grey Heron, Greylag Goose, Mallard, Teal and Osprey, occur on both oligotrophic and eutrophic waters. On both types, some species are found on the open water itself (mostly diving ducks, grebes and divers), while others occur mainly round the margins (mostly dabbling ducks and Moorhens, some of which also feed on land). Most water-birds nest in the vegetation around the edge or on islands which offer security from most mammalian predators. Other species, such as geese and gulls, now rely on lakes mainly for nesting or roosting, and get almost all their food from nearby farmland. Common Terns frequently nest on islands in eutrophic lakes, and feed on fish and aquatic insects. In addition, several wader species which nest in wet grassland, such as Lapwing, Redshank and Snipe, feed around the edges of water bodies, especially in the non-breeding period.

FIG 176. Two birds of eutrophic waters: left, Great-crested Grebe Podiceps cristatus (Richard Chandler); right, Pochard Aythya ferina (Alan Martin).

FIG 177. Two birds that nest on islets in lowland lakes and reservoirs; left, Black-headed Gull Chroicocephalus ridibundus (Allan Hale); right, Common Tern Sterna hirundo (Frank Snykers).

The main beneficiaries of new water bodies created during the 20th century have been dabbling ducks such as Mallard, Shoveler, Gadwall and Teal, and diving ducks such as Tufted Duck and Pochard. In addition, Mute Swans, Greylag, Canada, Barnacle and Egyptian Geese have found safety and nesting sites at these new wetlands, and gulls both breed and roost there, their numbers largest in winter. Many of these species move out onto nearby farmland to feed, gulls eating mainly soil-dwelling invertebrates or spilled grain, and waterfowl various crops and crop-waste (Chapter 6). Many artificial lakes are now regularly stocked with fish, which provide additional food for birds such as Cormorants, whose numbers have expanded greatly in recent decades. In reeds around the edges, Reed and Sedge Warblers occur, sometimes parasitised by Cuckoos, and larger reed-beds also hold Bearded Tits, Water Rails, Bitterns and Marsh Harriers. In addition, the history and spread of the Great-crested Grebe, Common Tern and Little Ringed Plover in Britain have been closely linked with the increase in sand and gravel pits.

FIG 178. Two introduced goose species which have benefited from man-made lakes on low ground: left, Canada Goose Branta canadensis (Ian Newton); right, Egyptian Goose Alopochen aegyptiacus (Richard Chandler).

FIG 179. Cormorant Phalacrocorax carbo numbers have greatly increased in association with the stocking of new lakes and reservoirs with fish (Alan Martin).

These open waters thus support an avifauna somewhat different in composition from that of the marshland lost in earlier centuries (Chapter 15). While Bitterns and Marsh Harriers are more restricted now than in earlier times, open-water species such as Tufted Duck and Great-crested Grebe are probably more numerous and widespread. Some of the larger lowland reservoirs, with their shallow, nutrient-rich water and fringing vegetation, have become hotspots of biodiversity within farmed landscapes, attracting a wide range of breeding and wintering birds, as well as passing migrants and rare vagrants. One of the best known is Rutland Water in central England, which has a surface area of around 1,086 ha and was completed in 1976. An area of 417 ha at the western end is managed specifically for birds, and has become one of the best places for waterfowl in Britain. Up to 2008, some 268 bird species had been recorded there, with about 70 species breeding regularly. In some years, flocks of moulting Tufted Ducks reached nearly 10,000 and Pochard more than 1,000, making Rutland Water one of the most important moulting sites for these species in Europe.

Another well-known reservoir is Chew Valley Lake in Somerset, completed in 1956 and covering an area of around 486 ha. By 2010, more than 270 bird species had been recorded there, while in some years moulting Great-crested Grebes numbered more than 600, and wintering ducks (of 12 species) up to 4,000. A staggering 55,000 gulls have roosted there in winter, mainly Black-headed and Common Gulls, spreading widely over the surrounding land to feed. Further north, the much smaller Ogston Reservoir (83 ha) in Derbyshire constructed in 1958 had accumulated a bird list of 242 species by 2012, of which about 85 species are known to have bred; while Carsington Reservoir in the same county was constructed in 1991, and by 2012 had a bird list of 222 species, supporting winter roosts of up to 10,000 Lesser Black-backed Gulls and more than 2,000 Coots (Frost & Shaw 2013). Similar details for other reservoirs situated in lowland farmland can be found in county bird books and the annual reports of ornithological societies. The important point is that, while many birds at these reservoirs obtain their food from the wetland itself, some of the most numerous species obtain some or all of their food from surrounding farmland. Without the open water for roosting, these birds could not be present, and without the productive farmland within easy reach, they could not be present in such numbers.

FIG 180. Ogston Reservoir in Derbyshire from the air (Roy Frost).

Farm ponds

In the past, some form of wetland was present on almost every farm, if only in the form of a pond, dug to provide drinking water for livestock, often at places where several fields met, so that animals in each field could gain access. Such ponds were often stocked with fish, and were used by domestic ducks and geese. Other ponds resulted from clay or marl digging. In addition, larger ponds were often dug in villages to provide water for drinking or fire dousing. New ponds of any kind are quickly colonised by aquatic plants and animals. They provide feeding, drinking and bathing opportunities for many bird species from the surrounding land, safe roost sites for some, and mud for nest-building by others. With the advent of troughs and piped water, many of these ponds were filled in or became silted and overgrown.

FIG 181. Two birds that take advantage of farm ponds: left, House Sparrows Passer domesticus bathing (Chris Knights); right, House Martin Delichon urbicum collecting mud for nest-building (Chris Knights).

As long as some open water remains, small ponds are occupied particularly by Moorhens, which can make do with less open water than most other aquatic birds, perhaps partly because they obtain some of their food from surrounding land. Other species are sometimes found on larger farm ponds: Reed Buntings, Sedge and Reed Warblers inhabit tall vegetation around the edges, while Pied and Yellow Wagtails feed at pond edges bordered by short vegetation or mud.

FIG 182. Little Grebe Tachibaptus ruficollis (Richard Chandler).

However small, ponds are important for the contribution they make to insects and other biodiversity. Among 57 farmland bird species examined on Common Birds Census (CBC) plots, ponds emerged as the most important feature influencing the presence of five species – particularly Moorhen – but the numbers of 28 other species were also enhanced by the presence of ponds (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986). Only the bigger farm ponds, created more recently to provide water for irrigation, are large enough to hold a wider range of species, such as Little Grebe, Coot and various ducks.

At a regional level, however, ponds have been found to support substantially more species overall, more unique species and more scarce species than other water-body types. This is partly because ponds differ so much from one another, and from some other wetlands, in the plants and animals they hold. The collective biodiversity value of small farm ponds scattered over a region can therefore be considerable, providing they are not too polluted (Williams et al. 2003).

In recent decades, some farmers have created reservoirs to store water which is collected during winter when it is surplus to needs, and used for irrigation during summer droughts. Some of these farm reservoirs are strictly utilitarian rectangular troughs lined with clay or polythene. They nevertheless support some invertebrates and provide resting places for ducks and gulls, which may retreat in the evening to larger inland waters or the coast to roost. However, other farmers have shaped their reservoirs to encourage suitable fringe vegetation and provide refuges for ducks and other wildfowl. This is one way in which grants to farmers, ostensibly for irrigation, have benefited wildlife.

According to successive Countryside Surveys, the numbers of ponds in Britain (excluding garden ponds) increased by 6% between 1990 and 1998, and by a further 13% to 2007. This increase was driven mainly by agri-environment funding, but was nowhere near enough to offset the losses of earlier decades. In the late 19th century there had been more than a million ponds in Britain, but in 2007 there were only 478,000 (Williams 1997, Carey et al. 2008). Moreover, in 2007, the biological condition of only 8% of ponds was classed as good, most being ranked as poor or very poor, largely because of their continuing contamination with agrochemicals. Invariably, well-vegetated good-quality ponds with clear water and high species diversity were surrounded by wide buffer strips of unfertilised grass running around the entire pond. This buffer zone was evidently enough to significantly reduce the flow of agrochemicals into the water.

RIVERS, STREAMS AND DITCHES

Rivers offer varied environments for birds, with species changing according to gradient and speed of flow, nutrient status, and associated features. Upland rivers are distinguished by faster rates of flow, rocky substrates and the rarity of floodplains. Lowland rivers are generally wider and deeper, flow more slowly, and usually have at least one extensive floodplain in the lower reaches. In both summer and winter, they support more bird species than upland rivers. Along narrow waterways, trees and bushes produce shade which reduces plant productivity in the water, but they provide habitat in their own right, and add nutrients to the stream in the form of leaves and other debris. Insects falling from trees also provide food for fish and birds.

Apart from the fish-eating Grey Heron and Cormorant, the commonest large birds of lowland rivers include the Mute Swan, Mallard and Moorhen, all three of which feed to some extent on neighbouring farmland. Other riverine species make little use of farmland, although the migratory Yellow Wagtail is primarily associated with wet meadows beside rivers, but also breeds in cereals and other crops on better-drained land (Chapter 10). The less migratory Pied Wagtail is one of the most widespread riparian species in Britain but also occurs commonly around farmyards away from running water. The Reed Bunting also breeds beside rivers and other wetlands, but forages widely over farmland.

FIG 183. Mute Swan Cynus olor, one of the most familiar birds of slow-flowing lowland rivers and lakes (Ian Newton).

Few, if any, of Britain's lowland rivers and streams remain in a natural state. Over the centuries, the courses of many rivers have been altered, and their channels straightened, widened and deepened to achieve more rapid flow and reduce the flooding of adjoining fields. Through these actions, many lowland rivers have now lost their original banks and meanders, together with many of their other natural features, such as shoals, beaches, islands, riffles, deep pools, oxbow lakes and muddy margins (Chapter 15). During 1994–97, a survey by the Environment Agency of some 5,600 sites throughout Britain revealed evidence of past river widening, deepening or straightening (often all three) at 80% of these sites. Engineering work to restructure bank-sides, farming to the water's edge and removal of aquatic and emergent vegetation had further degraded much riverine habitat.

Carried out over considerable lengths of river, these processes have had profound effects on many birds. Various studies revealed lower densities and numbers of breeding species on 'managed' stretches than on more natural ones (Fuller 1982). The removal of bank-side and emergent vegetation clearly affect those species that nest, feed or roost there, including Reed and Sedge Warblers, Pied Wagtails and Reed Buntings (Williamson 1971). Birds that depend on special features such as vertical earth banks (Kingfisher, Sand Martin), shingle banks (Oystercatcher, Ringed Plover), or shallows (Grey Wagtail) suffer from the destruction or alteration of these features. In 1978, natural stretches of the River Wye held an average of 146 pairs of 25 bird species per 10 km, while equivalent managed stretches held only 43 pairs of 11 species per 10 km (RSPB report, cited in Mason et al. 1984).

FIG 184. Birds that require steep earth banks in which to dig their nest burrows: left, Kingfisher Alcedo atthis (Frank Snykers); right, Sand Martin Riparia riparia (Chris Knights).

More than 90% of river catchments in Britain drain farmland, at least over part of their area (Raven et al. 1998), so rivers have not escaped the other changes associated with agricultural intensification. Increases in agrochemical inputs are widespread, as are silting through soil erosion and destruction of waterside vegetation. Enhanced drainage that results from river management also affects flood meadows and other riverside habitats. In addition, many small lowland rivers have changed through excessive water abstraction which has resulted in lower rates of flow and in some rivers drying out in summer, altering the conditions on which many plants and animals depend. Water needs are greatest in years of drought, and river flows are lowest when the need to irrigate crops is greatest. At the present time, about 15% of river catchments are deemed to be 'over-abstracted'. All these changes act to reduce the wildlife value of lowland rivers and streams. Overall in Britain, with few exceptions, the best-quality riverine habitats are now found in the uplands where most waters are oligotrophic. The Goosander, Common Sandpiper, Dipper and Grey Wagtail are confined to fast-flowing rivers and streams in the uplands during the breeding season, but the Grey Wagtail also breeds sparsely across the lowlands.

FIG 185. Some birds of fast-flowing, oligotrophic rivers: upper left, Grey Wagtail Motacilla cinerea (Edmond Fellowes); upper right, Dipper Cinclus cinclus (Keith Kirk); lower left, Common Sandpiper Actitis hypoleucos (Edmund Fellowes); lower right, Goosander Mergus merganser and ducklings (Keith Kirk).

Over the last two decades of the 20th century, under EU legislation, attempts were made by government to strengthen environmental regulations and improve the management of rivers and streams. In CS1990, around 40% of streams across Britain were judged to be in good condition, and by 1998 that figure had risen to around 60%, with further improvement through to CS2007. Plant species richness increased in this time, as did the abundance of species that prefer clean water. This was in contrast to the situation with farm ponds. However, improvements in physical and biological condition were most marked in headwater streams, less so in the lowlands with more intensive agriculture. Bank-side vegetation changed in this period, and under reduced physical disturbance, more bushes such as bramble and hawthorn became established. CS2007 estimated that rivers and streams in Britain occupied 58,000 ha, just over 0.26% of the total land area (Carey et al. 2008).

Ditches

Ditches are man-made surface drains that can range from permanently wet channels up to several metres wide and deep to small, often dry, channels less than a metre wide and deep. Ditches can hold a variety of plants and animals, and also can trap chemicals and sediments, thus acting as a filter for water and improving its downstream quality. The small drainage ditches that run along the boundaries of many fields receive their water largely from pipe drains that discharge into them, chiefly after heavy rain. At other times such ditches contain no water, and therefore support little or no aquatic life. However, their bottoms are sometimes damp enough to support reeds and other tall plants suitable for Reed Warblers, and remain soft enough in summer for Song Thrushes and other birds to find soil-dwelling invertebrates.

In low-lying flat regions, such as the East Anglian Fens, the larger ditches often contain water year-round. Most of those situated between fields are only 1–2 m across, but others, often bearing names like 'sixteen foot' or 'forty foot', are much wider and often navigable, supporting abundant water plants, fish and invertebrates, and birds such as grebes, ducks, Mute Swans, Greylag Geese, Coots and Moorhens. The sloping banks of these large ditches provide cover, used by birds and small mammals, and often attract vole-hunting Kestrels and Barn Owls.

FIG 186. Modern ditch-clearing operation, an essential job to maintain ditch function, and usually undertaken every few years (Ian Newton).

Ditch clearing was one of the traditional jobs for farm labourers in winter. Nowadays, the job is done mechanically, and the tendency is to remove all shrubs and other vegetation to give easy access to machinery. A recently cleaned-out ditch has sides neatly plastered with clay dug from the channel, with no vegetation growing on the banks or on the bottom. But both ditch and spoil are soon re-colonised by plants and animals. Birds nest and feed in the vegetation that develops, perhaps Reed Buntings, Sedge and Reed Warblers, plus other species as shrubs begin to grow. Sometimes ditches are left for several years between clearings, during which time their conservation value may rise, only to be destroyed again when they are next cleaned out. But periodic clearing is necessary for their long-term persistence and effectiveness in drainage. With larger ditches, clearing opposite banks in different years can provide continuity of habitat through time.

IMPORTANCE OF OPEN WATERS IN FARMLAND

As agriculture and land drainage have intensified, remaining wetlands have become increasingly important in lowland Britain because of the diversity of plants and animals they often support. They are a good source of insect food for birds, attracting Pied and Yellow Wagtails, Song Thrushes, Starlings, Reed Buntings, Tree Sparrows, and waders. The once widely distributed Tree Sparrow has declined by around 90% in recent decades; the species needs insects to feed its young, and over much of Britain most remaining colonies are close to water. And as wet grassland has declined, the edges of open water have become a more important nesting habitat for birds such as Grasshopper Warbler and Reed Bunting. Clean open waters are also important for other vertebrates, including fish and amphibians, Water Voles and Otters. However, they also provide habitat for the introduced American Mink, which since the 1960s has become a serious predator of many wetland birds. Mink prey extensively on the eggs, chicks or adults of ground-nesting birds, including gulls and terns, waterfowl and divers. They swim well, so can get to islands to raid nests which hitherto had been safe from mammalian predators. In some areas, Mink have been held responsible for declines in the distributions and numbers of several wetland species, notably Black-headed Gulls, which over the years have become concentrated in fewer and larger colonies (Dunn, in Mitchell et al. 2004). Mink are much less numerous now than in the 1990s, their decline in some areas having coincided with the recovery of Otters, which limit their numbers. Mink are also controlled by trapping in some game-rearing areas and wetland nature reserves.

By providing secure roosting sites, lakes and other open waters enable waterfowl and gulls to exploit feeding areas on farmland that would not otherwise be available to them. Their numbers are greatly swollen each winter by immigrants from distant breeding areas, extending from Greenland east to Siberia. In recent winters, more than 2.5 million migratory waterfowl have been counted in and around Britain, including some 18,000 swans, around 785,000 geese, more than 1.5 million freshwater ducks and over 226,000 sea-ducks (Musgrove et al. 2013). To these could be added up to 180,000 Coots. Apart from the sea-ducks, many of the most numerous species feed partly or entirely on farmland.

Benefiting from the greater numbers of man-made lakes available as habitat, some wintering waterfowl have increased markedly in recent decades. During the last 40 years of the 20th century, routine counts suggested that wintering Gadwall had increased about tenfold, Pochard about fourfold, and Teal and Tufted Duck about threefold. Wintering Mallard numbers increased and then decreased over the same period, but the figures were affected by the artificial rearing and release of Mallards by shooting interests, with up to 400,000 birds released in some years (Owen et al. 1986, Cabot 2009).

The larger waterfowl that roost on open waters feed heavily on farmland, mainly on crop-waste, grass and young cereal plants. Their marked increases in numbers since the mid-20th century can be attributed partly to the provision of safe roosting sites and reduced shooting pressure, but also to the nutritious feeding available on farmland (Chapter 6).

Gulls on farmland feed mainly on invertebrates (especially earthworms and beetles and their larvae), but the larger gull species take greater proportions of larger items, such as mice and voles, the eggs and chicks of other birds, and sometimes adult birds, in addition to carrion. The Great Black-backed Gull, in particular, hunts mainly birds and mammals, and can kill and swallow items as large as small Rabbits and ducks. It is viewed as a threatening presence around lambing fields, to which it is attracted by afterbirths and stillborn lambs. The smaller Black-headed, Common and Mediterranean Gulls feed more in fields than the larger gulls, and all three frequently follow the plough, seizing any invertebrates turned to the surface. The larger gulls in turn take more food from rubbish dumps. All species also eat grain whenever it is available, and occasionally rob food from other species (Chapter 12). The overall numbers of gulls in Britain were estimated at 3.8 million in the winters of 2003–04 and 2004–05, the resident birds being joined by immigrants from abroad (Burton et al. 2013).

FIG 187. Two large gulls which frequently roost on large reservoirs and feed on surrounding farmland or rubbish dumps: left, Herring Gull Larus argentatus (Frank Snykers); right, Lesser Black-backed Gull L. fuscus (Edmund Fellowes).

AGRICULTURAL POLLUTION OF WETLANDS

Open waters on farmland may be insulated from the urban and industrial pollutants that had previously affected many of our major rivers and lakes, but they have been more affected by agrochemicals, a diffuse cocktail of fertilisers and pesticides which are washed from the soil by rain. Some are dissolved in rainwater while others are attached to soil particles transported to wetlands by erosion. These chemicals greatly reduce the range of species that can live in farm wetlands, and fish and amphibians have been eliminated from many ponds and streams since the 1950s. Contamination of freshwaters with nitrate and phosphate fertilisers and slurry initially increases their productivity, but further input causes eutrophication, resulting in algal growth that chokes out the remaining life. The water becomes turbid, reducing light penetration. Submerged water-weeds and the animals they support rapidly disappear, and it becomes hard for birds which hunt underwater to find their prey. Rotting organic matter reduces oxygen levels, owing to respiration by the bacteria involved, which in turn kills many aquatic animals, including fish. Blue-green algae are sometimes associated with eutrophication, producing toxins to which fish and terrestrial animals are susceptible. Most pollutants that reach rivers end up in the sea, and many eastern coastal areas have periodically suffered from eutrophication and its associated toxin-producing dinoflagellate blooms, sometimes obvious as 'red tides'. These toxins have in turn caused periodic mass die-offs of seabirds (Armstrong et al. 1978, Newton 2013a).

In addition to fertilisers, pesticides have become widely distributed through the freshwaters of Britain. A survey of 3,500 sites in England and Wales by the National Rivers Authority in the 1990s revealed that 100 out of 120 pesticides checked for were detected, and five herbicides (atrazine, diuron, bentazone, isoproturon and mecoprop) regularly exceeded the limits set for drinking water. At sufficient concentration in water, pesticides can wipe out practically all aquatic life, but at the levels they are usually found, they kill only the species that are most sensitive to them, notably mayflies, stoneflies, caddisflies and amphipod crustaceans. In effect, then, agrochemical pollution means that many lowland ponds and streams can no longer support the range of plants and animals that they once did. Frogs, toads and newts rapidly disappeared from most farmland ponds in the 1950s–60s, and on low ground survived chiefly in suburban gardens and other places largely untainted by agrochemicals. Even mountain streams are not immune to the effects of pesticides, as they can be contaminated by the insecticides used in sheep-dips. Contamination of public water supplies is a big problem, costly to deal with, and where water authorities own the land around reservoirs, they often ensure that it is farmed with minimal agrochemical use.

Discharge of pollutants from point sources, such as sewage and factory waste, is fairly easy to control, and became regulated under two EU Directives. Some agricultural pollution, resulting from seepage from silage or manure heaps or from careless pesticide disposal, are also relatively easy to pinpoint and control. Single pulses of pollutants are less easy to detect in rivers, as they are rapidly washed away, killing organisms as they pass downstream. For this reason, aquatic pollution is often monitored in the organisms it affects, whether by their presence or absence or by pollutant levels in their tissues. However, diffuse agricultural pollution, involving sediments, fertilisers and pesticides washed into water bodies by rainwater draining in from all sides, is much more difficult to tackle. Not only do these pollutants enter the water via the soil, rather than directly, but any one water system may be bordered by land belonging to many different people, making it difficult to attribute pollution to any one of them. In any case, these major polluting activities arise chiefly from routine pesticide and fertiliser use, and are thus regarded as legitimate.

Improved management

The management of freshwaters has improved from the 1990s. Changes to environmental legislation provided new obligations to protect water bodies, largely under the EU Water Framework Directive. Under this Directive, a healthy eutrophic lake is seen as having clear water, with lots of water plants, low algal populations and good light penetration. The initial legislation called for restoration of all freshwater areas in the EU by 2015, a deadline later extended to 2027. Nevertheless in Britain, pollution from sewage fell greatly, owing to tighter regulation of the water companies and more rigorous law enforcement (Environment Agency 1997). Agri-environment grants allowed farmers to improve the management of existing wetlands on their farms and to create new ones. Some measures were designed to reduce diffuse water pollution by agrochemicals. They included the creation of uncultivated buffer strips next to watercourses, reduced use of fertilisers, and better management of nitrate runoff, together with support for ditch, river and pond management, organic farming and woodland restoration.

Riparian buffer strips, managed separately from the rest of the field, can reduce sedimentation and agrochemical pollution, as well as downstream flood risk (Environment Agency 1996a, 1996b, Castle et al. 1999). Such strips of uncultivated land bordering rivers and streams also enhance visual amenity, and provide habitats for terrestrial and freshwater wildlife, and corridors for their movements. Localised introduction of these strips increased the wildlife of farm wetlands, and provided fresh habitat for a range of different bird species (Carey et al. 2008). Compared to many other habitats, wildlife-rich wetlands can be restored or created in a relatively short time. Once the input of pollutants has been reduced, many small wetlands recover quickly. Aquatic insects colonise naturally, but amphibians, fish and Water Voles may often have to be reintroduced.

Although many river systems remain in a poor state, other formerly damaged rivers have improved as a result of sewage treatment, and control of industrial effluent and agrochemical pollution. The River Thames in London is perhaps the best-known example, but another is the River Rother near Chesterfield. In the 1950s when I was a child there, this river was a lifeless waterway, stinking of industrial effluents and sewage. It is now a clean natural-looking waterway re-stocked with native fish species, and supporting Kingfishers, Herons and other birds. Some lakes have also been improved, although the process can take much longer because of the continuing release of pollutants accumulated in sediments. For example, the large freshwater Loch Leven in southeast Scotland was for many years polluted by phosphorus-rich effluent from a factory. From a peak in the 1960s and 1970s, input from this source was progressively reduced to almost nil by 1989, and from 1995 attempts were also made to reduce the diffuse input of agrochemicals by use of uncultivated buffer strips along the main feeder stream. These measures were successful, but it took about 20 years from 1989 for nutrients in the lake water to decline, and for the water to become clear enough for larger water plants to return to their former levels, bringing clear benefits for invertebrate, fish and bird populations (Carvalho et al. 2012). Wintering herbivorous birds, such as Coot and Pochard, showed marked increases.

In the Norfolk Broads, eutrophication became evident from the 1960s, caused by a combination of fertilisers from farmland and sewage discharges from neighbouring towns and villages. As in other cases, the once-clear water became turbid, with a greenish or brownish tinge from phytoplankton; bigger water plants largely disappeared, and invertebrate diversity declined. There were widespread losses of plant and animal life, bird deaths from botulism, and fish deaths from other toxins produced by particular phytoplankton species. Over time, nutrients concentrated in the bottom mud, and removal of this mud from Brundall Broad, which is isolated from the polluted nutrient-rich River Yare, was followed by recovery of larger water plants and benthic invertebrates (George 1977).

CONCLUDING REMARKS

Wetlands are important for the wildlife they hold, including bird species which rest on water but get most of their food from surrounding farmland. Some large reservoirs support many thousands of gulls and geese in winter, with the gulls feeding mainly on soil-dwelling invertebrates and the waterfowl on crops and crop-waste. Without these artificial lakes, these birds could not exploit the resources of inland farmland to the same extent. Most wetlands in farmland are contaminated with agrochemicals. Fertilisers cause eutrophication and algal blooms, sometimes to the level that few other plant and animal species can live there. Pesticides that get into the water kill some plants and animals, in extreme cases removing most species from small ponds and streams.

Upland lakes in Britain are mostly nutrient-poor (oligotrophic), deep with stony shores and little vegetation, whereas lowland lakes are nutrient-rich (eutrophic), mostly shallow with muddy edges, and much lush edge vegetation. Some bird species are found only on eutrophic waters, while a smaller number are found only on oligotrophic ones. Eutrophic lakes are generally rich in plant and animal life, including birds, but further input of nutrients from fertilisers leads to reduction in the variety of plants and animals they hold. Not surprisingly, lowland waters have suffered much more from agricultural impacts, particularly agrochemical use, than upland ones.

Lowland rivers tend to be large, slow-flowing and nutrient-rich, while upland ones tend to be narrower, fast-flowing and nutrient-poor. Largely different species of birds occupy the two types. Most catchments in Britain contain farmland, so their streams and rivers have not escaped the effects of agricultural intensification. River channels have often been straightened and deepened to promote rapid land drainage, features such as sand banks, meanders and oxbow lakes have been removed, and banks have often been cleared of trees and bushes to allow machines access for management. All these activities are likely to have reduced bird populations, mainly by removing habitats.

Farm ditches vary from large ones, several metres across, which hold water year-round, as found mainly in the flat lands of East Anglia, to narrow ditches on the edges of fields that receive their water through drainage pipes, and hold it only at times of heavy rain. They nevertheless support some plants and small animals that could not otherwise occur on farmland, and provide nesting and feeding places for birds. To be effective as drainage channels, they need clearing out every few years, recovering their plant and animal life between times.

Farm ponds enhance the local diversity of plant and animal life, and many bird species use them for drinking, bathing, foraging or as a source of mud for nest-building. During the 20th century, about half of all farm ponds in Britain were filled in, with adverse effects on local bird populations. In studies in the 1960s, farmland plots containing ponds supported more bird species than those without. Most remaining ponds are still polluted, but agri-environment measures promote their recovery. Across farming landscapes, aquatic plant and animal diversity does not depend solely on larger rivers and lakes, because small water bodies, such as ponds and ditches, can make significant contributions.

The condition of lowland wetlands has generally improved since the 1990s, mainly because of measures taken under the EU Water Framework Directive, together with agri-environment measures taken by individual farmers. Plants and animals have responded positively to reductions in agrochemical pollution. Other attempts have been made to clean polluted waters through reductions in point-sources of pollutants (such as sewage or factory effluent), and through the use of buffer strips of uncultivated land around still-water bodies and alongside streams. These strips reduce the input of fertilisers and pesticides.

## CHAPTER 17

## Woods, Heaths and Farmsteads

MANY BIRDS OWE THEIR presence in farmed landscapes to patches of non-farmed, semi-natural habitats scattered among the open fields (Chapter 1). Woods and hedges are in this category, and so are ponds and lakes, streams and rivers, marshes and bogs, heaths, quarries and farmsteads. Typically, each of these habitat types holds some bird species which are confined to it and also others which obtain part or all of their food from neighbouring farmland. Without these habitat features, farmland would be devoid of many of its most familar species. Part of the loss of birds from farmland over recent decades has resulted from the reduction of these 'semi-natural' or unfarmed places, as many were destroyed in the drive for more food production. The importance of wetlands to farmland wildlife was discussed in Chapter 16, and the drier habitats of woods and heaths, farmyards and farm buildings, hedges and other field boundaries are discussed in this and the next chapter.

The importance of other habitats within farmland has been shown by specific studies. For example, the Cambridgeshire parish of Hilton covered 537 ha, and held around 1,225 territorial bird pairs, with 650 pairs of 42 species in the 70 ha of village and 575 pairs of 36 species in the 467 ha of farmland (Wyllie 1976). The average density of birds in the village was therefore more than seven times that of the farmland (9.3 pairs/ha versus 1.2 pairs/ha). Moreover, nearly three-fifths of the birds on farmland nested in the hedgerows. In the year of this study (1973), Skylarks were the most numerous bird in the overall area, and Corn Buntings also occurred across the arable land. In the following decades, Skylarks greatly declined and Corn Buntings disappeared completely, further raising the contrast between farmed and non-farmed areas.

Another study area in the Lothians of southeast Scotland covered 1,735 ha of land, which held some 2,980 territorial bird pairs in 1984 (da Prato 1985). Some 1,321 pairs of 51 species were found in the 1,525 ha of farmland, while 1,459 pairs of 53 species were found in 113 ha of other habitats (woods, scrub and derelict land). The overall density of birds in these latter habitats was therefore over 15 times the density on farmland (14.6 pairs/ha versus 0.9 pairs/ha). Moreover, two-thirds of the birds on farmland nested in the hedgerows and shelter belts. Species that occurred only on farmland included waders such as Oystercatcher, Lapwing, Snipe and Curlew.

Neither of these studies recorded nesting Rooks, and in Hilton 'no attempt was made to estimate the huge populations of Starlings and House Sparrows'. In general, though, both studies emphasise the importance of non-farmed habitats in influencing the overall bird numbers in farmed landscapes. The difference arises partly because non-farmed habitats have greater vertical and spatial structure, and so provide more niches for birds than the low dense monoculture vegetation of fields. In addition, the food sources of birds in farm crops are usually much reduced through pesticide use.

Other types of studies have also revealed the importance of non-farmed habitats. For example, on CBC plots examined in 1965, overall bird densities increased with rise in the densities of hedgerows present (m/ha), and also with the densities of woodland and scrub (% of total farm area) and farm ponds (number per km2) (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986). All three correlations were mutually independent, although farms rich in hedgerows often also had at least one pond. Particular habitat features benefited more species than those that were wholly dependent on them. For example, hedgerows containing mature trees were the most important habitat element for 15 bird species but had significant influence on the numbers of another 28. The equivalent figures for woods were 8 and 24 species, for farmsteads 3 and 12, and for ponds 5 and 28. The wider effects of these habitats are not hard to explain. As described in Chapter 16, the importance of ponds extends well beyond the aquatic species wholly dependent on them, and the same is true of the habitats discussed in this chapter.

Later studies served to confirm these early findings, emphasising the importance of diversity in landscapes, including not only the semi-natural habitats present, but also the range of crops that were grown, and the nature of field boundaries. In general, the more varied the landscape, the greater the abundance and variety of bird species present (Fuller et al. 1997, 2004, Gillings & Fuller 1998, Pickett & Siriwardena 2011, Siriwardena et al. 2012, Henderson et al. 2012). However, not all species benefited from the presence of semi-natural habitats, as some thrived on open uniform landscapes that happened to provide the conditions they needed. For example, the numbers of Skylarks and Yellowhammers in study plots were related to the extent of cereal crops (Fuller et al. 1997).

Semi-natural habitats in farmed landscapes now occupy much smaller areas than in earlier centuries, but most of the remaining patches still fall under the management of farmers. For example, in 2012, woodland associated with farms (agricultural holdings) was estimated to total around 827,000 ha, while other non-agricultural habitats totalled around 332,000 ha (Defra 2012). After decades of woodland and hedgerow removal on farms, planting of new woods was encouraged by government grants from the late 1980s, and the planting and restoration of hedgerows from the late 1990s. However, these new plantings have nowhere near compensated for the losses over previous decades. In addition, any patch of semi-natural habitat on farmland is affected by what goes on in adjacent fields, and is subject to the effects of drainage, eutrophication through fertiliser use, and drift of pesticides. Most of these influences are likely to adversely affect native plants and animals.

WOODLANDS

From the start of the Neolithic period, around 6,500 years ago, the original forest that covered most of Britain was progressively removed by human action. Most had gone by Norman times, around 1,000 years ago, when around 15% of England and Wales remained wooded. By AD 1900, only 5% of Britain was under woodland. Most consisted of small patches scattered through lowland farmland, with a few more substantial areas mainly in the Scottish Highlands. These patches, together with hedgerows and scattered trees, maintained the woodland bird populations of Britain through to the latter half of the 20th century, when extensive efforts were made to increase the woodland acreage. After timber shortages during the First World War, the Forestry Commission was established in 1919, with a view to creating a strategic reserve of timber for use through the next century. Most of this new planting occurred in the uplands, and involved conifer species from continental Europe or North America. By 1940, about 6% of Britain had become wooded, by 1970 about 8%, and by the end of the 20th century around 12%, comprising nearly 2.7 million hectares (Forestry Commission 2003). As a result of this surge in planting, some four-fifths of the woodland in Britain is now less than 100 years old. About half of this total is classed as broad-leaved or mixed broad-leaved/coniferous woodland, and the rest as coniferous. Most native broad-leaved woods are now in the lowlands, chiefly in England, and most conifer forests are in the uplands, chiefly in Scotland. More than two-fifths of the total woodland in Britain now consists of introduced conifer species, largely a result of Forestry Commission policy.

FIG 188. Well-wooded landscape around Drumlanrig Castle, Dumfriesshiere (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

The category 'broad-leaved woodland' includes areas of scrub, coppice and wood pasture, along with more mature stands. Nowhere in Britain does any mature woodland remain in a wholly natural state. The term 'ancient woodlands' refers to sites that have been wooded for centuries (at least since 1600) and where the trees have arisen by natural regeneration or regrowth from cut stumps, rather than by planting. These places are often home to special plant and invertebrate communities that reflect the age of the wood and its long history of management. Such sites cover only 1.2% of the total land area of Britain, and less than 10% of the total woodland area (Hayhow et al. 2016).

Today, we tend to view agriculture and forestry as separate activities, but in earlier times farmland and woodland were managed together to meet the needs of local communities. Both provided forage for livestock, and woods also provided material for buildings, fences and fuel, as well as food for people. Almost all the present broad-leaved woods in Britain have been managed for much of their history, many as an integral part of farming. Traditional woodland management commonly involved wood pasture or coppice. Individual trees were managed specifically to produce a continual supply of new growth, by cutting the trunk close to the ground (coppicing) or higher up (pollarding), so that new shoots would emerge from around the cut surfaces.

FIG 189. Above, Coppiced Hazel Corylus avellana with one year of growth between widely spaced standard trees, Bradfield Wood, Suffolk (Rob Fuller); below, pollarded Black Poplar Populus nigra tree with young growth, Buckinghamshire (Rob Fuller).

Probably from Neolithic times on, and extending into the 20th century, many woods were managed as wood pastures, consisting of well-spaced trees in grassland. The trees were left to provide timber, or pollarded to produce regular crops of young shoots for feeding to livestock, or longer shoots for building and other purposes. The crown of the tree was cut at some 2–4 metres above ground so that the new shoots could escape browsing by livestock. These new branches were cut on an appropriate rotation, depending on their use. Fresh growth intended for livestock was cut and fed to cattle and other animals towards the end of their first summer, while the leaves were still green. The underlying grass was grazed seasonally or year-round, and if the trees were oak or beech, pigs were given access in autumn to consume the fallen mast. Ancient wood pastures in Britain include parts of the New Forest, Burnham Beeches and Epping Forest, famous now for their large numbers of old trees, while willows with signs of past pollarding can be seen in many parts of the country. Old pollarded trees often provide an abundance of dead wood and nest holes, ideal for woodpeckers and other hole-nesting species. The woodpeckers feed on the insects and insect larvae that live in the decaying branches. Nowadays, new wood pastures are being created accidentally across the uplands, wherever fences are no longer maintained and sheep and other grazing animals have access to remnant deciduous woods. Such unfenced woods have low ground cover and no shrub layer. They favour species such as Redstart, Pied Flycatcher and Wood Warbler. Parkland can be regarded as wood pasture, with large old trees (often oaks) widely spaced across grassland. The most characteristic birds are again hole-nesters and, because of the size of the trees, some of the cavities are large enough for Jackdaws, Stock Doves, Barn Owls and Kestrels.

In a second common system, prevalent mainly in southern England, some widely spaced trees, often oaks, were left for more than 100 years to grow as standards and produce timber, while the under-wood was managed as coppice, with the new growth cut close to the ground every several years. When some broad-leaved trees such as Hazel, Ash, oaks or willows are felled, the stump sends up shoots and becomes a stool from which successive crops of poles can be cut every few years indefinitely. In the past, the shoots were used mainly for fencing, wattle-work and other purposes, but also as fuel and for making charcoal, while oak bark was used for tanning leather. In some other trees, such as Aspen, cherries and elms, the stump usually dies after cutting but the roots live on and send up successive crops of suckers. The coppice rotation varied with tree species and the intended market: Hazel was typically cut every 7–10 years, Sweet Chestnut every 15 years, Ash and Oak every 25–35 years. The year after cutting, when sunlight hit the forest floor, magnificent carpets of flowers often developed, which were shaded out in subsequent years as the coppice regrew. Coppice and sucker shoots are eaten by cattle, sheep and deer, so the practice of coppicing entailed fencing out large grazing animals. Coppicing declined in Britain by about 73% between 1947 and 1980 (Locke 1987). It survives mainly in parts of the southeast, but in other areas its legacy can be seen in neglected woods as groups of large closely spaced trees derived from the original stools.
