FIG 190. Two summer visitors of the open sheep-grazed woods of western Britain: left, Pied Flycatcher Ficedula hypoleuca; right, Redstart Phoenicurus phoenicurus (Keith Kirk).

In most remaining coppices, the mature standard trees are widely spaced, with the coppice below usually arranged in a mosaic of different-aged patches, cut on rotation. They give conditions suitable for a wide range of birds, especially shrub-dwelling species such as Nightingale, Garden Warbler, Dunnock and in more open areas also Tree Pipit, which is absent from closed-canopy forest. A succession of breeding birds occurs in relation to the age of the coppice growth, with Nightingales, for example, being most numerous in stands of 4–8 years. The standard trees increase the range of vertical and spatial structure in a wood, providing habitat for additional species, and nest sites for cavity-nesters.

Nowadays the types of trees present in individual woods are greatly influenced by those chosen in the past for planting or removal, but different types prevail in different regions. Among broad-leaved woods, oak is the most widespread type in Britain, with Pedunculate Oak mainly in the south and east and Sessile Oak on the poorer soils of the north and west. In the far north of Britain, birch and locally Scots Pine replace oak as the dominant trees, while throughout Britain Alder and willows prevail on damp ground. Most other trees show local variations of abundance, with Ash and Beech found especially on calcareous soils.

FIG 191. The Nightingale Luscinia megarhynchos is found in an early growth stage of coppice woodlands, nesting on the ground (Bobby Smith).

Woodland structure and birds

Woodland is the most structurally complex of all terrestrial vegetation. It holds more bird species in Britain than any other habitat, about 113 species in total, although 26 of these are only incidental (Fuller 1995). Despite Britain holding less forest than almost every other European country, most of our common birds are woodland species, many of which also occur in parks, gardens and hedgerows.

In general, the number of woodland bird species in Britain is greatest in the southeast and declines towards the north and west, even within similar types of woodland. Woods in southeast England typically hold more than twice as many species as those in northwest Scotland (Fuller 1982). In addition, woods at higher altitude hold fewer species and smaller overall numbers than lower-lying woods (Newton et al. 1986). Within these general trends, the main factors that influence the composition of woodland bird communities include the tree species (especially broad-leaved versus coniferous), the physical structure of the wood, and its extent. Broad-leaved woods generally support more breeding species and individuals than conifers; and the more complex the internal structure of a wood, with its ground vegetation, bushy understorey and high canopy, the more diverse is its bird community (Moss 1978a). Larger woods also tend to support more breeding species than small ones, partly because larger woods usually show more structural variation (Bellamy et al. 1996, Hinsley et al. 1996). Soil fertility and dampness are further factors that influence the overall abundance of woodland birds.

FIG 192. Four common resident woodland birds: upper left, Blue Tit Cyanistes caeruleus (Stan Wilson); upper right, Chaffinch Fringilla coelebs (Stan Wilson); Lower left, Nuthatch Sitta europaea (Stan Wilson); lower right, Goldcrest Regulus regulus (Sean Gray, GrayImages).

Insects are probably the most important foods that trees offer birds (Box 15), but buds and flowers are eaten by some species (notably Bullfinch, Black Grouse and Capercaillie), and seeds and fruits by many (Newton 1972). In autumn and winter, acorns are favoured by Jays and Woodpigeons, Beech-mast also by various tits, Chaffinches and Bramblings, Hornbeam seeds by Hawfinches and Greenfinches, Ash seeds by Bullfinches, and the tiny Birch and Alder seeds by Redpolls, Siskins and Goldfinches. Conifer seeds provide almost the entire diet of Crossbills, but are also eaten by a range of other finches when the cones open. Tree seeds tend to fluctuate greatly in abundance year to year, and at times of good crops the woods may seem full of seed-eating finches and other birds, leaving farmland largely vacated.

BOX 15. The numbers of insects associated with different tree species

Trees are important to birds partly because of the insects they support. Willows (5 species) hold the greatest variety of foliage-dwelling types with at least 445 recorded species, followed by oaks (2 species) with 421 and birches (2 species) with 330, then Hawthorn 204, poplars (4 species) 186, Blackthorn 147, Alder 135, Crab Apple 118, elm (2 species) 117, Hazel 102, Beech 94 and Ash 65, lime (2 species) 53, Hornbeam 50, Field Maple 46, Sycamore 38*, Rowan 36, Sweet Chestnut 11*, Holly 10, and Horse Chestnut 4*. Among conifers, Scots Pine holds 172 insect species, Norway Spruce 70*, Larch 37*, Juniper 31, fir 16*, and Yew 5. Those trees marked with an asterisk* were introduced to Britain, so would be expected to support fewer insects than similar native trees.

These figures only partly reflect the value of different trees to insectivorous birds. They were originally based only on insects which specialised on the foliage of those trees, and excluded insects that fed on other parts of the tree or on a range of different trees. Nor do the numbers of insect species necessarily reflect the biomass of insects that individual trees might hold. Of particular importance to birds are the various leaf-eating caterpillars which develop in abundance in early summer, sometimes reaching plague proportions, especially on oak. Many birds eat these caterpillars, including, in peak years, flocks of Rooks and Starlings that move into woodland at that time to exploit the glut.

(Data from Southwood 1961, Kennedy & Southwood 1984, Alexander et al. 2006)

Several species benefited from extensive conifer planting in the 20th century, expanding greatly in numbers and range. They include the Firecrest in the southern lowlands, and the Siskin, Crossbill, Crested Tit and possibly Capercaillie further north. These species are all conifer specialists, while the Goldcrest and Coal Tit also breed much more frequently in coniferous than in broad-leaved areas. Many other bird species are specialists of broad-leaved woods, and avoid pure conifer areas in Britain. They include the Hawfinch, Nuthatch, Marsh Tit, Garden Warbler, Blackcap, Wood Warbler, Chiffchaff, Nightingale, Redstart, Spotted Flycatcher, Pied Flycatcher and Lesser Spotted Woodpecker, while the Blue and Great Tit breed at much higher densities in broad-leaved than conifer woods. Most of these species occur in mixed woods which have both tree types. However, the virtual lack of natural cavities in conifer trees tends to exclude most hole-nesters, unless nest-boxes are provided. All other woodland birds, including Chaffinch, Robin, Song Thrush, Blackbird and Wren, seem to occur commonly in both broad-leaved and coniferous areas, providing the internal structure is right for them (Fuller 1982, 1995). Some species are found only in the early shrubby stages of growth, but species numbers and overall bird densities tend to increase with woodland age to reach a maximum in mature stands with a well-developed understorey.

Traditional woodland management, giving rise to coppice and wood pasture, affects birds differently from the modern methods involving tree monocultures, clear-fells and replants. Instead of concentrating on the management of individual trees, as in the past, modern methods typically involve clear-felling and replanting whole sections at a time. With modern machinery, it is more economic that way, and in any case the demand for young wood for fuel, charcoal, hurdle-making or livestock feeding has almost disappeared.

Trends in bird and other wildlife populations

Although woodland has been largely protected from the impacts of modern agriculture, many of its wild plants and animals have declined. As reported in the 2016 State of Nature report, of 1,256 woodland plant and animal species that have been studied in recent decades, 60% have decreased, and 34% strongly so, with an average decline in woodland birds since 1970 of around 20% (Hayhow et al. 2016). Nearly two-thirds of all invertebrate species that had been monitored had declined, as had 58% of flowering plants. Some of the declining bird species, such as Nightingale, Willow Tit and various warblers, rely on younger woodland growth stages, so are likely to have been affected by the reduction of coppicing and the absence of a shrub layer. Most of the birds that had increased or remained stable, such as the Blue Tit, Great Tit and Great Spotted Woodpecker, are associated with large trees, and have benefited from the developing maturity of many planted woods, as well as from garden bird feeding, of which they are major beneficiaries.

Based mainly on studies in the 1960s and 1970s, broad-leaved woodland in Britain was found to contain around 800–1,800 bird pairs per km2, depending on its type and structure. This is roughly four times as many as uniform-aged conifer monocultures at 200–500 pairs per km2 (Moss 1978b, Fuller 1982, Petty & Avery 1990). Woodland species which have declined since 1970 by more than 50% include the Lesser Spotted Woodpecker (–82%), Willow Tit (–94%), Marsh Tit (–71%), Wood Warbler (–58% since 1995), Song Thrush (–56%), Mistle Thrush (–59%), Spotted Flycatcher (–87%), Tree Pipit (–68%), Lesser Redpoll (–85%), and Woodcock (–61%) (Hayhow et al. 2015a). Yet others had apparently declined markedly, but were not well enough sampled to measure the extent, namely the Long-eared Owl, Capercaillie, Hawfinch and Nightingale. In most decreasing species, declines were more marked in the south of Britain than further north. However, other species had increased by more than 50% in the same period, namely Buzzard, Sparrowhawk, Woodpigeon, Green Woodpecker, Great Spotted Woodpecker, Great Tit, Long-tailed Tit, Chiffchaff, Blackcap, Nuthatch and Redstart. Some of the smaller species on these lists can fluctuate by more than 50% from one year to the next, but the figures refer to net long-term trends.

Several hypotheses have been proposed to account for these population changes, but no single explanation seems pertinent to all. However, the most generally applicable factor acting within Britain was change in woodland structure, resulting from the maturing of woodland, a reduction in active management, and increased numbers of deer (Fuller 2001, Amar et al. 2006). Grazing and browsing by deer greatly alter the composition and structure of woodland, removing some plant species altogether. In addition to the two native deer species (Red and Roe), four non-native species (Fallow, Reeves' Muntjac, Chinese Water Deer and Sika) have spread widely in recent years (Chapter 7). High deer density is a new phenomenon in the British lowlands. It has developed in parallel with agricultural intensification, and several deer species now feed widely on farm crops.

The effects of deer cascade through the whole woodland ecosystem. Deer remove favoured low plants, such as bramble and palatable herbs, so that unpalatable vegetation increases, leaving more grassy areas and bare ground. They prevent tree and shrub regeneration, reducing the understorey and changing the internal microclimate of the wood (Fuller & Gill 2001, Gill & Fuller & 2007). The feeding and nesting habitat of many bird species, especially those of the shrub layer (including the outside edges of the wood) eventually disappears. If this level of browsing continues, whole areas of woodland could eventually disappear, because dying trees would not be replaced. The deer would destroy the habitat for themselves and for other wildlife.

Even at low densities, as deer concentrate on browsing the growing tips and fresh leaves of trees and shrubs, they consume those parts of plants also favoured by herbivorous insects, including caterpillars. Their browsing therefore removes a large insect supply that would otherwise be available to birds, and as herbivorous insects decline, so do predatory insects and detritivores, with effects spreading through the invertebrate community (Gill & Fuller 2007). Deer browsing also removes many shrub and tree flowers, hence reducing the production of seeds and fruits important to birds (Perrins & Overall 2001). In effect, therefore, even relatively low levels of deer browsing can cause substantial reductions of bird food supplies.

Such findings have been confirmed by experiments in which deer were excluded from areas by fencing, allowing trees to regenerate, shrubs and other plants to grow, and other animals to recover (Putman et al. 1989). Some experiments specifically examined the effects of deer exclusion on birds. In each case, breeding birds associated with low vegetation were less numerous in browsed than in protected areas of young woodland, especially coppice (Fuller & Gill 2001, Gill & Fuller 2007, Holt et al. 2011). Effects were particularly marked on some warblers and other breeding migrants, as well as resident Dunnocks and others. In the fenced plots, once the recovering vegetation had reached an appropriate stage, Nightingales bred at 15 times the density found in unfenced browsed plots; and individuals that were radio-tracked spent 69% of their time in the 6% of a study area protected from deer (Holt et al. 2010). Resident ground-feeding species also increased after deer exclusion, benefiting in winter from the extra cover afforded against weather and predation. As expected, high-canopy feeders were unaffected.

FIG 193. The Hawfinch Coccothraustes coccothraustes is found in deciduous woodlands in Britain, feeding on large hard tree seeds, but has declined greatly over recent decades (Frank Snykers).

In addition to such detailed local studies, national monitoring data confirm that deer-related habitat modification may now be affecting some bird species over large parts of lowland Britain. Birds of the woodland understorey are most affected, with the greatest apparent impacts on Nightingale and Marsh Tit (Newson et al. 2012). Discussion of these impacts may seem far removed from farmland birds, but many of the affected woodland birds also occur on farmland, and the issues associated with deer grazing are not so different from those associated with livestock grazing (Chapter 19). Despite research, the marked declines seen in some woodland species, such as Lesser Spotted Woodpecker and Hawfinch, still remain unexplained.

Recent changes in woodland types

For much of its history, Forestry Commission policy involved planting large forests of conifers, especially in uplands, and replacing many existing deciduous areas with conifers in the lowlands. This policy came in for increasing public criticism, and since the 1990s more emphasis has been placed on native broad-leaved trees. Over recent decades, the likely roles of forests of all kinds in carbon storage and water management have also been increasingly recognised.

In the 20th century, most new woods on low ground were planted on heathland, while on farmland some existing woods were destroyed to create more farmland. However, in recent years some new woods have been planted on farmland, under the Farm Woodland Premium Scheme, which provided grants for establishment and care. Many farmers planted a hedge of shrub species around the edges of a new wood, and this provided another kind of habitat, as well as shelter for the interior. However, these woods lack a true woodland ground flora, and many are used as sites for Pheasant release pens. In such situations, the Pheasants eat much of the ground vegetation and many small animals, so the value of these new woods for wildlife is less than was intended. In recent years, some 40 million Pheasants have been released annually by the shooting industry. These birds spend their early lives in large pens in woodland, from which they are later released, a practice which is likely to have major impacts on woodland flora and fauna – but so far this has been largely unstudied (but see Larkman et al. 2015). Overall, the planting of new woods on farmland in recent years has not compensated in quantity or quality for the loss of older woods from farmland in the preceding decades. The net loss of woodland area from lowland farmland since the 1950s has been estimated at around 8%.

SCRUB

On open land, in the absence of cultivation, mowing or grazing, shrubs establish naturally, eventually forming areas of 'scrub'. Such scrub patches develop mainly on abandoned land, whether former farmland or industrial sites, but also among coastal sand dunes. The first pioneering shrubs grow from seeds deposited in the droppings of birds or blown in by wind. Sometimes bushes spread out from wood edges or hedgerows into neglected fields. In many areas, Hawthorn is one of the first colonists, but other species soon follow, including Bramble, Privet, Dog Rose, Elder, Blackthorn, Silver Birch and in some places also Rowan, Common Gorse, Juniper or Yew. Hawthorn grows well on neutral or alkaline soils; Blackthorn often dominates on deeper more fertile soils, expanding by suckering to form sizeable clumps; Elder often establishes on recently disturbed or enriched soils; birch, gorse and broom grow well on dry acid soils; and willows on damper ground. As more shrubs become established, they cover progressively more of the original open land. Eventually, bigger tree species take hold, and if left, the scrub eventually gives way to woodland in which the original colonising shrub species are mostly shaded out by bigger trees.

Scrub is an important but underrated habitat. It can support all the plant and animal species of mature hedgerows, and others besides. For example, clumps of tall Hawthorn can provide nest sites for species such as Sparrowhawk, which would not normally nest in a narrow hedge. Areas that contain a variety of bushes of differing heights and spacing, with patches of shrubs interspersed with areas of grass and flowering plants, generally contain the greatest diversity of birds. Clumps of Bramble and Rose provide good nest sites for shrub-nesting birds, and together with Hawthorn, Elder and Rowan, an abundance of fruits for thrushes and other birds from late summer into winter. Well-developed scrub patches are also used as winter roost sites by many species, including flocks of finches, buntings, thrushes, and Starlings which fly in each evening from surrounding land. Scrub on sea coasts provides food and shelter for newly arrived migrants, Sea-buckthorn being prevalent on some sand-dune areas.

Depending on location, young shrubs scattered in lower herbaceous vegetation attract Linnets, Yellowhammers and Whitethroats, which are commonly found in hedgerows, plus Grasshopper Warblers, Whinchats, Tree Pipits and Woodlarks, which are generally absent from hedgerows. As the bushes grow and spread, the composition of the bird community changes, and overall numbers rise. Dunnocks, Garden Warblers and Willow Warblers colonise low-growing closed-canopy scrub and remain as it grows, Blackbirds and Robins come in at a slightly later stage, while Turtle Doves, Song Thrushes, Bullfinches and Chaffinches favour older taller stands (Fuller 1982). In the southeast, Nightingales may also colonise dense stands of, for example, Blackthorn or Bramble; and in the past, sparse thorny scrub was the main habitat of Red-backed Shrikes in Britain. Because bushes mostly lack cavities, however, hole-nesting birds are usually scarce or absent. Some other birds are found in wet scrub, consisting of willows or Alder, including Redpolls, Sedge Warblers, Cetti's Warblers, Willow Tits and, in more mature areas, Lesser Spotted Woodpeckers. The number of species and individuals breeding in well-grown scrub can exceed by many times the number in the original open land (Fuller 1982). Diverse scrub patches containing shrubs at various growth stages have been found to support up to 2,250 bird pairs per km2 (e.g. da Prato 1985). This is more than in most areas of mature woodland.

FIG 194. Scrub development: upper, on abandoned farmland in Sussex, showing well-grown trees, bushes of various sizes and open herbaceous vegetation (Ian Newton); lower, growth of gorse on pastureland in Kirkcudbright (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Over Britain as a whole, according to one survey, some 60% of scrub present in 1965 had gone by 1980 (Locke 1987). This was partly through succession to woodland, but mainly through removal to create more farmland or building sites. The total loss since 1965 could be much higher, but I know of no reliable estimates. For many years, scrub removal was funded by agricultural grants. The main additions in recent decades were on the ungrazed slopes of downland too steep to plough, on various abandoned industrial sites and waste tips, on some motorway verges, on heathlands with insufficient grazing or burning, and on former wetlands affected by drainage. In Countryside Surveys, scrub was included with more mature woodland, but from the 1990 survey, scrub was estimated to cover just over 0.4% of the land surface of Britain (some 90,000 ± 20,000 ha, Mortimer et al. 2000).

HEATHLANDS

Lowland heathlands are associated with areas of sandy or gravelly, acid and infertile soils. Most are probably very old, dating back to early forest clearance. Many of the wastes of old England would be described today as heathland, and the fragments that survive give some idea of what large parts of the south may have looked like in former times. Much heathland in the south of Britain and moorland in the north are both dominated by the same plant, namely Heather (Ling). Yet the two habitats are of quite different character and hold different bird communities. Dry southern heathland is home to the Dartford Warbler, Woodlark and Nightjar, while damp northern moorland is home to the Red Grouse, Golden Plover and Ring Ouzel.

FIG 195. Dunwich Heath in Suffolk, showing heather, gorse and regenerating trees (Ian Newton).

Once heathland or moorland is formed after forest destruction, fire and grazing maintains it, or it grows up with trees, especially birch and pine, with their light wind-borne seeds. If heathland is 'overgrazed', Heather is replaced by grass and Bracken. Southern heathland has long been used for grazing livestock, and formerly as a source of fuel (gorse) and thatch, and as a place for enclosed Rabbit warrens. Up to the mid-20th century, periodic burning of southern heathland was a routine practice aimed to benefit grazing animals. Conducted in spring, it probably destroyed the early nests of many ground-nesting birds, including Montagu's Harriers, as records show (Underhill-Day 1990). Nowadays, most heathland fires are accidental and uncontrolled. In the long term they help to maintain the habitat, but in the short term they can temporarily destroy the habitat of some animal species, and kill portions of their populations.

Owing to the poverty of the dry acid soil, and the low nutrient content of the vegetation, heathland can support only low densities of grazing livestock. The vegetation is inadequate for modern high-yielding breeds, but can itself be strongly affected by grazing. Under sustained and intensive grazing by Rabbits or sheep, the Heather is converted to short sandy grassland, suitable for Stone-curlews and Wheatears, as on the Brecks of East Anglia. Other birds, such as Woodlark, Tree Pipit and Stonechat, require bushes or other tall vegetation among bare or short-grass areas, a situation produced under lower-density livestock grazing. However, under too little grazing, Heather grows tall and shrubs and trees invade, creating conditions suited to other species. Dartford Warblers are found in areas offering a mixture of mature Heather and medium-height gorse, and obtain most of their invertebrate food from gorse, whatever proportion it forms of the overall heathland vegetation. Nightjars favour areas where trees encroach upon heathland. As an area becomes more tree-covered, other woodland species move in. Maintaining heathland in the right state for these desired species therefore requires careful management. By the 1980s, most remaining areas of heathland in southern Britain had become 'under-grazed' for the key species, and subsequent conservation management mainly entailed re-establishing appropriate levels of grazing, tree removal and careful control of fires (for Stone-curlew see Green & Griffiths 1994, Green & Taylor 1995; for Woodlark see Sitters et al. 1996). Recreational disturbance had also risen, with adverse effects on Nightjars and Woodlarks (Liley & Clarke 2003, Mallord et al. 2007).

FIG 196. Six birds of heathland: upper left, Dartford Warbler Sylvia undata (Allan Hale); upper right, Stonechat Saxicola rubicola (Edmund Fellowes); mid left, Wheatear Oenanthe oenanthe (Richard Chandler); mid right, Woodlark Lullula arborea (Chris Knights); lower left, Nightjar Caprimulgus europaeus (Allan Hale); lower right, Tree Pipit Anthus trivialis (Allan Hale).

Between the years 1800 and 2000, the overall area of lowland heath in Britain was reduced by more than 80%. Initially most losses were due to conversion to farmland, but in the 20th century also to plantation forests and housing estates, leaving remaining heathland more fragmented. These processes led to corresponding national declines in the species associated with heathland. In addition, on the remaining heaths, some 65% of plant and animal species that have been studied have declined over recent decades, in association with inadequate management, tree invasion, nitrogen pollution and human disturbance. Nevertheless, Britain still holds 20% of the world's lowland heath, which in 2007 was estimated to cover 93,000 ha, almost all in southern England (Carey et al. 2008). Heathland is the sole habitat of the Dartford Warbler in Britain, and also holds substantial proportions of all our Woodlarks, Nightjars and Stone-curlews, and provides good habitat for Hobby and Stonechat, among others, and in the past also for Montagu's Harriers and Red-backed Shrikes. The valley mires and bogs of the New Forest still hold breeding waders such as Lapwing, Curlew, Redshank and Snipe. On the other hand, the Black Grouse had disappeared entirely from lowland heathland by the end of the 19th century, and is now restricted to some upland areas (Holloway 1996). During the course of the 20th century, the Ringed Plover, once estimated at 400 pairs in Breckland (Clarke 1925), gradually disappeared, but Curlews expanded to all Breckland areas with sufficiently long vegetation to provide nesting cover. Some characteristic heathland species (including Nightjar) obtain some of their food from neighbouring farmland, while other species found commonly on lowland heathland, such as the Wren, Bullfinch, Long-tailed Tit, Skylark, Meadow Pipit and Cuckoo, also nest widely elsewhere.

FIG 197. Short-grass sandy heathland: left, Rabbits Oryctolagus cuniculus which through their burrowing and grazing create the bare and short-vegetation habitat suitable for Stone-curlews Burhinus oedicnemus and Wheatears Oenanthe oenanthe; right, Stone-curlew pair at nest (Chris Knights).

In general, as befits their poor soils, heaths support relatively sparse birdlife, with densities varying according to vegetation structure, and recent estimates falling within the wide range of 25–125 pairs per km2 calculated years ago by Lack (1935). Nevertheless, more than 30 species breed regularly on heathland, although most in small numbers or sporadically (Fuller 1982). The smaller fragments often hold species more often associated with neighbouring farmland.

The dry impoverished soils, sparseness of berry-bearing shrubs and low invertebrate densities also make heathland unattractive as winter habitat for most birds. Many of the most characteristic breeding birds are absent or remain in much reduced numbers in winter, when they move to other habitats (especially farmland) or to distant wintering areas. However, other birds move in, including the occasional Hen Harrier, Merlin, Short-eared Owl and Great Grey Shrike.

About three-quarters of remaining lowland heaths in Britain are protected, but in recent years grasses have spread in relation to Heather, a process probably encouraged by atmospheric nitrogen deposition (de Smidt 1995, Carey et al. 2008). But under appropriate habitat management on protected areas, the breeding populations of some heathland species have increased significantly in recent decades. For example, the estimated number of Woodlark territories in Britain increased from around 240 pairs in 1986 to 3,064 pairs in 2006, giving a roughly 12-fold increase in numbers and a fourfold increase in breeding range (Sitters et al. 1996, Conway et al. 2009). Much of this increase occurred on heathland, in association with the reinstatement of light grazing or burning. But numbers also increased greatly within clear-felled areas of lowland conifer forests, again through sympathetic management. Likewise, an increase in the numbers of Stone-curlews breeding in remaining open parts of Breckland, from 87 pairs in 1991 to 142 in 1998, was attributed partly to the reinstatement of sheep grazing on many of the grass heaths, helped by agri-environment funding (Swash et al. 2000). The Dartford Warbler, whose populations usually decline during periods of severe winter weather, expanded from a national total of just 11 pairs after the hard winter of 1962–63 to more than 3,200 pairs in 2006, following a long run of predominantly mild winters (Wotton et al. 2009). Numbers of calling male Nightjars increased nationally from around 2,100 in 1981 to around 4,600 in 2004. This was attributable partly to heathland management, and partly to an expansion of suitable habitat in newly planted or clear-felled areas in conifer plantations (Conway et al. 2007). These population expansions, largely brought about by targeted management, provide striking contrasts to the general downward trends of most bird species on farmland.

FARM BUILDINGS

Farm steadings, holding livestock and stored foodstuffs, are important components of farmed landscapes, offering shelter, nest sites and food for a range of birds and other wildlife. Old, traditional farm buildings, made from natural materials, support much more wildlife than modern ones. In the past, every lowland farm had a farmstead, with house and garden, orchard and sheltering trees, barns, stables and byres, space for corn and hay ricks, and a source of water for livestock, usually a pond. Traditional farm buildings still provide nest sites and shelter for various bird species, acting as centres for House Sparrows and hirundines. Almost any species that uses cavities in trees or rocks can also use suitable buildings. Most Swallows in Britain nest in cowsheds and other open buildings, many Barn Owls nest in barns or bale-stacks, while House Sparrows, Starlings, Swifts, Pied Wagtails and others make use of holes in walls. All these species also nest in other sites, so none is wholly dependent on farm buildings.

Few farmyards now consist entirely of old buildings, except in some hill districts. In recent decades, as many adjacent farms have been combined, some farmsteads have been abandoned altogether, with their buildings demolished or used only for storage. Many of the old farmhouses have been sold off, while other buildings have been converted to housing. This means that most of the nest sites formerly available in the old buildings no longer exist, greatly reducing the nesting opportunities for species such as Swallows and Barn Owls (Ramsden 1998). Moreover, in modern arable farms many of the old buildings have been replaced by much larger steel and concrete structures which can be used to house bigger equipment and to store crops. Such buildings offer few useable nest sites for birds – no thatch, no lofts or roof spaces, no vents in walls, no broad tops to walls, little in the way of ledges, and so on. But birds still use new buildings as roost sites if they can gain access, sitting on the metal or concrete beams. Storage buildings are usually designed to keep out rodents and birds, which therefore no longer have access to the food within. The bird-proofing of farm buildings has probably been a major cause of the decline in some birds, such as House Sparrows and Starlings. In addition, farmyards have increasingly become concreted and uncluttered, enabling the easier movement of equipment year-round, and with a lack of livestock on many arable farms, much of the food formerly available for birds in traditional farmyards is no longer there. In recent decades, new buildings have also spread even in hill districts, where purpose-built lambing sheds have appeared in increasing numbers.

FIG 198. Left, old farm buildings in Cumbria, no longer in regular use but providing nesting sites for various bird species (Ian Newton); right, Starling Sturnus vulgaris, one of the typical inhabitants (Keith Kirk).

FIG 199. Four birds that nest on or within farm buildings: upper left, House Martins Delichon urbicum nest-building (Chris Knights); upper right, Swift Apus apus emerging from nest cavity (Chris Knights); lower left, House Sparrow Passer domesticus at nest (Bobby Smith); lower right, brood of recently fledged Barn Swallows Hirundo rustica (Stan Wilson).

Old farmsteads usually supported an abundance of rats and mice. The ricks of harvested cereal sheaves often stood for several months before they were threshed, and until then supported hundreds of rodents (Chapter 7). These animals caused great damage to grain, but provided a food source for Barn Owls and others, buffering them to some extent from the effects of hard winters and of cyclic lows in vole populations living in the fields. Yards where livestock were fed on hay or grain products could attract exceptional numbers of birds during periods of severe weather, when many species moved in to feed among the animals. Up to a thousand birds could occur around a single cattle yard, and,

FIG 200. The Pied Wagtail Motacilla alba frequently nests in farm buildings and feeds around farmyards (Ian Newton).

in extreme weather, if you walk among the cattle you can get within a few feet of Corn Buntings, Skylarks, Meadow Pipits, Yellowhammers, Reed Buntings, Redpolls, Linnets, Chaffinches, Wrens and Dunnocks. (Wareing 1973)

While structural features, such as old buildings, generally serve to diversify bird populations, they also render parts of the landscape unattractive to certain species. Birds such as wild geese and waders, which rely on wide open landscapes and rapid flight to escape predation, tend to avoid feeding or nesting close to any structural features that could hide predators, or which they associate with frequent disturbance. Villages, farmsteads, roads, wind turbines, overhead wires, woods and tall hedgerows are normally shunned by these open-country birds, rendering some otherwise suitable habitat unused. For geese and swans, wind turbines and overhead wires also represent a flight hazard that kills birds every year. The activity around farm buildings, and the presence of cats and dogs, deters most ground-nesting birds from settling nearby.

Cattle sheds and Swallows

Swallows, known internationally as Barn Swallows, occur mainly around farms. They are usually associated with cattle, probably because these animals and their dung attract flies on which Swallows feed. These insects can proliferate in great numbers in fresh cattle droppings, and others in older dung heaps. In recent decades, the numbers of Swallows breeding in Britain have declined in the east and increased in the west, paralleling trends in cattle numbers (Henderson et al. 2007a). Despite their name, Barn Swallows much prefer cattle byres over storage barns for nesting. They like smaller and darker buildings with fewer access points, more reminiscent of their ancestral nesting caves (Roberts 2001). Studies in Denmark found that, as farms switched from cattle to arable, the Swallows left (Møller 1983), and the same has been observed by bird ringers in Britain. The main causal factor seems to be loss of the flies associated with cattle. But in the absence of cattle, byre doors are often left closed through summer, denying access to Swallows, and the insect-rich pastures and meadows that fed the cattle are usually replaced by insect-poor cereal fields (Chapter 14). Whatever the factors involved, these findings suggest that changes in the numbers of farms housing cattle have influenced long-term trends in regional Swallow populations in Britain. But this does not exclude rainfall in African wintering areas as a cause of year-to-year fluctuations, again through its influence on insect populations (Møller 1989, Robinson et al. 2008).

OTHER CHANGES AFFECTING BIRDS IN RURAL AREAS

FIG 201. Great Spotted Woodpecker Dendrocopos major, one of the main beneficiaries of garden bird feeding (Stan Wilson).

Other recent developments in the countryside have been centred on the thousands of villages and their gardens, minor industrial sites, roads, railways and other infrastructure, and their associated wasteland. According to CS2007, such areas covered about 1.3 million hectares, nearly 6% of the total land area of Britain. This is nearly the same total area as is covered by towns and cities, so overall in 2007, about 12% of Britain was under some sort of built development (Carey et al. 2008).

Over recent decades, as farmland birds declined, the feeding of garden birds became increasingly popular. An estimated 12.6 million (48%) households in Britain frequently provide food for birds (Davies et al. 2009). This supplementary food is especially important in winter, and may have helped to increase the numbers of some species or at least to prevent them from declining. Major beneficiaries include the Greenfinch, Goldfinch, Siskin, Chaffinch, Blue Tit, Great Tit and Great Spotted Woodpecker, all of which have increased over recent decades (although disease has now caused widespread decline in the Greenfinch). All these species are more frequent in gardens in winter, when food is shortest in the general countryside, and some are more frequent in winters with poor tree-seed crops than in winters with good crops (Newton 2013a).

CONCLUDING REMARKS

The various semi-natural habitats present in farmed landscapes of Britain today not only enhance the visual appeal and amenity value of the countryside, they also support the bulk of its wildlife. Most bird species now present on lowland farmland depend entirely or partly on patches of semi-natural habitat or farmsteads. These features provide most of the bird habitats and nest sites and some of the foods in farmed landscapes. Studies have shown how the numbers of bird species and individuals in areas of farmland increase with the proportions of semi-natural and other non-cropped habitats present. The fact that birds of the open fields have declined so much in recent decades only enhances the conservation value of whatever semi-natural habitat remains.

Most of these semi-natural and uncropped habitats declined in extent during the latter half of the 20th century, as some areas were converted to cropland or other uses. This process can only have brought about a substantial reduction in farmland bird populations. Those habitat patches that remain often hold fewer birds than in the past, partly in association with a lapse or change in management, altered grazing or browsing pressure, drift of pesticides from cropped land, greater nitrogen deposition favouring competitive plant species over others, and the varying consequences of greater habitat fragmentation. The rearing of large numbers of Pheasants in many of the remaining woods is almost certainly detrimental to many wild plants and animals, an issue which has so far been largely ignored.

During the 20th century, afforestation schemes (mainly in the uplands) increased the proportion of Britain under woodland to 12%, about half broad-leaved or mixed woodland and the rest coniferous. Some old broad-leaved woods that remain today show signs of past management, such as pollarding or coppicing. Bird numbers and diversity are greatest in woods with complex internal structure, with well-developed ground and shrub layers below a taller canopy. Many woodland birds have declined in recent decades, partly through decline of traditional management but mainly through increasing numbers of deer, which are eliminating the shrub layer on which many species depend.

Scrub-land is one of the richest habitats for birds in Britain, especially where it shows great spatial and vertical variation in structure. It provides breeding habitat for many bird species, good feeding areas for fruit-eaters and roosting areas for a wide range of songbirds. In recent decades, its total area has declined greatly in lowland Britain, partly through succession to woodland, and partly through its conversion to farmland or building sites.

Lowland heathland, mainly grass- and heather-covered, with some gorse, birch and pine, holds some characteristic species, including Dartford Warbler, Woodlark, Stonechat, Whinchat and Nightjar. Areas grazed to the ground by Rabbits provide habitat for Stone-curlew and Wheatear, and in the past also for Ringed Plover. Much former heathland has been lost to farming, afforestation and housing developments, and in areas that remain, the vegetation has often changed through eutrophication (nitrogen deposition), and reductions in burning and grazing, enabling tree establishment. However, about three-quarters of remaining heathland is now under conservation management, as a result of which former declining bird species are now on the increase.

Old farm buildings typically provide many nesting sites for birds, including Swallows and Barn Owls. New buildings are less bird-friendly, and many are deliberately designed to exclude birds. Farmyards are also tidier than in the past, with less spilled livestock food available for birds to feed on. Many arable farms now lack all forms of livestock.

Much of the remaining semi-natural habitat in Britain requires the continuance of old management practices if it is to retain its former aesthetic and wildlife values. Grazing influences habitat quality for many bird species. On lowland heaths, the problem has often been too little grazing, which allows the vegetation to grow too tall and trees to establish, while in many lowland woods the problem has become too much grazing and browsing by wild deer, causing the lower vegetation to disappear, along with the birds that depend on it. However, under appropriate management, several 'specialist' bird species have recovered to some extent in recent decades, including most heathland species. Not all habitats can readily be protected as nature reserves, however, and hedgerows seem particularly vulnerable, which takes us on to the next chapter.

## CHAPTER 18

## Hedges and Other Field Boundaries

HEDGEROWS ARE A CHARACTERISTIC and much-loved part of the British landscape. They were originally grown as stock-proof barriers around fields, and to mark property and parish boundaries and rights of way. So to some extent they signify the historical partitioning of land. Over the centuries, they have provided shelter and shade, protection against soil erosion, and products such as timber and firewood, fruits, nuts and herbs. They have also provided habitats for many native plants and animals that would be much scarcer in their absence. Occurring as continuous linear networks, rather than as discrete habitat patches, they facilitate the dispersal of many plants and animals through the countryside.

HISTORY AND MANAGEMENT

Many hedges were originally planted directly into the ground as lines of shrubs, and others on top of an earth or stone bank. The latter types are common in southwest England, where some date back more than 1,000 years. Other hedges are woodland remnants, left after the rest of the wood was removed and often containing woodland plants at their base, such as Bluebell, Wood Anemone, Primrose and Dog's Mercury. Yet other hedges were planted naturally, through birds sitting on fence wires, below which the fruit stones in their droppings grew into bushes. But whatever their origins, hedges soon develop lives of their own, and as the years pass they are progressively colonised by other woody and herbaceous plants, thus acquiring further species through time. Many shrubs, such as Dog Rose and Bramble, colonise in the early years, but the rate of new additions slows with time. Some trees, such as Oak and Ash, are commonly found in hedgerows, but others, such as Hornbeam and Lime, only rarely.

Hedges probably date back to the Neolithic period, and some of those established in the Bronze Age still persist (Rackham 1986, Pryor 2010). By Anglo-Saxon times, the country was apparently well hedged, mainly marking parish boundaries and other patterns of settlement. However, many old hedges were removed over time, partly to create the open-field system of farming which by the 14th century covered nearly one-third of the land surface of England. From then on, hedge planting regained momentum and, with the Enclosures of the 17th–19th centuries, an estimated 300,000 km of new hedgerows were planted in England. The process of enclosure also extended to Wales and Scotland, where it more often involved walls (Rackham 1986). From then to 1945, as maps confirm, little change occurred in field hedgerow and wall patterns across most of Britain. Because of this history of repeated hedge planting, removal and replanting, most hedges remaining in Britain today are probably less than 300 years old, although some are clearly very much older and appear on ancient maps.

The ages of hedges in southern Britain can supposedly be estimated by counting the number of woody plant species per 30 yards (27 metres). Count several stretches, and then take an average. This average reflects the age of the hedge in centuries (Pollard et al. 1974). So a hedge that holds an average of eight woody plant species per 30 yards would be 800 years old. This method of ageing hedges was developed by Max Hooper, who counted the tree and shrub species in 227 hedges of known ages from 75 to 1,100 years. The numbers of woody plant species were more strongly correlated with the age of the hedge than with soil type, climate or management. The method works well in many southern regions, but less well in the north. It does not work well for hedges more than 1,000 years old (by which time all likely woody species may have been incorporated), or for relatively new hedges in which several species may have been planted together. Not surprisingly, considering their prevalence in hedges, Hawthorn and Bramble are now the commonest and second commonest woody plant species in Britain (Carey et al. 2008).

FIG 202. The well-hedged pastoral landscape of Prolly Moor, Shropshire (Ian Newton).

Hedges in Britain now contain large trees of varying ages, but with a bias towards older ones. According to the 2000 Countryside Survey (CS2000), 30% of hedgerow trees were more than 100 years old, and too few young trees were being allowed to grow to maintain their numbers. The life span of hedgerow trees is now generally shorter than in the past, because the deaths of many are hastened by root damage caused by ploughing and by water shortage resulting from field drainage. Many are also removed because they are 'in the way' or judged 'unsafe'. New trees can easily be established by allowing selected saplings within the hedge to grow, but this practice is not popular with most farmers because it involves lifting the flail during mechanised hedge trimming. In consequence, the annual recruitment of new trees to hedgerows has in recent decades been well below the level needed to maintain tree numbers. Hedgerow and other isolated trees usually have more spreading canopies than those of similar age in woodland. They could probably therefore support more insect life, although their isolation and more exposed positions may sometimes act against this.

FIG 203. A country lane in Lincolnshire, with trees, tall hedgerows and wide flower-rich verges: ideal habitat for a wide range of hedgerow birds (Ian Newton).

For obvious reasons, hedgerows are more numerous in pastoral than in mainly arable districts, this difference being accentuated during a major period of hedge removal during the 1950s–90s. Over 600 plant species, 1,500 insects, 65 birds and 20 mammals have been recorded as living or feeding in hedgerows in Britain, although not all could be regarded as regulars. The plant community resembles that of open woodland, in terms of both the woody plants that form the hedge and the herbaceous plants that grow at its base. Hedges provide food and overwintering sites for insects, whose abundance is influenced by the diversity of food plants present and their flowering and fruiting patterns. In appropriate wind conditions, aerial insects are sometimes concentrated against hedges, providing rich pickings for hirundines and bats. In the south of England, south-facing hedge banks can provide basking and hibernating sites for reptiles. In landscapes lacking woodland, hedgerows are often the only places where many plants and animals can survive. They also serve as corridors along which plants and less mobile animals can spread gradually, or more mobile animals can travel day-to-day.

FIG 204. Different types of hedgerows: upper left, a neatly trimmed short-and-narrow hedge supporting a very limited range of bird species; upper right, an untrimmed taller and wider hedge, supporting a much wider range of bird species, at greater overall densities; lower left, a line of young bushes separated by gaps, much favoured by Whitethroats and Linnets; lower right, a 'green lane', with good hedgerows on each side of a track, the optimal habitat for hedgerow birds (Ian Newton).

The management of hedgerows varies according to their location and condition. Some thick hedges may need no more than occasional trimming, now done mechanically from a tractor. However, hedges which have been allowed to grow without trimming, and are exposed to grazing livestock, tend to become leggy and devoid of cover at ground level. Such neglected hedges may need laying to restore their stock-proof character, while others which have become too large may need coppicing so that the new growth can be laid at a later date. In the past, this labour-intensive operation was done every 20 years or so, with longer intervals for regularly trimmed hedges. In hedge laying, when vertical stems are 3–5 metres tall, some are cut out, and the rest are partly cut through at the base, and bent over almost horizontally along the hedge line, maintaining contact with the root system. These 'pleachers' are then fixed to vertical stakes driven in at 1–2-metre intervals (Fig. 205). Some lengths of pliable wood might then be woven in to produce a strong stock-proof barrier, which becomes thicker with subsequent growth. For many years such hedges need only to be clipped every few years. Occasional young trees can be left to grow on, providing shade for livestock, while gaps are filled by planting new shrubs between existing ones. If they are not managed, even ancient hedges lose their diversity, and lower plants are eaten out by livestock. Eventually, a hedge can become little more than a line of trees, no longer functioning as a barrier, or it can spread outwards from blackthorn suckers, obliterating the former ground flora (Garbutt & Sparks 2002).

FIG 205. Left, a degenerate hedge with the base eaten out by livestock, supporting few, if any, nesting birds (Richard & Barbara Mearns); right, a newly laid hedge, showing stakes and pleachers (Ian Newton).

An important feature of hedges, if they are to feed wildlife, is that they should produce flowers and fruit, as on Hawthorn, Bramble and Dog Rose. At least 15 bird species in Britain regularly eat fleshy fruits from trees and shrubs, and then disperse the seeds in their droppings. They include five thrushes, Waxwing, Robin, four warblers, Starling, two pigeons and three corvids. Some other species, notably the Bullfinch, Greenfinch and at least three tit species, discard the flesh, crack open the seeds and swallow the kernels, and therefore play no part in seed dispersal (Snow & Snow 1988). Pigeons can digest both flesh and seeds.

FIG 206. Birds and hedgerow fruits: upper left, Blackbird Turdus merula eating crab apples (Alan Martin); upper right, Redwing T. iliacus eating Holly fruits (Peter Harris); lower left, Bullfinch Pyrrhula pyrrhula eating shrivelled Bramble fruits (Sean Gray); lower right, Woodpigeon Columba palumbus eating Ivy fruits (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Most shrub and tree species do not form fruit on the current year's growth, so if a hedge is cut every year, each time removing the new growth, it can bear little or no fruit. But if it is cut at intervals of two or more years, flowers and fruits have time to form on wood that is older than the current year. And if different hedges on a farm are cut in different years, the rotation helps to prevent a dearth of fruit in any one year (Hinsley & Bellamy 2000). Cutting is best done in late winter, once the fruit has been eaten. If a hedge is left uncut year after year, it continues to fruit, but in time it grows into a line of tall bushes, and the important lower cover can be shaded out. In general, fruit is consumed during the period August–February, different types by different bird species in different months, until it has all gone. Bramble, Honeysuckle, Elder and Rowan are usually eaten early in the season, followed by Hawthorn and Dog Rose, and then Guelder Rose and Ivy. Some common herbaceous plants commonly found beside hedges also provide seeds for finches, including Meadowsweet (for Bullfinch, Redpoll and Goldfinch), Nettle (Bullfinch), docks (Bullfinch), Great Willowherb (Redpoll) and Burdock (Goldfinch).

HEDGEROWS AND BIRDS

The way that a hedge is managed affects its suitability as bird breeding habitat. Into the 20th century, when hedges were used primarily for stock-proofing, they were skilfully laid. In some parts of Britain, well-laid hedges can still be seen, but in others hedges look neglected. Some have grown into tall and wide thickets, while others have been turned, under severe grazing, into lines of stemmed bushes that look like small trees, or have been reduced to short tightly trimmed strips or a series of isolated bushes, lacking the original herbaceous plants. So in the British countryside today, a wide range of hedges can be found, whose height, width and structure greatly influence the numbers and types of bird species they support.

The presence of hedgerows has a large influence on the size and make-up of farmland bird communities. About half of all the bird species that regularly obtain food from farmland in Britain are associated with woodland, scrub or hedgerows (Table 1). Most hedgerow species are found in the lower bushes, and others in the bigger trees which provide nest sites and hunting perches for various corvids and birds of prey, and sites for hole-nesting species such as Starlings, Tree Sparrows, tits, Spotted Flycatchers, owls and Kestrels. Hedge-bottoms and grass margins abutting hedges can hold ground-nests of Grey and Red-legged Partridges, Pheasants, Yellowhammers, Whitethroats and sometimes Willow Warblers, and along with ditches these margins provide food for many species that nest in the hedge itself. Outside the breeding season, many of these same species find food in hedges, as do wintering thrushes, all of which also use hedges for roosting.

Bird numbers in hedgerows

From the 1930s on, many researchers attempted to count the numbers of breeding birds per unit length of hedgerow. These numbers varied greatly with the type of hedgerow involved: most fell in the range 5–14 pairs/km of length, but some short clipped hedges held less than three pairs/km, while some broad bushy hedges with big trees held up to 39 pairs/km, with even higher densities over shorter lengths (Pollard et al. 1974, da Prato 1985, O'Connor & Shrubb 1986, Hinsley & Bellamy 2000). Overall, the commonest hedgerow species at the time of these studies included the Blackbird, Song Thrush, Chaffinch, Dunnock, Robin, Linnet, Whitethroat and Yellowhammer.

The largest hedges today tend to occur mainly along roads and tracks, where there is less pressure to remove or trim them. Such big hedges can support about the same number of birds per unit area as the best patches of scrub, but both support many more birds than a similar area of interior woodland. This is partly because hedgerows represent 'edge habitat' (which is usually more structurally diverse and productive than dark woodland interior), and partly because the presence of trees as well as shrubs in hedges provides foraging for birds at different levels. In addition, many hedgerow birds obtain some of their food from neighbouring fields which are not counted in estimates of habitat area.

FIG 207. Some common hedgerow birds: upper left, Dunnock Prunella modularis (Richard Chandler); upper right, Robin Erithaca rubecula (Stan Wilson); lower left, Chaffinch Fringilla coelebs (Stan Wilson); lower right. Long-tailed Tit Aegithalos caudatus (Richard Chandler).

Several studies have shown how bird breeding numbers and species composition relate to the structure and character of the hedge itself, as well as to features of the surrounding area. Study sites were widely scattered around the country, but gave broadly consistent findings. In general, both total bird numbers and species numbers increased with the size or volume of the hedge: more birds nested in tall, wide hedges than in short narrow ones (typically three times as many species and five times as many individual birds). This relationship held whether hedge size was measured by height, width, cross-sectional area or volume. Bird numbers also increased with the number of taller trees in the hedge, with the variety of tree and shrub species present (= botanical diversity), with the occurrence of dense vegetation around the base, and with the extent of other boundary features, such as banks and ditches or grassy field margins. All these features added to bird numbers and diversity (Osborne 1984).

In addition, hedges that were near to other bird-rich habitats, such as woods, scrub patches or villages, tended to hold more nesting birds than similar but more distant hedges. The adjacent crop type also had some influence, with old grassland attracting the most hedge species, rape fewer, and cereals fewest of all, especially if they had been sprayed with pesticide (Green et al. 1994). Even though particular hedgerows may show several of these features, each feature could be shown to have its own individual influence on bird numbers. In addition, Hawthorn seemed to hold more birds than any other type of shrub, especially when allowed to grow into a wide, tall hedge thick at the base. It offered dense protective cover, and abundant food in the form of insects and fruit. However, Hawthorn and other hedges that had become open and leggy at the base were used by few species.

It is not hard to imagine why birds should respond to these various features, because they influence habitat structure and food. For example, tall trees in hedgerows provide additional foliage layers in which birds can forage, as well as nest sites such as cavities which are not usually available in shorter shrubs. They provide high perches and nest sites for species such as Carrion Crows which would not normally nest nearer the ground. In addition, mature hedgerow trees can contain high concentrations of insects and other invertebrates, especially in comparison to other habitat features in open arable landscapes (Kennedy & Southwood 1984, Henderson et al. 2007b, Merckx et al. 2010). Many birds forage for insects and other arthropods within the canopy of hedgerow trees, while Swallows exploit the concentrations of aerial insects around their canopies, and other birds pick fallen insects from the vegetation and ground below. Large hedgerow trees thus provide food for birds over a wider area than they themselves occupy. For smaller birds, such as Yellowhammers, trees also provide elevated song perches.

A mixture of different tree and shrub species provides yet more structural diversity, and more insect prey species associated with the different plant species, thereby increasing the variety and year-round availability of food for birds. Because hedgerows tend to gain more plant species as they age, this could in turn influence their value as sources of seed, fruit and invertebrates (Pollard et al. 1974, O'Connor 1987). A thick hedge also offers more cover from predators or shelter from weather, so may be favoured partly for these reasons, although some predators, such as Jays and Weasels, can be seen to search hedgerows for bird nests and other food sources. The presence of woods and scrub in an area gives additional feeding opportunities for hedgerow birds nearby. The influence of neighbouring crop types, as described above, broadly corresponds with the amount of insect and other invertebrate food that they would be expected to hold. Compared to cereals, oilseed rape offers more food (as leaves, seeds and invertebrates), while old grassland also offers an abundance of earthworms and other soil-dwelling creatures. In contrast to most birds, however, Yellowhammers, Corn Buntings and game birds are generally more closely associated with arable land, especially cereals (Donald & Evans 1994, Green et al. 1994, Parish et al. 1995).

Despite these general relationships, all of which emerged as statistically significant in the studies mentioned, different bird species preferred different types of hedgerows. Most species (including Chaffinch, Great Tit, Blue Tit, Song Thrush, Chiffchaff, Tree Sparrow) preferred tall hedges with many trees, but some (Dunnock, Wren, Lesser Whitethroat) preferred tall hedges with few trees. Other species (Whitethroat, Linnet, Yellowhammer) preferred low hedges with few or no trees, and Corn Buntings preferred low, sparse hedges in open country. Bullfinches and Turtle Doves were found only in tall thick hedges, with or without larger trees. In addition, the incidence of some species, such as Wren and Whitethroat, was positively influenced by the number of woody plant species present per unit length of hedge (Arnold 1983, Osborne 1984, O'Connor & Shrubb 1986, Green et al. 1994). Among larger birds, Stock Doves, corvids, owls and raptors generally required large trees, while Grey and Red-legged Partridges tended to avoid hedges with trees, preferring for nesting those with wide verges and dense vegetation near their bases. Standing dead trees provided nest cavities for some species and insect food for woodpeckers. Overall, then, because bird species differed in their habitat needs, farms with a wide range of hedgerow types supported a wider range of species than farms where all hedges were managed to the same pattern.

FIG 208. Four widespread hedgerow warblers: upper left, Whitethroat Sylvia communis (Edmund Fellowes); upper right, Lesser Whitethroat Sylvia curruca (Frank Snykers); lower left, Garden Warbler Sylvia borin (Frank Snykers); lower right, Blackcap Sylvia atricapilla (Frank Snykers).

Additional habitat adjacent to hedgerows may also increase the quality of hedgerow territories by increasing local food supplies and hence reducing the time and energy spent on foraging trips by parent birds feeding young in the nest. Ditches attracted Reed Buntings, and remained sufficiently damp in summer to provide soil-dwelling prey for Blackbirds and Song Thrushes. In wide verges, small mammal populations provided food for Barn Owls and Kestrels (Broughton et al. 2014).

In recent decades, with pesticides used in the fields, several bird species have been found to use grassy field margins preferentially when seeking food for their young, including Whitethroat, Tree Sparrow, Yellowhammer and Corn Bunting. Moreover, the nesting densities of Whitethroats and Yellowhammers along hedgerows were found to correlate with the width of the adjacent grassy margin, with densities greater along hedges with wide margins (Stoate 1999). Similarly, Corn Buntings were found to have a significantly greater amount of rough grassy field margin within 250 m of the nest than the average for the area as a whole (Brickle & Harper 2000). These and other studies indicated that, in modern arable land with heavy pesticide use, a field boundary consisting of a hedge with an uncropped margin is far more useful to birds and their food organisms than a boundary that is cropped up to the hedge, as formerly encouraged by subsidy payments.

Similar relationships between bird numbers and hedgerow structure held in winter, when by far the greatest densities of individuals and species were found in association with tall thick hedgerows in old pasture land. These places attracted not only resident species, but also wintering Fieldfares and Redwings which fed both on hedgerow fruits and on invertebrates from the neighbouring pasture. Moreover, birds are not the only animals whose abundance and diversity correlates with hedgerow size, as similar relationships have been found for small mammals, butterflies, moths and other insects (Garbutt & Sparks 2002, Merckx & Macdonald 2015). Hedgerows and other field margins also provide overwintering habitat for many insects that move into arable crops as they develop in spring (Collins et al. 2002). Some of these insects are important predators on the pests of crop plants, and help in their control (Duffield et al. 1996).

Hedgerows as travel corridors

In many landscapes, hedgerows may provide safe travel routes for woodland birds and other animals, facilitating their dispersal from wood to wood. The presence of some breeding birds (including Robin, Blue Tit, Great Tit and Long-tailed Tit) in particular woods was found to be influenced by characteristics of the landscape outside the woods, including the number of hedgerows connected to a wood and the total amount of hedgerow in the surrounding area (Opdam et al. 1985, 1995, Hinsley et al. 1995). This relationship may have arisen because the hedgerows provided additional habitat, but also because they acted as travel corridors. Some species, such as the Long-tailed Tit and Wren, can be seen to travel along hedgerows, while others are more abundant in woods connected by hedgerows than in isolated woods. The implication is that lack of hedgerows in the landscape may hinder dispersal between woods, a situation studied in the Marsh Tit, Nuthatch and, in the Netherlands, the Short-toed Treecreeper (Broughton et al. 2010, Broughton & Hinsley 2015, Clergeau & Burel 1997). The birds of particular woods or hedgerows clearly do not function in isolation from those in other woods and hedgerows nearby (Arnold 1983, Hinsley et al. 1995, Macdonald & Johnson 1995, Clergeau & Burel 1997, Fuller et al. 1997, Bennett et al. 2004).

So the wildlife content of hedges is influenced not only by the proportion they comprise of a farmed landscape, but also by the degree to which they form a network across the land, as opposed to isolated remnant sections. Broadly speaking, more hedgerow habitat in a given locality results in more hedgerow birds, and combining hedgerows into networks in conjunction with other semi-natural features such as woods and ponds, serves to further increase habitat and bird diversity and abundance (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986, Lentner & Landmann 1994, Shrubb et al. 1997).

LOSS OF HEDGEROWS

The removal of many hedgerows, chiefly in the 1950s–80s, was one of the most obvious changes on farmland during the latter half of the 20th century, particularly in eastern England. When this process began, there was no reliable estimate of the amount of hedgerow in Britain, against which to assess the losses. In the first systematic survey in 1954–57, field boundaries were measured in sample areas in 11 counties from south to north across Britain (Locke 1962). The figures were then extrapolated to produce an estimate of 1.54 million kilometres of field boundary for Britain as a whole, of which some 991,000 km (65%) consisted of hedgerow. If the average hedge was 2 m across, the total area of hedgerow in Britain at that time would have covered around 1,982 km2, about 1% of the total agricultural area, including the open uplands. However, hedgerows were not distributed evenly through the country, but were mainly in the lowlands, and were more abundant in pastoral than arable districts. In addition, their proportion of all field boundaries declined from south to north, with hedges commonest in the south and almost absent in the extreme north, where fences or walls prevailed (Locke 1962).

By the time of this survey, some hedges had already been removed, and we can never know accurately the total amount for earlier years. However, in the following decades many estimates were published of the rates of hedgerow removal for different regions and periods (Pollard et al. 1974, Joyce et al. 1988, Barr et al. 1993, Westmacott & Worthington 1997). For example, the annual losses in eastern England, calculated from aerial photographs, averaged 1,287 km per year in 1946–54, 3,862 km per year in 1954–62, 5,633 km per year in 1962–66, and 3,219 km per year in 1966–70 (Pollard et al. 1974). From these and other figures, the process of hedge removal in the country as a whole began in the 1940s, peaked in the 1960s, but continued well beyond the 1980s when, in response to public opposition and concerns about soil erosion, grant-aided hedge grubbing was replaced by grant-aided hedge planting and restoration.

Fresh estimates of hedgerow length for Britain as a whole then became available from successive Countryside Surveys. These gave figures (published in the 2007 report) of 624,000 km for 1984, 506,000 km for 1990, 508,000 km for 1998 and 477,000 km for 2007 (Carey et al. 2008). Evidently most of the loss had occurred before 1990 but, despite some grant-aided replanting, a net loss continued into the present century. Comparison with the estimate for 1954–57 suggests an overall loss over the 50 years of 514,000 km, or 52%. Because many hedges had been grubbed before 1954, well over half the post-war total is likely to have been removed.

While many hedges were removed from farmland during the 1950s–80s, the management of others lapsed. For various reasons, the densities of large trees in hedgerows declined greatly during the latter half of the 20th century, and this trend is set to continue. Hedges lose much of their wildlife value if they become 'gappy' (shrubs or trees lost and not replaced) or 'leggy' at the base (Fig. 205). The life span of the shrubs in a hedge depends on their management and protection. They can suffer from overzealous trimming, herbicide drift, heavy grazing at the base, or root cutting from close ploughing. Pesticide and fertiliser drift can also damage the plant and invertebrate life in the hedge bottom, and often results in a build-up of aggressive grasses, cleavers and nettles. Unsprayed buffer strips of at least 2 m width from the hedge base give some protection from agricultural operations.

EFFECTS OF HEDGEROW LOSS ON BIRD POPULATIONS

What effect could the loss of hedgerows have had on farmland birds? The presence of trees and shrubs is critical for many species, and the amounts of both woods and hedgerows are good predictors of the size and composition of bird populations in lowland landscapes. In other words, in any kilometre square of farmed land in Britain, we can usually expect that the numbers of breeding birds will increase with the amount of woodland, scrub or hedgerow within that square (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986, Fuller et al. 2001). The more hedgerows there are, the more hedgerow birds there are. This is true for the number of individual birds, but not for the number of species, which soon reach a plateau dependent on the local species pool from which hedgerow birds could be drawn. Based on CBC results, the number of bird species in hedgerows on a farm usually peaks at hedgerow densities of around 7–11 km per km2, but with further increase in hedgerow densities, there is no further increase in species numbers, only in overall bird numbers (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986). Some 30 bird species out of 57 present in CBC plots were found to increase in line with hedgerow density (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986). The pattern varied between species, depending partly on the amount of space they require. While many pairs of Wrens could nest in the hedges found in one kilometre square, the same square would be unlikely to hold more than 1–2 Kestrel or Tawny Owl pairs, because these species hold larger territories, and get their food from nearby open land. Removal of most of the hedges from a square could therefore make little difference to these large species, providing that remaining hedges were suitably spaced and prey supply was maintained.

Most of the species that nest in hedgerows are territorial, and pairs generally have elongated territories in order to gain sufficient foraging habitat. Some species, such as Wren, Chiffchaff and Chaffinch, locate their territories at the intersections of hedges more frequently than expected by chance. The individuals concerned thereby gain the maximum amount of hedge per unit area, which could make their foraging more efficient than if they occupied a similar length of a single hedge (Williamson 1971).

The effect of hedge removal on bird populations depends on the species involved and on the initial and final densities of hedges in the area concerned. However, if as a rough guide we take a mean density of 10 pairs per km of hedgerow, and if 514,000 km of hedgerow has been removed from Britain since the 1950s, this would imply a loss of 5,140,000 pairs of hedgerow birds over this 60-year period, mostly small songbirds.

However, there are several reasons why we should treat this estimate with caution. For one thing, it assumes that all hedgerows in Britain were occupied to the full with breeding birds, so that if some hedges were removed, this would inevitably result in a corresponding reduction in bird numbers. For some species, winter conditions might normally reduce the population to below the level at which all available nesting habitat could be occupied. In this situation, a proportion of hedgerow habitat could be removed without causing a further reduction in overall breeding numbers. Alternatively, winter conditions might reduce the population, but not sufficiently to leave some nesting habitat unoccupied. More birds might survive the winter than the nesting habitat could hold, leaving a surplus of individuals unable to obtain territories and breed. In this situation, the removal of some nesting habitat would be expected to cause a corresponding reduction of breeding numbers. This may often be the situation in some territorial species which get much of their food from hedgerows, such as Blackbird and Dunnock, but not for others, like some finches and buntings, which get almost all their food from fields or other open ground. Some finches such as Linnet and Greenfinch, which can nest in loose colonies and forage over wide areas, could probably lose a substantial proportion of nesting habitat, yet still have enough to accommodate the entire population. Yet other bird species, such as Great Tit and Chiffchaff, nest primarily in woodland, and only when woods are fully occupied do birds move into hedgerows (Krebs 1970, Benson & Williamson 1972). Their numbers in hedgerows therefore depend on the size of the overall population, which could fluctuate greatly from year to year, so that in many years large stretches of potentially suitable hedgerow habitat remain unoccupied. On the face of it, these species could also experience a substantial reduction in hedgerow nesting habitat without declining. Clearly, the situation is likely to vary between species (depending, for example, on whether hedgerow was a first-choice or second-choice habitat), and also between areas (depending on the amount of hedgerow per km2), and between years (depending on current bird population sizes). The evidence for these various scenarios is explored in more detail in Box 16.

FIG 209. The Yellowhammer Emberiza citrinella nests mainly in hedgerows, in apparent preference to other habitats, and may be seen singing from the hedge itself or from scattered hedgerow trees (Alan Martin).

The ultimate test of the importance of hedgerows for breeding birds is to remove some and check whether bird numbers decline. On a few farms, hedgerow bird populations were measured before and after a period of hedge removal. Invariably, the numbers of at least some species declined locally. On a farm at Cranworth in Norfolk, birds were counted in four years (1965–68) before and four years (1971–74) after the removal of 30% of all hedges (Bull et al. 1976). Some hedgerow species showed obvious declines between these periods, the Wren by an average of 38%, Blackbird by 25%, Dunnock by 20% and Song Thrush by 19%. In contrast, seed-eating hedge-nesting species showed little change, probably because they were not limited by nesting habitat and got most of their food from the fields; while birds that nested in the open fields, such as Grey and Red-legged Partridge, Lapwing and Skylark, increased somewhat, possibly in response to increased field sizes and cropping changes. The overall bird numbers on the farm changed little between periods, with 399–430 (mean 427) pairs in the pre-removal period and 424–446 (mean 435) in the post-removal period. Some of the species that declined after hedge removal were the same species as in the bird removal experiment described in Box 16, again implying that they were occupying their habitat to the full.

FIG 210. The Great Tit Parus major nests in hedgerow trees mainly when available woodland territories nearby are already occupied (Richard Chandler).

If hedgerow habitat was limiting bird densities, the composition of a hedgerow bird population would also be expected to change following a change in the structure of a hedge, which would have benefited some species and disadvantaged others. At one farm in Dorset, the hedgerow bird community was compared before and after the removal of most of the big trees through Dutch elm disease (Osborne 1982). There was a net loss of breeding birds from hedges following tree removal, with the loss twice as large (24% against 12%) in those hedges losing half or more of their trees. Hedges that continued to be used by Stock Doves and Magpies were those that lost the fewest trees (Osborne 1982, 1983). In another study, Robins, Goldcrests, Dunnocks and Chiffchaffs declined more on CBC plots where the disease killed trees than on other plots (Osborne 1983).

Although the removal of hedgerows has apparently reduced the numbers of many bird species which nest in them, other species which nest in hedgerows seem to have declined for other reasons, such as reduction in food supply (as in the Linnet; Newton 2004) or disease (as in the Greenfinch; Robinson et al. 2010).
