It is not clear that such species were ever limited by nesting habitat, but they are now clearly much scarcer over much of Britain than hedgerow nesting habitat would permit.

BOX 16. The role of hedgerows in limiting the breeding numbers of different bird species

HEDGEROWS AS FIRST-CHOICE HABITAT

Some territorial bird species use hedgerows and low scrub patches in preference to woodland, and in many areas, hedges are their only nesting habitat. Examples include the Yellowhammer and Whitethroat (Fuller et al. 2001). These species use other habitats, such as woodland, only sporadically, occupying the more open shrubby areas devoid of overhead trees. For these species, the removal of appropriately structured hedgerow would be expected to lead to reduction in local breeding numbers. Studies of the distribution of Yellowhammers in different years implied that farmland (with suitable hedgerows) was the first-choice habitat, and that woodland and other habitats were occupied by individuals unable to obtain territories in farmland (O'Connor 1980). Greater proportions of birds were found at openings in woods in years when the overall population was high than in years when it was low.

HEDGEROWS AS SECOND-CHOICE (OVERSPILL) HABITAT

Other species use hedgerows chiefly when more favoured habitat is fully occupied. In a study near Oxford, Great Tits nested primarily in woodland, where nest success was high, and occupied nearby hedgerows chiefly in years when overall numbers were high (Krebs 1970). When territorial Great Tits were removed from woodland in spring, their places were immediately taken by former hedgerow birds. In contrast, birds removed from hedgerows were not replaced. The birds in this study were ringed, so there was no question over their identities and movements. Breeding success was lower in hedgerows, and birds that bred there tended to be subordinate (typically first-year birds). The conclusion was that woodland was the preferred habitat, and could accommodate the entire population in years when numbers were low. But in years when numbers were higher, variable proportions of individuals were obliged to settle in nearby hedgerows. These places could therefore be regarded as secondary 'overspill' habitat, which may seldom or never have been occupied to the full. Similar conclusions were drawn for some other species, including the Wren, Chaffinch, Robin and Chiffchaff, by examining their distribution patterns in years of different overall population levels (Bull et al. 1976, Williamson 1969, 1971, Benson & Williamson 1972, Osborne 1982). In all these species, woods and adjacent hedgerows were occupied by preference, and only in years of unusually high numbers did pairs extend to more distant hedgerows.

Theoretically, then, these species could have lost some hedgerow habitat without declining, but with continued hedgerow loss some reduction in overall numbers was eventually inevitable. Even though hedgerows may be second-choice habitat for such species, they are better than no habitat, and possibly play a role in population persistence (Newton 1998).

BIRD REMOVAL EXPERIMENTS

For at least some bird species, available nesting habitat is insufficient to accommodate all potential breeding birds, leading to a surplus of non-territorial birds unable to breed (Newton 1998). At least some of these surplus birds are physiologically capable of breeding because, if territorial birds are removed from breeding habitat, their places are taken in the same season by former non-territorial individuals which then proceed to nest. When such removal experiments were conducted on hedgerow birds, some were replaced, implying that the hedgerow habitat before the removals was fully occupied (Edwards 1977). In one such experiment on farmland, Blackbirds, Song Thrushes, Dunnocks, Wrens, Robins, Great Tits and Yellowhammers were all replaced to some extent, and only Chaffinches were not replaced after removal (Edwards 1977). Species varied in the extent and speed of replacement, indicating different levels of population pressure for territories. The implication was that, for most of these species in this area, hedgerow habitat was filled to capacity, and some potential occupants had been excluded by territorial behaviour. In this situation, the removal of some hedgerows would have been expected to result in a reduction of breeding numbers.

NATIONAL BIRD POPULATION TRENDS

Because both bird populations and hedgerows at the national level declined during the latter half of the 20th century, the total stocks of both were inevitably correlated. In at least one species, however, the correlation was so close as to suggest a possible causal relationship. Using the annual data, a strong association emerged between Yellowhammer population size and total hedge length in Britain from 1966 to 2000. A change in total hedgerow length, upward or downward, was followed by a corresponding change in Yellowhammer numbers. Hedge length explained 74% of the annual variation in Yellowhammer numbers, and 81% of the annual variation 2–3 years later. The recovery of Yellowhammers may have lagged behind hedgerow availability because of the time needed for new hedges to grow tall enough and for Yellowhammers to colonise them. So hedgerow loss is a candidate explanation for Yellowhammer decline in Britain, even though winter food shortage or other factors may also have been involved or have taken over as the main current limiting factor (Cornulier et al. 2011).

Other benefits of hedgerows for birds

Although some bird species, such as Wren and Whitethroat, seem to get all or most of their food from within hedgerows, for other species hedgerows provide food in another way, by giving access to fields which would otherwise be unusable. This is because many small bird species do not move far from cover to obtain their food, darting back whenever danger threatens. Blackbirds, Song Thrushes, Robins, House Sparrows, Bullfinches and others seldom forage more than a few metres from a hedge or other protective cover, taking their food from low plants or the ground. They are not normally seen on open land lacking cover. We can assume, therefore, that in the absence of hedgerows, these birds could not exploit the food available in fields, and that as hedgerows have disappeared, much potential feeding area has been lost to such species, with possible effects on their population levels.

Sparrowhawks use hedges to approach their avian prey, while Kestrels, Barn Owls and Tawny Owls hunt for rodents along the grassy margins next to hedges. Birds such as Kestrels, Buzzards and Crows use hedgerow trees as high perches to watch for prey in the fields. These species may be much less able to exploit farmland effectively without these high look-outs. For all of these species, then, we can assume that hedgerows provide access to food supplies that would otherwise be largely unavailable.

In winter, many bird species are no longer territorial, so they have greater freedom of movement, often foraging in places where they could not breed. For example, while Blue Tits breed in hedgerows only if large trees are present to provide nest cavities, in winter they can be seen foraging in any kind of hedgerow, including low ones only a metre or so tall. At this season, as in summer, some hedgerows provide food, but unlike in summer, more birds can access that food, including visiting Fieldfares and Redwings. In coastal areas, hedgerows also provide welcome resting and feeding places for newly arrived migrants, and at bird observatories it is standard practice to check the local hedgerows daily for fresh arrivals. Many a rare vagrant has been discovered in this way.

Another indirect effect of hedgerow removal is that it causes some species to have to move further from remaining hedges to reach food sources. This holds for species, such as Linnet, in which individuals seek food on open land at varying distances from their hedgerow nest sites. The fewer hedges there are in a landscape, the further, on average, Linnets have to fly if they are to exploit all the local food supplies effectively. This can cause a reduction in nest success through starvation or chilling of nestlings, as found after hedge removal in a part of Brittany (Eybert et al. 1995).

COMPARISON OF BIRD NUMBERS IN HEDGEROWS AND WOODS

Not all woodland bird species also breed in hedgerows – the Sparrowhawk, Goshawk, Pied Flycatcher and Wood Warbler being obvious examples. Several other species breed mainly in woodland but are scarce in hedgerows, such as Marsh Tit, Willow Tit, Treecreeper, Nuthatch and Nightingale. However, for some other species hedgerows seem to be preferred over woodland. In a study based on BTO data, the Dunnock, Common Whitethroat, Lesser Whitethroat, Linnet, Goldfinch, Greenfinch and Yellowhammer all emerged as hedgerow specialists, being scarce or ephemeral in woodland (Fuller et al. 2001).

There is a widespread perception that Britain's hedgerows hold more birds overall than Britain's woodland, because hedges extend over so much more of the countryside. This may have been true in the past, and may still be true for parts of the lowlands where many people live, but following widespread afforestation in the 20th century, it is no longer true for the country as a whole. If the total length of hedgerow in Britain is taken as 477,000 km (see here) and its average bird density as 10 pairs per km, then fewer than 5 million pairs of birds breed in these hedgerows. But if the total current area of woodland and forest in Britain is taken as 27,000 km2 (Chapter 17), and their average bird density conservatively as 500 pairs per km2, then 13.5 million pairs would breed in this habitat, nearly three times as many as in hedges. Using any estimates of average bird densities that are close to plausible would not alter the conclusion that hedges in Britain currently hold fewer breeding birds overall than woods and forests, however crucial hedgerows may be for some species or in some areas.

VULNERABILITY OF HEDGEROWS

Despite their agricultural advantages as sheltering windbreaks and livestock barriers, hedgerows may be one of the most vulnerable habitats in Britain. This is because many farmers in eastern Britain have given up on livestock, and switched so completely to arable crops that they no longer need hedges, at least not in the same quantity. In arable agriculture, several factors have favoured hedge removal. Larger machines operate most efficiently in large fields, and for every hedge removed more land is gained for cropping. If the width of land occupied by a hedge is 2 m (and some are much wider), removal of 1 km of hedge will free another 0.2 ha for cropping. Tall hedges with trees cast shade and slow crop development, so that part of the crop may be unripe when the rest is ready for harvest. Hedges are seen by some farmers as reservoirs for weeds, crop pathogens and pests such as Rabbits, which they would rather not be there. And lastly, despite mechanisation, hedgerow management costs money, whether spent on planting, protective fencing, laying, coppicing or trimming (Doubleday et al. 1994, Semple et al. 1994). All these considerations conspire against hedges, and favour 'prairie farming'.

Even on livestock farms, fewer hedges are needed than in the past because cattle are now more often kept indoors or in enclosed yards, and grazing patterns are more intensive, with moveable electric fences giving flexibility. Despite these reasons for hedge removal, even in the most arable of areas, some hedges have been retained as farm boundaries, and along public roads and tracks, while others may have been saved by the presence of ditches necessary for drainage, or for reasons of good public relations.

Other threats to hedgerows result from introduced tree diseases. One reason that trees are much less common in hedgerows now than in the past is the occurrence of Dutch elm disease, which appeared in Britain from 1967 and within two decades had spread widely, killing millions of hedgerow elms (both Common and Wych Elm). The disease was caused by a virulent strain of a fungus, Ophiostoma novo-ulmi, whose spores were spread from tree to tree by the bark beetles of the genus Scolytus and by transmission along the root systems that linked some trees together. For a few years after tree death, woodpeckers benefited from an increase in beetle larvae in the dead wood, and nested in elms more often than formerly. Overall during the 1970s, Dutch elm disease killed an estimated 17–20 million trees, mainly in hedgerows, leaving many farms in some western areas bereft of any large trees. Elms were important because of the many cavities they provided for hole-nesting birds, and because their seeds, produced in May–June, were relished by several finch species, notably Hawfinch, Greenfinch and Bullfinch.

FIG 211. The Little Owl Athene noctua nests in the cavities of hedgerow trees and feeds mainly on adjacent grassland, taking worms, beetles and small mammals (Andrew Everitt).

Despite the disease, small elms still occur in hedges, largely because the disease does not kill the roots, which continue to sucker. These new trees rarely survive beyond 15–20 years, when they become attractive to the beetles that carry the fungus. However, elms can bear flowers before this age, producing seeds that can give rise to new trees. So if a hedge is left untrimmed for several years, any elm suckers may reach flowering size and produce seeds, even though over most of Britain mature elms are a thing of the past.

Another newer threat to hedgerow trees is 'ash die-back disease', caused by the fungus Hymenoscyphus fraxineus (also known as Chalara fraxinea). Since its detection at a tree nursery in 2012, this disease has been recorded at hundreds of other sites, as it spreads rapidly across Britain. It could kill more trees than Dutch elm disease years ago, because over much of the country Ash is now by far the commonest hedgerow tree and also abundant in woodland. The demise of Ash would therefore have a large effect on hedgerows, woods, landscapes, birds and other wildlife. Another new but slower spreading disease is 'acute oak decline', thought to be bacterial, and so far reported from occasional trees across southern Britain. Its symptoms include lesions or vertical splits in the bark oozing a dark liquid. It affects both species of native oak in Britain, mainly trees older than about 50 years, which can die within 4–6 years of symptoms emerging.

After the late 1980s, grant schemes encouraged the creation and restoration of hedges and other boundaries, and further tree planting. Most farmers opted to plant the trees in patches, creating small woods or 'game coverts' rather than hedgerow trees. Since 1997 the Hedgerow Regulations have improved protection for 'important' hedges through the planning system. The stipulations of agri-environment schemes have also helped to curtail severely the removal of hedgerows in England and Wales. The biggest management threats to the remaining hedges are neglect and over-trimming. All agri-environment schemes currently operating in Britain provide financial support for the management of hedgerows and the land adjacent to them, rules on the timing of trimming (to help protect breeding birds) and advice on their creation, restoration and management. In the longer term, however, without the continued encouragement of grant aid, further removal of hedgerows seems likely.

OTHER FIELD BOUNDARIES

Hedges are only one of several linear features which add interest and diversity to the British countryside. Dry-stone walls are common in areas such as the Cotswolds, the Lincolnshire and Yorkshire Wolds, the Derbyshire Peak District and many more northern areas, having been constructed in some places from stones cleared from the fields. Many are now in need of repair. Compared to hedges or tree lines, walls are of little use to birds, although in some areas they provide nest sites for Pied Wagtails, Wrens and sometimes Wheatears and Twite. In the arable land of the fens, fields are separated mainly by ditches that hold water year-round and are edged by extensive grassy banks. The wider ditches, often fringed with reeds, hold Moorhens, Coots, Little and Great-crested Grebes, Mallards and other ducks, and the grassy areas provide nest sites for Reed Buntings and others (Chapter 16). Elsewhere, field boundaries consist of unploughed grassy strips which, unless maintained in this open state, tend in time to become hedgerows, because shrubs arise there from seeds dispersed by birds. Fences of various types have increased greatly in recent decades, in the uplands as well as in the lowlands, partly because they have been grant-aided and partly because of their ease of management. In earlier centuries, fences were made of wood, and only from the 1840s did wire become readily available. Their main value to birds is as perches, from which individuals can watch for prey on the ground below. They can be hazardous to game birds and bustards which fly into them, but replacing barbed wire with plain wire reduces the deaths (Potts 2012).

FIG 212. Dry-stone wall, south Scotland, providing nest sites mainly for Pied Wagtails Motacilla alba and Wrens Troglodytes troglodytes (Stan Wilson).

Grassy field margins and road verges can hold substantial numbers of small mammals. There are supposedly around 370,000 km of roads in Britain, most of which have grass verges. A survey of road verges in Cambridgeshire revealed the presence of five rodent and three shrew species, on average 3–4 species per verge. The main species were Bank Vole, Wood Mouse and Field Vole, which occurred at overall mean densities of 115 animals per km2 in summer and 281 animals per km2 in autumn (Bellamy et al. 2001). Species composition varied with the features of the neighbouring hedgerow and of the verge itself. Field Voles were present only in tall grass verges more than 4 m wide.

Following the main period of hedge removal and cut-back in the 1950s–80s, field boundaries in Britain were examined on a random sample of nearly 600 1-km squares as part of CS2007 (Carey et al. 2008). These samples showed that managed hedges then accounted for only 30% of all field boundaries in Britain, and lines of trees, shrubs and relict hedges for another 14%. Walls accounted for 11%, banks and grassy strips for 4% and fences for 41%, the latter having become by far the commonest field boundary out of a total of around 1.6 million kilometres. Comparisons with earlier surveys indicated that, while many hedges had been removed, some of the field boundaries had been retained, either as grassy strips or as fences. Hedgerows thus formed a smaller proportion of field boundaries in the early 21st century than they had 50 years earlier.

Among the different types of field boundaries, hedges and water-containing ditches support most wildlife; and grass banks (including 'beetle banks') and dry-stone walls considerably less. Fences provide little more than hunting perches for birds seeking prey in the fields, but they generally have grass beneath them, providing habitat and travel corridors for smaller animals.

CONCLUDING REMARKS

Over Britain as a whole, more than half of all the hedges present in the late 1940s have now gone. This implies the loss of around 5 million pairs of breeding birds, although the actual loss was probably considerably less. Not all species were limited by the availability of hedgerow nesting habitat, as they were not occupying suitable stretches to the full; some species would in any case have declined from other changes on farmland. Over the same period, many other hedges were reduced in size or lost most of their large trees. With the current use of tractor-mounted mechanical cutters, it is easier for a farmer to trim off saplings with the rest of the hedge than to cut around them. This contrasts with times past when hedges were trimmed by hand, and trees were valued for the wood, shade and shelter they provided. As old trees die, the total stock of hedgerow trees in Britain continues to decline year by year. In terms of bird habitat, neither the quantity nor the quality of hedgerows in Britain is what it once was.

Hedgerows add interest and diversity to the countryside, and their importance to birds and other wildlife is clearly established. In some landscapes, hedgerows offer the only places where some plant and animal species can persist. The structure of a hedge and its neighbouring boundary features have a large influence on the birds and other animals that use it. Total bird densities tend to increase with the cross-sectional area of the hedge (more birds in taller, wider hedges), with the number of tall trees in the hedge, and with the presence of other boundary features, such as wide grassy verges or ditches. Hedgerows managed optimally and located so as to link woodland fragments do much to maintain the matrix of woody habitat that characterises wildlife-rich countryside in lowland Britain. However, variations in habitat requirements between bird species mean that only a varied hedgerow structure, available every year on individual farms, can accommodate the full range of local bird species.

It is ironic that each human generation seems to value the landscape it is losing. The poet John Clare (1793–1864) protested bitterly at the hedge planting that was dividing and destroying the open field system whose wildlife he celebrated. And even more ironic that he had to engage in hedge planting because he needed the money. His sentiments were shared by land-owning agricultural writer, Chandos Wren Hoskyns (1857), who described hedges as 'hideous and useless strongholds of roots, weeds, birds and vermin'. The aesthetic appeal of hedges may be subjective, but their importance in wildlife conservation is beyond doubt. There are many parts of lowland Britain where woods and other semi-natural habitats are scarce, and where hedgerows provide the primary refuges for many indigenous plant and animal species. The conservation case for retaining hedges is clear and strong. It is largely public opinion, and opposition to their removal, that has kept hedges at their present level. But much depends of farmers, and without active management and more sympathy for trees on farmland, the contribution of hedges to landscape and wildlife will continue to decline.

## CHAPTER 19

## Hill Farming

FOR MANY PEOPLE IN BRITAIN, the hills and mountains of the north and west provide some of our finest scenery – our most natural-looking landscapes where wilderness remains. Such areas are sparsely populated, but their impoverished vegetation is largely a product of human use – the destruction of the original wildwood followed by centuries of livestock grazing and sward burning. The high land is too difficult to cultivate, the climate too harsh, and the growing seasons too short. So the grazing of livestock is the only agricultural use that is feasible on the open uplands (above the fence-line), exploiting the short summer season of vegetation growth on high ground. Traditionally, livestock were taken to the hills in summer, while the lowland vegetation was preserved for winter use. For hundreds or thousands of years, depending on area, both cattle and sheep have grazed the hills but, from the late 18th century, sheep came to predominate. The smaller numbers of horses have now virtually disappeared from the hills, except for some ponies kept locally. Goats seem never to have been widespread, but have now largely gone, leaving a scattering of ancient feral herds. In addition, the hills and mountains are also grazed by wild herbivores, including deer, hares, rabbits and voles, and at least the deer can have substantial effects on the vegetation.

While livestock grazing is by far the major use of the British uplands, other uses include (1) grouse management on heather moors; (2) deer management on other open upland (called deer forest); (3) crofting – low-intensity farming now largely restricted to the lower parts of western Scotland and its islands (Box 17); (4) forestry, chiefly through the planting of non-native conifers on former open land; (5) water catchment for electricity generation and urban water supplies, usually involving the damming of rivers; (6) electricity generation through use of wind turbines; (7) wildlife conservation, mainly in nature reserves; and (8) tourist recreation, as on ski slopes. Not all these uses are mutually exclusive, and many areas of grouse moor, deer forest and energy production also hold sheep at low densities, and are thus subject to agricultural policy. Forestry in its early stages is incompatible with livestock and deer (which eat young trees), and at all stages of its growth with the sward burning that is associated with sheep and grouse. The way the uplands are managed, together with climate and underlying soil type, largely determine the vegetation prevailing in different areas (Box 18).

BOX 17. Crofting

Crofting in the Scottish Highlands and Islands is a form of farming which, strictly speaking, only occurs on agricultural holdings which have the legal status of croft. Crofts are mostly worked part-time by crofters living on site, and whose family incomes are often supplemented by other means (such as forestry, fishing or council work). The pattern of mixed livestock rearing practised by crofters (including enclosed fields of cultivated land, meadow and pasture and a larger expanse of communal grazing land) is widespread in western Scotland and the Outer Hebrides. Most such farms are relatively small (perhaps 5 ha), and largely self-sufficient. Crofters usually live in communities (crofting townships) and share certain jobs, such as gathering in sheep from common grazing land. The rearing of livestock, mainly regional breeds, is central to the system. Cattle are reared by natural suckling and sold in autumn as 'stores' to be fattened on better land elsewhere before being slaughtered. A traditional cropping pattern in the enclosed area produces root crops, cereals and hay (or more recently silage) to be fed to livestock in winter. This system is generally good for birds because it is 'mixed' and not intensive, and involves the late cutting of grass and cereals. It can therefore support a range of bird species at relatively high densities, including some that are rare elsewhere. The recent trend from hay and cereal grain to silage, however, has brought a loss of habitat suitable for Corncrakes, and food for seed-eating birds such as Corn Bunting and Twite. Reduction of cattle keeping has also led to other changes, notably the loss of Swallows from many crofts. As a way of life, crofting is at best economically marginal, being sustained by subsidies (including agri-environmental). The risks to wildlife often stem more from agricultural abandonment than from intensification, as people leave to seek a better life elsewhere (Bignal & McCracken 1996).

As they are today, the British uplands support extensive areas of peat, especially in the wetter north and west. Peat formation has probably accentuated through the period of human use. Wherever the soil becomes waterlogged, the resulting anaerobic conditions slow the decay of dead plant remains, which therefore build up as peat above the original soil or bedrock. With contuinuing accumulation, the peat eventually separates living plants from the rock below, so that these plants become almost entirely dependent on atmospheric fall-out for essential nutrients. Mineral nutrients formerly in circulation become immobilised in the peat, or leached out by rain. With low pH and low fertility, the moorland and bog vegetation which result are far less productive than the original forest. In some flattish western areas, blanket peat can now be metres thick, but in drier eastern areas, peat is usually shallower, in some places only centimetres thick. Peat is increasingly valued as a carbon and water store, but in recent decades, upland peatlands have been damaged by several activities, including drainage for pastoralism, grouse management or forestry, or track building, while on lower ground the more neutral peat has been extensively drained and extracted for horticultural use (Chapter 15).

BOX 18. Major vegetation types in the British uplands

The term upland is often applied to the uncultivated land above the enclosed fields of the lower ground. In the southern half of Britain, it is usually above about 240 m above sea level, but it becomes progressively lower with increasing latitude, down almost to sea level in parts of the northwest. The term upland thus refers more to a range of uncultivated and largely unfenced habitat types than to a particular altitude zone. Omitting built-up areas and water bodies, the uplands thus defined cover around 6.8 million hectares, some 31% of the total land surface of Britain. They comprise nearly 1.6 million hectares of acid grassland (7.3% of Britain's total land area), 1.3 million hectares of heather and other dwarf-shrub moorland (5.9%), 2.2 million hectares of peat bog (10.0%) and 1.3 million hectares of forest and woodland (5.9%). Smaller areas consist of Bracken-covered land (260,000 ha, 1.2%) and montane vegetation above the original tree-line (42,000 ha, 0.2%). As expected, the uplands experience lower temperatures than lower ground, as well as higher rainfall and stronger winds, all accentuated with increasing altitude. On the higher ground, winter snow can lie into summer.

(Countryside Survey 2007)

Over the centuries, particularly in recent decades, human use has arguably affected the uplands more adversely than the lowlands, probably leading to greater reduction in productivity from the original forest (McVean & Lockie 1969). While in the lowlands much has been done over the centuries to maintain and enhance soil fertility, little or nothing has been done in the open uplands to achieve the same result. On the contrary, the generally acid bedrocks, wetter climates, peat formation and prevailing management practices of grazing and burning have almost certainly combined to reduce the productivity of the uplands over the millennia of human use. Throughout this period, annual 'crops' of meat have been removed from the open uplands, with no attempt to replace the nutrients thereby lost. The history of the British uplands is mainly a history of the impacts of livestock on landscapes, vegetation and soil fertility, providing examples of some of the most destructive of all land-use practices.

UPLAND BIRDS

Almost all bird species that breed on the low ground of northern and western districts of Britain can also be found in nearby uplands, wherever suitable habitat is available. Nevertheless, 11 bird species in Britain are currently restricted in the breeding season to mountain and moorland, namely the Red Grouse, Black Grouse, Ptarmigan, Golden Eagle, Hen Harrier, Merlin, Dotterel, Golden Plover, Greenshank, Ring Ouzel and Snow Bunting. Some of these species, such as Black Grouse and Hen Harrier, also bred widely in the lowlands in recent centuries, but disappeared as conditions became unsuitable there. For several other species, such as Curlew, Wheatear, Whinchat and Meadow Pipit, a similar withdrawal is occurring, and the uplands now hold the bulk of their British breeding populations.

As in the lowlands, many species breed in the uplands only by virtue of specific habitats, such as woods and trees, cliffs and buildings, or streams and lakes. Excluding these species, we are left with at least 28 other birds of the open uplands that regularly nest on or close to the ground in herbaceous or shrubby vegetation. They include all those mentioned above (apart from Golden Eagle), plus the Grey Partridge, Short-eared Owl, Lapwing, Snipe, Curlew, Whimbrel, Wood Sandpiper, Redshank, Dunlin, Cuckoo (here parasitising the Meadow Pipit), Grasshopper Warbler, Skylark, Meadow Pipit, Wren, Stonechat, Whinchat, Wheatear and Twite. This is a far greater number of ground-nesting land-bird species than breed in the lowlands. In general, then, the uplands are known mainly for their ground-nesting grouse and waders, and also for their birds of prey, two of which habitually nest on the ground. The most numerous and widespread of all upland species, however, is the ground-nesting Meadow Pipit, which breeds on all open land up to the highest vegetated mountaintops.

In association with the more severe winters on higher ground, relatively more open-land birds than in the lowlands leave their breeding areas for the winter. Year-round residents include Raven, Carrion and Hooded Crows, Golden Eagle, Buzzard, Peregrine, Ptarmigan, Red and Black Grouse, Wren, and, at least at lower elevations, Dipper and Stonechat. In contrast, virtually all the waders and some passerines vacate the hills totally for the winter. The remaining species are partial migrants in which some individuals stay while others leave to winter elsewhere. Some winter visitors, including Snow Bunting, Redwing and Fieldfare, move in to exploit the seed or fruit crops available on open ground. So quite a wide range of species can be seen sparingly on the open hills in winter, at least in the lower parts. Largely different species occur in the forests and other treed areas.

SHEEP AND HILL FARMING

Sheep rearing in Britain developed markedly from the 12th century on, spreading from lowlands to uplands as the demand for wool increased. The arrival of sheep in one upland district after another led to the progressive destruction of many remaining areas of forest and scrub. Only in the 18th and 19th centuries, however, did sheep farming reach northern Scotland, giving rise to the Highland Clearances when crofters were driven from the land in order to create open pastoral landscapes ideal for these animals. Then, during the 19th century, sheep declined in some upland areas with the rise in grouse shooting and (in parts of Scotland) deer stalking.

FIG 213. Three Blackface tups on the Galloway hills (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Typical hill farms today still embrace both low and high ground, with enclosed pastures and meadows in valley bottoms and lower slopes (the in-bye land) and more extensive open areas of rough grass, heather moor and blanket bog on the higher ground (the out-bye land). In many areas, the latter is common land shared between several farms, or tenanted as part of a larger estate. Lambing in spring normally takes place on the lowest ground near the steading, where grass growth begins earlier than on higher ground. In late May or June, the ewes and their young lambs are driven up to the open hills where grass growth has then begun and where they will spend the summer, freeing the lower fields for growing hay, haylage or silage for winter use. However, in July the sheep are driven down to the steadings for a day or two, where the ewes are sheared. They and their lambs are also dipped in insecticide to kill external parasites (mainly scab mites and blowfly larvae) and treated with anthelmintics to kill internal parasites, and the lambs are vaccinated against other diseases. All the animals are marked to signify ownership, and are then returned to the open hills. There they will stay until autumn when grass growth ends and they are again driven to lower ground. By then, the lambs are well grown and can be separated from their mothers. Next year's breeding stock is selected, new rams may be bought in, and at an appropriate date rams are introduced to the ewes to ensure next year's crop of lambs. Surplus animals are sold for slaughter in the autumn or after a period of fattening on lower ground. In some milder regions, some sheep may be returned to the hills and remain there over winter, fed with hay or other supplementary food when necessary, and sometimes lambing there in spring. Nevertheless, unless the hill farmer can rent additional land or purchase extra food, the number of animals that can be kept over winter is limited mainly by the area of low ground available and the amount of grass that can be harvested there in summer.

FIG 214. Hill farms in the Ewes valley near Langholm, Dumfriesshire, showing the enclosed in-bye land in the valley bottom and lower hillsides, and the open sheepwalk on the upper hillsides with rough grass and heather (Keith Kirk).

FIG 215. The hill ground in early spring, showing traditional sheep pens at Mitchellslacks, Dumfriesshire (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

FIG 216. Cheviot sheep before and after shearing in July, Bentpath, Dumfriesshire (Ian Newton).

This pattern of seasonal activity has persisted fundamentally unchanged for centuries. However, patterns vary somewhat between regions, according to the timing of spring, the altitude of the hill country and the amount of low ground available. Since the advent of man-made fibres, wool is in less demand than previously, and nowadays its sale seldom covers the costs of shearing. In addition, the preference is now for 'lamb' meat, so most of the animals are slaughtered in their first year of life, there being little demand for the tougher but more flavoursome 'mutton' from older sheep. In the past, most hill farms housed a few dairy cows, kept year-round on low ground near the steading. Nowadays, any cattle that are kept are used for beef production, sometimes grazing the hills in summer and brought to the lower ground for winter, after separation of calves, many of which are sold for fattening elsewhere.

In contrast to their lowland neighbours, most hill farmers survive today by using a minimum of external inputs and expenditure, reverting largely to traditional ways that work, and spending as little as possible on pesticides, fertilisers and processed foods. However, lambing is more frequently done in sheds, rather than in the open fields, and chemicals are used in the control of parasites. The higher farms can be up to two months behind lowland ones in the start of grass growth. Yet lowland and upland still form part of an interconnected meat-producing system, under the same or different ownerships.

GRAZING ANIMALS

The breeds of livestock kept on hill farms tend to be those which can best fend for themselves on the open hills. They are slower growing and smaller than popular lowland breeds, but better able to survive the harsh nutritional and climatic conditions of the uplands. In many hill regions distinct hardy breeds of cattle were developed, such as the Welsh Black in Wales, the Galloway in southern Scotland and the Highland further north, all of which can survive on the hills year-round. Black cattle became important in the rural economy of Scotland in the latter half of the 18th century, and many thousands were exported each year to markets further south. This was the breed from which modern Highland cattle were derived, the paler golden colour of most of today's animals having arisen by mutation and selection from the original black. Over the uplands as a whole, a much wider range of sheep breeds was developed, adapted to the conditions in different areas. They include the Welsh Mountain in Wales, the Herdwick in the Lake District, the Swaledale in northern England, and the Northern Cheviot and Scottish Blackface further north. The Welsh Mountain and the Scottish Blackface and now the most numerous of all sheep breeds in Britain.

In its food needs, one cow is roughly equivalent to about five sheep, but the two species graze differently, and have different effects on vegetation (Chapter 11). Left to themselves, sheep concentrate on areas of the most palatable grasses, such as fescues and bents, nibbling them down to almost ground level, and creating lawns of heavily grazed areas scattered among areas of coarser herbage which they largely ignore. Sheep also depress many broad-leaved plants, eating the flowering stems before they can bloom and seed. At high density, they can also depress heather, which becomes replaced by grasses (see later). In contrast, cattle are less selective feeders, tearing off the vegetation from further up the stem. They are better able to deal with tougher plants, and thus help to keep rushes and other species in check; they also tread down Bracken and slow its spread. Part of their effect on vegetation comes from their trampling and dunging, through which they kill some plants but provide seed-beds for others. Even at low densities, cattle can destroy heather and other dwarf shrubs, and can also puddle river and stream banks and pollute the water.

FIG 217. A Galloway bull, the traditional hill breed of south Scotland (Ian Newton).

Among wild herbivores, the most important in many upland areas are deer, which have increased greatly in recent decades (Chapter 7). In the Scottish Highlands, during the latter half of the 20th century, the total population of Red Deer more than doubled to reach over 350,000. Deer tend to graze by biting rather than tearing, but are more effective browsers than sheep or cattle, removing any new growth within reach from trees and shrubs. Like sheep, they prevent the regeneration of young trees, and in addition they can reach up and create a browse line on older trees. In severe winters, when other foods are scarce, Red Deer also remove bark from well-grown trees.

THE ENCLOSED IN-BYE LAND

The fields of hill farms are mostly used for livestock grazing and hay or haylage production, with occasional fields cultivated. In most regions, they are usually delineated by stone walls or post-and-wire fences, rather than hedges. This mid-altitude terrain of the in-bye land forms a transition zone between the lower more cultivated land and the upper more open moorland. Until recently it was often poorly drained, forming damp rushy pastures rich in breeding waders or hay meadows full of colourful flowers and butterflies in summer. It has long acted as a frontier, pushing upward in good times to claim more of the open hill, and retreating down again in bad times. In some places, the ruins of dwellings and walls signify past retreat. Traditionally, fields were given a light dressing of farmyard manure in late winter, and then left to produce hay, which was mown in late July or early August, and kept to feed livestock in winter. Any new growth on these fields was then grazed into winter, as long as it lasted. The fields received no other treatment apart from occasional liming to reduce their natural acidity.

FIG 218. Typical rush-infested fields of hill farms, pre-drainage, ideal nesting habitat for several wader species (Ian Newton).

The in-bye land of hill farms has been subject to changes similar to those that have affected lower ground. They occurred mainly in the 1960s to 1990s, under grant aid. Many of the old pastures and hayfields were drained, ploughed, fertilised and sown with more productive grass varieties, replacing most of the indigenous vegetation. In many areas, application of fertiliser became an annual routine. Many areas of damp rushy grassland, around the lower margins of the uplands, were thereby turned into lush green pastures, causing big reductions in waders and other birds. In the past, nearly every upland farm also grew some arable crops on the in-bye land: oats to feed the horses and cattle, turnips for sheep and cattle, and potatoes for the family. However, arable cropping gradually declined, adversely affecting the finches, buntings and other birds that largely depended on it. Over the same period, manufactured foods for livestock became available, and could be used as a supplement in winter.

The process of 'agricultural improvement' raised productivity in terms of grass yields and livestock densities, but also resulted in: (1) a lowering of the water table and reduction of soil moisture; (2) increased homogeneity of vegetation structure by removal of hummocks and tussocks and the production of more uniform green swards; (3) reduction in the number of plant species, rendering the vegetation more uniform and above-ground insect populations less abundant and diverse; (4) reduction in the invertebrates of damp soil, except for earthworms, which benefited from the increase in plant material resulting from fertiliser use (Chapter 5). Most conspicuously, improved fields lost the clumps of rushes which formerly grew in amounts correlated with the water table. With higher livestock densities on pastures, trampling of ground nests presumably became more likely (Chapter 13).

FIG 219. A patch of green 'reclaimed' grassland in the midst of rough hill vegetation, Liddesdale, Roxburghshire (Ian Newton).

Effects on waders and other birds

These changes had huge effects on bird populations, especially on the waders for which the in-bye land was known. Throughout the period of change, the commonest species was the Lapwing, with smaller numbers of Redshank, Curlew and Snipe, the last of these closely tied to the wettest rushy areas. In the northern Pennines during the process of 'improvement' in 1985–87, Baines (1988) compared the densities of various waders between unimproved and improved grass fields, some 300–500 m above sea level. Overall, unimproved pastures held wader densities averaging around 87 pairs per km2, and improved fields only around 17 pairs per km2. These figures implied an immediate overall reduction in breeding waders following drainage of 80%. For hay meadows, the effect of drainage was initially less, with an overall decline of 52% in wader numbers. However, in both pastures and meadows, initial declines differed between species, and Snipe – which required the softest ground – disappeared totally following drainage. As the years passed, more and more fields became devoid of waders, and the remaining occupied fields were settled at lower densities.

Similar events were repeated time and again throughout the hill pastures of Britain. Drainage came later than in the lowlands, so for one or two decades the upland margins held many more waders than lowland grassland. Only on the low-lying undrained machair land of the Outer Hebrides were waders found at higher densities than in upland pastures (Fuller et al. 1986).

Given the scale of marginal land reclamation since 1970, and the fact that combined wader breeding densities of up to 140 pairs per km2 were found on the best traditional hill grasslands (Baines 1988), the overall losses nationally of waders from these habitats were massive. There was no indication that the birds moved elsewhere after drainage: their local declines contributed to a wider population collapse, evident in this habitat across the British uplands. Only the Oystercatcher increased on some improved pastures, but the numbers involved were small.

Improvement of marginal hill pastures was also accompanied by declines in Black Grouse, Yellow Wagtail, Skylark, Meadow Pipit, Whinchat and Cuckoo. In one study, bird population changes were assessed from CBC counts made during 1966–81 and again in 1999–2000 in 13 different areas of hill farms (Henderson et al. 2004a). In the early period, most of the ground surveyed consisted of rough pasture, but in the later period most had been 'improved' and some silage was grown. Of 35 species examined, 13 had declined, five had increased, while 17 showed no significant change. Declining species included the Grey Partridge, Snipe, Redshank, Skylark*, Meadow Pipit, Yellow Wagtail*, Dipper*, Whinchat*, Wheatear*, Ring Ouzel*, Linnet, Reed Bunting and Yellowhammer*. Apart from the Dipper, all these species depended on unimproved grassland, and those marked with an asterisk* had declined by more than 80%. Seven of these species were found in the final survey on fewer than half the plots on which they had been present earlier. The five species that increased (Woodpigeon, Pied Wagtail, Carrion Crow, Jackdaw and Goldfinch) were less specialised in their habitat needs and could survive on improved land, while most of those that showed no significant change were woodland or woodland-edge species. In other words, most of the species that were strongly associated with traditional upland grass fields had declined, whereas others on the same farms had not.

FIG 220. Four waders of wet grassland on hills farms: upper left, Curlew Numenius arquata (Bobby Smith); upper right, Snipe Gallinago gallinago (Bobby Smith); lower left, Lapwing Vanellus vanellus (Alan Martin); lower right, Oystercatchers Haematopus ostragelus, one of the few waders to survive on farmland after 'improvement' (Stan Wilson).

FIG 221. Four ground-nesting songbirds of hill grassland: upper left, Meadow Pipit Anthus pratensis (Keith Kirk); upper right, Yellow Wagtail Motacilla flava (Chris Knights); lower left, Whinchat Saxicola rubetra (Richard Chandler); lower right, Wheatear Oenanthe oenanthe (Frank Snykers). All these species have declined in recent decades.

FIG 222. Cuckoo Cuculus canorus is now commoner in the uplands than in the lowlands. Its main upland host species is the Meadow Pipit Anthus pratensis (Frank Snykers).

Two other sites in the southern Pennines were monitored annually over long periods (1968–99 and 1972–94 respectively). During this time grassland became more intensively managed and dairy cows were replaced mainly by sheep (Fuller et al. 2002). In both areas, large declines occurred in the numbers of breeding Lapwing, Snipe, Curlew, Redshank, Skylark, Meadow Pipit, Twite and Reed Bunting, while large increases were apparent in Carrion Crows. Species declines were most obvious in the area that was most modified. Nevertheless, on this high ground, dairy cattle were less of a problem for nesting waders than on lower ground. At this altitude, cattle were kept inside until late May, by which time most Lapwing eggs had hatched, so losses due to trampling were small. Cattle grazing also produced a sward of varying texture, with patches of shorter and longer vegetation into which sitting Lapwings merged well, unlike the heavily sheep-grazed swards in which sitting birds were conspicuous. In addition, the spreading of farmyard manure in late winter may have increased the invertebrate food for birds. As dairy cattle disappeared from more and more farms, breeding Lapwings became increasingly restricted to those that retained them.

Reclamation of open hill ground

In addition to the draining and reseeding of existing pastures, much reclamation and fencing of previously open hill ground occurred during the 1960s–90s (e.g. Mackay et al. 1998). Following the conversion of this land to fresh green pasture, typical moorland birds, such as Red Grouse, Black Grouse, Golden Plover, Dunlin, Merlin, Hen Harrier, Short-eared Owl, Ring Ouzel, Twite, Stonechat and Whinchat, disappeared, while others, such as Curlew, Snipe, Skylark, Meadow Pipit and Cuckoo, declined. However, conversion often provided improved feeding opportunities for other species, and in some places newly created fields were colonised by Lapwings, Oystercatchers and others that had previously been absent (Ratcliffe 1990, Jenkins & Watson 2001).

The transition zone between enclosed lowland and open upland is known in Wales as fridd. It is often more varied than its equivalents elsewhere, with mosaics of grassland, dwarf shrubs, Bracken, scattered shrubs and trees and occasional clumps of Gorse. It is usually restricted to slopes steeper than 10 degrees, which are difficult for farmers to work. The fridd usually has more shrub growth than the land above or below and in places is wooded, so it adds diversity to the landscape and supports some species such as Tree Pipit, Whinchat, Linnet and Yellowhammer at higher densities than land above or below. Livestock graze most of it, but seldom intensively (Fuller et al. 2006).

THE OPEN OUT-BYE LAND

In contrast to the lower ground, the open hills of the out-bye land are still covered with indigenous plant species and are not normally subject to agrochemical use, apart from the anti-parasite chemicals used on livestock and grouse. The main agricultural impacts of recent decades have resulted from sward burning and land drainage, and from increased densities of sheep, all of which affected the structure and composition of the vegetation, and in turn wildlife.

Sward burning

From well before the Neolithic period, people may have started fires in order to drive prey animals out of particular areas or to promote the growth of fresh vegetation on which game could later be hunted. Yet over the last 300 years or more, sward burning (called muirburn in Scotland) has become routine in the management of most upland vegetation for sheep and grouse. Its main purpose is to remove old and dead plant material and to stimulate new nutritious growth, supposedly benefiting from minerals in the ashes of the fire. Burning also destroys any young trees that may have taken hold, helping to keep the landscape open, in an ideal state for sheep. If grazing and burning were withdrawn, sooner or later trees would re-establish, and except where the land was too wet or too high, the uplands would revert to forest.

Where the priority is sheep, burning is often done every few years, in large patches, sometimes whole hillsides at a time. But where the priority is Red Grouse, heather moorland is ideally burned less often (every 10–15 years) and in smaller patches or strips of 0.5–1 ha (Jenkins 1964, Miller 1964). The aim on grouse moor is to produce a mosaic of different heights of heather, the young growth providing nutritious feeding and the older providing cover and shelter, but on a small spatial scale so that each grouse should have access to both young and older stands in its territory. Because older heather often protrudes through snow, especially in windy places, it also provides food for grouse and other animals in hard weather.

FIG 223. Sward burning in Lanarkshire (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Whether for sheep or grouse, the overall aim of burning is the maintenance of a larger stock of animals than would be sustainable in its absence. However, despite short-term benefits, this process may in the long term reduce the fertility of the land. This would occur if more nutrients were lost at each burn than could be replenished before the next. Some plant nutrients go up in smoke, while others are lost by leaching and soil erosion (Allen 1964). They can subsequently be regained from chemicals contained in rainwater and airborne dust, as well as by rock weathering, a process irrelevant where plant roots do not reach through the peat layer. The net effect of these various processes probably varies between areas, but no good quantitative field data are available. When regular burning first began, the initial losses of nutrients from the land may have been great, but they are likely to have declined through time, so that they may now have reached a balance, with the losses more or less matching the gains from atmospheric input. Some wider environmental impacts of sward burning, based on recent studies, are described in Box 19.

Since the mid-18th century these nutrient losses have been offset to some extent by industrial and other pollutants added from the atmosphere. As well as soot and other particulate matter, they include acidifying sulphur-based and nitrogen-based compounds. Over recent decades, nitrogen is likely to have had major effects, both as an acidifier and as a fertiliser, contributing (along with grazing pressure) to the decline of heather moorland and Racomitrium heath (de Smidt 1995, Lee et al. 1988, Thompson & Brown 1992, Baddeley et al. 1994).

Whatever its effect on long-term land fertility, repeated burning and associated soil drying release more carbon dioxide into the atmosphere than would otherwise occur in such a short time, potentially contributing to climate warming. The practice also reduces floristic diversity, quickly to begin with, and more slowly with each additional burn. Over time it tends to produce either extensive stands of heather (mainly in dry eastern districts) or stretches of the poorest grasses and sedges (in wetter western districts). Reduction of plant diversity brings a similar reduction in animal life, and often violent fluctuations in the numbers of some species, such as the Heather Beetle, which at high densities can defoliate large areas of its food plant, presumably with repercussions on bird populations (de Smidt 1995). Surveys show that sward burning has increased in recent decades, but mainly on grouse moors rather than sheepwalk (Yallop et al. 2006, Douglas et al. 2015).

BOX 19. Impacts of upland sward burning

The wider environmental impacts of sward burning over peatland were studied over a five-year period in northern England (Brown et al. 2014). This study was based mainly on comparisons between five river basins in which regular sward burning took place and five river basins in which no burning occurred, together with measurements on 120 widely distributed soil plots. Burning was shown to have clear effects on peat hydrology, chemistry and physical properties, and on the chemistry and animal life in river waters. Burning reduced the organic content of the surface peat so that it was deprived of chemicals important for plant growth and for buffering acid rain. These findings did not, therefore, support the idea that burning enriches the peat with nutrients from ash, which in these areas were rapidly leached out in rainwater.

Water tables were found to be significantly lower in burned catchments than in unburned ones, giving greater scope for degradation of the peat and loss of carbon to the atmosphere. The drying peat became less conducive to the growth of Sphagnum, which is an important peat-forming plant. Burning also led to greater extremes of near-surface temperatures in the years following burning, but this effect declined as insulating vegetation regrew.

River waters draining burned catchments typically had lower calcium concentrations and lower pH than river waters draining unburned catchments, together with higher concentrations of silica, manganese, iron and aluminium. In burned catchments, more peat particles were deposited on river beds, and invertebrates became less diverse, dominated by a few groups such as non-biting midge larvae. Mayflies were particularly sensitive to reduced pH, increased aluminium and the fine peat sediment on the river bed. So while sward burning over peat may have had short-term benefits for sheep and grouse, allowing more heather growth, it also had wider detrimental effects leading to impoverishment of important plant nutrients, drying and erosion of surface peat (and consequent carbon dioxide release), and adverse effects on nearby river systems and their animal life. It also increased the risk of downstream flooding. The adverse consequences of burning thus extended from upland to lowland, and was a cost to society at large.

Drainage of hill ground

Following the development of appropriate machinery and the availability of grant aid, the cutting of open drainage ditches ('grips') became common practice on wetter moors and peat bogs from the 1960s to the 1980s. This was done ostensibly to benefit livestock grazing, and in some areas to permit tree planting. But it also led to the widespread drying, erosion and oxidation of peat, reduction of its water-holding capacity, coloration of drinking water in upland reservoirs, sedimentation of rivers, and release of much carbon dioxide to the atmosphere (Royal Commission on Environmental Pollution 1996). Across the uplands, an estimated 30,000 km of grips were cut through peat, some of which soon developed into major erosion gullies. In other places, further erosion of peat resulted from the careless laying of thousands of kilometres of vehicle tracks through hill country, a practice which greatly increased from the 1990s, especially on grouse moors. In consequence, although peatlands represent the largest expanse of semi-natural habitat remaining in Britain, more than 80% has recently been classed as 'damaged' to a greater or lesser extent, and as a result is emitting an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of carbon per year (Bain et al. 2011).

FIG 224. New drainage ditch cut through peat, Dumfriesshire (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Moor gripping also had adverse effects on wildlife. By lowering the general water table, it dried out many botanically interesting flushes and marshes which were favourite feeding places of Snipe and other waders, and trapped or drowned any chicks of grouse and waders that fell into the ditches. Most of the birds that breed on moorland, including plant-eaters such as grouse, depend on insects or other invertebrates to feed their chicks. These invertebrates are most abundant around flushes or other wet ground. Drainage therefore affects all bird species requiring damp ground or invertebrate prey that are dependent on damp ground. Associated declines of crane-fly larvae living within the peat affected both breeding output and breeding numbers of Golden Plovers (Pearce-Higgins et al. 2010). Newly emerged crane-flies are important in the diets of many moorland birds, from corvids to Meadow Pipits. Not surprisingly, many of the interesting plant and animal species found on peat bogs have shown marked population declines over recent decades (Bain et al. 2011, Burns et al. 2013). For these various reasons, drainage of moorland is no longer subsidised, and re-wetting programmes have been funded instead. Peatland can be restored by blocking or filling in ditches and by reseeding eroded areas (Armstrong et al. 2009). These processes are expensive, but provide one of the most cost-effective options for mitigating climate change.

FIG 225. Erosion of peat by various human-induced processes: upper, severe erosion on the summit of Bleaklow Hill in Derbyshire, started mainly by the past destruction of its covering of peat-forming Sphagnum moss caused by industrial atmospheric pollutants (Courtesy of Moors for the Future Partnership); lower left, erosion in a gulley following ditch digging (Ian Newton); lower right, erosion on a quad-bike track where peat has washed away to the underlying rock (Ian Newton).

Grazing pressure

Between 1950 and 2000, the summer sheep population of Britain more than doubled from about 20 million to over 44 million animals. These latter numbers were roughly similar to those in the late 19th century, but at that time a much greater proportion of the total was on low ground, with concentrations in East Anglia and the chalk downs of southern England. From then on, sheep became progressively more concentrated in the uplands, giving average densities there much higher than in earlier times. Numbers increased slowly to the mid-1970s, and then much more rapidly, under the influence of 'headage' payments, through which hill farmers were subsidised according to the number of sheep they kept. This system was introduced from 1947, but the subsidy increased greatly after Britain joined the European Common Market in 1973. It encouraged farmers to put as many sheep as possible on the hills, a practice which had huge effects on the vegetation and to some extent on the sheep themselves, as reflected in higher mortality and poorer lambing success (Hudson 1984). With poor nutrition caused by overstocking, average lamb production on most hill farms in northern England fell in the 1980s to less than one lamb per ewe, compared to more than 1.5 per ewe in earlier times (Hudson 1984). For several decades, grants were also available for land drainage and other measures designed to improve the quality of pasture, as were other payments associated with living in 'disadvantaged areas'.

Increases in sheep densities were especially rapid and marked in southwest England, Wales, the Welsh Borders, northern England, southern Scotland and Orkney (within 25 years tripling in some of these areas). Increases were less marked elsewhere (Fuller & Gough 1999). Sheep numbers remained roughly stable in the Scottish Highlands and Western Isles, but Red Deer increased greatly in the Highlands. From the mid-1970s, the open uplands over most of Britain therefore became ever more heavily grazed. In addition, in earlier times much high ground was spared from winter grazing because sheep were brought to lower ground then, owing to the difficulty of conveying supplementary food to high ground. But from the 1970s the use of quad-bikes and other vehicles for this purpose allowed more sheep to be overwintered on high ground, with the result that grazing pressure was often maintained year-round.

Effects of overgrazing

Heavy grazing keeps landscapes open, for any accessible young trees that appear are quickly consumed. The herbaceous vegetation that remains varies with soil type, and the species and densities of grazing animals that occur there. Light grazing tends to encourage fresh growth and maintains the diversity of plant species present, but beyond a certain level, grazing can weaken and even kill plants. Some plant species, such as grasses, are better able to withstand grazing than are others, so that under continued hard grazing, sward composition changes over time. Sensitive and palatable plant species gradually disappear while tougher less palatable plants take over. This change in vegetation happened over large upland areas during the latter half of the 20th century, when many became seriously overgrazed, reducing the height, productivity and diversity of the sward, and eventually the ability of the land to support the grazing animals themselves (Box 20). And as plants are cropped close to the soil by sheep, erosion can also cause soil to be washed from the hills and deposited in rivers (Chapter 15). By the late 20th century, the effects of overgrazing had become especially evident in much of Wales, the Peak District and the Lake District.

Poorer management of the sheep exacerbated the effects of their increased numbers. Traditional shepherding aimed to move the animals around to utilise large areas fairly evenly and prevent the overgrazing of heather, which was valued as winter feed when shorter vegetation was under snow. With increasing labour costs, these practices largely ceased. The supplementary feeding of sheep in hard weather made heather less important as a winter food, removing any incentive for the farmer to protect it. In addition, regular feeding at specific places led the sheep to concentrate there, leading to locally intense overgrazing. These long-term changes in stocking densities and management thus had profound effects on hill vegetation, with repercussions on bird populations. The situation differed on well-managed grouse moors, where sheep are generally kept at lower density, moved around more frequently, and often removed altogether in winter.

BOX 20. Definitions of overgrazing

In broad terms, overgrazing occurs when too many livestock are kept on an area for too long to allow the grazed plants to recover. However, the term overgrazing means different things to different people. To some, it means only that natural plant succession has been halted, as for example when any tree seedlings that emerge on moorland are eaten by grazing animals, thereby preventing forest regeneration. Others use the term for situations where the composition of the vegetation is changed for the worse, as palatable plant species are gradually replaced by less palatable ones. Where this process affects domestic livestock, the term 'agricultural overgrazing' is sometimes used, and where it also leads to loss of biodiversity it is sometimes called 'ecological overgrazing'.

A different way of defining overgrazing stems from the condition of the grazing animals themselves. To some farmers, ground is not overgrazed until livestock lose condition badly or show reduced reproduction. They would claim that, while ever extra livestock can be kept alive and well on a piece of ground, its vegetation is not overgrazed, even though the plant composition may be changing in the long term so as to support fewer animals. For decades, agricultural authorities tended to this livestock-based view, recommending more livestock than the natural vegetation could sustain. This stance contributed substantially to the decline over recent decades in the quality of vegetation in the uplands. The government's current definition states that 'overgrazing means land with livestock in such numbers as to adversely affect the growth, quality or species composition of the vegetation.' If this policy were enforced, it could prevent further degradation of vegetation, but would not necessarily allow areas already seriously overgrazed to recover.

Destruction of heather

Heather forms the main food of Red Grouse and Mountain Hares throughout the year and of Red Deer in winter. It is a poor source of nutrients for sheep, but it provides some edible forage in winter, and at times of snow it is more readily available than lower-growing plants. In some winters, virtually all recent growth may be removed. The effect of grazing on heather can be easily seen at fence-lines which separate areas of low and high sheep densities, or on roadsides and steep slopes that sheep cannot reach (Fig. 227). Over a period of years, it can also be seen in places where a substantial change in the density of sheep is paralleled by a change in the abundance of heather.

On good basic soils, which occur only locally in the uplands, decline in heather allows an increase in fairly nutritious grasses, such as fescues and bents, raising the carrying capacity of the land for livestock. However, on poor acidic and damper soils, which cover much wider areas, heather is usually replaced by nutritionally poor grasses, such as Mat-grass and Purple Moor-grass, thus reducing the carrying capacity of the land for livestock (Welch 1986). Sheep and deer generally avoid these grasses, and so do nothing to constrain their spread. However, swards of both species can be improved agriculturally by cattle grazing or by regular burning, which for a time gives other more palatable grasses a chance to develop. While in most areas these grasses are the main replacement species for heather, in the lower parts of the uplands rushes and sedges can develop on poorly drained land, while Bracken can spread under heavy sheep grazing on drier ground.

FIG 226. Throughout its British range the Red Grouse Lagopus l. scoticus is closely associated with Heather Calluna vulgaris (Edmund Fellowes).

Some once-productive heather moors were lost or reduced in area during the 20th century through excessive sheep grazing. The break-up of some large estates encouraged this change, as owners sold parts of their hill land to sitting tenants who were more concerned with raising sheep than grouse.

In many upland areas, loss of heather has been quantified from written records, from dated aerial photographs, and in recent decades from successive Countryside Surveys (Haines-Young et al. 2000, Carey et al. 2008). Many regional studies have assessed heather loss over different periods of years. For example, in the Peak District, heather cover declined by 36% from 154 km2 to 99 km2 between 1913 and 1979, a period in which local sheep numbers trebled and grouse bags declined by one-third (Anderson & Yalden 1981). In England and Wales, an estimated 27% of heather moorland was lost between 1947 and 1980 (Hunting Surveys 1986), and in Scotland over a roughly similar period 18% was lost, rising as high as 67% in some areas (Tudor & Mackey 1995). By 1995, a quarter of the remaining heather moorland in England and two-fifths of that in Wales was judged as suppressed and under threat of disappearance (Bardgett et al. 1995). However, between the 1940s and 1980s, losses of heather in Scotland were less in areas maintained for grouse shooting (10% loss) than in areas where grouse shooting had been abandoned (29% loss) (Robertson et al. 2001). The same was probably true for England and Wales.

FIG 227. The effect of sheep grazing on hill vegetation. Left, on Langholm moor, the fence line on the upper left shows the boundary between high and low densities of sheep, the heather having almost disappeared from the land on the left (Ian Newton). Right, heather has totally disappeared from the land to the right of the fence, which is heavily grazed by sheep, and remained on the left, where sheep have been excluded (Ian Newton). This photograph was taken in 2010 on the Long Mynd in Shropshire, where heather persisted on the current grassy area until the 1980s.

Estimates of the sheep densities needed to tip the balance from heather to grass have varied between areas, partly according to the underlying rock, the age and growth rate of the heather, its degree of fragmentation, and whether it was grazed in summer only or year-round (winter grazing being more destructive). In general, critical June densities ranged between 100 and 200 sheep per km2 (1–2 per ha) in the lower and more fertile parts of the uplands, falling to less than 50 sheep per km2 on higher ground or on peat bogs. These crude figures were calculated as densities that would prevent further decline in heather, not as densities that would allow its recovery (suggested as 50 sheep per km2 on heather moor and 10 sheep per km2 on blanket bog, Evans & Felton 1987). Nevertheless, for several decades, large parts of the British uplands held sheep densities far in excess of these figures, sometimes three or four times higher (up to 700 ewes per km2), and after several years of heavy grazing, heather and the more palatable grasses gradually disappeared, and the less palatable grasses took over, along with Bracken on the better ground. So under years of intense grazing pressure, the carrying capacity of the land for sheep diminished, as did heather-dependent birds.

The estimates of critical sheep densities cited above refer to situations where heather was likely to disappear within a matter of a few years or decades. But pollen records from lake sediments reveal that heather may have been declining for a much longer period, traceable in some places back to the 17th or 18th centuries, and almost universally back to 1850–1900 (Stevenson & Thompson 1993). Heather decline proved to be greatest in those areas that had the longest tradition of intensive sheep grazing, dating from medieval times, such as Wales and southwest Scotland, in contrast to parts of northwest Scotland and Ireland where both sheep and deer densities were low until the 20th century. The effects of sheep grazing may thus have been accumulating for 150 years or more, perhaps accounting for the long-term declines in some upland bird species such as Ring Ouzel, Dotterel, Black and Red Grouse (Smout 2000).

Compared to sheep, cattle can have an even more severe impact on heather. On areas in northeast Scotland studied by Welch (1984), densities of only 20 cattle per km2 were enough to reduce heather cover over time, whereas 270 sheep per km2 were needed to have the same impact. It is hard to find by direct observation what contribution wild grazing animals make to heather loss, because on easily accessible ground they feed mainly at night, but studies indicate that, at equivalent densities, deer have similar effects to sheep. However, over the British uplands as a whole, deer are still much more restricted in distribution than sheep and tend to occur at much lower densities.

FIG 228. The high tops of the Lowther Hills in the Southern Uplands which, before their vegetation was changed under sheep grazing, are said to have supported Ptarmigan Lagopus muta and Dotterel Charadrius morinellus (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

On high mountain tops, short growing seasons and slower plant growth mean that the effects of trampling and grazing take longer to heal than lower down. Effects of overgrazing are often evident, as where former areas of shrub-heath (favoured by Ptarmigan) and Racomitrium heath (favoured by Dotterel) have become dominated by grasses (see here). Even on the high plateaux of the Cairngorms, sheep have been found locally in summer at surprisingly high densities of up to 110 animals per km2 (Welch & Scott 2000). Here the combined impact of sheep and deer can be substantial, and not only through their effects on vegetation, for in some areas more than one-fifth of recorded Dotterel nests were trampled (Thompson & Whitfield 1993).

Spread of Bracken

Bracken fronds are generally regarded as poisonous to livestock. In Britain, no animals are known to eat them, although pigs will dig up and eat the rhizomes. The general spread of Bracken through the uplands of Britain coincided with a period when hill cattle were still declining while sheep were increasing. In many well-drained hill areas, Bracken now forms a more or less continuous blanket over many hectares of land, which in consequence have much less value for grazing livestock. The plant is now estimated to cover 1.3–2.8% of the total land area of Britain (Carey et al. 2008). It can spread from rhizomes or spores, and on open ground the rhizomes can spread outward at up to 3 m per year (Marrs & Pakeman 1995). In its natural woodland habitat, Bracken is kept in check largely by shading.

FIG 229. Bracken Pteridium aquilinum on the Long Mynd in Shropshire, where it has increased over recent decades of heavy sheep grazing, now covering hundreds of hectares (Ian Newton).

The plant grows best in well-drained and fairly fertile soils by upland standards, benefiting from fires and heavy sheep grazing which suppress competing plants. Its own deep rhizomes are unaffected by burning, and after a fire they soon produce new shoots. However, Bracken is sensitive to spring frosts and waterlogging, so it does best in the lower drier parts of the hills, seldom reaching more than 350 m above sea level. Its fronds in places grow more than 2 m high, and together with the litter from previous years, it tends to smother out any lower plants. The one selective herbicide (asulam) that can control it to some extent has now been withdrawn from regular use in Britain, leaving mechanical methods (such as ploughing or repeated cutting) as the only way to get rid of it from open land. Where Bracken is dominant, it excludes most moorland bird species, and holds fewer arthropods than more open areas. The Whinchat uses scattered Bracken fronds as perches from which to search for prey on the short-grass pasture below, and nests among the collapsed dead fronds (Murray et al. 2016). Many other ground-nesting birds nest among dead Bracken fronds occasionally, but none can be said to depend on them.

INCREASED GRAZING AND BIRDS

The large increase in national sheep numbers between the 1970s and 1990s caused reduction in habitat quality for many upland bird species, and was probably the underlying cause of some observed population declines (Fuller 1996). At least five aspects of change are likely to have been involved: (1) changed structure of the sward, making it less heterogeneous, shorter and more uniform; (2) changed composition of vegetation, leading to loss of preferred types, notably heather; (3) reduction of food supplies (fresh leaves, fruit, invertebrates, small mammals) through the greater removal of fresh growth from vegetation; (4) increases in predator numbers and changes in vegetation which make eggs and chicks more vulnerable, and (5) increased incidence of parasitic diseases, as a result of interactions with livestock. Other associated changes, such as land drainage, are also likely to have affected many birds adversely, as mentioned above.
