For most of these potential drivers of bird population declines, little direct evidence is available, except for grouse, but they are discussed below mainly on the basis of inference from parallel studies elsewhere. Other factors, such as excessive or poor sward burning, atmospheric pollution or proximity of new forests, almost certainly also contributed to the decline of some upland bird species.

Changes in vegetation structure

On open land, grazing pressure affects birds in different ways, with heavy grazing benefiting a few species but not the majority. Most ground-feeding birds avoid uniformly dense tall vegetation, preferring areas with patches of long and short intermixed, kept in an ideal state by light to moderate grazing. Birds hide their nests in the tussocks or other taller patches, and obtain most of their food from the shorter areas. More intense grazing produces a generally shorter and more homogeneous lawn-like sward favoured by Lapwings and Wheatears, the latter hiding their nests in holes or rock crannies. At higher altitudes, Golden Plovers nest on areas of short heavily grazed vegetation, along with recently burnt areas, while in some western coastal areas Choughs feed on turf or heath kept low by Rabbits or sheep, combined with wind exposure. Short swards are also favoured foraging areas for Starlings, Ring Ouzels, Crows, Rooks and Jackdaws, which generally avoid tall vegetation. Dung from livestock may help to increase the densities of soil-dwelling invertebrates in those areas, and most of the bird species just mentioned take invertebrates directly from dung, as well as from the soil (Coulson 1988, Keiller et al. 1995). Of these various species, only the Lapwing and Golden Plover nest on the ground surface, so are at risk from trampling. On the other hand, any level of grazing that destroys tussocks to give more uniform short swards could be disadvantageous to species which conceal their nests in tussocks, as is the case for most other ground-nesting birds in the uplands, from Meadow Pipit and Skylark to Black Grouse and Snipe. Variation in the spatial and vertical structure of upland vegetation also increases the abundance and diversity of arthropods present, and both measures decline under increased grazing pressure, presumably reducing the food supply of insectivorous birds (Dennis et al. 1998).

Change in plant composition

From an ornithological viewpoint, the most significant vegetation change caused by heavy grazing involves the replacement of heather and other dwarf shrubs by grass. In Britain, only one bird species, the Red Grouse, is confined to heather moorland, but four others (Golden Plover, Black Grouse, Merlin, Hen Harrier) breed mainly in this habitat, while for 15 others heather moorland is considered a 'major breeding habitat' (Thompson et al. 1995a). Other birds of the open uplands, such as Meadow Pipit and Skylark, generally occur at lower densities on heather than on grass, while Dunlin seem to avoid heather altogether. Stretches of Mat-grass and Purple Moor-grass that often replace heather are relatively poor in breeding birds, but the latter may hold more birds in winter than in summer. Snow Buntings feed on its seeds in winter, as do Twite when they return to the moors in spring (Armitage 1933, Orford 1973).

FIG 230. Two species which nest on the ground among heather: left, Merlin Falco columbarius; right, Hen Harrier Circus cyaneus (Ian Newton).

Substantial changes in bird communities would therefore be expected to accompany any change from heather to grass. Red Grouse, Black Grouse, Ptarmigan, Dotterel, Merlin, Hen Harrier and Ring Ouzel would be expected to decline in distribution, while Meadow Pipit, Skylark, Curlew, Lapwing, Carrion Crow, Hooded Crow and Raven would be expected to increase. During the 20th century, most of these expected changes occurred, although in the most recent decades some of the grassland species also swung into decline (Chapter 2). Meadow Pipits increase as heather gives way to rough grass, but then decline as the grass is shortened and unified by further sheep grazing (Smith et al. 2001). These are the more obvious examples of recent change but, because many upland birds seem to require mosaics of different vegetation on which to breed, and because these mosaics can be destroyed by heavy grazing, we can expect that other species have also declined from this form of habitat change (Fuller 1996).

Over the years, the effects of sheep grazing have become apparent even on the highest mountains, above the natural tree-line, and especially on mountains south of the Scottish Highlands. Here the resulting vegetation changes could account for the loss of Dotterel from places in the Lake District and Southern Uplands where they bred regularly into the late 19th century. Flat-topped hills of sufficient altitude also occur in north Wales, from which Dotterel may have largely disappeared in earlier times, before ornithologists could record them, but occasional pairs were found breeding there into the 1960s. Similarly, the Ptarmigan of the high tops depend on dwarf shrubs for food, and their disappearance from mountains south of the Highlands has been attributed to the general eradication of high-altitude dwarf-shrub and Racomitrium moss heaths through heavy sheep grazing and indiscriminate moor burning, with fires occasionally reaching high altitudes (Ratcliffe 1990). These mountains also receive the greatest deposits of atmospheric pollutants, which may have accentuated the effects of sheep grazing (Baddeley et al. 1994). Dotterel are still in rapid decline, as indicated by the halving of their numbers between 1987 and 2011 (Hayhow et al. 2015b).

FIG 231. Two species of the high tops which have disappeared from some regions in association with vegetation change, probably resulting from grazing pressure: left, Dotterel Charadrius morinellus (Edmund Fellowes); right, Ptarmigan Lagopus muta (Edmund Fellowes).

The important point, however, is that although the higher mountains of Britain extend well above what would be regarded as traditional grazing land, the vegetation and birdlife of the montane zone have been adversely affected by sheep which graze there in summer. Although recorded contractions in the breeding ranges of Ptarmigan and Dotterel could plausibly be attributed to this cause, other factors cannot be excluded.

Food resources

Grazing can affect food supplies for birds either directly, as livestock remove plant-parts that might otherwise be available to birds (heather shoots eaten by grouse), or indirectly by removing fresh growth, flowers and seed-heads which could otherwise support insects that could be eaten by birds. Many species of arthropods are associated with particular plant communities, often with a single or small number of plant species. Loss of diversity in plant communities could therefore have adverse effects on any bird species in which food needs of adults and chicks differ, or in which a diversity of plant species is needed to provide food through the season. Grazing could also change vegetation structure in such a way that it reduces food availability – for example, spiders tend to live at higher densities in complex taller vegetation, which is unlikely to persist under heavy grazing (Keiller et al. 1995). The abundance and diversity of both spiders and ground beetles were found to fall when upland pastures were agriculturally improved, producing a uniform sward similar to more intensively managed pastures at lower altitudes (Rushton et al. 1989).

Most caterpillars and other leaf-feeding insects consume mainly the fresh growth before it becomes fibrous or develops toxins. The more of this fresh growth is removed by sheep and other mammalian herbivores, the fewer of these insects it can support, and the fewer can complete their development. This greatly reduces the insect foods of birds. Evidence comes from studies of Black Grouse, for which suitable caterpillars and other insects were found to be much scarcer on heavily grazed than on lightly grazed moorland. This difference was reflected in grouse density and breeding success, both of which were higher on lightly grazed than heavily grazed moors (Baines 1996). Similarly, within open pine forest, ground vegetation in areas grazed by Red Deer held on average only one-fourth as many caterpillars as similar vegetation in ungrazed areas, one-third as many Hymenoptera (mainly ants), and half as many beetles (Coleoptera), flies (Diptera) and stoneflies (Plecoptera) (Baines et al. 1994). Whatever the mechanism, grazing clearly has big effects on the composition and abundance of arthropod populations, with effects documented not only for lepidopteran caterpillars but also for carabid beetles, dipteran larvae, spiders and other arthropods (McFerran et al. 1994, 1995, Keiller et al. 1995, Dennis et al. 2008, Evans et al. 2015). Grazing in spring and summer also reduces the production of fruit, by removing potential fruiting shoots of low plants such as Bilberry, Cowberry and Crowberry. Most game birds eat Bilberry fruits, including Capercaillie, Red and Black Grouse, Grey Partridge, Pheasant and Ptarmigan, as do other species such as Mistle Thrush, Ring Ouzel, Woodpigeon and several corvids. To these various grazing impacts can be added the effects of land drainage, which reduces insect populations dependent on wet flushes and other damp ground, as mentioned above.

Grazing and predation rates

Many ground-nesting birds place their nests within concealing vegetation, which presumably gives some protection against predation and adverse weather. Merlins and Hen Harriers prefer to nest in tall heather, several waders nest within tussocks growing in generally shorter swards, and Meadow Pipits, Skylarks and grouse also hide their nests in ground vegetation. Extreme heavy grazing results in a uniform lawn-like sward unsuitable for these species. Where the density or height of the vegetation is reduced less severely, birds may continue to nest, but with lower success. Evidence that nesting cover can influence nest success in ground-nesting birds is available for various waterfowl, Grey Partridges and other birds studied in lowland areas, whose more exposed nests suffer greater predation, but I know of no comparable studies for upland birds (Hill 1984, Rands 1988). Chicks of precocial species that leave the nest soon after hatch also hide in cover, so loss of cover could make them more vulnerable to predation too.

In addition, livestock may step on nests during their daily feeding movements, with trampling rates varying in relation to cattle or sheep densities (Chapter 13). Moreover, sheep have also been seen to eat bird eggs and chicks, especially in areas of suspected nutrient deficiencies. But whether this habit is widespread or has much impact on bird populations is unknown (Beintema & Müskens 1987, Furness 1988, Pennington 1992, Burton 2002).

Over recent decades, some predators have greatly increased in numbers (Chapter 2). This has been attributed to reduced persecution and increased food supplies, created by various human activities, including changes in agricultural practice. In the open hills, Foxes, Badgers, corvids and others are all likely to have benefited from the abundance of sheep carrion, and from the increased areas of short pasture on which earthworms and other invertebrates are readily accessible. Any such increase in predators is likely to have repercussions for bird populations, and evidence for population impacts is available from various predator removal studies conducted in the uplands and elsewhere (Chapter 13, Newton 1998, 2013a, Fletcher et al. 2010). Some species, notably waders, may now be unable to persist in many upland areas unless Carrion/Hooded Crows and Foxes are controlled.

It is not only grouse and waders that are affected by predation, but other ground-nesters too. On one grouse moor near Langholm in Dumfriesshire where Hen Harriers, Peregrines and Merlins were allowed to increase over an eight-year period, Meadow Pipits and Skylarks declined markedly, whereas declines were less marked on other moors where raptor populations remained more or less stable at lower levels. Predation rates on pipits and larks, as assessed from prey brought to harrier nests, implied that predation in June was sufficient to remove up to 40% of pipits present in that month and up to 34% of larks. So at least in this area of high harrier density, harriers alone could have limited the numbers of Meadow Pipits and Skylarks, and caused their decline over a number of years (Amar et al. 2008). On the same moor, Golden Plovers also declined over the same period, but Curlews and Lapwings did not. Crows and Foxes were killed by gamekeepers, so were of little significance as predators.

An additional factor which has raised predation rates on open-land birds, and contributed to their declines, is afforestation. Not only has tree-planting removed habitat for open-land birds, it has provided secure harbourage for Foxes also and other predators which spread out to hunt over neighbouring open land. Both directly and indirectly, then, large-scale afforestation has been implicated in the declines of waders such as Curlew, Golden Plover, Dunlin and Snipe in several parts of upland Britain (Stroud et al. 1987, Hancock et al. 2009, Amar et al. 2011a, Douglas et al. 2014, Wilson et al. 2014).

Large herbivores and disease

Herbivores, including sheep and deer, often carry ticks, which at high densities can debilitate and even kill the chicks of ground-nesting birds. They also carry many kinds of parasitic diseases which they can transmit between different hosts. This raises the question whether tick-borne diseases carried by livestock could have affected bird populations, and whether any such effects could have risen over the years as sheep and deer numbers have increased. There is at least one example from the British uplands, involving the louping ill flavivirus, which affects the central nervous system mainly of sheep, but also of other animals, including Red Grouse (Chapter 7). This virus was probably introduced to the uplands in sheep, and is now a major factor limiting Red Grouse numbers in some areas (Hudson 1992, 1995). In recent decades sheep have been used as 'tick-mops', put out on grouse moors in summer, moved around and routinely dipped in insecticide to kill any ticks they may have picked up. This practice was started years before louping ill was suspected, but has become more important where the disease has taken hold. Sheep ticks are also responsible for transmitting Lyme disease, which has affected increasing numbers of people in recent decades.

SHEEP CARRION AND BIRDS

On the open hills, sheep can provide a source of carrion for scavenging birds and mammals. At lambing times, they also provide stillborn lambs and afterbirths. The main beneficiaries include the Golden Eagle, White-tailed Eagle, Buzzard and Red Kite, Raven, Carrion and Hooded Crows, and large gulls, but many other species take carrion occasionally. Sheep carrion is usually available year-round but peaks in late winter and spring, when sheep are in poor condition. This is a time when alternative foods eaten by scavenging birds are often scarce. In winter, carcasses can remain available for weeks at a time, providing food over a long period, whereas in summer fly maggots quickly dispose of uneaten carcasses. In the Highlands, Red Deer carcasses and afterbirths provide additional carrion, as do the discarded gut-piles ('grallochs') from shot deer. Nowadays, in the interests of disease control, farmers are required to have sheep carcasses removed by an approved collector. But these regulations are relaxed in remote areas, such as the Highlands and Islands of Scotland, and in any case the rapid detection and removal of carcasses from open hill ground in winter is often impracticable.

FIG 232. Dead sheep picked clean by scavengers (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

If the number of carcasses had increased over the years in strict relation to the numbers of sheep on the hills, the carrion supply would have doubled in the latter half of the 20th century. But if the mortality rates of sheep had risen as well, through increased competition for food and poorer shepherding, this could have raised the carrion supply even more. The situation is likely to have varied between areas, according to altitude and climate, the state and quality of the vegetation, the levels of supplementary feeding, the densities and body condition of the sheep, and whether they gave birth in the hills, on lower ground or protected within sheds.

I know of no figures on the long-term trends in carrion availability, but studies in the uplands of Wales and Scotland in the 1970s revealed no shortage of carcasses, especially in late winter and early spring. For example, in each square kilometre of two sample areas of sheepwalk in mid-Wales, there were on average about 150 sheep in midwinter. During the winter and spring, about five adult sheep died, and subsequently about 45 newly born lambs, giving a total of at least 190 kg of edible carrion per km2 annually (Newton et al. 1982). This was equivalent to 19 tonnes of 'meat' left on the ground per 100 km2. This figure was an average from four 'normal' winters (1975–78), but the following severe winter produced about three times as much. Similar surveys in two areas of northwest Scotland gave figures of 65–152 kg carrion per km2 per year (Houston 1977, Hewson & Wilson 1979, Hewson 1984). So despite considerable annual and regional variation, all these open hill areas in the 1970s provided an abundant supply of sheep and lamb carrion. At most times of year, carcasses were consumed rapidly within days of their appearance, but in March–June – the peak time for deaths – some carrion remained unconsumed by birds and mammals, evidently surplus to needs.

In a previous study from the early 1960s, the amount of carrion was calculated indirectly from official figures on sheep densities and mortality rates for different parts of Scotland (Brown & Watson 1964). This gave annual amounts of carrion (sheep and lambs combined) of 472 kg/km2 for the southwest Highlands, 227 kg/km2 for the northern Highlands, 180 kg/km2 for the northwest Highlands, and 'negligible' amounts for the eastern Highlands. Exclusion of Red Deer carcasses made little difference to the totals because at that time (as in the areas mentioned above) most of the carrion was contributed by sheep. More recent transect counts made by Watson et al. (1992) showed the same geographical pattern of carrion availability, despite much smaller variation in sheep densities between areas.

The breeding densities of both Golden Eagles and Ravens in different parts of upland Britain were found to be correlated with the amounts of winter carrion on the hills, either sheep or deer (Marquiss et al. 1978, Dare 1986, Newton et al. 1982, Watson 2010). The greater the supply of winter carrion, the greater the densities of these scavenging birds. And as sheep numbers declined in some areas as a result of tree planting on hill ground, both Ravens and Golden Eagles declined (Marquiss et al. 1978, 1985, Mearns 1983). Carrion supply apparently had little or no influence on the brood sizes of eagles, but affected the clutch sizes of Ravens (Newton et al. 1982). Ravens begin breeding early in the year, and their young are in the nest when carrion reaches its seasonal peak (Newton et al. 1982). An increase of Raven densities in Snowdonia between the 1950s and 1980s to a density of 11 pairs per 100 km2 was attributed to an increase in sheep carrion (Dare 1986). Over the same period, within the adjacent Migneint–Hiraethog upland area, the Raven population remained stable at four pairs per 100 km2 despite an increase in sheep numbers. But this area had different terrain, with far more of the land enclosed and carcasses more readily removed by farmers. In addition, shortage of secure nest sites limited Raven numbers here, in contrast to Snowdonia.

FIG 233. Golden Eagles Aquila chrysaetos feeding on deer carrion (Frank Snykers).

FIG 234. In the uplands of Britain, the Raven Corvus corax is the main carrion-feeding species, nesting early in spring to coincide with the peak period of carrion supply (David Boyle).

While adult eagles can survive on carrion, they need smaller live prey, such as grouse and hares, for their chicks. Only then can the chicks obtain enough bone and other essentials for their growth. But as sheep and deer have increased over the decades, smaller herbivores, including grouse and hares, have declined. This has been attributed to competition for fresh green vegetation (Watson 2010). In contrast to the situation in the 19th century, grouse and hares are now extremely scarce over much of western Scotland; as the land is so poor and sheep or deer so abundant, competition for fresh vegetation is intense, and the smaller herbivores suffer:

Put simply, populations of naturally occurring small herbivores have been almost completely displaced as a result of grazing by excessive numbers of large herbivores such as sheep and deer (Watson 2010).

This contrasts with the situation in eastern Scotland where grouse moors prevail, sheep are scarcer, and grouse and hares are still abundant (except where hares are killed to prevent the transmission of disease-carrying ticks to grouse).

In parts of Scotland where domestic livestock ate almost all the fresh vegetation from the hills each year, many former Golden Eagle territories were abandoned, but where livestock densities were lower, leaving enough vegetation to support hares and grouse, eagle territories remained occupied (Whitfield et al. 2008). It is almost inevitable that livestock should win over wild herbivores in competition for food, because their larger body size enables them to last longer on poor nutrition; they are also less disturbed by the presence of people, and receive supplementary food at times of shortage, as well as veterinary drugs. However, any benefits to vegetation and smaller herbivores through reductions in sheep numbers are now unlikely to be realised in the Scottish Highlands without simultaneous reductions in Red Deer numbers and sward burning (Hope et al. 1996, Albon et al. 2007).

RESTORATION OF VEGETATION THROUGH REDUCED GRAZING

Headage payments on hill sheep were abandoned from 2005. From that year, subsidies were finally decoupled from current livestock numbers, and based instead on previous livestock numbers or the area of land farmed, in the Single Payment Scheme. National sheep numbers then fell from more than 40 million to about 30 million by 2012, giving lower average densities on the hills. Fewer sheep were wintered on the hills, as opposed to the enclosed lower land, and more were brought into sheds for lambing. These changes gave easier handling, better control over nutrition and improved lambing success in spring, and they also reduced the pressure on hill vegetation.

Relaxation of grazing cannot necessarily be expected to reverse all the vegetation changes that occurred in years of high sheep densities. Much depends on the composition of remaining vegetation, on proximity to other seed sources, on numbers of other herbivores such as deer, whether the sward is burnt, and whether remaining sheep are present only in summer or year-round. In the absence of remnant heather, most areas could develop into tall grassland, unsuitable for birds that require some short-grass areas for foraging, and under very low grazing pressure, trees and shrubs could take hold.

Even within a few months, vegetation without sheep can look remarkably different and more diverse. During an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in 2001, many hillsides in northern England and southern Scotland were cleared of sheep, for the first time in living memory allowing plants to flower and seed. Some areas were white with flowering cottongrass, and some rare flowering plants were recorded in previously unseen profusion (Roberts 2002). These changes revealed for all to see the impact of sheep on visible floral diversity, and of how the uplands could look – at least for a time – under reduced sheep grazing.

FIG 235. Cottongrass Eriophorum flowering in profusion after the removal of sheep from Langholm Moor (Ian Newton).

Long-term experiments have provided some quantitative data. On one Welsh hillside, sheep were removed from an area of mainly fescue/bent grassland. Two years later heather formed 20% of the total herbage, and 15 years later 88% (Jones 1967). The area was again subjected to grazing, and 12 years later heather had been reduced to just 10%. In other areas, the removal of sheep led to increase in heather cover at up to 5% per year. Once heather grows tall, it can shade out grasses. Regeneration of other shrubs and trees can also occur, but at rates that depend largely on proximity to seed sources. Sheep removal can also lead to recovery of upland bog vegetation, with heather, cottongrass and other bog plants spreading (Rawes 1983).

In the Scottish Highlands, sites where sheep had been removed for periods of up to 25 years were compared with areas where stocking rates had remained unchanged (Hope et al. 1996). At five sites where sheep had been removed, the vegetation was generally taller, patches of heather and other dwarf shrubs were larger, while patches of grass were smaller, with more signs of vole activity. One of these sites was also being invaded by birch trees. At the remaining six sites, removal of sheep resulted in little obvious change in the vegetation, probably because at these sites grazing by Red Deer had increased greatly, and sward burning had continued. It was concluded that, in the Scottish Highlands, sheep removal was likely to cause significant vegetation change only where Red Deer were few and heather burning infrequent. Other studies in the Highlands showed that, where sheep were removed from hill areas, Red Deer used them more, and had greater effect on heather (De Gabriel et al. 2011). Mixed grazing by sheep and deer gave more diverse vegetation than either one alone.

FIG 236. Red Deer Cervus elaphus stag in Galloway. The species expanded greatly in numbers and range during the latter half of the 20th century, with effects on upland vegetation similar to those caused by sheep (Keith Kirk).

Deer can suppress tree regeneration more effectively than sheep, by cropping seedlings and de-barking saplings and older trees. On the open hill, Red Deer at 3–7 individuals per km2 have been found capable of preventing tree regeneration altogether, depending on conditions. On some estates, however, such as Glenfeshie, Creag Meagaidh and Abernethy, deer have been heavily culled, greatly reducing their densities and promoting an astonishing burst of plant growth and tree regeneration.

Other studies have examined the effects of livestock grazing on birds directly. Effects of reduced grazing on Black Grouse were studied on 10 experimental plots where summer sheep numbers were reduced to less than 1.1/ha and winter densities to less than 0.5/ha. Each plot was paired with a control site which held sheep at twice (summer) to three times (winter) these densities. Male Black Grouse counted at leks increased by an average of 4.6% per year on the 10 sites with reduced grazing, but declined by 1.7% per year on the control sites with the higher sheep densities (Calladine et al. 2002). Some 54% of females were seen with well-grown broods at sites with reduced grazing, compared with 32% on the more heavily grazed sites. On the other hand, the experimental plots supported about 60% fewer Grey Partridges, Lapwings and other waders (Baines et al. 2002).

FIG 237. Black Grouse Tetrao tetrix have been declining in Britain since the 19th century, and have long since disappeared from lowland heaths (Edmund Fellowes).

Other field experiments have shown the importance of sward heterogeneity. For example, mixed sheep and cattle grazing at low intensity improved the abundance of breeding Meadow Pipits after two years (Evans et al. 2006b). Plots stocked with sheep alone (at high or low density) or left free of livestock held fewer pipit territories. The combination of cattle and sheep at low density generated greater heterogeneity in sward structure, which benefited pipits, perhaps through its effect on prey availability. In another study, a doubling of sheep numbers on Orkney between the early 1980s and late 1990s was accompanied by a marked decline in Hen Harriers. Subsequently, as sheep numbers declined by 20% between 1998 and 2008, rough grassland expanded, bringing an increase in the Orkney Vole and in turn in its main predator, the Hen Harrier. Overall, Hen Harrier breeding output over a 33-year period was negatively correlated with sheep densities, as well as with spring rainfall (Amar et al. 2011b).

Afforestation, voles and vole-eaters

Similar vegetation changes occurred throughout the uplands wherever sheep and deer were fenced out of grassland areas prior to afforestation. After fencing, the land is ploughed in strips to give lines of upturned sod in which young conifers are planted, separated by lines of the original grass. In the absence of sheep, Ravens soon disappear, but the grass and other vegetation grows tall, and plants can flower and seed. Meadow Pipits nest at increased densities, and other species are attracted by the dense ground vegetation, some using the bushy young trees as song posts and nest sites. These young forests often attract Wrens, Robins, Stonechats, Whinchats, Willow Warblers and Tree Pipits, and on lower ground also Grasshopper Warblers and Whitethroats. Red Grouse persist wherever heather makes some recovery and Black Grouse often flourish among the young trees, while Merlins and Hen Harriers occasionally nest until the canopy closes. However, the birds found in young plantations vary with region and altitude, and also with the age of the trees, and whether the original open habitat was grassy or heathery. Some waders, such as Curlew, may persist for several years, but others, such as Lapwing, Golden Plover and Dunlin – if present at all – usually drop out within a year or two of planting. This profusion of wildlife lasts only 10–15 years after the removal of sheep, until the canopy closes. At this point all the herbaceous vegetation is shaded out and disappears and the birds of open land are replaced by common woodland species (Moss et al. 1979, Newton 1983, Avery & Leslie 1990, Ratcliffe 1990).

The growth of grass and other vegetation that follows the removal of sheep usually promotes a big increase in Field Voles. These small rodents thrive in the dense ground cover, achieving higher densities in grassy areas than in heather, and feeding on the young shoots of grasses, sedges and other plants. After tree planting, vole densities remain high for about 15 years, fluctuating in 3–4-year cycles, until the developing trees shade out the grass below. During their period of abundance, voles provide plentiful food for many vole-eating predators. Kestrels are usually present from before planting, but increase in density, while up to three species of owls may move in to take advantage of the new food supply (Village 1990).

FIG 238. Young conifers planted on former sheepwalk (Ian Newton)

FIG 239. Short-tailed Field Voles Microtus agrestis, main prey of Kestrels Falco tinnunculus and various owl species in the uplands (Keith Kirk).

At Eskdalemuir in southern Scotland, after tree planting in the 1970s, vole densities were many times greater in the young ungrazed plantations than in the neighbouring grazed sheepwalk (Charles 1981). High vole densities had a big influence on vole-eating predators, including Kestrels, Barn Owls, Short-eared and Long-eared Owls among birds, and Foxes and Weasels among mammals, all of which fluctuated in line with vole cycles. Kestrels depended for nesting mainly on existing cliffs or trees within the recently planted area, Long-eared Owls depended on old stick nests in existing tree clumps or shelter belts, while Barn Owls used deserted shepherd's cottages and other buildings. All three species increased in response to vole abundance but were eventually limited by shortage of nesting places, which restricted the extent to which they could respond to this food bonanza. However, Short-eared Owls, nesting on the ground, were free of this constraint, and reached densities exceeding three pairs per km2, raising up to 10 young in a brood (Village 1987). In peak vole years, some Barn Owl pairs raised up to eight young in a brood, and sometimes two broods in a year. These events helped to confirm the effects of livestock grazing on the growth of grass, and the resulting densities of voles and their predators (see also Wheeler 2008, Evans et al. 2006a).

Similar observations were made in earlier years in other areas whenever sheep were removed or reduced in numbers (Adair 1892, 1893, Goddard 1935, Lockie 1955). Together, they revealed how productive of wildlife upland grassland could be in the absence of high sheep densities. The abundance of open-land wildlife would be only temporary, however, lasting until the area grew up with planted or naturally colonising trees, changing the open habitat to woodland.

FIG 240. Four predators that benefit from outbreaks of Short-tailed Field Voles Microtus agrestis: upper left, Kestrel Falco tinnunculus (Richard Chandler); upper right, Short-eared Owl Asio flammeus (Frank Snykers); lower left, Long-eared Owl Asio otus (Bobby Smith); lower right, Barn Owl Tyto alba (Chris Knights).

Not all bird species would be expected to benefit from reduced grazing pressure, and the studies cited above gave examples of Lapwings, Golden Plovers and Wheatears – species which prefer short swards – declining with the growth of vegetation and recovery of heather. Around bog and pool complexes, vegetation growth might reduce the numbers of Dunlins and Greenshanks. Crows are also likely to decline because of reduction in areas of short grass and animal dung, bringing reduced availability of invertebrate prey. And if the total amount of carrion were to decline as a result of sheep removal, this could reduce the breeding densities of Golden Eagles and Ravens, although other prey would develop in the absence of sheep.

CONCLUDING REMARKS

In the open uplands, recent agricultural policy has had very different impacts from that in the lowlands. Changes result primarily from increased livestock densities and consequent overgrazing, coupled with associated land drainage and sward burning. The open uplands support indigenous vegetation, free from agrochemical use, but which can change rapidly in response to grazing pressure and other management. In Britain as a whole, sheep numbers doubled during the latter half of the 20th century, but in some hill districts their densities trebled. In northern Scotland, little change occurred in sheep densities, but Red Deer densities on open hill ground more than doubled over the same period, so the effect of grazing in much of northern Scotland became similar to that in other overgrazed parts of the British uplands. Over the same period, relatively few cattle grazed the uplands, and their numbers continue to decline.

In addition to changes on the open hills during the 1960s–90s, most of the enclosed in-bye land was drained and agriculturally improved to support greater numbers of livestock, but at the expense of wader and other bird populations. Arable crops were much reduced on hill farms over this period, and wild flowers disappeared from meadows, both changes detrimental to seed-eating birds.

By the time that headage payments were stopped in 2005, much good upland habitat, particularly heather moorland, had been lost or degraded, while less palatable grasses and Bracken had spread, reducing the carrying capacity of the land for sheep, as well as for wildlife. While high stocking levels and associated sward burning were the primary causes of most of the recent vegetation change, reduced shepherding, out-wintering of more sheep, supplementary winter feeding and other changes were also involved. Over the same period, large areas of peat bog and other moorland were drained in attempts to improve the vegetation for sheep, but causing erosion and drying of peat, and decline in bog-dwelling plants and animals.

On the open hills, many bird species declined in association with increased grazing pressure. Potential mechanisms include: (1) creation of shorter, more uniform swards unsuited to many birds; (2) decline in plant species such as heather and other dwarf shrubs, and their replacement by grasses or Bracken; (3) reduction of the amount of fresh vegetation available for wild herbivores, including grouse and voles; (4) reduction of the invertebrate food supply, resulting from simplification of vegetation structure and composition, and the removal of fresh leaf growth, flowers and fruit that would otherwise support insects and their larvae; (5) increases in predator numbers, along with changes in vegetation that made eggs and chicks more vulnerable; (6) increased incidence of parasitic diseases, as a result of interactions with livestock; and (7) land drainage, which leads to the loss of wet flushes on moorland and to a general lowering of the water table, further reducing the food organisms of many birds. The effects of overgrazing on vegetation and birds are likely to be accentuated by inappropriate sward burning and deposition of atmospheric pollutants. Such a large proportion of the natural land productivity over recent decades has gone into sheep that little has been left for other animal life, whether insects, wild mammals or birds. In addition, high densities of livestock can lead to more disturbance of nesting birds and trampling of nests, lowering reproductive output, with potential effects on population levels.

Although all these mechanisms affect birds, they have been well studied only in a few species. But this does not mean that other species have escaped unaffected, or that their declines had other causes. Nor can we assume that other factors, such as climate change, have not also been involved in the declines of some species (for Golden Plover, see Pearce-Higgins et al. 2010). Migratory species could also have been influenced by conditions on passage, or in their wintering areas, independently of any changes in their breeding areas.

In contrast, the chief positive effects resulting from recent management practices in the hills have included: (1) increased sheep and lamb carrion, which has provided an abundant source of winter–spring meat for carrion-feeding birds and other animals; and (2) the temporary benefits that accrue to many birds from sheep removal prior to new tree planting.

The restoration of upland habitats is not merely a matter of reducing sheep numbers. To reverse the trends of recent decades will probably require a more mixed grazing regime with a greater use of cattle, lower stocking rates, some positive management and more regard for the nature of the habitats involved. Most upland vegetation has changed markedly at various times in the past, whether for biological or socioeconomic reasons (Hanley et al. 2008). Without strong government support, most current hill farming could not pay its way. In the 1960s, hill farming occupied about one-third of agricultural land in Britain, but employed about one-tenth of people who worked in agriculture. Yet it contributed only one-thirtieth of the gross agricultural product. These differences between upland and lowland can only have widened in the ensuing decades. Moreover, lowland agriculture could quite easily replace most of the production from the open uplands. Hill farming is funded mainly for political and social reasons, to keep people on the land and avoid rural depopulation. The uplands currently provide livelihoods for about 60,000 farmers, many of whom love the way of life. Their incomes are low, compared to farmers in the arable sector, and as a result their numbers are dwindling, with few new entrants. Politicians sometimes argue that farmers are important to 'look after' the uplands, but the short-term benefits of reducing the densities of domestic livestock are plain for all to see, and in the long term if livestock were removed, some form of forest would reassert itself in most areas. Nevertheless, farming remains the main economic activity in the uplands, and still employs most of the people living there. The meat products of the uplands are still in demand, even though they can be produced more efficiently on lower ground. But their production in the uplands frees some lower ground for other uses. However, the fact remains that intensive livestock grazing is not necessarily the best use for the uplands in modern Britain, and, together with grouse management, it brings many wider societal costs.

## CHAPTER 20

## Agri-Environment Schemes

BY THE MID-1980S, maintaining the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) was absorbing 70% of the total EU budget. This policy was generating huge surpluses of food and causing serious environmental problems. The need for reform was widely acknowledged, and agri-environment schemes were eventually introduced across Europe in attempts to save some of the most valued landscapes, wildlife and archaeological sites. In later years, additional emphasis was placed on reducing soil erosion and water pollution, on carbon sequestration (because of its role in climate change), on promoting pollinating insects (because of their role in crop production), and in some parts of Europe on maintaining traditional farming systems or rare livestock breeds.

Money for agri-environment schemes came from the CAP budget, but national governments could decide within limits how the money was spent, and could also supplement it from other sources. For farmers, participation in such a scheme was either compulsory or optional, depending on the scheme. Within the context of productive agriculture, money could be spent on managing semi-natural habitats, such as hedges and ponds, heathland and flower meadows, or it could be spent on cropped land, soil and water management. Some schemes also provided funds for 'income forgone' in which farmers were paid not to undertake some environmentally damaging activity that might otherwise benefit their business.

The idea of paying farmers to forgo part of their production income in the interests of the wider environment and society took shape gradually. The first such scheme in Britain was introduced in 1987, as the Environmentally Sensitive Area (ESA) scheme, aimed to safeguard parts of the country of high scenic, wildlife or cultural value. Farmers in each such area were issued with instructions on what they needed to do or not to do in order to earn their payments. Agreements with individual farmers covered 10 years, and eventually the scheme was applied to 32 areas of Britain, totalling about 10% of all farmland. However, less than half the farmers within ESAs elected to join the scheme, and no new entrants were accepted after 2004.

The next step was an additional system of payments open to a wider range of farmers nationwide, but again designed to protect landscapes, wildlife and other valued features. This came in 1992, along with other measures designed to shift agricultural support from product (through guaranteed crop and livestock prices) to producer (through income supplements). These 'MacSharry reforms' were aimed primarily to improve the competitiveness of EU agriculture, to stabilise EU expenditure and markets, and to encourage farmers to diversify their production. But they also removed some of the incentive to raise crop and livestock production to maximum levels regardless of the environmental consequences. Compulsory set-aside was introduced at this time, as a way of cutting surplus production, and further agri-environment options were made available. But it was not until 2003 that financial support was finally decoupled from production, and this, along with further agri-environment measures, opened the door more widely to less destructive farming.

At each subsequent review, made every few years, earlier agri-environment programmes were modified and relaunched, usually under new names, but some of the main components of the schemes remained throughout. Programmes were labelled differently in different countries of the UK and had somewhat different priorities adapted to regional conditions. In England, for example, the ESA scheme was accompanied by Countryside Stewardship (CS) from 1991, and then both these schemes were amalgamated into Environmental Stewardship (ES) from 2005, reverting to Countryside Stewardship from 2016. For simplicity, all these programmes, in each country of the UK, are here referred to as agri-environment schemes (AES).

In the simplest schemes, farmers were presented with a number of management options from which to choose. These included improved hedgerow management, pond restoration, planting of seed crops for wild birds, and other measures as shown in Box 21. As time passed and experience grew, options were modified and more were added. For example, in the 1990s arable land was still out of the system, even though declines of birds and other wildlife were most marked there. In consequence, an Arable Stewardship Scheme was trialled in England from 1998 to 2000, after which successful measures were incorporated within prevailing schemes. These arable options included maintaining overwinter stubbles, summer fallows, low-input spring crops and crop headlands, including uncultivated field margins, and growing special mixed crops designed to provide seeds for birds in winter. Later schemes (from 2005) adopted 'broad and shallow' or 'narrow and deep' approaches. The first offered relatively simple, low-cost management options in an Entry Level scheme (ELS) to any farmer who could choose from a list of options, each worth a number of points. Providing that the grand total of points came to at least 30 per hectare averaged over the farm, the farmer then received a flat payment of £30 per hectare per year over five years. The main idea behind ELS was to extend agri-environment measures over more of the country, including the intensive arable and dairy farming areas. The alternative 'narrow and deep' approach, as in the Higher Level scheme (HLS), offered more targeted and more demanding management options to fewer farmers, focusing on priority species and habitats. This payment was not fixed but depended on the measures implemented, and ran for ten years rather than five. It was also competitive, because the funds available were insufficient for all farmers who applied.

BOX 21. Some agri-environment options relevant to birds

All these options have been at some time included in agri-environment schemes in Britain, but not necessarily over the whole agri-environment period or in every region.

• Woodlands. Planting of new woods and restoration of old ones, for example by fencing to allow regeneration and the development of an understorey.

• Hedgerows. Planting new hedgerows or restoring old ones by filling gaps, fencing out livestock to allow lower parts to thicken, and trimming existing hedges less often. Other requirements include not trimming during the bird breeding season so as to protect active nests, and not applying fertiliser or pesticide within 2 m. The growth and protection of hedgerow trees is also encouraged.

• Trees in fields. Protection of trees, including their roots, by not ploughing underneath the canopy.

• Old orchards. Maintenance and preservation.

• Dry-stone walls. Repair and maintenance.

• Traditional farm buildings, and designed landscapes, such as parkland. Repair and maintenance.

• Field margins and other uncultivated areas. Creation of uncultivated grassy areas free from agrochemical use, including buffer strips, beetle banks, field margins and corners. Strips around the edges of fields are usually 2–6 m wide.

• Birdseed and cover crops, as field-margin strips or as small patches. Known as 'game-cover crops' and 'wild-bird seed crops' according to their main intended use and the plants that are grown.

• Pollen and nectar mixes. Usually sown as strips 2–6 m wide or patches in arable fields to promote pollinating and other insects.

• Winter cereal stubbles. Stubbles left unploughed until at least mid-February; chemical inputs restricted.

• Under-sowing of organic cereal crops with a grass/legume mixture to establish a ley, supporting insects and birds through the winter.

• Bare patches in arable land. Creation of bare patches in areas where most crops are sown in autumn and are therefore too tall for Stone-curlews, Lapwings and other species in spring.

• Conversion from arable to grassland on steep slopes to prevent soil erosion, especially that associated the growing of summer maize crops on erosion-prone slopes.

• Reducing or eliminating fertiliser and pesticide use on grassland and arable land.

• Maintaining and creating species-rich grassland. No fertiliser or pesticide use.

• Encouraging mixed stock, such as sheep and cattle, on the same ground to promote plant species diversity and heterogeneity of sward structure.

• Restoration and creation of ponds, to support aquatic plants and animals, add to the overall diversity of farmland, and provide additional insects for birds.

• Re-creation of other previously destroyed habitats, such as reed-beds, heathlands, flower-rich meadows, fens, raised bogs and others.

• Maintaining ditches, so that they remain open and functional, with limited and rotational cutting and grazing of adjacent vegetation.

• Establishment of 12–24 m (mainly grassy) buffer strip beside waterways, to reduce pollution of the water.

• Planting cover crops after harvesting to prevent soil erosion and nitrate leaching.

• Fencing to protect regenerating areas from grazing livestock or ground-nesting birds from mammalian predators.

All these schemes then operated in line with the farmer's receipt of a single payment, decoupled from production, but conditional on farming to basic environmental standards, plant health, and animal health and welfare. It brought us to a period in which agri-environment management throughout Britain operated within a three-tier 'pyramid': (1) 'good agricultural and environmental condition', with which all farmers had to comply if they were to receive any subsidy payment (cross-compliance); and on top of this, either (2) an ELS available to all; or (3) an HLS based on competitive application for more targeted and costly management options. Soon after the introduction of this system, however, EU funding for the period 2007–13 was substantially reduced, limiting the amount that could be spent especially on HLS projects. By 2013, agri-environment measures were applied on around 70% of farms in Britain, the remaining farmers opting out of any AES. These schemes operated alongside other funded programmes which also benefited wildlife, including organic farming and compulsory set-aside, which ran from 1992 to 2007 (Chapter 9). Although AES were applied throughout the EU, unless stated otherwise, the findings reported here refer specifically to Britain. The latest scheme, for 2016–20, should take us through the period when Britain leaves the EU, beyond which the future of AES and farmland birds remain uncertain.

ASSESSING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF AGRI-ENVIRONMENT SCHEMES

Despite the many options, only a small part of the CAP budget (less than 10%) was spent on AES, while the remaining 90% or more was still spent on intensive agriculture which is environmentally damaging in one way or another. Although, at their peak, AES covered more than two-thirds of farms in Britain, on most only a small proportion of the land was affected (mostly less than 5–7%). Such schemes cannot therefore have been expected to restore national bird populations to their 1950s levels. However, they could have helped to stem further population declines or raise populations to higher than their 1980s levels. Continued evaluation of the effectiveness of AES has helped to ensure value for money and to improve the design of the various measures.

To assess population trends in birds, counts are usually made in spring to check whether breeding numbers are up or down from the previous year, or whether the average trend over a period of years is upward or downward. The effects of agri-environment measures can then be tested at the level of the individual farm, the wider landscape or nationwide. Any one species is not likely to respond to every change made, but only to those which are limiting its numbers at the time and place of study. For example, if Yellowhammers were short of winter food, their numbers would be expected to respond positively to the provision of more winter stubble fields containing suitable seeds. But if they were limited by shortage of hedgerow nesting places, they would be expected to respond to provision of extra hedgerows, but not to extra stubble fields. In theory, the limiting resource could vary from one locality to another, so that particular species might respond to a particular measure only on a proportion of farms on which it was applied.

Tests of the effectiveness of agri-environment measures have included: (1) assessments of the numbers of a target species before and after a scheme was implemented; (2) simultaneous assessments of numbers or trends of target species in scheme and non-scheme (control) areas managed conventionally. Often these assessments have been made simultaneously on a number of different AES and control sites, or assessments of population changes have been made in multiple areas with different amounts of particular measures (such as areas of seed crops or grassy field margins). Such replication gives greater reliability to the findings. This is important because, although some measures might attract more birds onto the farm at particular times of year, they may not necessarily lead to sustained population growth, either on the farm or in the wider area.

For example, over recent years, the creation of wet meadows attracted many Lapwings to breed there (suggesting scheme success), but on many of these meadows too few young were reared to maintain the numbers of adults, which therefore declined (suggesting scheme failure). High rates of egg and chick loss, mainly from predation and trampling, emerged as the cause, and these problems needed to be tackled before any newly created meadow could achieve its potential (Chapter 13). Similarly, seed-eating birds require a seed supply throughout the winter if they are to survive to the following spring when seed production begins anew. Planted seed crops often attract large numbers of seed-eating birds in autumn and early winter (suggesting scheme success), but not in February–April when seeds have been shed and often ploughed under, so that breeding numbers may not rise (indicating scheme failure). In both these examples, it was important that limiting factors were identified, so that the scheme could be modified or other actions could resolve the problems, enabling particular measures to perform better.

RESULTS FROM AGRI-ENVIRONMENT SCHEMES

In an early review of the effectiveness of agri-environmental schemes, the findings from 62 published studies from six European countries were examined (Kleijn & Sutherland 2003). Three-quarters of these were from Britain and the Netherlands. Overall, 54% of the plant and animal groups that were studied showed increases in species richness or abundance compared with control areas, while 6% showed decreases. Another 17% of studies showed increases for some species and decreases for others, while 23% showed no change at all in species numbers or abundance. Responses varied between different animal and plant groups. Of 19 statistically robust studies on birds, four showed significant increases in species richness or abundance, two showed decreases, while nine showed both increases and decreases, depending on species. In other words, 13 (68%) indicated some significant benefit of agri-environment measures. These early results were encouraging, but suggested that modifications might make the measures more widely effective.

In a later study spanning five countries, the species densities of plants, birds, bees, grasshoppers, crickets and spiders were assessed on 202 paired fields, one within an agri-environment scheme, the other conventionally managed (Kleijn et al. 2006). In all five countries, agri-environment measures had slight to moderate positive effects on these various plants and animals. Common species usually benefited more than uncommon ones, suggesting that, while some agri-environment options could benefit many species, a mosaic of different options over a sufficiently large area would be required to benefit wildlife as a whole.

Returning specifically to birds in Britain, some studies examined local population trends within BBS study plots (1 km2) in relation to different agri-environment options applied in the surrounding areas (Davey et al. 2010, Baker et al. 2012). In the latter study, plots were chosen that had been surveyed in two or more years in the period 2002–10. Some species showed positive associations with particular options, while others showed negative or no associations with the same options. The clearest findings concerned seed-eating birds whose numbers increased more (or declined less) in areas offering winter stubble fields or wild-bird seed crops, both of which provided additional food.

Another study focused on the Higher Level options within AES, comparing changes in bird densities between 2008 and 2011 on 65 farms under Higher Level management and 21 farms lacking AES interventions (Bright et al. 2015). After allowing for any impacts of predator control undertaken on some farms, changes in the densities of six priority species were more positive on farms under Higher Level management. Five of these species (Grey Partridge, House Sparrow, Tree Sparrow, Yellowhammer, Reed Bunting) were mainly associated with field edges, and had probably responded to food provision (insects in summer or seeds in winter), while the sixth (Lapwing) had probably responded to habitat provision (field-centre fallow plots). In addition, Grey Partridges increased on farms with predator control, while Tree Sparrow and Reed Bunting declined on farms with no predator control. These changes all occurred within a three-year period.

In a different type of assessment, birds were counted in 28 different 100 ha farmland sites across southern England over three summers during 2007–10 (Henderson et al. 2012). In the same years, three other measures were taken: (1) the amount of cropped land in each site, (2) the amount of semi-natural habitat, such as hedgerows, woods and ponds, and (3) the amount of uncropped land, including fallow land, field margins and wild-bird seed crops. After allowing for differences in the amounts of hedgerows and other semi-natural habitats present, and for whether the farm was conventional or organic, the numbers of farmland birds at each site were found to correlate with the proportion of uncropped land at that site. On plots with less than 3% of their area as uncropped land, overall densities of birds were significantly lower than on plots with more than 10% of their area uncropped, in which bird abundance levels were roughly 60% higher. Independently of other factors, then, an appropriate amount of uncropped land had significant positive effects on a range of farmland birds. This amount had to be more than 3–5% of farmland area to have a noticeable impact on local bird numbers.

FIG 241. Some major beneficiaries of wild-bird seed crops and game cover crops: upper left, House Sparrow Passer domesticus (Richard Chandler); upper right, Tree Sparrow P. montanus (Richard Chandler); lower left, Yellowhammer Emberiza citrinella (Alan Martin); lower right, Reed Bunting Emberiza schoeniclus (Alan Martin).

Different agri-environment measures are designed to benefit different bird species. The sections below describe a number of measures and their effects, while Chapter 21 examines some initiatives designed to benefit particular target species, or to raise the entire bird populations of particular farms. Some of the assessments below were made during the process of developing specific measures, but most were made after their widespread establishment in agri-environment schemes. Wide-scale testing proved possible for some popular options, such as seed provision, but other options were taken up by too few farmers in bird count areas to provide sufficiently robust results.

WINTER FOOD SUPPLIES

Winter mortality, resulting from reduced food supplies, is thought to have been the main cause of population declines in some seed-eating birds in the 1970s–90s (Chapter 10). On game-rearing estates, the planting of game crops to provide food and cover for Pheasants increased over this period, along with the numbers of Pheasants released. Several researchers looked at the potential of these crops to benefit a wider range of farmland birds by trialling different crop-mixes, and studying their use by different species. Much of the early work was done by the Game & Wildlife Conservation Trust (GWCT) at their farm at Loddington in Leicestershire (Boatman et al. 2001, Stoate et al. 2003).

Planting seed-bearing crops for game birds became permissible on set-aside land from 1993, and payments to farmers for growing mixed seed crops for these and other birds became available under agri-environment schemes from 2002. Two main types of crops were eligible, namely: (1) 'game-cover crops' intended mainly to provide cover and food for Pheasants and partridges, and usually containing a high proportion of cereals, such as maize or triticale (a wheat/rye hybrid); and (2) 'wild-bird seed crops' intended to feed a variety of seed-eating species, including finches and buntings, and usually containing fewer cereals than game crops and more broad-leaved plants, such as quinoa. These crops are usually grown in small patches or strips of 0.4–2 ha and remain unharvested. They provide nesting cover and insects for various birds in summer, and cover and seeds into winter, but most remain sufficiently open at ground level for game-bird chicks to move easily between the stems.

Some mixtures consist entirely of annual plants (which seed in their first summer), while others consist of a mixture of annual and biennial plants (which seed in their second year, such as kale, chicory and teasel). Providing the patch is left unploughed, some annual plants regenerate during the second year from seed produced in the first, adding to the range of seeds available in the second year of a two-year crop.

FIG 242. Greenfinches Chloris chloris and Linnets Linaria cannabina feeding on wild-bird seed crop (Chris Knights).

Because different bird species have different seed preferences and feeding methods, mixtures can be tailored to the needs of desired species (Table 7). Most small species cling to the stems to pick the seeds from the plants, while larger species stand on the ground and reach up to pluck the seeds; all birds can also pick up fallen seeds from the ground (Fig. 242). Also, while some species (such as Pheasant and Dunnock) habitually walk under the crop canopy in search of food, others (such as Skylark and Rook) prefer to remain in the open on bare patches or places where plants have collapsed.

Seed mixtures can be sown in spring or autumn, and their seed production can be increased by use of fertiliser, although inputs are limited under AES. In the absence of other chemical use, invertebrates can flourish, and the presence of broad-leaved weeds within these crops further increases their value for birds because of the seeds and insects these weeds produce. The insect fauna can be enhanced by including plants, such as rape, linseed or Phacelia tanacetifolia, that attract pollen- and nectar-feeding insects. Moreover, biennial crops give a two-year break from cultivation, which enables biennial weeds to seed and insect populations to grow. Various small mammals also benefit from seed crops, especially Wood Mice.

Surveys have confirmed the importance of wild-bird seed crops for insects, as well as birds. For example, at Loddington in Leicestershire, the abundance of 13 arthropod groups was assessed in wild-bird seed crops for comparison with different commercial crops (cereals, beans, rape and grass) and field boundary vegetation (Moreby & Southway 2002). Overall, wild-bird seed crops contained the greatest numbers of arthropods important to birds, including Araneae (spiders), Homoptera (aphids, scale insects, leaf-hoppers), Heteroptera (bugs), Chrysomelidae (leaf beetles), Cantharidae (soldier beetles) and Carabidae (ground beetles). They also contained the greatest numbers of sawfly larvae, which are particularly important as food for birds. The sawfly pupae benefit from undisturbed soil in winter, so reach peak abundance in the second year of a two-year crop. In contrast, aphids were least abundant in wild-bird seed crops and most abundant in commercial cereals, and in some years also in rape.

Of various plant species commonly used in seed mixtures, kale, quinoa and wheat were eaten by the largest range of bird species, and linseed, rape, and various cereals by a smaller number (Table 7). Other crops were taken by only one or two small species – sunflower, fodder radish, borage and hemp by Greenfinches, and teasel and evening primrose by Goldfinches. Because of its large seeds, maize was mainly eaten by game birds, pigeons and corvids. Buckwheat was seldom used by any birds other than Grey and Red-legged Partridges and Pheasants, while canary-grass seemed little used by any birds except buntings. Nationwide, at least 26 bird species have been recorded feeding in these crops (Table 7). Some plants listed in this Table were seldom used in seed mixes, so the number of potential consumers may have been under-recorded. In general, however, buntings specialised on cereals, and finches and sparrows on other seeds. On the basis of these findings, at least three crop species are required in a mix to attract a wide range of bird species.

Bird species concentrate on different seeds through the season, as particular types become available or depleted at different times. Sunflower and borage shed their seeds early in autumn, although these seeds remain on the ground for a few further weeks. In contrast, kale, quinoa, linseed and millet retain some seeds at least into January. Among cereals, wheat and triticale retain grain in the ear for longer than barley and especially longer than oats, which shed their seeds on ripening. So kale, quinoa, linseed and to a lesser extent cereals can support birds well into winter (Boatman et al. 2001). Cereal grains often rot or germinate soon after dropping, whereas the oily seeds of other species last longer on the ground.

FIG 243. Goldfinch Carduelis carduelis feeding on teasel Dipsacus fullonum, a plant which seeds in its second year (Edmund Fellowes).

The important point, however, is that all the plant species listed in Table 7 have shed almost all their remaining seeds by late February, which seem to be eaten or otherwise disappear, while fresh seeds of wild herbaceous plants do not become available until April or May. In any case, most game-cover crops are ploughed in early February, after the end of the shooting season (Chapter 10). This leaves a period of 2–3 months in which food for farmland seed-eaters is scarce. Bridging this 'hungry gap' may entail the use of different plant species, or the artificial provision of food, for example by scattering or hopper feeding. Often cereals are provided in this way for game birds, but such large hard seeds are not suitable for all small seed-eaters. In the past, this gap was filled by grain released at threshing and at livestock feed sites, by spring sowings, and by dormant weed seeds turned to the surface by ploughing, a resource which has now been much depleted (Chapter 10).

It is not only the plant species that are grown which influence the numbers and kinds of birds found on seed crops. Usage also depends on the general abundance of different bird species in the surrounding landscape and on the position of the seed patch with respect to hedgerows and other features. Chaffinches, Tree Sparrows and Yellowhammers prefer plots adjacent to tall hedges to which they can retreat when alarmed, whereas Skylarks and Corn Buntings prefer more open areas with lower cover (Henderson et al. 2004b, Siriwardena & Stevens 2004). Linnets feed near tall hedges, but also exploit more open areas, gaining security in larger flocks.

Whereas in winter birds from wide areas can converge on wild-bird seed patches, in summer they are mostly constrained to feed fairly close to their nests. At Loddington, maximum foraging ranges in summer of Yellowhammers, Tree Sparrows and Skylarks were roughly 300, 220 and 200 m from the nest respectively (Stoate et al. 2004). Elsewhere, estimates for Dunnock fell within 50 m and Blackbird within 500 m of the nest (Holt et al. 2010). For territorial species which feed their young on insects, it is therefore advantageous to distribute such crops in small patches across the farm, rather than in one bigger patch, so as to bring the crops within reach of a greater number of nesting pairs. This is less important for cardueline finches, such as the Goldfinch, Greenfinch and Linnet, which can store large quantities of food in the gullet, feeding their young by regurgitation (Newton 1972). These finches therefore need to return less often to the nest than other small birds, so can forage at greater distance. All have been found to feed at times more than 1 km from the nest. In winter, small seed-eaters, such as Yellowhammer, Chaffinch, Greenfinch and Goldfinch, commonly moved up to 500 m between different feeding sites on the same day, and occasionally greater distances, as shown from radio-tracked and colour-ringed individuals. Tree Sparrows also sometimes moved more than 1 km. Creating seed patches up to 1 km apart could therefore be a cost-effective way of feeding these various species in winter (Calladine et al. 2006, Siriwardena et al. 2006).

Effects of seed provision on bird numbers

On 21 farms across eastern Scotland in summer, up to 80 times more birds per hectare were recorded in pesticide-free game crops than in nearby conventional crops (Parish & Sotherton 2004a). Weeds important to birds were nearly three times as plentiful in game crops as in conventional crops, while butterflies and bumblebees were up to 15 times and 40 times more abundant. In winter in these same fields, up to 100 times more birds per hectare were counted in game crops than in commercial crops, the latter including unmanaged set-aside and cereal stubbles, which are usually considered good for birds (Parish & Sotherton 2004b). There can be no doubt, then, that game seed crops, free of pesticide use, attract a much greater abundance of birds in both summer and winter. They also attract a wider range of species, with 25 species recorded in the above game crops in summer and 21 in winter.

Other studies have given similar results. Between one winter and the next, a massive increase in bird numbers was noted on a large arable farm in County Durham following the planting of wild-bird seed crops (Stoate et al. 2003). In the winter when these crops were available, the density of birds over the farm as a whole averaged 10 times higher than in the previous winter before the crops were planted. So most of the birds present in the second winter could only have moved in from elsewhere.

In another study, almost all common seed-eating species during autumn–winter preferred seed-bearing crops over adjacent commercial crops, stubble or grassland (Henderson et al. 2004b). Four other species used seed crops, but three (Grey Partridge, Skylark and Corn Bunting) were more strongly associated with the more open habitat of cereal stubbles, while the fourth (Rook) was most often seen on grassland. The results for Corn Buntings were unexpected, for in other areas these birds preferred cereal-based seed crops over stubbles, presumably because of the greater quantities of food available in the seed crops. This finding led to 'unharvested cereals' being included as an agri-environment measure for Corn Buntings in Scotland (Perkins et al. 2008).

At Hillesden near Buckingham, the number of birds counted in seed crops through the winter averaged 79 per hectare, while the number of species averaged 8.7. These figures compared with 0.3 birds and 0.2 species per hectare in conventional crops (Hinsley et al. 2010). Densities of individuals and species therefore averaged 263 times higher and 44 times higher in seed crops than in conventional crops, such as growing cereals or rape. Moreover, these figures refer to small birds only, and exclude corvids, pigeons and game birds.

Despite late-winter shortages, seed provision at Hillesden was associated with greater bird densities in both winter and the following summer (Hinsley et al. 2010). When seed patches became available, significant increases at the farm scale in winter were found for all species combined, for all seed-eating species combined, and for nine individual species. In order of level of increase, these species included Linnet (37-fold), Yellowhammer (9-fold), Tree Sparrow (7-fold), Chaffinch (3-fold), Dunnock (3-fold), Great Tit (2-fold), Blue Tit (nearly 2-fold), Song Thrush (nearly 2-fold) and Reed Bunting (absent to present). Their increases tended to be greatest in areas where most of the patches were located. However, not all these increases may have been due to seed crops, because other aspects of farm management also changed under AES. Nevertheless, the species that showed the biggest increases were those that fed most heavily on the seed crops provided.

In the breeding season at the farm scale, the total numbers of territories, both for all species combined and for all seed-eating species combined, increased significantly when seed patches had been provided in the previous winter. In order of increase, species showing statistically significant increases in breeding numbers compared with the previous year were Linnet (2.3-fold), Robin (1.3-fold), Chaffinch (1.2-fold) and Dunnock (1.2-fold). The Dunnock and Robin were perhaps surprising, because they eat fewer seeds than most other species, but the dense vegetation of cover crops enabled them to gain access to both seeds and invertebrates over wider areas than in previous years, by feeding on the ground beneath the crops. The provision of winter seed crops therefore appeared to raise not only winter bird numbers but subsequent breeding numbers too. Evidently, sufficient nesting habitat was available locally to accommodate the extra birds.

FIG 244. The Dunnock Prunella modularis is an unexpected beneficiary of wild-bird seed crops, feeding on the ground below the canopy, accessing both seeds and invertebrates, while protected from avian predators (Peter Harris).

Other studies that demonstrated increased breeding numbers following the provision of winter seed crops are discussed in Chapter 21. In addition, a wide-scale study of Skylarks and Yellowhammers revealed that population trends in different areas were related to the amount of winter cereal stubble available locally which provided seeds for both species. However, Skylarks may also have benefited from the associated area of spring-sown cereal crops used as nesting habitat (Gillings et al. 2005a). Other studies found evidence that provision of harvested seeds over winter increased the breeding numbers of Yellowhammers and other small seed-eaters (Siriwardena et al. 2007), while the provision of winter food for House Sparrows on a farm where numbers had declined was followed by local increases in winter survival (39% to 65%) and in subsequent breeding numbers (Hole et al. 2002).

Other research, comparing bird population trends in many different 100 ha areas across England, showed that, since 2005, management to enhance winter seed availability was associated with significantly reduced rates of local population decline in several species, such as Yellowhammer, Reed Bunting, Linnet, Tree Sparrow, Skylark and Stock Dove, compared with other areas (Baker et al. 2012). Management involved the provision over winter of cereal stubble and wild-bird seed crops. Because providing extra seeds only slowed population declines rather than reversing them, it seemed that much wider uptake of winter feeding options was needed if the numbers of seed-eating birds were to grow nationally. In addition, the scheme probably needed modifying to ensure that more food remained available during the 'hungry gap' of late winter. This has been achieved in the latest AES by the inclusion of hopper feeding in late winter, which has proved beneficial at least for grain-eating species (Stoate 2012). In general, however, it seems that seed provision can increase the numbers of many small seed-eating birds, not only in winter but also in the subsequent breeding season.

FIG 245. Stock Dove Columba oenas feeding beside a wild-bird seed crop (Chris Knights).

In some of the species mentioned above, response to winter seed provision may be limited by the availability of other resources such as nest sites or insects to feed the chicks. This is apparent, for example, in the Tree Sparrow, which in modern farmland is largely dependent on wetlands to provide sufficient insects. In several nature reserves and working farms, thriving colonies have been re-established where nest-boxes and winter seeds have been provided next to wetland vegetation where insects still abound. All three resources are needed for populations to grow.

WET GRASSLAND FOR WADERS

Agri-environment funds have been used to maintain or re-create wet grassland areas suitable for waders and other meadow birds. Ideal management entails the reinstatement of winter flooding, maintenance of a high water table through the breeding season, delayed or minimal exposure to livestock on pasture until after hatch, and mowing in hay or silage fields delayed to July or August when young can fly (Chapter 13). These various measures came as different options in AES and, in general, waders responded most strongly on land where all measures were incorporated into a single management regime, especially when coupled with predator control (a practice outside AES payments).

An opportunity to assess the effectiveness of agri-environment measures for wet grassland waders came from counts in 2002 at the same sites where waders had been previously counted in 1982 (A. M. Wilson et al. 2007). These counts enabled population changes to be compared between sites that had come under AES management in the intervening years and sites that had remained under conventional management. For Lapwing, Snipe and Redshank, populations increased or declined less rapidly in the more expensive Higher Level AES options aimed at improving habitat; while the less expensive options maintained habitat and benefited Redshank, but had little or no effect on Lapwing or Snipe.
